Armenian premier says talks continue with Russia on railway concession

Burc Eruygur
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said Thursday that negotiations with Russia on the concession management of his country’s railway are ongoing, according to state news agency Armenpress.
Speaking at a media briefing in the capital, Yerevan, Pashinyan said there has been no change in the situation with regard to the topic, and that discussions are continuing.
“This is a very sensitive issue. It is our property, and we should have the ability to manage our property the way we want,” said Pashinyan.
He stated that Armenia has set no deadline for resolving the issue, noting it is calmly discussing the issue in conjunction with other issues, and that Yerevan is working for a resolution “as quickly as possible and in as friendly a manner as possible.”
Armenia’s rail network is operated by South Caucasus Railway, a company owned by Russian Railways, under a 30-year concession agreement signed in 2008.
Armenia argues that the agreement deprives the country of certain competitive advantages, which Moscow has accused the West of “blackmailing” Yerevan on the issue.
Pashinyan said that as part of agreements he reached with Russian President Vladimir Putin during negotiations in the Kyrgyz capital on Aug. 31, Yerevan continues to take stock of its relations with Moscow to “see what layers they consist of.”
He also renewed his country’s position on not objecting to Russia withdrawing its military base in Gyumri in northwestern Armenia if it wants to do so, stating that the base has “no vital significance for Armenia’s security.”
"There has not been a single case when any of our officials raised such an issue or raised such a question with any Russian official. If they decide to withdraw it, we will not object," he added.
On Sept. 2, Putin said the presence of the Russian military base was ultimately a sovereign decision for Armenia."If Armenia believes that the Russian military base is not needed, we will leave as early as tomorrow. We will not impose anything on anyone," he said,
One day later, Pashinyan said Armenia has not raised the issue of withdrawing the base with Russia.

Russian Drone Strike Near Polish Border Forces Jet Scramble and Airport Closures
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk stated on September 17, that Russian drone strikes occurred near the Ukrainian-Polish border in the Volyn region, according to Reuters.
In response to the incident, Poland deployed military aircraft, and operations at airports in Lublin and Rzeszów were temporarily suspended.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Tusk, a gas station located near the Yahodyn border checkpoint was likely targeted during the attack.
The Operational Command of the Polish Armed Forces reported that an unmanned aerial vehicle crashed or was shot down approximately 4 kilometers from the Polish-Ukrainian border.
Military officials confirmed that no violation of Polish airspace took place, while Reuters noted that Ukrainian authorities stated no impacts occurred directly at the border crossing facility.
A similar border attack had already occurred just two days prior when Russian aerial strikes triggered a air defense alert in the same region. Poland scrambled fighter jets overnight on September 15 in response to renewed Russian attacks on western Ukraine involving jet-powered strike drones, according to Poland’s Armed Forces Operational Command.
The command reported that Polish and allied aircraft were deployed around 4 a.m. while ground-based air defense and radar systems were placed on heightened readiness.
The measures were taken as a precaution to protect Polish airspace, and by 6:30 a.m., officials announced that the potential threat had passed with no recorded violations of Polish airspace.
The incidents follow another recent airspace breach involving a NATO member. On September 8, Romania deployed two F-18 fighter jets after military radar detected an aerial object entering Romanian airspace at around 4:47 p.m., roughly 18 kilometers north of Roman.
The detection prompted air raid warnings in several nearby communities. Shortly beforehand, at approximately 4:20 p.m., neighboring Moldova reported that a drone, preliminarily identified as a Shahed, had entered its territory.

Lebanese foreign minister urges Britain to pressure Israel to halt attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
20:35:27 UTC
05:35:27 KST

Naim Berjawi and Lina Altawell
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
Lebanese Foreign Minister Youssef Raggi asked Britain on Thursday to pressure Israel to halt attacks on Lebanon, as Beirut continues to urge implementation of an agreement providing for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese territory, according to a statement from the Lebanese foreign minister’s media office
Raggi made the request during a call he received from UK Minister of State for the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan Stephen Doughty.
It said Doughty reaffirmed the UK’s “steadfast and enduring support for Lebanon.”
The two ministers discussed developments in Lebanon and the region, as well as the period following the end of the mandate of the UN Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL).
“I called on the United Kingdom to exert pressure on Israel to halt its ongoing attacks against Lebanese territory,” said Raggi.
The Lebanese minister also briefed Doughty on progress made toward placing weapons exclusively under state control, without providing details.
UNIFIL’s mandate is due to expire at the end of 2026. The force has been deployed in Lebanon since 1978 under UN Security Council resolutions to monitor the cessation of hostilities and help maintain security and stability in the area.
Raggi’s call came on the day Lebanese President Joseph Aoun said, during a preparatory meeting in Paris for an international conference to support the Lebanese army and Internal Security Forces, that completing implementation of the agreement with Israel and consolidating stability cannot be achieved while Israeli attacks, violations and occupation of parts of Lebanese territory continue.
Aoun urged Lebanon’s friends and partners to help fully implement what has been agreed and deal with Lebanon’s sovereignty and territorial integrity as a fixed principle that is not subject to selectivity.
On June 26, Beirut and Tel Aviv signed a US-sponsored “framework formula” in Washington providing for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese territory and deployment of the Lebanese army in areas vacated by Israeli forces.
Israel continues to carry out attacks on southern Lebanon despite the agreement, and still occupies areas in the south, some for decades and others seized during recent wars and military operations.
At the end of the call, Rajji invited Doughty to visit Lebanon, and the British minister promised to accept the invitation at the earliest opportunity, according to the statement.

Italian authorities issued weather warnings in 12 regions for Friday as severe thunderstorms and heavy rainfall swept parts of the country, including Florence, the broadcaster Sky TG24 reported.
An Atlantic weather system moving across central Europe brought intense thunderstorms Thursday to northern and central Italy, with additional heavy rainfall expected.
The Civil Protection Department issued yellow alerts for Friday for parts of Abruzzo, Basilicata, Lazio, Campania, Lombardy, Marche, Molise, Puglia, Sardinia, Sicily, Umbria and Tuscany.
Storms affected or were forecast in Liguria, Emilia-Romagna, Lombardy, Veneto, Friuli-Venezia Giulia, Tuscany and Campania, with authorities warning of intense downpours, strong wind gusts and frequent lightning.
Florence was hit by particularly heavy rainfall, described by the media as a "water bomb."
At the Uffizi Gallery, water seeped into the museum and splashed onto the exterior glass of the protective case housing Caravaggio's Bacchus. No damage to the artwork was reported.
Orange weather alerts were in place Thursday in large parts of Liguria and sections of Emilia-Romagna, while several other regions were under yellow warnings.

Suspect in ‘Putney pusher’ case told family that investigation was ‘murdering him’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
20:33:37 UTC
05:33:37 KST

Days before Nicholas Brandram, the man suspected of being the “Putney pusher”, killed himself, he told his family that the police investigation was “murdering him”.
He had “no fight left” in him, he told his sisters, Alexia Hicks and Sophie Voelcker, and could not see an end to the Metropolitan police investigation, or the online abuse.
Brandram’s lawyers warned the Met last week that his mental health had deteriorated and he was receiving treatment in a psychiatric hospital after renewed press reporting that he had been released under investigation.
“He said a couple of days ago that this investigation was murdering him. Day by day, he was slowly being murdered,” Hicks, 40, said through tears.
“He saw no end to this investigation,” added Voelcker, 45. “My sister and I were keeping a close eye on him because he was telling us he couldn’t go on. He said it more than once in the week before, that he couldn’t keep going. All we could do was just reassure him. We had faith in the system, we had faith in the police, and they neglected him. They failed in their duty of care to him, to the wider family, and we do not want to see another family going through this.”
The pair insisted that Brandram, 44, was not the “Putney pusher” and that he died thinking no one would believe in his innocence.
He was arrested on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm on 15 June, nine years after a jogger shoved a woman headfirst into the path of an oncoming bus on Putney Bridge in south-west London.
The case attracted considerable media attention but appeared to elude detectives, who wound down their investigation in 2018, after interviewing 50 men and arresting three suspects.
But there was renewed interest in the case after Brandram’s arrest, which his family described as heavy-handed and disproportionate. A number of officers in body armour reportedly swooped on his home address, his sisters said, while a reporter who had been tipped off about the arrest filmed the ordeal.
Although Brandram’s name was not published in the media because he had not been charged, his family said that biographical information in reports made him easily identifiable. He was described as a wealthy banker who lived in a £1.4m west London home and an army veteran with links to royalty. Brandram was the grandson of Princess Katherine of Greece, who was a great-granddaughter of Queen Victoria, which made his arrest all the more newsworthy.
While in police custody in June over the Putney Bridge incident, he was also arrested on suspicion of possession of class A and class B drugs.
His sisters said there was no forensic evidence linking Brandram to the Putney incident and that he had a prominent military tattoo and a withered calf which, they said, distinguished him from the man in footage of the attack on 5 May 2017.
That morning, Brandram had walked from his home in Notting Hill Gate to his office in Bond Street and sent his sisters an email from his work account, which they said he could only access from his workplace. They said that evidence was passed on to the police.
They added that Brandram had volunteered to take part in an identification parade and provided his DNA for comparison with a sample recovered at the time of the incident. Hicks said detectives told Brandram just days ago that they still did not know when the DNA analysis would be completed.
“Our brother willingly provided DNA in an attempt to obviously help clear his name and to complete the investigation, and for weeks now we’ve been asking the police just to complete the DNA test,” Voelcker said.
“We’ve always maintained that he’s innocent. He always maintained he was innocent. We just needed the police to complete their inquiry, and it just felt particularly egregious that they were just hanging this DNA test over him.”
Hicks said as details of the case kept being reported in the press, her brother became preoccupied by online abuse on forums such as Reddit.
“His reputation within a couple of days was in tatters. People saying he’s the alleged pusher, and you can imagine the vitriol that was coming out online,” Voelcker said.
“You can imagine what people might say about somebody they think tried to push a woman in front of a bus. There was a lot of people had a lot of views about our brother, about his background, about where he worked.”
“And the problem was he was reading it all every day,” Hicks said. “The vitriol is still there and that’s what’s so heartbreaking for us, is that when he took his own life he died thinking that effectively everyone hated him and thought he’d done something awful and that no one would see that he was innocent and he knew that his family were behind him but it wasn’t enough.”
The sisters said Brandram had stayed with them in recent days after his mental health deteriorated following the publication of an update about the case that said he had been released under investigation.
“He was really talking about ending his life and ending things. And he was very low and said he felt like he had no fight left in him. He couldn’t see the end,” Voelcker said.
Brandram was admitted to a psychiatric hospital for six days before being discharged on Sunday.
His family insisted the Met police were warned about his mental health.
Voelcker tried to boost his mood on Tuesday by telling him it was a beautiful day and that he had many friends and his family supporting him. He was found dead at his home in Chiswick, west London, later that day.
The family said their priority was to clear their brother’s name and “to ensure another family does not have to go through what we have as a result of the police delays and leaks to the media”.
Hicks said: “Nick was really very loving, enthusiastic. He had an infectious character to be around, very funny. He was an extrovert, so he loved people. He was a much-loved father and uncle.”
Voelcker added: “He spent a long time in the army before going into the city. And his reputation was important. He was a proud man. I think that’s the thing and even the fact that he needed to seek help from a psychiatric hospital was a big deal for him.”
Ch Supt Dan Knowles, in charge of policing for south-west London, said: “Our thoughts are with Mr Brandram’s family and friends at this deeply distressing time. We recognise the significant impact his death will have on those who knew and loved him. We also understand the strain that being subject to a police investigation can place on individuals and their families.
“The investigation remains ongoing. Following Mr Brandram’s release under investigation, it was made clear that inquiries would continue while officers progressed outstanding lines of inquiry and forensic examinations. This remains the position, and further investigative work is ongoing.
“Investigations of this nature, particularly those involving complex evidential and forensic work, can take a number of months to complete as officers gather and assess all available evidence.”
He added that the force had made a mandatory referral to the Independent Office for Police Conduct on 16 September.

Argentina sends Falkland Islands sovereignty bill to Congress
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
20:31:20 UTC
05:31:20 KST

Maryam Ashalem de Andres
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
Argentine President Javier Milei’s government sent a bill to Congress on Thursday, seeking to strengthen legal measures related to the country’s sovereignty claim over the Falkland Islands and increase penalties for unauthorized exploitation of natural resources in the area.
“The initiative is based on three pillars: punishing those who illegally exploit our natural resources, encouraging them to stop such activities and giving the state tools to protect itself against external threats,” the Office of the President said in a statement.
The legislation would replace a 2011 law governing activities involving natural resources in the territory and surrounding maritime areas claimed by Argentina.
It would expand sanctions beyond the hydrocarbons sector to cover any unauthorized activity involving the exploitation of renewable or nonrenewable natural resources, according to the government and Argentine media reports.
Penalties proposed under the bill include fines ranging from 4,000 to 500,000 units, or legal monetary reference units under Argentine law, as well as the cancellation or suspension of permits, and disqualification from operating for periods of between five and 20 years.
The legislation would also establish a National Security System coordinated by a National Security Council.
The framework would bring together diplomatic, economic, defense, legal, intelligence and cybersecurity functions, as well as measures related to critical infrastructure and national sovereignty.
The bill comes as Argentina has increased pressure on companies involved in natural resource projects around the Falkland Islands.
The move also follows an Argentine federal court’s decision Wednesday to order works linked to the Sea Lion offshore oil project to be suspended. The project involves Israeli company Navitas Petroleum and British firm Rockhopper Exploration.
The government has opposed the project, arguing that resource exploitation in the area requires authorization from Argentine authorities.
The bill will be reviewed by congressional committees before being considered by the Chamber of Deputies.

PETROPAVLOVSK·KAMCHATSKY, September 17. /TASS/. The first day of a three·day voting for the election of deputies to the State Duma has started in the easternmost regions of Russia -- in Kamchatka and Chukotka.
At 8:00 a.m. local time (8:00 p.m. GMT) 178 permanent polling stations opened in Kamchatka, and 54 in Chukotka, officials at the regional election commissions told TASS.
"At 8:00 a.m. (local time) on September 18, 178 permanently operating polling stations opened in Kamchatka, and 225,107 voters were registered," an official at the regional election commission said.
In Chukotka, 54 polling stations opened.
The elections will be monitored by 385 public observers on the peninsula.
Earlier, until 8 p.m. (local time) on September 17 early voting was held in the remote and hard·to·reach areas in the regions. In Kamchatka, about 12,000 people made their choice early, and in Chukotka about 5,000.
Polling stations in Sakhalin and the Magadan Region will open in an hour -- at 00:00 Moscow time on September 18 (9:00 p.m. on September 17); in the Maritime and Khabarovsk regions and the Jewish Autonomous Region, they will open in two hours -- at 1:00 a.m. Moscow time on September 18 (10:00 p.m. GMT on September 17). Subsequently, in the Amur Region, Transbaikalia, and Yakutia, voting will take place at 02:00 a.m. Moscow time (11:00 p.m. GMT); in Buryatia, at 3:00 a.m. Moscow time (00:00 GMT).
The single voting day to elect lawmakers to the 9th Russian State Duma will take place on September 18-20. For the first time ever, residents of the recently incorporated Donetsk and Lugansk People’s Republics, as well as the Kherson and Zaporozhye Regions, will participate in legislative elections for the lower house of the Russian parliament. A total of ten parties are taking part in the election: United Russia, the Communist Party of the Russian Federation (CPRF), the Liberal Democratic Party of the Russian Federation (LDPR), New People, A Just Russia - For Truth, the Party of Pensioners for Social Justice, the Communists of Russia, Rodina, the Party of Direct Democracy, as well as the Greens Ecological Party.

Merve Aydogan
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
 The US Treasury Department on Thursday sanctioned an Iranian cryptocurrency exchange, accusing it of helping transfer hundreds of millions of dollars in Bitcoin to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
The sanctions, imposed by the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), target BitBank, its developer Pishtaz Simorgh Electronics, and three associates of Iranian financier Babak Zanjani.
Treasury accused Zanjani of using BitBank between June and July to facilitate the transfer of hundreds of millions of dollars’ worth of Bitcoin to Iran’s Revolutionary Guards as part of alleged efforts to evade US sanctions.
The department claimed that BitBank was a key component of infrastructure allegedly used by Zanjani to launder funds and transfer money to Iranian state-linked entities.
"Today’s designations of Iranian digital asset infrastructure make perfectly clear that efforts to finance the Iranian regime using cryptocurrencies are not beyond OFAC's reach," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement.
"If you support the Iranian regime, the Department of the Treasury will sanction you," he added.
Treasury further claimed that Zanjani has promoted BitBank on his social media accounts since at least 2024 and that the exchange has been listed as a partner by companies within his sanctions evasion network.
The three individuals designated are Hossein Ali Zaker Hossein, Mohammad Mahdi Zaker Hossein, and Seyed Adel Heidari, whom Treasury accused of being executives involved in Zanjani’s digital asset activities.

Rep. María Elvira Salazar, a Florida Republican up for re-election in November, released an ad on Thursday in which she criticized President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, just months after he endorsed her campaign.
“Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” Salazar said in the ad. “The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today.”
"You can be for immigration what Lincoln was for slavery and Reagan was for communism," she continued. "I’m not talking about giving them amnesty. I’m talking about giving them a dignified life in this promised land. And only you can do that.”
The video marked a stunning break from the President who backed Salazar’s re-election bid earlier this year. In February, Trump said in a Truth Social post that the Congresswoman was “doing a truly fantastic job representing the wonderful people of Florida’s 27th Congressional District!” and that she “knows the Wisdom and Courage required to confront the Corrupt Fake News.” He said that she had his “Complete and Total Endorsement for Re-Election” before telling voters that Salazar “WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN!”
Salazar joins a growing number of Republicans who have publicly pushed back on Trump’s policies.
Trump has railed against other members of his party who have broken with him, going so far as to endorse several of their challengers in the primaries. The President endorsed Ed Gallrein, for instance, who ultimately defeated Rep. Thomas Massie in the May Republican primary for the Kentucky Congressman’s seat, after Massie broke with Trump on various issues, including objecting to the “One Big Beautiful Bill” and leading the effort to push the Department of Justice to release the so-called “Epstein files.”
Salazar’s campaign said that the video released on Thursday is the first of multiple ads that it plans to run before the upcoming midterm elections, in which Salazar is facing off against Democratic nominee Eliott Rodríguez. Both Salazar and Rodríguez are Cuban American, and previously worked as journalists.
The Cook Political Report indicates that Salazar, a three-term Congresswoman, is expected to hold on to her seat come November, rating it as “Likely Republican.”
In the district Salazar represents, the foreign-born population makes up more than 54% of the total population—one of the largest proportions of all the districts in the lower chamber.
Thursday’s ad isn’t the first time that Salazar has expressed concerns about the Trump Administration’s immigration enforcement efforts. Earlier this week, she responded to reports that Luis Galeano, an exiled Nicaraguan journalist whose U.S. asylum application has been pending for years, had been detained by federal immigration agents.
“America must always know the difference between a criminal and a political exile,” Salazar said in a statement shared on social media. “Luis is a respected journalist who paid a price for telling the truth about the Ortega-Murillo dictatorship. The regime persecuted him, forced him into exile, and stripped him of his citizenship. That history matters. He cannot be sent back into the hands of the people who targeted him.”
“I have been clear with the Administration: enforce the law and deport dangerous individuals, but do not treat political exiles like criminals,” she continued.
Salazar has also been backing a bipartisan measure in the House that would grant immigrants who don’t have a criminal history a route to secure legal status in the U.S., but not a pathway to citizenship.

Budget day 2026: a renewed drive to safeguard prosperity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
20:29:50 UTC
05:29:50 KST

The Dutch economy is strong, despite economic shocks and global insecurity. What is more, the government is making funds available to support the purchasing power of households. This is the message set out in the Budget Memorandum and the Tax Plan for 2027 which the Minister of Finance, Eelco Heinen, presented to the House of Representatives today.
The government will seek to stimulate economic growth to safeguard the Netherlands’ continued prosperity. It is placing a strong emphasis on three pillars: investment, reform and international cooperation. Issues relating to grid congestion, regulatory pressure and the permitting system must be resolved in order to encourage private investment. Reforms are needed in order to deliver greater productivity and an increase in the labour supply. And international cooperation is crucial so that the Netherlands remains strong at a time when international relations are under great strain.
Minister Heinen: ‘Whether we’re talking about our security, our public services or the opportunities we want to give future generations, they all depend on the strength of the economy. And it’s that economic strength which is under pressure. So our country must recommit to the task of generating economic growth. That means we have to invest, reform, and step up international cooperation. Sound public finances are a prerequisite, and they will be safeguarded by this budget.’
Key measures
The Netherlands Bureau for Economic Policy Analysis forecasts that, next year, households will on average be 0.1 percentage points worse off, partly as a consequence of the war in the Middle East and higher prices. The government is taking measures that will on average improve households’ purchasing power by 0.2 percentage points relative to earlier estimates. In addition, lower rates of excise duties on petrol and diesel will provide a reduction in the tax burden at the petrol pump totalling €1.4 billion.
In addition, the government will make a one-off investment of €1.5 billion – and invest €300 million on a structural basis – in infrastructure. As a stimulus to home building, €425 million will be invested annually in housing associations, by means of policy measures, to increase their capacity to build more homes. To foster the energy transition, a subsidy of €1.3 billion will be made available for carbon storage with a view to mobilising investment. In addition, some €370 million will be allocated to international cooperation annually over the next three years, partly for Ukraine.
In the government’s view it is important to look carefully at the final design of the tax on the actual return on savings and investments in box 3. It was agreed in the coalition agreement to evolve the new box 3 system, based on actual return, into a capital gains system. Over the coming period the government will therefore present concrete and broadly supported proposals to work towards this objective in line with the coalition agreement. They will be processed at the next budgetary decision-making moment.
Cooperation with parliament, subnational authorities, civil society and business is crucial in order to effectively tackle the major issues confronting Dutch society. With this Budget Memorandum, the government is reaching out to the social partners (representatives of employers’ and employees’ organisations) to come to the table and discuss these issues. The plan to directly link the state pension age to life expectancy has been definitively abandoned. In addition, the measure included in the coalition agreement to lower the maximum daily wage for the calculation of social security benefits by 20% has been scrapped. It has also been decided to postpone a number of proposed social security measures by a year. This offers scope for discussion between the government and social partners about the reforms to the social security system and to conclude a broadly supported social accord.
Public finances
The government’s commitment to fiscal discipline and a trend-based fiscal policy is undiminished. During the term of this government, the budget deficit will remain below 3% of gross domestic product (GDP) and public debt below 60% of GDP. The deficit will amount to 2.9% in 2027 and fall gradually to 2.2% in 2030. The level of public debt will gradually increase from 45.6% in 2026 to 46.9% in 2027 and 48.9% in 2030. Sound public finances are crucial. Without intervention, expenditure will shift increasingly towards consumption, whereas the government wishes to use the scarce resources to invest in economic growth.
2027 Tax Plan
The Tax Plan presents proposals by which the government seeks to address public concerns relating for example to home building. Besides scrapping the limit on interest deduction, the government also aims to address these concerns by abolishing transfer tax for housing associations. Furthermore, the government intends to reduce transfer tax for investors from 8% to 7% from 2027.
In addition, the government wants to amend the measures for the waste processing sector, so that waste incineration plants will have more time to make their operations more sustainable, and to avoid a situation where Dutch waste is incinerated abroad. To this end, waste disposal charges and the CO2 levy on industry will rise more slowly than previously planned. Measures are also being proposed that will improve the functioning of the tax system and contribute to sound public finances. Tax reliefs that no longer serve their intended purpose or have become too complex for the people for whom they are intended are being abolished. This also helps implementing agencies. Through these measures the government is ensuring that the tax system will continue to improve in 2027.

US: Trump administration weakens Endangered Species Act
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
20:29:00 UTC
05:29:00 KST

US: Trump administration weakens Endangered Species Act
September 17, 2026
The US government is planning a major reinterpretation of the Endangered Species Act (ESA), The New York Times reported and officials confirmed to AFP on Thursday.
The policy shift was delivered in a new memo signed by Brian Nesvik, director of the Interior Department's Fish and Wildlife Service.
In it, the department will reduce the term "take," a term that relates to pursuing, killing or capturing of a species, to simply "affirmative conduct intentionally directed against a particular animal or animals."
This change would no longer treat the unintentional killing of protected wildlife as unlawful.
Wildlife deaths resulting from foreseeable risks posed by activities such as commercial fishing or logging would end up exempt from the landmark 1973 law.
The Interior Department confirmed the memo's authenticity to AFP.
"The memorandum accurately reflects the US Fish and Wildlife Service's guidance for implementing the Endangered Species Act following the final rule rescinding the regulatory definition of 'harm,'" the department told AFP.
"Under the guidance, the ESA's prohibition on 'take' continues to prohibit conduct including harassing, pursuing, hunting, shooting, wounding, killing, trapping, capturing or collecting protected wildlife," it added.
Broad overhaul of Endangered Species Act
Last year, the Trump administration declared it would consider "economic considerations" when deciding whether to protect species at risk of extinction.
The move is the latest attempt to loosen the landmark ESA's rules. Combined, the changes overturn five decades of precedent in how the law is interpreted and applied.
Interior Secretary Doug Burgum has argued that the changes are necessary, claiming the ESA has been "weaponized" to stop economic projects, weaken competitiveness, undermine national security, and ultimately hurt Americans.
Among the changes to ESA is the redefinition of the term "harm," which would allow oil drilling, mining and other activities in endangered habitats as long as those activities do not directly kill or injure the animals.
The automatic application of endangered species protections to those listed as "threatened" was also halted.
Additionally, the Trump administration announced that it was shrinking two vast stretches of protected land in Utah by more than 90%, to open millions of acres of protected land for fossil fuel extraction and mining.
States sue the government
Last week, the attorneys general of 20 Democratic-led states, along with Washington, DC, submitted a lawsuit against the administration over its overhaul of ESA.
One lawsuit tackles the redefinition of "harm," while a second lawsuit challenges a rule that removes protections for newly threatened species, and the new business-related considerations taken into account when declaring "critical habitats."
"The Trump administration is trying to undermine the law, the will of Congress and the will of the people who overwhelmingly support protections for endangered species," Washington Attorney General Nick Brown said.
"Instead of stewardship, this administration's approach to our land, to our water is one of exploitation," he added.

Syria to abolish Assad-era ‘Terrorism Court’ to restore rights in 90,000-plus cases
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
20:26:41 UTC
05:26:41 KST

Sahin Demir
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
Syria’s People’s Assembly unanimously approved a bill Thursday to abolish the Assad-era “Terrorism Court,” according to state-run SANA news agency.
The move is to reverse the effects of rulings in more than 90,000 cases handled by the court and restore confiscated property and other rights to those affected.
The court was established under Law No. 22 of 2012 during the rule of Bashar al-Assad and had jurisdiction over cases involving civilians and military personnel.
SANA said the exceptional legal framework under which the court operated had drawn criticism because of fair-trial guarantees and the right to defense.
Abdul Nasser Houshan, head of parliament’s Constitutional and Legislative Committee, said the bill abolishes the law establishing the court and assigns the Supreme Judicial Council responsibility for addressing the consequences of its rulings.
Specialized judicial committees will be formed to nullify the effects of previous rulings, including returning confiscated property. Pending cases will be closed or transferred to the competent judicial authorities.
At least 90,560 cases were brought before the court, according to figures cited by SANA from the Syrian Network for Human Rights (SNHR).
The rights group documented at least 40,602 property seizure and confiscation orders between 2012 and 2024, affecting 320,000 people under the broader seizure and confiscation system established by the Assad regime.
SNHR said the court relied on security reports and confessions extracted under torture in some cases, while imposing restrictions on the right to defense and lacking transparency in its rulings.
The bill also exempts those recovering confiscated property from taxes, fees and other costs associated with transferring ownership back to them. The provision covers property confiscated under rulings by the “Terrorism Court,” Military Field Courts and military courts between March 15, 2011, and Dec. 8, 2024.
The Assad regime abolished the separate Military Field Courts in 2023 and transferred pending cases to the military judiciary.
Following Assad’s fall in December 2024, authorities began reviewing the legacy of the “Terrorism Court.” In 2025, the Justice Ministry referred judges who had served in the court for investigation and established a specialized judicial committee to review rulings and procedures issued by the court and other exceptional judicial bodies.

Zelensky, von der Leyen plan to meet at UN as EU releases $3.7 billion for Ukraine

The call comes a day after von der Leyen delivered her annual State of the EU address to the European Parliament.
The EU will disburse another 3.3 billion euros (over $3.7 billion) to Ukraine on Sept. 18, von der Leyen said in a press release after her conversation with Zelensky. The aid package will go towards purchases of missiles and drones for Ukraine's defense forces, she said.
The funds are part of the 28.3 billion euros ($32.9 billion) earmarked for Ukraine's defense under the EU defense support loan this year. With the latest disbursement, Ukraine will have received 11.7 billion euros (about $13.4 billion) of the total funding.
Ukraine will also be able to use funds from the support loan to purchase U.S.-made PAC-3 Patriot interceptors, urgently needed to defend against Russian ballistic missile strikes.
The upcoming tranche is smaller than the 4.7 billion euros ($5.5 billion) previously promised by EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius on Sept. 11. The smaller disbursement is the result of delays in processing Ukrainian receipts for military equipment.
A senior EU official previously told the Kyiv Independent that the disbursement would likely be lower than $5.5 billion due to this reason. Disbursements from the support loan can only be processed once Ukraine has provided receipts for cross-checking.

"We discussed the issue of funding for Ukrainian defense in great detail," the president said. "We are working on solutions to this problem and agreed to meet in New York on the sidelines of the General Assembly."
World leaders will convene at the U.N. headquarters in New York from Sept. 22-28 for the organization's 81st General Assembly. Zelensky is expected to meet with multiple leaders at the event, including a potential one-on-one with U.S. President Donald Trump.
In her statement after the call with Zelensky, von der Leyen indicated that she would lobby Kyiv's non-European allies for increased support during her time at the UNGA.
"Next week, I will be at the U.N. General Assembly in New York," she said. "My message to Ukraine's friends around the world will be simple: Europe is stepping up. Now others must step up their support too."

 Impartiality is sometimes treated by philosophers as if it were equivalent to moral impartiality. Or, at the very least, the former word is often used, without the qualifying adjective ‘moral’, even when it is the particularly moral concept that is intended. This is potentially misleading, since impartiality in its broadest sense is best understood as a formal notion that can be applied in a number of contexts, including non-moral contexts….

Big space mirrors could bring Earth on-demand light — and upend our night sky
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
20:23:22 UTC
05:23:22 KST

Big space mirrors could bring Earth on-demand light — and upend our night sky
Reflect Orbital satellites could make the darkest skies look like nighttime in the suburbs
Since 1989, astrophysicist Jonathan McDowell has tracked every human-made object in space. McDowell’s meticulously maintained catalog, updated every few weeks, is more comprehensive and detailed than that of most governments.
From his front-row seat, he has watched with growing alarm as private companies launched dozens, then hundreds, then thousands of satellites over the last decade. So when McDowell heard that a space company called Reflect Orbital plans to launch a satellite to reflect the sun’s light onto the night side of Earth, he heaved a deep sigh.
“It’s an insane project,” says McDowell, who retired from Harvard this year and is now an honorary professor at Durham University in England. “There’s a failure to understand that darkness is a good thing.”
Reflect Orbital, based near Los Angeles, hopes its satellite and others like it some day offer “sunlight on demand,” illuminating disaster areas for search and rescue efforts, lighting up nighttime events and festivals and allowing solar farms to run all hours of the day.
“We believe that exploring how new technologies can help the world forgo fossil fuels is a responsible application of the scientific process,” Christopher Buscombe, a spokesperson for Reflect Orbital, wrote in an email to Science News. “We will continue to work closely with scientific partners who share this belief.”
But many space observers and dark sky enthusiasts are in an uproar. The consequences to astronomy could be catastrophic, they say, and the reflected light could threaten human health and safety and disrupt wildlife. In March, the American Astronomical Society petitioned the Federal Communications Commission to deny Reflect Orbital’s request to operate the test satellite. When the FCC granted approval in July, nonprofit organizations including DarkSky International asked the agency to reverse its decision.
The response to Reflect Orbital reflects growing concerns about the crowding of space more generally. The number of active satellites orbiting Earth has ballooned from 2,000 in 2018 to over 16,000 today, McDowell says. Many more are expected to launch in the years ahead.
This traffic jam, along with the proliferation of space junk from dead satellites and discarded rocket stages, has space scientists worried about collisions that could wipe out GPS navigation and other essential tools. The satellites are also a problem for astronomers, interrupting observations by leaving streaks on telescope images.
But there’s not much scientists can do to appeal the launches, says international environmental lawyer Dana Zartner of the University of San Francisco. Space satellite deployments are governed (sometimes loosely) by a patchwork of domestic regulations and international treaties. “The law has not caught up to the reality of what is happening,” Zartner says.
The Reflect Orbital launch, expected this year, could change that. The satellite’s unique brightness and the risks it may bring could mark an inflection point in the way we regulate the night sky. The project “amplifies the issue to the point where it’s impossible to ignore,” says astronomer Stephen Hummel of the McDonald Observatory in West Texas.
Who’s in charge?
Space law’s roots are planted in the Cold War. Some of the earliest international treaties about activities in outer space grew from agreements banning nuclear tests high in the atmosphere.
“People [were] saying, ‘Let’s not nuke the sky, please,’” says Cristian van Eijk, an expert in international space law at Newcastle University in England.
Over 100 nations have signed the Outer Space Treaty of 1967, which declares space “the province of all mankind.” No nation can occupy or claim sovereignty over any portion of outer space, it says, and space must be used for peaceful purposes and be kept clear of harmful contamination. Four other international treaties have dealt with issues such as the registration of space objects and the liability they might cause.
But such treaties are voluntary, and it’s difficult to enforce compliance. “Nobody can make a state do any of these things,” Zartner says. “You cannot throw a state in jail.”
Individual countries have their own regulations about what goes into space and how. In the United States, the Federal Aviation Administration oversees rocket launches and reentries. But the FCC oversees licensing of commercial satellites that communicate with Earth, and it has become the de facto gatekeeper for satellite approval. The FCC has traditionally been required to consider whether applications serve the public interest, but it has not generally considered factors such as light pollution.
The explosion in satellites in low-Earth orbit, between about 100 and 2,000 kilometers in altitude, has exposed gaps in the system, says astronomer Samantha Lawler of the University of Regina in Saskatchewan, Canada. That’s because current approval processes look at launches one by one without addressing what thousands of satellites mean in aggregate. “There are some serious loopholes,” Lawler says.
Bugs on the windshield
To reduce the impact to science, companies like SpaceX have worked with astronomers to dim the appearance of their commercial satellites, by changing their orbits or painting the satellites black, for example. But there are still problems.
Astronomer Meredith Rawls likens existing satellites to “bugs on the windshield.” She and colleagues have spent years preparing the new Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile to cope with the light streaks left by overhead satellites.
Those streaks can mess with searches for transiting exoplanets, the mysterious sources of gravitational waves, objects in and beyond the distant Kuiper Belt and asteroids that could cross paths with Earth. Satellites in low-Earth orbit, including SpaceX’s Starlink constellations, are mainly visible just before sunrise and after sunset; that’s prime time for many types of astronomical observations.
“One of the most frustrating parts about it is you won’t know what you didn’t discover,” says Rawls, of the University of Washington in Seattle. “We can’t know what we didn’t see.”
The space community is also alarmed by the growing potential for orbiting objects to crash into each other, hurtling space junk toward Earth or creating an unnavigable debris field around the planet. Most commercial satellites have thrusters to avoid such collisions. But the proliferation of objects means those satellites are engaging thrusters frequently, sometimes weekly. Scientists wonder what will happen when they fail.
And there is a growing concern about the potentially hazardous residue such satellites could leave in the atmosphere when they de-orbit. “We are now using space as a species at an unprecedented level,” McDowell says. “A lot of effects that were previously trivial are now no longer trivial.”
Space scientists, amateur astronomers, Indigenous peoples and many others are mourning the night sky as it has existed for millennia — or soon will be. “This represents far more than mere loss of environment,” wrote astronomers Aparna Venkatesan of the University of San Francisco and John Barentine, cofounder of the Center for Space Environmentalism, in 2023 in Science. “We are witnessing loss of heritage, place-based language, identity, storytelling, millennia-old sky traditions and our ability to conduct traditional practices grounded in the ecological integrity of what we call home.” The pair proposed a term for “sky grief”: noctalgia.
That grief could grow as companies put ever more satellites into space. SpaceX alone plans to launch one million as part of orbiting data centers starting in late 2027. Other companies and countries, including China’s space agency, plan to launch hundreds of thousands more. Even if not all of them get off the ground, the number of fake stars in a dark night sky could rival the number of visible real ones by 2030, McDowell says.
Mirrors in the sky
Reflect Orbital’s satellite, named Eärendil-1, is an 18-by-18-meter sheet of reflective material that will fold up for launch and unfurl in space. Motors will maneuver it to bounce light in any direction the company desires. It will orbit 600 to 650 kilometers high, a popular altitude for commercial satellites. Eärendil-1 will be able to shine light on a spot about five kilometers wide, making it as bright as if a full moon were overhead. The mirror will move at about 7.5 kilometers per second, meaning it will illuminate the same spot on the ground for four minutes before disappearing over the horizon.
“Our first demonstration mission will enable Reflect Orbital to test the operation of a commercially built spacecraft and deployable reflector, including the built-in safeguards governing precisely how, where and when the service is delivered,” Buscombe told Science News. “The mission will provide real-world data that shapes the design of future satellites, the markets we serve, how we engage communities and the operational practices we put in place. We expect this to be the first of several test missions.”
This isn’t the first time such a scheme has been proposed or even attempted. In the 1960s, NASA and the U.S. Department of Defense ran a study called Project Able to determine the feasibility of putting a 600-meter-wide mirror into a geosynchronous orbit 36,000 kilometers above Earth. One of the motivations was to light the sky over Vietnam to aid combat.
“They say history doesn’t repeat itself, but it does rhyme,” says Lisa Ruth Rand, a California-based space historian who is writing a book about waste in Earth’s orbit.
Practicalities and cost meant the mirror never got off the ground. But in 1993, the Russian space agency deployed a 20-meter space mirror that swept a spot of light across Europe. The project sought to show the feasibility of lighting up Siberia during long winter nights. Though the beam was mostly blocked by clouds, astronauts aboard the Mir space station filmed the event.
Reflect Orbital says its spotlight will be fully controllable and can be turned off in an instant by tilting the mirror away from Earth. Outside the beam, the light will look like just another star, according to Buscombe. And it shouldn’t shine on places where no one ordered it.
Space scientists aren’t so sure. As light travels from space to the ground, it scatters off molecules in the atmosphere, says astrophysicist Gaspar Bakos of Princeton University. “That is why the sky is blue, why we see the clouds,” he says.
Bakos and colleagues ran computer simulations of the light from a Reflect Orbital satellite overhead under various conditions. Between scattering in the atmosphere and reflections from the ground, Eärendil-1’s beam could appear as a hazy chimney on the horizon from as far as 14 kilometers away, the team reported in a paper posted in August on arXiv.org.
Only one satellite is cleared for operations, Reflect Orbital and the FCC note. But critics worry that there’s nothing in the licensing logic that would stand in the way of more. If the test is successful, Reflect Orbital says it wants to launch 5,000 mirrors by 2030 and 50,000 by 2035. They would be larger, about 54 meters across. Light from such a mirror could brighten the night sky to as much as four full moons. Arranged in a chain, they would keep the lights on longer, because a new mirror would come into view just as an old one sets.
“It’s quite a dance, if you think about it,” Hummel says. “A lot of things need to move very accurately in order to provide the levels of illumination that they’re claiming.”
Within the beam, you’d see no stars. The effect outside the beam would vary depending on distance and existing levels of light pollution. In a dark area, one 54-meter satellite would leave a concentrated glow that outshines the full moon from more than 30 kilometers away, Bakos and colleagues calculate. Even a person in an average suburb could see the beam from 20 kilometers away, Bakos says. For astronomers, the beam would be disruptive from up to 100 kilometers away.
Barentine, who is based in Tucson, has seen renderings of the simulations. “The only word I can think of to describe what they look like is horrifying,” he says. “If you are within a few kilometers of a beam, it looks like the mother ship is landing.”
Meanwhile, the McDonald Observatory is preparing for Eärendil-1 by developing tools to track and avoid the satellite’s path, Hummel says. Staff plan to pause telescope observing as needed. Seeing the beam through a moderate-sized telescope could damage observers’ eyes or harm research equipment, he and others assert.
Reflect Orbital counters that the risk of eye damage is extremely low, and that even intentionally tracking the satellite for 100 seconds through a 12-inch diameter telescope would stay within international eye-safety limits.
The company’s planned fleet could change the night sky dramatically, adding several hundred objects as bright as Venus by 2035, Munich-based astronomer Olivier Hainaut of the European Southern Observatory reported in August in Astronomy & Astrophysics. Because of light scattering, the full fleet could make the night sky three or four times as bright as it already is anywhere within a few hundred kilometers of the beam, Hainaut concludes. That would make skies at even the darkest sites appear more like those in the suburbs.
Reflect Orbital disputes those findings as well as Bakos’.
It’s not just astronomers who are concerned. Glints from rotating satellites could distract pilots or drivers. Nighttime light can also disrupt circadian rhythms, the behavior of nocturnal animals, and migration patterns of birds and insects.
The effects of one intermittent beam are unclear, says biologist Brett Seymoure of the University of Texas at El Paso. “If it’s a few days a year, is that going to have a big effect? Probably not. But we don’t know.” More troubling is the idea of permanently lighting up the night sky, which could alter critical ecosystem services, Seymoure says. “It’s an existential crisis for me.”
Reflect Orbital says it will maintain strict exclusion zones for astronomy and sensitive environments, which the company is developing with the National Science Foundation. It plans to adjust the exclusion zones based on the satellites’ actual brightness post-launch. “We are committed to ongoing dialogue with scientists, astronomers, environmental researchers and other interested stakeholders,” Buscombe told Science News.
Fighting back
Previous efforts to block satellites have relied on arguments about orbital debris and the environmental impact of light pollution. DarkSky International, for instance, challenged an FCC decision that granted SpaceX a license for its second-gen Starlink satellites in 2023, arguing the agency should have required an environmental review. DarkSky lost.
Typically, government-approved projects are subject to the National Environmental Policy Act, which requires environmental impact assessments. But since 1986, the FCC has said that most of its activities are excluded from the act because space is outside of Earth’s environment.
The FCC’s stance isn’t likely to change. In 2025, President Trump directed federal agencies to revise their environmental review processes to “prioritize efficiency and certainty over any other objectives.” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr has announced plans to speed the satellite application process by creating a “licensing assembly line” and to clarify that FCC’s space-related activities don’t require environmental review.
But if the FCC won’t consider the environmental impact of satellite operations, critics ask, who will? It “becomes this buck passing thing,” Barentine says. “The FAA says we find nothing wrong with your launch, the FCC says we find nothing wrong with your radio communications, and there’s nothing to check the environmental impacts.” The FCC did not respond on the record to requests for comment.
Mirrors designed to send light to Earth might change the legal landscape, Barentine says. If an individual gets hurt by looking at the mirror through a telescope, that individual could have the right to sue in court. That’s not an ideal strategy for policy making, he says, because “we might actually have to wait for something to happen, for somebody to be injured.”
Scattered light also could count as a public nuisance, depending on where it shines, Zartner says. If it spills over an international border, Reflect Orbital or even the United States could be liable for any harm done in another nation’s territory.
Simply by being so visible, Reflect Orbital’s satellites could bring wider awareness of the concerns over space crowding. “Satellites up in the air are so intangible for most people,” Zartner says. “For the law, you need something tangible. To get support, you need something that people can see and latch onto.”
Zartner, Barentine and Venkatesan have outlined legal strategies to protect the darkness, drawing on individual rights, community rights and the rights of nature. Though those efforts haven’t succeeded to date, “I don’t believe that will be the case forever,” Venkatesan says. “We have to keep trying.”
What follows depends on how the public and policy makers respond. Could they be moved to action by sunbeams at night? Or are people already too acclimated to starless, satellite-filled skies? Spotting artificial objects in space has become a pastime in its own right.
What comes of this moment could determine what future generations experience when they look to the night sky. In one possible future, there’s a sense of awe for ancient celestial phenomena, their light traveling hundreds or thousands of light-years. In another, we may look up and applaud only the stuff we made and sent up ourselves.

A street vendor sells walnuts on the occasion of the Sayar festival, in Mandi on Wednesday. (ANI Photo)
KOKERNAG: In Gohan village, around 100km south of Srinagar, Shabir Ahmad was among many harvesting walnuts from a towering tree. The work has become increasingly difficult. “My back aches now,” Ahmad said. J&K produces 3.5 lakh tonnes of walnuts annually, around 90% of the country’s total output.Like other villagers, Ahmad had no safety gear and he was proud of it. “We have been doing it for centuries,” said Ahmad, also a clerk at a local court. However, the bravado doesn’t help in harvesting seasons. Dr. Mohd Yaqoob Bhat, a surgeon at Paras Hospital in Srinagar, said Valley healthcare units treat dozens of patients each year after falls from walnut trees, some with serious spinal injuries. “There is no mechanism to address the issue,” Bhat said.Ahmad’s younger brother sold one walnut for one rupee and no two fruits are similar. For generations, Kashmir’s walnut trees have been grown from seeds. J&K and Sher-e-Kashmir University of Agricultural Sciences and Technology (SKUAST) are now promoting medium-sized, grafted walnut trees to bring greater uniformity and help the produce compete globally amid competition from soft-shelled varieties grown in California and Chile.
The initiative aims to replace scattered plantations with organised orchards of known varieties, allowing farmers to grow more trees in the same area and produce walnuts more consistent in size and color.J&K has about 80,000 hectares under walnut cultivation, most of it made up of seedling-origin trees. “When someone plants a walnut seed in the ground, whatever grows becomes a tree. Every tree is a variety of its own,” Ashfaq A. Pandit, professor and head of fruit science at SKUAST, said. This natural variation, once considered an advantage, has become a challenge in the modern market where buyers seek consistent produce.Traditional walnut trees can take about 15 years to bear fruit without using pesticides. Unlike traditional seedling-origin trees, grafted walnuts belong to known varieties.Imtiyaz Ahmad Lone, professor and head of SKUAST’s Walnut Research Centre, said the university released new walnut cultivars and grafting-based cultivation had spread over nearly 90,000 hectares despite lack of subsidies.Farmers argued, however, that the grafted varieties are no match for the traditional Kashmiri walnut. “It is no match in taste. The new varieties are brittle, tasteless. They are a no-show,” Mohammad Sultan, a Pulwama farmer in the business for 50 years, said.
Researchers differed. Lone pointed out that grafted trees have early bearing, give faster returns as orchards and nut quality are uniform. “They have higher productivity and better export potential. There is a gradual opportunity to replace unproductive seedling trees,” he said.The transition has impacted walnut woodcraft industries. Walnut trees cannot be cut in J&K without govt permission. The matter was debated in the assembly in March when CM Omar Abdullah opposed a bill allowing landowners to cut walnut trees on private property. Omar defended the restrictions, saying the law served a broader purpose of conserving walnut and chinar trees.

Migrant arrivals to Europe fall 39%, while deaths rise: UN migration agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
20:15:54 UTC
05:15:54 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
Migrant and refugee arrivals to Europe by sea have fallen sharply in 2026, but the number of people dying or missing during the journeys has risen, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said Thursday.
Nearly 60,000 people arrived by sea this year, as of Sept. 15, down 39% from last year's 98,040, according to data from the IOM's Displacement Tracking Matrix and Missing Migrants Project.
At least 2,292, however, have died or gone missing while attempting the crossings, compared with 1,999 during the same period in 2025.
The IOM cautioned that the actual toll is likely higher because many shipwrecks and disappearances are never recorded.
The sharpest decline in arrivals was seen on the Central Mediterranean route to Italy, falling 55% from 48,231 to 21,393. Deaths on the route climbed from 844 to 996.
"Fewer people are arriving by sea in Europe than at this point last year. But people are still dying and going missing in alarming numbers trying to reach safety," IOM Director General Amy Pope said in a statement.
Greece received 20,428 sea arrivals, about 5,000 fewer than a year earlier, while deaths along the Eastern Mediterranean route rose to 417 from 284.
Arrivals via routes to Spain also declined, with 16,794 people reaching the country through the Atlantic and Western Mediterranean, compared with 22,855 last year. At least 879 fatalities were recorded along those routes.
Pope urged greater international cooperation to save lives, combat trafficking, and expand safe and regular migration pathways.

Spread across 40 acres at Choglamsar and Stakna, the gardens house more than 25 lakh high-value flowers,
JAMMU/SRINAGAR: On Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s 76th birthday, Ladakh Lieutenant Governor Vinai Kumar Saxena inaugurated the world’s highest and India’s largest twin flower fields in Leh, at an altitude of 10,600ft, on Thursday as part of the administration’s efforts to diversify agriculture, build skills and create new livelihood opportunities in the Union Territory.Spread across 40 acres at Choglamsar and Stakna, the gardens house more than 25 lakh high-value flowers, including 24 lakh Lilium and 1 lakh Gladiolus. The Choglamsar field was developed in just two months, with plantation beginning on July 16 and the first blooms appearing in the first week of Sept. At Stakna, nearly 1.4 lakh lilies were planted in Aug, with the first blooms expected by Oct-end.
Saxena said the initiative was the first experiment of its size and nature at such a high altitude in Leh, adding that its successful execution could pave the way for replication elsewhere in Ladakh. The gardens will open to the public on Sept 18, with an entry fee of Rs 25 for adults and Rs 10 for children, officials said.Floriculture, as a high-value agricultural activity, can complement traditional farming, increase cultivators’ incomes and create opportunities for employment and entrepreneurship, the LG said. The Choglamsar flower park will serve as a training, demonstration and model floriculture centre for farmers and youth, where Lilium, Gladiolus, Tulips and other ornamental flowers will be cultivated for national and international markets.
“The facility will provide exposure to modern cultivation techniques, scientific farming practices and improved post-harvest management, enabling farmers to acquire the knowledge and skills required to take up floriculture at farm and village levels,” Saxena said. “Besides functioning as a recreational and educational space for residents and tourists, it will create an ecosystem where not only flowers, but also knowledge, skills and enterprises can grow,” he added.

From African shepherd to Australia's marathon record holder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
20:13:41 UTC
05:13:41 KST

Haftu Strintzos's remarkable journey from shepherd to marathon record holder
Australia's men's marathon record holder, Haftu Strintzos, thrives on hard work, but still finds it hard to believe where life has taken him.
Born in eastern Tigray in northern Ethiopia, he grew up standing barefoot in fields for hours, helping provide for his family from dawn to dusk.
"I feel as though I have lived a double life in a way," he said after celebrating his 27th birthday in Melbourne.
"I consider myself very privileged to live this life.
"I spent my early days as a shepherd, herding goats and sheep through the mountains of my local village. I grew up without a TV or running water."
In his remote community, 2,300 metres above sea level, the only source of information he had until age 10 was a mobile phone.
Haftu lost both biological parents by the time he was six, and was taken in by his maternal grandmother, living with his aunt and cousins.
A Greek-Australian aid worker by the name of Maria Strintzos came calling, meeting Haftu in 2007 at the age of eight.
After decades working across Ethiopia, she asked him if he'd like to be her son, adopted him and helped him migrate to Melbourne in 2011 — more than 12,000 kilometres from the mountains of Tigray.
Today, Haftu speaks five languages, Tigrinya, Amharic, Greek, Japanese and English, holds a Master of Electrical Engineering from Villanova University in the USA, and recently broke the national marathon record.
Feeling the 'weight of the world'
Maria always felt compelled to help others. Growing up in South Melbourne in the 1960s, she found strength in the local Greek community, even while migrant families faced racism.
"We had absolutely everybody there. As much as I loved growing up there, it built a strength in me," she said.
"I grew up knowing what social injustice and inequality looked like."
Her aid work took her through Indonesia, Ethiopia, Eritrea, and Sudan, supporting famine relief, water schemes, food security, women's empowerment, and communities affected by conflict, spending 35 years around wars and disease, but also hope, in the Horn of Africa.
But something different about young Haftu stood out.
He would walk barefoot through dry riverbeds, guiding his almost blind grandmother, Shifta, through the mountains to meet Maria.
"He was very respectful," she said.
"And he would sit there really quietly … didn't muck around like the other kids.
"He always had this sort of sad and serious look about him. It's like he had the weight of the world on his shoulders.
"But the way he looked after his grandmother and the way the grandmother would talk about him was very moving at the time too."
With the pull of family ties in Australia, Maria found herself at a crossroads.
"I was challenged at that time because I didn't particularly want to leave Ethiopia," she said.
"I loved my life. I loved what I did … I felt like I was achieving something."
Embracing the challenge of two different worlds
Excelling at school and winning education awards, Haftu embraced every opportunity.
When he migrated to Australia in 2011, he took nothing for granted in his new environment.
Growing up without electricity, he became fascinated by anything electrical.
Maria bought Haftu toy cars that he would unpack and dismantle anything he could get his hands on.
"He literally pulled them apart with the motors, everything, and reassembled them," she said.
Having never seen a TV, he would sit on the couch for hours waiting for people to appear outside the screen.
"Sometimes I'd catch him sort of looking behind the TV because he thought there was people in there,"
"I still can't believe it. It was quite incredible that given his background, that he had this innate gift, something about electricity."
Maria said she's most proud of how Haftu has risen above adversity in his life.
"Where he's come from it was a rock hut, and they would sleep on the floor and the animals were next to them," she said.
"The uniqueness of Haftu is that he's managed to retain the positive qualities of his experience. I'm in awe of him."
But the culture shock wasn't easy; different foods, subtle racism, and grappling with Western values were also some of Haftu's greatest tests.
"My biggest challenges in assimilating to Australian culture were learning the English language and motion sickness while riding in cars," he said.
"I remember a time in my early days where the only way I would not throw up while Mum drove the car was if I sat in the front passenger seat and kept my eyes on the road in front."
From a school oval to an athlete with no fear
It wasn't until he moved to Australia that Haftu realised his potential in athletics, having grown up in Tigray not knowing it was even a sport or profession.
"My PE teacher at school encouraged me to pursue it when he saw me run a cross-country race at the school oval," he said.
In that school race, he just kept running and didn't stop after the finish line, such was his determination for long-distance.
"I have grown up through this sport and learned my most valuable life lessons through it,"
"Running helped me connect with my local community, just getting out and about and meeting like-minded people."
His talent soon attracted attention, including from Cathy Freeman, who became like a mentor and even attended his birthday party during his teens.
Training up to 190 kilometres a week under coach Adam Didyk, Haftu broke the Australian men's marathon record in 2 hours 6 minutes and 20 seconds, at the Gold Coast Marathon in July.
He became the first Australian winner in 20 years, smashed the course record and set a new Oceania record — all on his fourth attempt at the distance.
Didyk, who also coaches Australian women's marathon record holder Jessica Stenson, has guided Haftu remotely from Adelaide for two years.
"He's a fairly no-fuss kind of individual. He'll just take the work and get it done," Didyk said.
"He's obviously very capable when it comes to longer distances and feels confident running at the pace he needs to for the marathon, quite extraordinarily, mind you."
Didyk said Haftu's college experience and early development give him a strong understanding of racing, matched by mental strength.
"He backs himself. He has a lot of confidence in his ability, and he believes in what he can do.
"He's one of those no-fear athletes who sets a goal that looks pretty daunting, but it excites him more and more the scarier he makes it."
Australian records are just the beginning
Haftu's talent comes as a package. Didyk said the physical ability, mental strength and calmness on race day is all put together to make good decisions, ultimately which led to the record-breaking performance at the Gold Coast Marathon.
"He's just a sensible, quite an intelligent young guy, and that all comes together to match what he can physically do as well," he said.
Haftu's calmness and patience at the Gold Coast reinforced Didyk's belief that he has world class potential.
"There's so many positives about Haftu that he can go and achieve what no Australian has before in the marathon," Didyk said.
"He's very determined to be successful in international level … it was a phenomenally strong close.
"I think what's probably most important to us now with seeing that is if he's going to be competitive at an Olympic or World Championships level, he's going to need that ability to be able to close really fast over those last 10 kilometres.
"He's shown he's got the foundations to do something like that."
"Off the back of that, it started to give us the knowledge of him to go, that's the game he can play when he goes to a major championship, he can put himself in there and he can put himself in a competitive situation late in the race.
"And that's ideally what we're aiming to do with him over the coming years."
From his humble beginnings in Ethiopia, Haftu's dreams of standing on an Olympic podium remain his driving force for motivation for the 2027 World Championships in China, and Los Angeles Olympics in 2028.
Australia hasn't had an Olympic marathon medallist since Lisa Ondieki won silver in 1988.
"I am very fortunate to have the support systems I need to help me to achieve my goals — something that not every athlete gets to have," he said.
"I want to continue to break records. After all, records are there to be broken."

Why is Trump shifting millions in military aid to South America?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
20:07:31 UTC
05:07:31 KST

Why is Trump shifting millions in military aid to South America?
The US has decided to redirect $52 million in foreign military financing to four countries in South America, the Associated Press reported on Tuesday.
The funds, which subsidize purchases of American military equipment, are being reallocated from Slovakia, North Macedonia, Tunisia, and Iraq to Panama, Peru, Ecuador, and Colombia, the news agency said, citing a State Department notification to Congress.
The shift comes as US President Donald Trump has placed greater emphasis on the Western Hemisphere under what he has called the ‘Donroe Doctrine’, his version of the 19th-century hegemonic Monroe Doctrine. The Trump administration has said it intends to strengthen US influence in the Americas while preventing rival powers from gaining strategic positions in the region.
The State Department said the previous distribution of foreign military financing did “not align with the administration’s prioritization of” the Western Hemisphere. Spending the money in South America will help recipients “combat narcoterrorism in our backyard and help continue to secure the Panama Canal” and “prevent adversaries from establishing strategic footholds in our hemisphere,” the department explained.
How did the South American recipients align with Trump?
Since Trump returned to office in January 2025, all four recipients have taken steps aligning themselves more closely with his administration’s priorities.
Panama withdrew from China’s Belt and Road Initiative and expanded security cooperation with Washington, though President Jose Raul Mulino pushed back on Trump’s suggestion that the US should retake direct control of the Panama Canal.
Mulino’s government has scrapped contracts with Hong Kong-based firm CK Hutchison Holdings, which Washington cited as evidence of a slow Chinese takeover of critical ports in Peru. The company owned by billionaire Li Ka-shing’s family is seeking $1.5 billion in damages.
Ecuador has signed a trade agreement with the US, lowering trade barriers and making other concessions to American exporters. President Daniel Noboa has also expanded counter-narcotics cooperation with Washington, tacitly endorsing Trump’s controversial tactics that involve airstrikes on boats in international waters that the Pentagon deems suspicious.
Noboa’s proposal to once again allow foreign military bases in Ecuador was rejected by voters last year.
Peru has joined Trump’s signature Shield of the Americas initiative under new President Keiko Fujimori, the daughter and political heir to dictator Alberto Fujimori, and otherwise expanding security cooperation with Washington.
Colombia too took a right-wing turn and realigned with Washington this year, after controversial President Abelardo de la Espriella came to power.
The millionaire nicknamed El Tigre (The Tiger) owns a personal luxury brand and used to represent drug traffickers as a lawyer. He has pledged to be tough on organized crime as president, including by resuming fumigation of coca with herbicides.
How is the ‘Donroe Doctrine’ being enforced?
The Trump administration has also used military and economic pressure elsewhere in the Western Hemisphere.
In January, US forces abducted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, and brought them to the US to face federal “narco-terrorism” charges. Trump subsequently said Washington would temporarily “run” Venezuela and tap its vast oil reserves.
During his first term from 2017 to 2021, Trump recognized opposition politician Juan Guaido as Venezuela’s interim president and supported his bid to replace Maduro.
Washington also tightened its trade blockade of Cuba this year, cutting off Venezuelan oil supplies and threatening retaliation against countries providing fuel to the island nation. The resulting fuel shortage has contributed to prolonged blackouts and a severe energy crisis.
Trump intervened directly in Honduras’ 2025 presidential race by publicly endorsing conservative candidate Nasry Asfura. He also pardoned former President Juan Orlando Hernandez, a fellow member of Asfura’s National Party who had been convicted in the US on drug trafficking charges.
In Colombia, former President Gustavo Petro alleged that the election won by de la Espriella had been digitally manipulated from abroad, pointing to alleged Israeli involvement and criticizing US interference in the campaign. Colombian electoral authorities rejected his fraud claims.
How is the ‘Donroe Doctrine’ different from the Monroe Doctrine?
US President James Monroe declared the Western Hemisphere off limits for European great powers in 1823.
While he framed his policy as anti-colonialist, in practice it prevented any military threat to the US homeland from emerging in South America and ensured preferential treatment of US businesses, particularly their access to natural resources, from bananas grown in Guatemala to copper mined in Chile.
US hegemony manifested during the 20th century in the so-called ‘dirty war’ against left-leaning political projects in South America. Washington supported right-wing dictatorships across the continent as long as they pledged to oppose Communism.
Since the end of the Cold War, Washington has defended its interests in South America under the guise of promoting human rights and democracy and dismantling narcotraffic, with the messaging shifting depending on which of the two US parties was holding the presidency.
Trump’s version distinguishes itself in its blatant approach rather than essence.

US to allow Iranian leaders to attend UN General Assembly
UNITED NATIONS - The Trump administration will allow top Iranian officials to attend the United Nations General Assembly in New York next week, the State Department said on Sept 17, even as Washington and Tehran remain at war and continue intermittent talks aimed at ending the conflict.

Iran’s Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to Reuters’ request for comment.
Under the 1947 UN “headquarters agreement,” the United States is generally required to allow access to the United Nations for foreign diplomats. But Washington says it can deny visas for “security, terrorism and foreign policy” reasons.
