It has been nearly eight months since Kazmierczak lunged towards the congresswoman and sprayed her with a dark water-and-vinegar mixture from a syringe, which landed on Omar’s clothing and skin.
The attack was captured on video and showed Kazmierczak, who sat in the front row of the town hall, leaping from the audience, after which he could be heard yelling, “You must resign” and that Omar was “splitting Minnesota apart”.
Kazmierczak was promptly subdued by Omar’s security team before being arrested. Omar was not injured in the attack and proceeded with the town hall.
The assault came as Omar had been calling for the abolition of the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency and the resignation of then-Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Kristi Noem over her management of federal border agents in Minneapolis during the shootings during “Operation Metro Surge,” President Donald Trump’s federal immigration crackdown in the state of Minnesota. The crackdown involved more than 2,000 officers in Minneapolis and Saint Paul and provoked intense civil unrest and led to the deaths of two US citizens, Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti, at the hands of federal agents.
In an earlier hearing, Kazmierczak could not explain what happened in the assault.
“It’s fuzzy,” he told US Judge Ericksen when asked what he remembered.
The government sentencing memorandum, submitted to the court by prosecutors, said he had texted at least three people indicating his actions were premeditated, though he refused to answer questions about his specific intent.
He also messaged a neighbour to arrange for dog care and contacts for a bail bond company.
The sentencing memo said Kazmierczak had long struggled with alcohol abuse, had “a history of mental and emotional health concerns”, and also had a string of health issues tied to a 2022 diagnosis of Parkinson’s disease. His lawyer, John Fossum, had argued that Kazmierczak had not been taking his mental health medication before the attack, lowering his inhibitions and contributing to what happened.
“I’ve spent enough time in jail thinking,” Kazmierczak said Thursday. “I really apologise to her for having put her through that,” he said, referring to Omar.
Kazmierczak wrote to Omar after the attack, “I’m sorry if I scared you.”
In social media posts, Kazmierczak had denounced former President Joe Biden and referred to Democrats as “angry and liars”, writing that Trump wants the US to be “stronger and more prosperous”.
“This assault is yet another example of a dangerous national trend: people channeling political hatred into criminal acts,” said US Attorney Daniel N Rosen after Kazmierczak pled guilty in May.
Omar, a Somali-American refugee and naturalised US citizen, has faced sustained mocking and anti-immigrant rhetoric from Trump throughout her congressional tenure.

'A struggle every day': There's a hidden side to Australia's student visa debate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:41:10 UTC
04:41:10 KST

IN BRIEF
- The government says the changes will help cut net overseas migration to 245,000 this financial year.
- Students and migration experts have raised concerns about how some of the new restrictions could affect migrants.
For almost nine years, Bashshar Khalid has been building a life in Australia.
He arrived as an international student in 2017, completed a three-year bachelor's degree in business and then a two-year master's degree before entering the workforce.
But graduating was only the beginning.
Khalid first moved onto a temporary graduate visa, known as a subclass 485, and recently secured a subclass 482 work visa after finding employment in sales.
He told SBS News that making the transition from international student to skilled worker was far from straightforward.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
One of the biggest difficulties was convincing an employer to invest in someone whose ability to remain in Australia had an expiry date attached to it.
"We basically have to work twice as hard, or we just have to prove our skill set to our employers," he said.
At one point, Khalid's temporary graduate visa was approaching expiry while his employer-sponsored visa application was still being processed.
He moved onto a bridging visa while he waited for an outcome.
"Every day when you wake up, or every day you're going into the office to work, you're not sure whether the application will be approved or not ... It's basically a struggle every day."
Government's migration crackdown
Now, the federal government has announced another suite of changes aimed at tightening Australia's migration system and further reducing net overseas migration (NOM).
The changes include measures targeting so-called "visa hopping", restrictions on secondary applicants on most student visas and stronger measures to ensure people without valid visas leave Australia.
The government will also introduce a 'no further stay' condition on all visitor visas and crack down on migration agents it says knowingly support applications without merit.
Announcing the reforms on Thursday, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said the government was targeting people who would "never" meet the requirements for permanent residency but continued moving through the migration system to extend their stay.
"They effectively jump from visa to visa, use the appeals process to be able to stay here as long as possible until it eventually becomes absurd to not just let them stay," he said.
Critics say the crackdown could limit legitimate study and work opportunities.
Khalid said he believes there should be a clearer distinction between people switching courses simply to stay in the country, and migrants legitimately progressing through study and skilled employment.
"We have contributed to the economy. We have paid our taxes. We have done everything right by the book," he said.
"There couldn't be one single hard and fast rule about everything.
"If they could genuinely prove that the change of career is more of a personal choice and not just for a visa hopping case, then I think they should be given a fair chance."
Former immigration department deputy secretary Abul Rizvi also supports reducing visa hopping but cautioned against applying restrictions too broadly.
"As a general rule, I think reducing visa hopping is a good idea," he said.
"The question will be how broadly those measures are applied, because if they're applied too broadly, there will be unintended consequences."
Rizvi pointed to businesses that bring workers into Australia on business visas when they urgently need their skills while waiting for a skilled temporary visa to be processed.
If those transitions are restricted while skilled visa processing times remain lengthy, he said, businesses could face difficulties.
'It would have definitely affected my decision'
For Khalid, the uncertainty of Australia's migration system has already made planning a career difficult.
Khalid said policy changes could mean migrants made significant decisions based on one set of rules, only to find the pathway had shifted.
"If my pathway was not as clear ... it would have been a major decision for me whether I should stay on in the country or leave the country," he said.
Had the pathway been more restrictive when he was studying, Khalid said it "would have definitely affected" his decision.
His recently granted 482 visa now provides a potential pathway towards permanent residency.
"After spending a good amount of time in this country, you sort of feel like it's your second home," he said.
What will the changes mean for students with families?
The government's reforms also restrict secondary applicants on most student visas, potentially affecting students seeking to have family members join them in Australia.
Muath Alqarni, a Saudi master's degree student at the University of Melbourne, told SBS News that he understood the government wanted greater control over migration involving international students' families but was concerned about broad restrictions.
"I recognise there is an issue with international students' families' immigration, and I understand that the federal government is trying to control it," he said.
"However, as an international student who used to live with his family, my situation is different."
Alqarni urged the government to examine the data and circumstances of different groups rather than applying broad measures.
"It's a lifetime chance for me to bring my family to Australia and spend a good time with them in Australia," he said.
Rizvi also raised concerns about students undertaking lengthy courses who may be affected by restrictions on bringing partners to Australia.
"If you're doing a four-year nursing degree or a five-year engineering degree or a six-year medicine degree and you're married, to be without your partner for four or six years is really, really difficult," he said.
He argued Australia risked losing some prospective students to competing destinations if they could not bring their partners.
Will the changes bring migration down?
The government says the reforms are designed to help bring NOM down to 245,000 this financial year and 225,000 in 2027-28.
Rizvi believes those forecasts will probably be achieved if the changes are combined with the high student visa refusal rates he says have been in place since November 2025.
International students have played a significant role in recent movements in NOM, he said.
"The biggest increase in the big surge in net migration in 2023 was students, and the biggest reduction since then has been students," Rizvi said.
Burke said migration also needed to slow sufficiently for housing supply to "catch up", but rejected the suggestion migration itself was responsible for Australia's housing shortage.
"The housing shortage we have is not caused by immigration," he said.
"But immigration needs to be part of the solution for the housing crisis."

Prime Minister Donald Tusk outlined in the Sejm the "most likely" scenario for the months ahead, warning of serious events and hybrid attacks on Poland and other Ukraine backers.

According to the prime minister, Russia's aim is to destroy Ukraine's economy and logistics on as large a scale as possible. "For now, Ukraine's," he added pointedly.
Six main Ukrainian cities in Russia's sights
The Polish prime minister said constant strikes of very high frequency and intensity are expected on six key Ukrainian cities, along with the destruction of stockpiles of supplies essential for the country's defence and of railway infrastructure. Tusk recalled that in the past several weeks Russians have destroyed more than 300 Ukrainian railway locomotives.
The head of government said that "in the assessment of intelligence services, Russia's plans also include hybrid strikes with drones and missiles on states supporting Ukraine, including Poland". Such possibilities have been mentioned for some time, but now, Tusk stressed, the information is already "highly consistent and, unfortunately, persuasive".
In the prime minister's view, potential strikes will be "so-called 'accidental'", aimed at paralysing or weakening NATO members' motivation to invoke alliance provisions in the event of aggression.
"There is a real risk that the territory of one or several NATO countries on the eastern flank may be entered by drones or other types of missiles, which may even cause destruction. And the official narrative will be that this is an accident and that there is no reason for anyone to contemplate any response from NATO," he said.
Russia's objective, he said, is "to weaken NATO's overall cohesion and, above all, to convince NATO countries that Article 5 is more theoretical than practical". Such "accidental" strikes may be repeated.
Tusk: on security, we must speak with one voice
Continuing, the prime minister said that Russia's new strategy also envisages possible political changes in some European countries. He recalled the forthcoming elections and the presence of forces that can be described as an openly pro-Russian option. He appealed to politicians, regardless of party colours – addressing in particular MPs from the Confederation party – "under no circumstances to take part, whether inadvertently or deliberately, in promoting narratives that Russia cares deeply about".
"Whipping up hostility towards the European Union, towards our allies, towards Ukrainians, is directly implementing Russia's strategy. Everyone must finally understand this," he underlined.
In closing, Tusk called on everyone present in the Sejm chamber to "speak with one voice, take joint decisions, hesitate no longer and show that, regardless of political views, we are all patriots in a moment of trial" when it comes to the security of borders, Polish airspace and people's homes. He pointed out that some politicians in Europe "are just waiting for an alibi" so that, in the event of conflict, they can argue: "We will not die for Poland, we will not perish for Latvia or Lithuania".
"Article 5, allied loyalty, fidelity to commitments must become our hallmark," he declared. He added that Poland wants and needs certainty that, in the event of a more serious threat from Russia, it can "count on a swift and effective response from the entire bloc".

Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev has said that activities with neighbouring Türkiye further strengthen stability in their region and beyond.
Aliyev said at a meeting on Thursday with security officials of Organization of Turkic States (OTS) member states in the Azerbaijani capital that relations between his country and Türkiye “occupy a special place and play a special role.”
Expressing that there are “no similar relations anywhere in the world,” Aliyev was quoted by the presidency as saying it is impossible to find a “second pair of countries so closely bound to each other,” with a multitude of factors converging such as historical ties, cultural connections and people-to-people relations.
“That is to say, Türkiye-Azerbaijan relations today constitute a vital factor in our region and the wider world, as a unified space. Our joint activities further strengthen stability in our region and beyond, especially in the current difficult geopolitical situation,” he said.
Aliyev described the Shusha Declaration signed with Ankara in 2021 as representing the “peak of our relations,” saying that while they were allies prior to the signing, the declaration formalised their alliance.
“More than five years have passed since that day, and with every passing year and month, our unity grows stronger and our role in the world is further reinforced,” said Aliyev.
Relations between Baku and Ankara were elevated to the level of an alliance with the Shusha Declaration, which Aliyev signed with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan during a two-day visit to the South Caucasus nation by Erdogan.
The OTS was established in 2009 and adopted its current name at the Istanbul Summit in 2021. Türkiye, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan are members, while Turkmenistan, Hungary and the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus hold observer status.
OTS Aliyev said that the overall sentiment among leaders of OTS member states is aimed at bolstering the role and position of the organisation on the international stage.
He said the potential of their countries is quite substantial and continues to grow, noting they are situated across a vast geographical expanse where crucial energy and transport routes and corridors pass through.
"To the west and east of the OTS region, our organisation is being closely watched with great interest as it strengthens its positive role in international affairs, including in matters related to connectivity, transport security, energy security, and security in general," said Aliyev.
“Therefore, I am confident that these issues will also be discussed at today’s council meeting, because today, without energy security and transport connectivity, it is virtually impossible to speak about overall security.”
He also described the stability, peace and security prevailing in their countries as a key factor in the successful development of the OTS, arguing that it is an important factor for development in today’s political and foreign policy realities.
"It is well known that no country can develop without stability and security. Neither investment, technology nor innovation will come to a country if there is no stability or political and economic security there. Therefore, today this is also a key factor that distinguishes our countries from many of the surrounding regions where we are located," he said.
Aliyev also said OTS countries are demonstrating strong economic growth, particularly at a time when they see opposite trends occurring in various parts of the globe.

See the first new species of cat discovered in more than a century—it’s adorable
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:34:46 UTC
04:34:46 KST

Deep in the Bolivian Yungas cloud forests, there stalks an utterly adorable beast: smaller than a house cat and spotted like a leopard, the creature has long been known to local communities as a tilcayo. Scientists, however, have only just formally discovered it—marking the first new wildcat species to be identified in more than a century.
The new species, Leopardus tilcayo, is a type of tiger cat, a group of small felines in the genus Leopardus that are native to South America. In a paper published on Thursday in Current Biology, the researchers identify five distinct species of tiger cats in South America, including the tilcayo.
The discovery came by accident, said the study’s co-lead author Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz to NBC News. A man had brought one of the kitties into the sanctuary that she volunteered at, and she noticed that it didn’t quite match any existing tiger cat species. After a series of genetic tests, she and her team discovered the cat must be a new species that had likely diverged from its closest tiger cat relative some 1.4 million years ago.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The discovery of a new mammal, especially a cat, is rare. It’s even more rare to find an entirely new species rather than a variation of a known species. The study analyzed the genomes of 38 cats, including 26 Leopardus cats, comprising “the most complete genetic study yet,” said the study’s co-lead author Jonas Lescroart, an evolutionary ecologist at the University of Antwerp in Belgium, to Gizmodo.
It’s unclear how many tilcayos are out there, and the authors have said that the study should be a catalyst for intensified conservation efforts across tiger cat species.
“Describing a new cat species after more than 100 years shows how much we still have to learn about the biodiversity around us. But it also reminds us that we need to protect the Yungas forests, which are home to so many species—including some we are only beginning to understand,” Nogales-Ascarrunz said in a statement.

The world is just enough: Ursula von der Leyen goes Bond villain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:32:02 UTC
04:32:02 KST

The world is just enough: Ursula von der Leyen goes Bond villain
As a historian who also happens to be German, that was my spontaneous reaction to Ursula von der Leyen’s annual grand – and always grandiloquent – “state of the union” address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg.
It’s not really a “union,” of course, and not really a “parliament,” either: technically, the EU is a confederation messed up by the ideological construct of “supranationalism”; and the parliament has no independent legislative power, but let’s not dwell on the obvious.
At the head of her Commission (read: over-reaching Central Committee) of career bureaucrats, von der Leyen is the unelected de-facto leader and personification of the Frankenstein wanna-be-super-state that has long gobbled up idealistic dreams of European unity.
Once, those dreams may have been about democracy, sovereign equality, prosperity for all, and peace. But real-existing EU-Europe is very different: the European dream has come true as a nightmare, dominated by a smug and self-empowered globalist establishment, thoroughly insulated from popular participation, economically stagnant and crisis-prone, as well as unequal, and ever more militarist.
When von der Leyen boasted that, in effect during her tenure, EU-Europe had become “stronger” and “more independent,” while “securing its prosperity” and increasing armament spending “by 80% in the last five years alone,” only the last point bore any resemblance to reality, as the preponderant majority of the over 450 million EU citizens – really subjects – experience it.
But there is no misery a Eurocrat worth her (or his!) salt cannot make worse. Now von der Leyen seems hellbent to take the worst of bad old German traditions to a whole new, all-EU level. As is well-known from the history of the last two world wars, Germany not once but twice first deftly maneuvered itself into being surrounded by (mostly) enemies and then lost, the first time crushingly, the second one even worse, in fact so badly it took a short half-century (and much Russian good will, as it happens) to put the country together again.
The Kaiser’s Germany and the Fuhrer’s were – to be fair even to the Kaiser – quite different, but what their establishments had in common was a bad case of Germanophrenia, a relative of the contemporary Russophrenia syndrome: The core delusion of Russophrenia, as it is now ravaging Western minds, is to hallucinate Russia as on the verge of collapse and of conquering the world at the same time. Those afflicted by Germanophrenia believed Germany was in existential danger but also capable of taking on Europe at least and, if need be, the world, too.
Enter the all-EU version, compliments of the very, very German von der Leyen. Quoting Charles Dickens’ already much overused “it was the best of times, it was the worst of times” line in her impeccably Germanic version of English, von der Leyen proceeded to do two things: assert that the EU is at peak strength and, at the same time, as precarious as ever. Clearly aware that sane listeners would find that combination of claims extremely counter-intuitive, she insisted that even if they “may seem incompatible,” they are still both true. Orwell for beginners really: two plus two is five, if Big Sister from the Commission says so.
Inducing debilitating cognitive dissonance, though, is the least of von der Leyen’s powers. The real payload of her rambling speech was her combative declaration of if not war then defiance against, in essence, almost everyone who matters on planet Earth.
In true paranoid fashion, von der Leyen first declared that the EU faced a “hostile world,” no less. Then, she got more specific: Russia – surprise, surprise – led her enemy list; and she congratulated, in effect, herself for ridding the EU of a “toxic” dependence on its fossil fuels. What a way to describe cutting yourself off from a reliable and comparatively inexpensive energy source to shift to exorbitant prices and uncertain delivery from, for instance, the unpredictable US and the war-torn and blockade-prone Middle East!
She had tough words and warnings for China as well. Those clearly must be seen in the context of ongoing EU attempts to play trade hardball with Beijing. Desperate to make up for the badly declining competitiveness of European industry and currently especially carmakers, the old continent – once happily exploiting the rest of the world for its own gain – has discovered what von der Leyen and her officials think of as fairness.
But throwing down the gauntlet to China and Russia – the core of the emerging multipolar order – was not enough for von der Leyen in attack-mode. Surprisingly, the same woman who almost literally kissed Donald Trump’s feet at Turnberry, delivering a full, unconditional trade war capitulation – so much, by the way, for her claim that the EU is “the greatest trading power on the planet” – loaded her speech with barely concealed challenges to the US. That is, the much diminished but still regrettably powerful center of the old West, as well as the state on which the EU is, of course, toxically dependent in reality.
The single most aggressive of von der Leyen’s sallies against Washington was her bizarre call for giving Canada “associate membership,” a status that does not even exist under the EU treaties, would need the very unlikely agreement of all 27 member governments, and makes no sense geographically or geopolitically.
But while unrealistic, the idea does have the capacity to make Washington very angry indeed. President Donald Trump has already warned that he considers the idea a “hostile act” and is ready to escalate his economic warfare against the EU. Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney, who was in Strasbourg for von der Leyen’s strange offer, has already switched into damage-control mode.
But then again, von der Leyen’s real motive in suggesting a Canadian-EU play that cannot be but against US interests may be something else entirely. In true von der Leyen spirit, the EU has recently made much noise about claiming interests and, quite simply, a say, in the Arctic. That makes fairly little sense except you count Greenland as “Danish,” which it is formally but hardly in reality. Not to speak of the well-known US ambitions to take it over in one way or the other. Some creative minds may have discovered that adding Canada’s northern coastlines would help make Arctic ambitions more plausible.
And that in turn may very well also explain the speed and ferocity of the US response. In other words, the challenge to Washington may be even worse than “merely” offering Canada a counterweight against traditional and entrenched US hegemony. If the Arctic is the real target, the stakes could not be higher. Way to go, Ursula: your EU against everyone at once. Some of your German ancestors would have been so proud.

Russia ‘sabotaging’ power supply lines at Zaporizhzhia plant: Greenpeace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:30:12 UTC
04:30:12 KST

Russia ‘sabotaging’ power supply lines at Zaporizhzhia plant: Greenpeace
Investigation finds no evidence of Russia’s claims that Ukrainian attacks hit the nuclear power plant.
Russia is sabotaging the Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant in occupied southeastern Ukraine and blaming it on Kyiv to “confuse and distract” from the threats posed by its “illegal occupation and war”, Greenpeace has warned.
In a report published on Thursday, the environmental group concluded that Moscow is “deliberately sabotaging” the plant’s electricity supply while engaging in a “disinformation campaign” about the attacks.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3India warns new US tariffs over Russian oil could impact ties
- list 2 of 3At least 19 injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine
- list 3 of 3US tariffs against Russian oil buyers pass: What it means for China, India
Greenpeace Ukraine and London-based McKenzie Intelligence Services (MIS) analysed satellite imagery of the site and found no evidence of Russian claims that Ukrainian attacks had occurred.
“The satellite imagery and evidence is clear – Ukraine did not attack its own Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant electricity system,” said Shaun Burnie, a nuclear specialist at Greenpeace Ukraine. “This is part of a massive disinformation campaign, enacted by Moscow to confuse and distract from the real safety threats caused only by their illegal occupation and war.”
“The repeated loss of external power at [the plant] is the result of Russian military attacks on Ukraine’s electricity grid and sabotage operations at [the plant] and associated switchyards,” he said.
MIS analysed several satellite images of the 330 kV Ferosplavna-1 power line near the Zaporizhzhia plant provided by Airbus’s defence and space division. The images were taken between October 2025 and June 2026 and analysed to assess whether damage at the site was caused by Ukrainian artillery fire on February 10 and a Ukrainian drone strike on June 4, as Moscow alleged.
MIS concluded that the damage to the power line was inconsistent with artillery fire or drone strikes.
It added that artillery fire would usually leave a pattern of impact craters and dispersed damage across the targeted area, which was not visible.
MIS also found that the damage allegedly caused by a Ukrainian drone strike on June 4 was already visible before the supposed attack.
According to the United Nation’s nuclear watchdog, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), Ferosplavna-1 is Zaporizhzhia’s only remaining external power line. Last month, the IAEA stressed the importance of a stable electricity supply at the plant to ensure nuclear safety.
Greenpeace echoed that warning on Thursday, saying that a stable electricity supply is crucial to “operate essential reactor safety systems, including pumps that provide cooling for nuclear fuel in reactor cores and spent fuel pools”.

Nato head: Britain must show ‘credible path’ of annual defence budget increases
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:29:44 UTC
04:29:44 KST

Britain needs to show “a credible path” of annual increases in its defence budgets to meet a Nato target of spending nearly £30bn more on the military by the middle of the next decade, the head of the alliance said on Thursday.
Mark Rutte, Nato’s secretary general, said that Britain could not wait until just before 2035 to lift defence spending to 3.5% of GDP, in an unusually pointed intervention a day after he met prime minister Andy Burnham.
In an interview with the Press Association, he said: “And that is why you need a credible path towards that 3.5%, and yearly increments.”
The alliance’s secretary general, a former Dutch prime minister, made similar remarks to the BBC, where he said that the UK understood that the target could not be met “in one go in 2034” and that it would have to be achieved gradually.
Earlier on Thursday, Rutte met with Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, and Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary. He saw Burnham on Wednesday, at a business park in Didcot, and also met representatives from the defence industry.
Keir Starmer signed the UK up to a Nato-wide target of increasing defence spending to 3.5% of GDP in the summer of 2025, under pressure from the US president, Donald Trump. The figure has since been endorsed by Burnham and his chancellor, former defence secretary John Healey.
Current spending plans, covering until 2028/9, show defence spending levelling off at 2.7%, nearly £30bn below the ultimate target, raising the question of how it would be achieved after the next general election. It is unclear if taxes or borrowing would have to rise, or other government spending cuts.
Healey resigned as defence minister in June because Starmer would not commit to lifting defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030. At the time Healey said Labour needed to set “a clear path” to meet the Nato commitment, similar language to that used by Rutte in his interviews.
But since then Healey and Burnham have avoided committing to the 3% by the end of the decade. Decisions on future spending are likely to be left to the next government spending review due next year, prompting the Nato leader to engage in public lobbying on his trip to Britain.
Rutte said he was certain the Burnham government remained behind the ultimate goal and the need to increase defence spending gradually. “I am absolutely confident that when it comes to the yearly increments, they totally take it and accept it, that they have to be there,” he told the BBC.
“There has to be a credible path. What that credible path exactly will be, we will see with the spending review next year,” Rutte added.
A day earlier, Rutte gave a speech to at Ditchley Park in Oxfordshire, in which he warned that the 32 country military alliance faced “the most dangerous and complex security environment in a generation” with wars in Ukraine, the Middle East coming at time of rising state competition.
Nato needed “more UK and more Europe”, he added, to take up the slack as the US reduces its military commitment to the alliance. Trump has long argued that the UK and Europe should match US levels of defence spending and take the lead in defending the continent from Russia aggression.

Istanbul Airport named world's most connected aviation hub
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:29:29 UTC
04:29:29 KST

Istanbul Airport in Türkiye has been named the world’s most connected aviation hub, overtaking London Heathrow, according to global travel intelligence company OAG’s Megahubs 2026 report published on Wednesday.
Istanbul Airport climbed from second place in 2025 to the top of the global ranking for the first time, with connections to 337 destinations worldwide.
Turkish Airlines operated 80 percent of flights at the airport, according to the report.
London Heathrow dropped to second place after potential connections on its busiest day fell 6 percent year-on-year, partly due to ongoing disruptions to Middle East schedules.
Amsterdam Schiphol ranked third after recording growth in both connections and the number of destinations it served.
Kuala Lumpur retained fourth place and remained the most connected airport in Asia, with the number of destinations it served rising to 154.
Chicago O’Hare climbed from seventh place in 2025 to fifth globally and remained the most connected airport in the Americas.
Asia Pacific dominates
Airports in the Asia Pacific region accounted for eight of the global top 20, the largest share of any region.
Chinese airports made notable gains, with Shanghai Pudong rising from 19th to 14th and Baiyun International climbing from 36th to 19th. Hong Kong also returned to the top 20, moving from 22nd to 20th.
Kuala Lumpur ranked first in OAG’s Low-Cost Carrier Megahubs Index, with nearly 15,000 possible low-cost connections.
The Asia Pacific region accounted for 64 percent of the top 25 low-cost airport hubs, while low-cost carriers represented 51 percent of all seats across Southeast Asia, compared with a global average of 34 percent.

"Great news! Thanks to the bold leadership of my friend, Karol Nawrocki, President of Poland, major progress is being made toward establishing a US Army base in Poland.
"If this happens, the location will be announced very soon. This will be a historic step for our great US-Polish Alliance," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.

Trump's announcement comes despite his administration launching a formal review of its military presence in Europe, raising fears among allies that it could cut back its forces in European nations.
But Poland, which borders both Ukraine and Russia on NATO's eastern flank and spends around five percent of its GDP on defence, is working to strengthen the US presence on its soil.
Political will
Polish deputy defence minister Pawel Zalewski said in August that his country was discussing with the United States whether to set up a permanent US base on its territory.
"We have already completed the initial stage (of the process), not to mention the political will, which was expressed long ago," Zalewski told public broadcaster TVP.
Almost 10,000 US soldiers are currently stationed in Poland, but almost exclusively on a rotational basis.
Washington has levied heavy criticism against several European countries that refused to allow US forces to use NATO bases on their territory in their war with Iran.
Hegseth had also threatened to reduce his country's contribution to the alliance's budget if certain states refused to honour the commitments made last year at the NATO summit in The Hague.
At that summit, NATO allies pledged to devote by 2035 at least five percent of their GDP to security spending, including 3.5 percent devoted strictly to military expenditures.

Militants kill 15 in overnight Cameroon raid, village sources say
YAOUNDE, Sept 17 - Suspected Islamist militants killed at least 15 people in a pre-dawn attack on a village in northern Cameroon, a local vigilante and an administrative authority said on Thursday, in the latest violence to hit the area plagued by a long-running insurgency.
• Armed insurgents entered the village of Madegoua, near the town of Makary, at around 2 a.m. (0100 GMT) on Thursday, pulling out men and tying them up before executing them, said the local vigilante member, who requested anonymity to discuss the incident for security reasons.
• The initial death toll had been 13 though two other victims later died from injuries at a Makary hospital, according to the vigilante.
• The victims initially confirmed dead were buried on Thursday, according to a video seen by Reuters, which was not immediately able to independently verify it.
• No group immediately claimed responsibility for the attack. A security analyst told Reuters it was likely carried out by Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) militants who are active in the area.
• Some villagers said they suspected the assault may have been enforcement of an earlier order from militants for them to vacate, given it sits on a strategic route towards Makary.
• Cameroon's Far North, which borders Nigeria and Chad, has for years been affected by violence involving Boko Haram and other Islamist militants operating in the Lake Chad basin.
• Cameroon is part of a regional multinational military force fighting Islamist militants around Lake Chad. REUTERS

US to allow Iranian leaders to attend UN General Assembly
UNITED NATIONS - The Trump administration will allow top Iranian officials to attend the United Nations General Assembly in New York next week, the State Department said on Sept 17, even as Washington and Tehran remain at war and continue intermittent talks aimed at ending the conflict.
A State Department spokesperson said a “core delegation from the Iranian regime” would be allowed to attend the meeting in line with the United States’ obligations as the world body’s host country.
That means officials including Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi will be granted visas, according to a source familiar with the decision.
President Donald Trump’s administration has held on-again, off-again talks with Iran’s leaders aimed at ending the war that began on Feb 28 when the US and Israel attacked Iran.
Tehran responded with strikes on Israel and Gulf states that host US bases.
“The delegation will be under travel restrictions and will face prohibitions on the purchase of luxury and other goods per our policy. The delegation is smaller than last year,” the State Department spokesperson added.
In the past, the US government has barred Iran’s delegation from shops and restricted its movements to travel between the United Nations headquarters, the Iranian UN mission and UN ambassador’s residence and New York’s John F. Kennedy Airport.
Iran’s Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to Reuters’ request for comment.
Under the 1947 UN “headquarters agreement,” the United States is generally required to allow access to the United Nations for foreign diplomats. But Washington says it can deny visas for “security, terrorism and foreign policy” reasons.
The Trump administration on Sept 16 said it would deny entry to Palestinian officials for the UN meeting, extending a ban in place since 2025, over actions they took to “internationalise the Israeli-Palestinian conflict,” including pursuing cases against Israel at international tribunals.
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas was denied a visa as part of the US move, a Palestinian official said. REUTERS

Russian birth tourism to Brazil increases
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:19:00 UTC
04:19:00 KST

Russian birth tourism to Brazil increases
September 17, 2026
Yulia and Dmitri (whose names have been changed for reasons of safety) flew from Russia to Brazil this summer so that their child could be born there. Yulia was 32 weeks pregnant at the time of travel.
"Of course, we didn't say that I was pregnant at border control," Yulia told DW.
Her daughter was born at a private clinic in Santos, a city in southern Brazil. Anybody born in the country has an automatic right to Brazilian nationality. The family is currently preparing all the paperwork.
"We've achieved our minimum goal," said Dmitri. "With a Brazilian passport, our daughter will be able to travel without a visa to almost any country in the world. She won't have to apply for an expensive and time-consuming Schengen visa. We want her to be able to decide for herself where she studies, works or lives."
He said that a colleague of his had traveled to Brazil in early August with his pregnant wife for the same reasons.
Yulia and Dmitri said that they had spent the equivalent of about €10,000 (about $11,500) during the first six weeks of their stay in Brazil, which included the costs for several days of treatment for their daughter in intensive care. Dmitri quit his job at a bank for the trip and hopes to find work again after the family returns to their home in the Russian capital Moscow.
However, they are only planning to return once all the documents for their daughter are ready and that could take months. Other Russian families have decided to stay in Brazil permanently.
According to organizations and lawyers that provide support to Russians in Brazil, there has been an increase in immigration from Russia, particularly since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, after which visa requirements for Russian nationals entering certain countries were tightened.
Argentina tightens visa regulations
Birth tourism to Brazil has also increased since Argentina, which used to be one of the main destinations for people wanting their children to be born in a country that automatically grants citizenship to newborns, tightened its regulations. People who want their children to obtain Argentinian citizenship now have to have resided in Argentina for at least two years. Since 2025, the access of people who do not have a permanent residence permit to free healthcare has also been restricted.
According to the Russian news outlet RBC, more than 7,000 Russians applied for a residence permit in Argentina in 2023. By mid-2025, the number had decreased to about 1,800.
Meanwhile, almost 500 Brazilian passports were issued to Russians in 2024 and more than 600 the following year. More than half of the new citizens were women.
The parents of a child born in Brazil can apply for a residence permit, which they can obtain within a year, under certain circumstances.
Yana (name changed) and her husband chose to do this in 2023.
"The events of 2022 certainly played a role, but we had already toyed with the idea of giving birth abroad," Yana told DW. "A lot can happen in Russia. I always wanted a second passport and to give birth to my child in another country. When I became pregnant unexpectedly, all we had to do was decide which country made sense."
Yana gave birth to a boy at a public hospital in Florianopolis, the capital of the southern state of Santa Catarina, and the family stayed in Brazil for about three years.
"It was important to get passports for us and our child. I really enjoyed living there, and I learned Portuguese," Yana said, adding that she and her husband have lived as "digital nomads" in various countries over the years.
Even though they no longer live in Brazil, they want their son to have a connection to his birth country: "We read Portuguese books and talk a lot about Brazil. I want him to be able to travel without a visa and remain open to the world."
Big Russian community in Florianopolis
One of the largest Russian communities in Brazil lives in Florianopolis, and it's growing. According to the local health authorities, 119 Russian women took advantage of prenatal consultations in the first six months of this year. In all of 2025, it was 136 Russian women.
A lawyer who preferred to remain anonymous told DW that Brazil neither expressly prohibited nor permitted foreign nationals to enter the country for the purpose of giving birth. Often pregnant women do not disclose their reason for traveling to Brazil at border control. And once they are in the country they have access to free public hospitals and medical facilities regardless of their immigration status.
As Russian birth tourism to Brazil increases, a whole industry has emerged. Often, recent Russian immigrants to Brazil act as intermediaries and help others find housing or medical care. They provide assistance with complicated administrative procedures or the language. Depending on the level of care, the cost can reach into the thousands of dollars.
However, providers of such services, lawyers, and volunteers report stricter controls by Brazilian authorities, particularly in cities with larger Russian communities, such as Florianopolis. They say authorities are requesting more documents than in the past.
"The police are conducting more thorough checks to verify whether people actually live at the addresses they provide," one lawyer said, explaining that in the past, false addresses had been given by people hoping to obtain residence permits more quickly.
No evidence of Brazil systematically denying entry to Russians
But DW did not find any evidence to suggest that Russians were being denied entry to Brazil en masse.
In late July, the Russian Telegram channel Baza reported that 10 pregnant women had been "deported" from Russia. The information was later picked up by various media outlets. However, the Brazilian police denied the veracity of the report to DW, explaining that decisions to deny somebody entry to the country were always made on a case-by-case basis, and that pregnancy played no role in the process.
DW was only able to find one documented case of a pregnant Russian woman being initially refused entry into Brazil. She was allowed to enter the country after a lawyer intervened. According to the court records, the Brazilian border authorities had doubts as to how the Russian national would be financing her stay in Brazil.
The woman did not respond to the DW's inquiries.
This article was originally written in Russian.

Italy to safeguard its ships in Bab al-Mandeb as concerns mount
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:18:00 UTC
04:18:00 KST

Italy announced Thursday it would deploy warships to ensure the safe passage of its commercial ships through the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, as maritime security concerns mount off the coast of Yemen.
The country does not intend to wait for a joint decision by the European Union, Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto said. "We have the capabilities to protect the passage."
Crosetto warned that if the waterway were to become impassable, this would have significant consequences for the economy and consumers.
"We cannot allow bureaucratic delays in decision-making to aggravate an already complex situation," he noted.
Crosetto said he and Italy's chief of defense staff had agreed to mobilize the navy to prepare "whatever is necessary" to guarantee the secure transit of Italian vessels.
The Bab al-Mandeb connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden, one of the most important shipping routes between Europe and Asia.
Fears for shipping in the Red Sea have surged this month after the Iran-aligned Houthis brought the entire west coast of Yemen under their control and captured strategically located islands.
This has given the Houthis virtually unrestricted access to the strait, a development seen as a significant setback for Saudi oil exports rerouted from the Strait of Hormuz and international shipping.
The United States and the European Union have already been attempting to better protect merchant ships from attacks by the rebels through military operations.
Crosetto did not spell out what measures were being considered or what naval assets might be sent to the area.
He said that disruptions to major shipping lanes would drive up transport costs, delay deliveries and ultimately push higher prices onto families and businesses.
"Every economic crisis hits the most vulnerable people hardest, putting social cohesion and the country's stability at risk," he said.
The defense minister also highlighted the vulnerability of undersea infrastructure, including data cables and energy links.
"For a major maritime nation such as Italy, monitoring and protecting the seas, both above and below the surface, means safeguarding its security, its prosperity and its future," he said.
"The Defense Ministry and the Italian Navy will continue to protect the sea, intervening with determination whenever necessary to safeguard national interests and the security of Italians," he said.

Six Convicted, €300M Confiscation Ordered in Mafia-Linked EU Tax Fraud
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:16:00 UTC
04:16:00 KST

A Milan court has sentenced six individuals to prison and ordered the confiscation of more than 300 million euros ($344.66 million) for their roles in a transnational tax fraud and money laundering syndicate tied to the Italian mafia, the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) announced on Thursday.
The convictions mark the latest judicial actions in "Operation Moby Dick," a massive EPPO investigation into a VAT carousel fraud scheme. Between 2020 and 2023, the network issued over 1.3 billion euros ($1.49 billion) in fake invoices for AirPods, laptops, and other electronics, resulting in 520 million euros ($597.35 million) in losses to EU and national budgets.
The Milan judge confirmed aggravated circumstances for the criminal syndicate’s aiding and abetting of a mafia association. According to the EPPO, one of the convicted defendants received illicit funds from a Camorra clan—which investigators previously linked to the Nuvoletta and Di Lauro groups—and funneled the money into the scheme to launder the mafia's proceeds.
“These verdicts confirm what the EPPO has been warning about for years: mafia organizations are investing in VAT fraud as a vehicle to launder their criminal proceeds,” European Chief Prosecutor Laura Kövesi said in a statement.
The six defendants, who opted for an abbreviated trial procedure to receive a one-third reduction in their sentences, were handed prison terms ranging from four years to seven years and two months. The judge also barred several defendants from holding public office or operating commercial enterprises, and ordered the seizure of real estate, company shares, and over 300 million euros ($344.66 million) in illicit profits.
Among those convicted was a ringleader of the syndicate who evaded arrest in Prague in November 2024 and remained a fugitive for six months before surrendering in May 2025.
The judge accepted the prosecution's reconstruction of a complex, federated network of "missing traders," brokers, and conduit companies operating across numerous European and third countries.
The overall proceedings in the Moby Dick investigation involve more than 400 individuals and legal entities as suspects. Authorities noted that some individuals hit with earlier seizure orders have already settled their debts with tax authorities.
The EPPO noted that the rulings were issued at first instance and remain subject to appeal.

Customer Data Permanently Lost in Iran Strikes on Amazon Data Centers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:15:00 UTC
04:15:00 KST

Half a year after Iranian drone strikes knocked out multiple Amazon data centers, the US tech company has acknowledged the permanent loss of some customer data that was hosted in Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates.
Amazon Web Services was “unable to restore access to the resources and data” hosted in some of the war-damaged data centers, according to an AWS dashboard update posted on September 15. The development was first reported by Reuters and suggests that the Iranian strikes inflicted catastrophic damage on the data centers.
Customer data was irretrievably lost in one of three AWS availability zones in the United Arab Emirates region, specifically the mec1-az2 availability zone. Each availability zone is serviced by one or more Amazon data centers.
The company is still working on “recovering regional resources” and restoring resources hosted in the other two availability zones in the United Arab Emirates. The AWS update described ongoing work to replace “affected infrastructure” and promised to update customers on a restoration of services in the coming months.
But the destruction was apparently even more widespread for the data centers in the Bahrain region, because Amazon said it was unable to restore access to resources and data across all three availability zones there.
“The damage to our infrastructure spanned multiple availability zones and exceeded what our regional and multi-AZ services are designed to withstand,” the AWS update said.
The company had already suspended customer billing in the affected AWS regions in Bahrain and the UAE and has spent the past six months attempting to restore normal operations.
The Iranian drones first struck the Amazon data centers on March 1 in the opening days of the ongoing war that began with US-Israeli attacks on Iran on February 28.
AWS immediately urged customers to migrate resources to other cloud regions and use remote backups to restore any “inaccessible resources.” The cloud service also reportedly issued $150 million in customer credits following the initial Iranian strikes in March.
A follow-up Iranian strike focused on Amazon’s data centers in Bahrain on April 1. The latest AWS update acknowledged this “disruption” of a second availability zone in the Bahrain region in April but described most affected customers as having already followed the company’s recommendations to migrate their cloud computing workloads elsewhere.
On July 24, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps launched yet another strike using missiles that specifically targeted a remaining Amazon data center structure in Bahrain. That damage was independently confirmed by satellite imagery.
“We remain committed to supporting our customers in Bahrain in the long term and will share a further update in early 2027,” the latest AWS update said.
Meanwhile, the US-Israeli war with Iran has since spiraled into a broader regional conflict and growing global energy crisis because of attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait. One of the few silver linings has been the surging interest worldwide in renewable power generation, such as solar rooftop panels.

“What Ukraine needs right now”: Poland to provide Ukraine with scarce F-16 missiles to shoot down jet-powered drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:11:13 UTC
04:11:13 KST

Poland will provide another aid package to Ukraine, which will include, among other things, “what Ukraine needs right now,” Deputy Minister of National Defense Stanisław Wziątek said, reports Polskie Radio. He said the package would include missiles for F-16 fighter jets, which the Ukrainian military uses to shoot down Russian drones.
Ukraine is critically short of missiles for F-16 fighter jets, which shoot down Russian UAVs. Recently, it was reported that pilots sometimes took off without missiles, using only the aircraft’s built-in M61A1 Vulcan cannon, which is dangerous for civilians. Poland’s newly promised aid will include these missiles for Ukraine.
Among other things, Poland will provide aviation equipment, the report said. Media reports added that the aid package may be worth around €50 million.
Ammunition for F-16s and possible aviation equipment
“Our aid is in the process of being prepared. Everything will happen in a moment. I cannot say what it contains, I can only say that it is what Ukraine needs right now. This includes basic ammunition. These are the ones mounted on F-16s to shoot down Russian drones,” Wziątek said.
AIM-9 and AIM-120 are air-to-air missiles that the Ukrainian Armed Forces use with F-16s to fight Russian aviation, Militarnyi says. The outlet adds that last year Ukrainian F-16s were spotted with APKWS II missiles, which are effective against drones. As for the aforementioned aviation equipment, Poland may provide decommissioned MiG-29 fighter jets or drones, the media outlet suggests.
The MiG-29 does not use the same scarce stocks of AIM-9 and AIM-120 missiles.
Missile shortage is not new
In July 2025, America abruptly suspended arms supplies to Ukraine, affecting some types of weapons. Among them were more than 90 US-made AIM air-to-air missiles that were in Poland and on their way to Ukraine, but were withdrawn by the US, according to a Wall Street Journal article. Since then, Ukraine has received Western aid for air defense systems, but missiles have remained among the items in short supply.
Ukraine faced a severe shortage of F-16 missiles from late November to mid-December, according to Reuters. One source said Ukraine had "nothing to put on its jets for almost a month."
While F-16s likely rank first by number in the Ukrainian Armed Forces, the Soviet-made MiG-29 ranks second, Euromaidan Press. Ukraine had enough R-73 missiles for this fighter, but when the Ukrainian Armed Forces also began using them for ground-based launchers after 9M33 missiles for Soviet Osa air defense systems ran out, the rate of consumption increased sharply.
Ukrainian forces were observed resuming the use of older missiles that had been considered obsolete. There is an alternative: using the fighter’s cannon. However, this practice is dangerous.

‘I don’t work for Netanyahu': Ofer Winter tries to be Israel's next kingmaker - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:08:44 UTC
04:08:44 KST

The demand for political renewal after the October 7 massacre was central to Ofer Winter’s election pitch: Give new people enough power, and they could change Israel’s Right, even under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Hamas’s massacre prompted expectations that a new generation of leaders would emerge, yet familiar figures continued to dominate. Former ministers Yoaz Hendel and Chili Tropper formed a joint party, then split. Tropper joined former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar slate.
Brig.-Gen. (res.) Winter, who had never served in the Knesset, offered another route. His Amcha Yisrael, or People of Israel, party made recruiting parliamentary newcomers part of its appeal, including immigrants, advocates for Israel abroad, and people whose families had been affected by the war.
Israelis vote for party lists. Governments normally depend on alliances commanding at least 61 of the Knesset’s 120 seats, allowing a small party whose support is essential to bargain for ministries and policy changes. Winter wants the Defense Ministry. First, he has to win enough votes to enter the Knesset.
He spoke with The Jerusalem Post from his temporary office in an old Jerusalem building, where he hosted activities for different parts of Israeli society. On the stairs, people approached him one by one: a haredi (ultra-Orthodox) man, a settler, a man without a kippah, and others.
Each person who approached expressed support for Winter
They expressed support. One asked why he had not joined forces with a small new haredi party advocating military conscription. Winter stopped for everyone, shaking hands, hugging people, and answering questions. His directness appeared to resonate.
“I don’t work for Netanyahu,” he said. “I don’t work for anyone.”
His candidates had other options, he said. “If we had been looking for a seat, we could have found a seat,” he added, meaning he was offered seats on different slates but declined immediately.
Winter acknowledged that supporting Netanyahu had cost him potential voters. He said he was choosing among available alternatives and seeking enough strength to change policy within government.
Calls to send all 120 MKs home were an impractical slogan, Winter said, adding that change would take time.
He refused pressure to merge with Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionist Party, and he resisted Netanyahu’s efforts to consolidate smaller parties. Parties that fall below the electoral threshold receive no seats.
Winter challenged the assumption that his voters would otherwise support existing right-wing parties. He also objected to the hostility toward him from that camp.
“I’m not Hamas,” he said. “Don’t confuse a friend with an enemy.”
“There are people who cannot bring themselves to vote for the current Right, for the existing government,” he added, citing younger voters and reservists as his core constituency.
Asked what distinguished him from Smotrich, Winter replied: “Look at my list.”
He described it as closer to what the Likud, Netanyahu’s party, should have been: “Religious, nonreligious, Jews, Arabs, Druze.”
No. 2 on his list, Yoseph Haddad, is an Arab Christian advocate for Israel who volunteered for military service and was wounded in the Golani infantry brigade. Winter wants him to become public diplomacy minister and defend Israel’s positions abroad.
Former television journalist Netali Shem Tov’s family was displaced from Metula, near the Lebanese border.
Sigal Kraunik-Atia lost her husband, Kibbutz Be’eri’s security coordinator, in the October 7 massacre.
Winter repeatedly highlights new immigrants to Israel
Winter repeatedly highlighted the olim (new immigrants).
Former Jerusalem deputy mayor Fleur Hassan-Nahoum immigrated from Gibraltar and became prominent in international advocacy.
Lali Deri arrived alone from France at age 14 and a half and became an activist and commentator. Her son, Saadia Yaakov, was killed fighting in Gaza.
Their experience connected his slate to Jewish communities abroad.
Winter also described a roots trip with his immigrant parents that reinforced his appreciation of having a Jewish state.
The diversity came with clear ideological boundaries. He opposed a Palestinian state and wanted Israel’s Jewish character preserved. He also opposed religious coercion and welcomed non-Jewish citizens who identify with Israel into its leadership.
Winter commanded Givati during the 2014 Gaza war, Operation Protective Edge, and later led the 98th Division. His religiously worded letter to soldiers before the 2014 fighting provoked controversy. He left the military in 2024 after being passed over for promotion to major-general.
“I lived with a sense of mission,” Winter said. “Otherwise, I would not have been able to do it, nor would my family.”
His wife raised eight children while working as a school principal, he said. He insisted he had left the army without anger.
As defense minister, Winter said he wants to change military doctrine “from containment to decisive victory.” He acknowledged wartime achievements but expressed disbelief that Hamas remained standing after years of fighting.
“Reservists are not supposed to serve in the IDF for three years,” he said. “Reservists need to be at home.”
They need to work, educate children, develop the economy, and help absorb immigrants, he added.
Winter described Eisenkot as an architect of the prewar security approach he opposed. Eisenkot could, nevertheless, join a broad government.
“But I don’t think he can be defense minister,” he said.
Winter also welcomed former prime minister Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Liberman into such a coalition “as ministers.”
Regarding Netanyahu’s responsibility, he was unequivocal.
“Netanyahu is responsible,” he said. “Whether he says it or doesn’t say it, he is responsible. He was prime minister. There wasn’t somebody else here.”
Winter distinguished the immediate failures of the military and Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency), Israel’s domestic security service, from political leaders’ responsibility for accepting assessments and approving policy. The failure had developed over at least a decade, he said.
“Nobody can take the responsibility away from Netanyahu,” he added.
Winter has publicly made military-service legislation a condition for joining the government.
His plan combines greater benefits for those serving, Defense Ministry oversight of yeshivas, and military units accommodating haredi religious requirements.
“The more you serve, the more you receive,” he said. Combat and reserve service should bring greater benefits, he added, and those failing to report would lose access to dealings with the state. He did not elaborate.
Drawing on his experience establishing a haredi company in Givati, Winter said recruitment required the army to honor its promises to religious soldiers.
“Don’t reeducate them,” he said.
Winter said there was room for women combat soldiers alongside religious accommodations, supported continued Torah study for exceptional scholars, and wanted other haredim to have routes into service, education, and work.
Regarding Gaza, he advocated what he calls voluntary emigration.
“Let them choose where they want to go,” he said.
Winter said the government had considered him to lead its emigration initiative, but then backed away after hearing his intentions. He did not identify the officials involved.
Winter’s account of his proposed wartime strategy included moving the population, besieging those who remained, and allowing emigration. He also advocated separating civilians from Hamas and striking the organization with full force.
The interview left unanswered how voluntary departure would operate alongside that pressure and what conditions civilians choosing to remain would face.
“Our soldiers come before enemy civilians,” he said, regarding his wartime instructions.
Winter hopes for a double-digit seat tally, drawing support from the Likud, other right-wing parties, the center, and first-time voters. That remained his assessment of the party’s potential.
Whether he could reshape a Netanyahu government depended on voters giving him enough influence to enforce his demands, he said.
“We will act from within, but we will not compromise on certain things,” Winter said.

Ten shades of Putin: Russia votes in first Duma election since Ukraine invasion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:05:55 UTC
04:05:55 KST

Nearly five years after ordering the full-scale invasion of Ukraine and launching a bloody war with no end in sight, Russian President Vladimir Putin will seek to project strength this weekend as Russians head to the polls in the country’s first parliamentary election since the war began.
The tightly controlled vote features 10 parties, led by the ruling United Russia party, all of which support Putin’s policies. The only registered party that openly opposed the war in Ukraine has been barred from the nationwide race.
The election comes at a difficult time for Putin’s government. In recent months, Russia has faced repeated Ukrainian drone attacks on oil facilities and e-commerce companies, causing significant economic damage and contributing to a prolonged fuel crisis. The strikes have also brought the war closer to Russian civilians, particularly those living relatively close to the Ukrainian border. Against that backdrop, the Kremlin hopes the election will underscore public support for the war and lend legitimacy to its policies.
Voting will take place over three days, from Friday through Sunday, with Russians choosing members of the State Duma, the lower house of parliament. Governors will also be elected in 11 regions and regional lawmakers in 39. The decision to spread voting over three days is intended to boost participation among the country’s 111 million eligible voters and includes the option of electronic voting.
For the first time, voting will also include residents of four Ukrainian regions — Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia — that Moscow illegally annexed after invading them in 2022. Voting is also taking place in Crimea, which Russia illegally annexed from Ukraine in 2014.
Elections to the Duma use a mixed system. Half of its 450 seats are allocated through nationwide proportional voting for party lists, while the other half are filled by candidates elected individually in local constituencies. Each voter therefore casts two ballots.
United Russia, the Kremlin’s main ruling party, currently holds more than two-thirds of the seats in the Duma. Other parties described as the “systemic opposition” generally vote in line with the government on major issues and also hold seats in parliament.
The liberal Yabloko party, the only registered party opposed to the war, was initially included on the ballot. In August, however, Russia’s Supreme Court barred it from the nationwide party-list contest and ordered its removal from the ballot. The court cited, among other arguments, claims that the party’s anti-war stance was equivalent to calling for a violation of Russia’s territorial integrity.
Yabloko is now fielding candidates only in individual constituency races, and some of those candidates have also been disqualified.
Long-serving foreign minister and Ukrainian drone survivor
United Russia, whose emblem features a bear beneath the Russian tricolor, won more than two-thirds of Duma seats in the previous election in 2021 and enters this election with overwhelming control of the chamber. The party benefits from extensive state media backing and tight government control over the electoral process.
Its candidate list is headed by several prominent political figures, including Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, 76, who has held the post for 22 years, and Sergei Sobyanin, 68, Moscow’s influential mayor. In an apparent effort to add a younger face to a party widely associated with officials and bureaucrats, war correspondent Yevgeny Poddubny, who was seriously wounded in a Ukrainian drone strike, was placed third on the list.
United Russia members have pledged support for the war effort and for Putin’s maximalist goals in what the Kremlin calls its “special military operation” in Ukraine.
At the same time, Sobyanin, widely regarded as a pragmatist, has rejected calls from Russian hard-liners for a large-scale mobilization of conscripts and for placing the entire economy on a war footing.
“To destroy a normal economy means destroying the entire country,” he said, in remarks reflecting the Kremlin’s desire to continue the war without risking another broad mobilization, a deeply unpopular step.
Another major political force is the Communist Party, which has been a leading presence in parliament since the 1990s. It has been led for more than three decades by Gennady Zyuganov, 82, a former Soviet official.
During more than a quarter-century of Putin’s rule, the Communists have criticized some aspects of government policy but have been careful to avoid personal criticism of Putin. They have also consistently supported the war in Ukraine.
“We strictly follow President Putin’s directives,” Zyuganov said last month while inspecting a shipment of military supplies.
The party has recently stepped up its social media activity in an effort to reduce its reliance on older voters and broaden its appeal among younger Russians.
A third major contender is the Liberal Democratic Party of Russia, whose name is misleading: In practice, it is an ultranationalist force. The party was founded by Vladimir Zhirinovsky, a fiery and often provocative politician who called for retaking former Soviet territories and threatened the use of nuclear weapons against Russia’s enemies.
The party has maintained a significant presence in parliament since the early 1990s and competes with the Communists in appealing to nostalgia for the Soviet Union. Since Zhirinovsky’s death in 2022, it has been led by Leonid Slutsky, a former university lecturer who has faced allegations of sexual harassment.
Like the Communists, the Liberal Democrats strongly support the war and emphasize the presence of military veterans in their ranks.
Among the party’s candidates is Viktor Bout, a former arms dealer nicknamed the “Merchant of Death.” Bout was serving a 25-year prison sentence in the United States before being freed in December 2022 in a prisoner exchange for WNBA star Brittney Griner, who had been detained in Moscow 10 months earlier for possession of cannabis oil.
Bout is a former Soviet Air Force officer who for decades sold weapons to governments and armed groups involved in some of the world’s bloodiest conflicts, including in Liberia and Angola.
He was arrested in Thailand in 2008 in a sting operation in which U.S. agents posed as members of Colombia’s FARC rebel group and told him they wanted to expand the Marxist organization’s weapons arsenal. His career helped inspire the 2005 film “Lord of War,” starring Nicolas Cage.
Putin approval at 76%: ‘We will show again that we are united’
Several smaller parties round out the ballot, including A Just Russia, which has been active in Russian politics for two decades. A social-democratic party, it competes with the Communists for older and middle-aged voters nostalgic for the Soviet era and supports the war in Ukraine.
Its leader, Sergei Mironov, 73, previously drew attention after posing with a symbol associated with Wagner Group brutality — a heavy sledgehammer given to him by Yevgeny Prigozhin, the late leader of the Wagner mercenary organization, shortly before Prigozhin’s failed 2023 mutiny against Putin.
Wagner fighters were alleged to have used such sledgehammers to execute people they considered traitors.
Also on the ballot is New People, founded shortly before the previous parliamentary election in 2021. It initially sought to position itself as a liberal voice representing younger voters and technocrats and won slightly more than 5% of the vote, enough to form a small parliamentary faction.
Although it initially presented itself as an opposition force, the party later embraced Putin’s policies, disappointing many supporters. It is led by Alexei Nechayev, who also heads a cosmetics company, and is widely viewed by Kremlin critics as a government-backed project designed to appeal to liberal voters while creating the appearance of political competition.
Other parties seeking seats include Communists of Russia, a smaller rival to the main Communist Party; the Party of Pensioners; the Greens; the Direct Democracy Party; and Motherland, or Rodina, a hard-line nationalist party.
Motherland is led by Alexei Zhuravlev, who petitioned the Supreme Court to bar liberal Yabloko from the nationwide vote.
It remains unclear how many Russians will turn out to vote. Polls indicate that Ukrainian attacks inside Russia and the worsening economic situation have hurt public morale. Putin’s approval ratings remain high, but the independent Levada Center recorded a decline from 87% in September 2025 to 76% in August.
Even some senior members of Russia’s establishment have publicly expressed concern about the situation.
Andrei Klepach, chief economist at state development corporation VEB.RF, recently warned of possible domestic unrest in Russia.
“We will not win this competition in a war of attrition,” he said. “Our costs are soaring. I am almost certain that we will face a social crisis.”
Klepach was dismissed after his remarks drew widespread attention.
In an address to Russians ahead of the vote, Putin sought to project confidence.
“Your choice and determination will once again prove that millions of people stand behind our fighters and that we are a united people, bound by shared values, historical memory and love for the Motherland.”

Ferguson Marine to build tugboats for commercial sale
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
20:05:04 BST
04:05:04 KST

Ferguson Marine is to begin building a small number of tugboats for sale on the commercial market, with the Scottish Government providing working capital to keep shipbuilding activity moving at Port Glasgow after delays on a proposed package of four further vessels.
Economy and Transport Secretary Stephen Flynn told Holyrood that he had agreed Ferguson Marine’s proposal for financial backing, describing it as a way of retaining productive work and critical skills during a gap in the yard’s order book.
He said: “I have agreed that this proposal should be taken forward because I agree with the board that it represents a sensible, commercial approach to maintaining productive activity within the yard.”
The tugboats are expected to be built for subsequent sale rather than against an existing customer order, with the state-owned yard then seeking buyers on the commercial market.
Ferguson Marine is expected to work with an established shipbuilder on a pre-packaged design, potentially Dutch shipbuilder Damen, allowing construction to begin relatively quickly. Flynn said the arrangement was intended to provide greater certainty while the Government continues work on plans announced earlier this year for four new vessels to be built at Ferguson Marine, including two CalMac ferries.
He said: “Providing working capital to the yard has the potential to retain critical shipbuilding capability and workforce skills during an important period for the business.”
Flynn added: “I have therefore asked officials to work with the company to progress the necessary commercial, financial and governance arrangements as quickly as possible.”
The proposed four-vessel package has not yet reached contract award, with Flynn telling MSPs that “robust due diligence” was still being carried out before the contracts could be placed. He said the working capital was intended to provide “certainty for the yard during the gap between the delivery of the Glen Rosa and the award of these new contracts by making sure we have a commercial alternative in place with tugboats.”
Ferguson Marine is currently completing MV Glen Rosa, the second of the two large CalMac ferries built at Port Glasgow. Delivery is expected before the end of 2026, after which the yard currently has no contracted shipbuilding work scheduled for 2027. The lack of confirmed follow-on work has increased pressure on the yard. Ferguson Marine announced in August that it was seeking voluntary redundancies, with up to 70 positions potentially affected.
The Scottish Government had previously pledged to award work for four smaller vessels directly to Ferguson Marine, including two ferries, but the necessary due diligence on those contracts is still under way.
The delay drew criticism from opposition parties. Scottish Liberal Democrat transport spokesperson Willie Rennie MSP accused the Government of failing to carry out the necessary legal work before announcing its intention to award contracts directly to Ferguson Marine.
Rennie said: “It’s now clear the government failed to carry out appropriate legal checks before it told parliament earlier this year that it would make a direct award of a ferry contract to the Ferguson yard.”
He added: “The consequences are being felt by the third of the workforce who have lost their jobs as a result of the government’s negligence.”
Rennie also called on Flynn to set out when a decision would be made on the contracts, saying: “The workers deserve not to wait another minute.”
The tugboat plan is intended to bridge the period between completion of Glen Rosa and any future vessel awards, while giving Ferguson Marine a product it can offer into the wider commercial market.
Flynn said the Government, which brought Ferguson Marine into public ownership in 2019, continued to believe the yard “can have a strong future as a modern and competitive shipyard.”

Third person dies from malaria in cluster near Germany’s Frankfurt Airport
