New US sanctions bill puts Russia's trade partners in crosshairs — RSPP deputy head
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:54:40 UTC
01:54:40 KST

MOSCOW, September 17. /TASS/. The newly proposed US bill tightening sanctions on Russia seeks primarily to make life difficult for Moscow's trading partners, Alexander Murychev, Vice President of the Russian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs (RSPP), told RBC TV.
"The main concern here isn't direct bans on Russian companies, but rather the pressure on our partners," Murychev said. "Secondary tariffs of up to 100% strike a blow not at us directly, but at those who work with us--the Chinese, the Indians, and even Europeans still buying our oil and gas. They will face a tough situation and will naturally seek ways to minimize risks."
Despite the threat, Murychev noted that Russian businesses have already adapted to ongoing restrictions.
"We are taking this in stride. There are already so many restrictions against our businesses that one more document is unlikely to radically change the landscape on its own," he pointed out.
According to Murychev, while adjusting logistics, payment systems, and partner relations will be "troublesome, costly, and time-consuming," Russian companies possess the necessary experience. "We will look for new options and negotiate with those willing to work with us," he assured.
"And yet, Donald Trump is a pragmatic president and will likely think twice before unleashing new trade tariffs against China and India. However, relying solely on that would be overly naive," the RSPP vice president concluded.
On bill toughening sanctions against Russia
Overnight on September 17, the US House of Representatives passed a bill to tighten sanctions against Russia, sending the legislation to President Donald Trump for his signature. Lawmakers in the Republican-controlled chamber voted 262 to 159 in favor of the measure, which the Senate had previously approved on August 7. Having cleared both houses of Congress, the bill now awaits the president's final approval to become law.
The legislation was primarily authored by US Senator Lindsey Graham (designated as a terrorist and extremist in Russia), who passed away on July 11. It mandates primary and secondary restrictions targeting Russia's top political and military leadership, as well as state-owned companies. Crucially, the bill authorizes the US to levy secondary tariffs of up to 100% against nations that remain major buyers of Russian oil and gas. Additionally, the package includes provisions to further toughen existing U.S. sanctions against Iran.

Abdulsalam Fayez and Sahin Demir
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
The Yemeni army said Thursday that it targeted Houthi supplies and positions in the southwestern cities of Taiz and Mokha.
The army’s media center said in a statement that air forces targeted Houthi supplies and positions in Taiz and Mokha in Taiz province, near the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait.
Earlier Thursday, the army said it had thwarted a Houthi attack and struck the group’s positions and reinforcements in Taiz.
There was no immediate comment from the Houthis on the army statements.
The Yemeni army has recently intensified strikes against Houthi positions and gatherings in several provinces, particularly Taiz, according to government forces.
The fighting has intensified along Yemen’s western coast over the past week, with the Houthis taking control of strategic districts in Hodeidah and Taiz provinces, including Mokha, as well as Red Sea islands, including Mayyun in the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
Government forces, meanwhile, have advanced in Al-Jawf province toward its capital Al-Hazm, while clashes continue in Marib, Al-Dhale and Al-Bayda.
The escalation, which began in July, is the broadest since the relative calm that followed the April 2022 truce, with fighting intensifying this month, particularly along the western coast and around Bab al-Mandab.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized Sanaa and several provinces in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.

Palestine rejects US visa restrictions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:53:57 UTC
01:53:57 KST

Palestine rejected a US decision to extend visa restrictions on Palestinian Authority officials and members of the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) ahead of the UN General Assembly in New York, calling the measure “unjustified” and harmful to efforts to rebuild confidence and advance a two-state solution.
The Palestinian foreign ministry said in a statement on Thursday that the restrictions run counter to efforts to improve Palestinian-US relations and create the political conditions needed for peace and stability in the region.
It said the PLO and Palestinian Authority remain committed to peace, international legitimacy and a two-state solution based on the June 4, 1967 borders, “with Palestine and Israel living side by side in security and peace.”
The ministry also rejected Washington’s argument that Palestinian recourse to the UN, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) and the International Criminal Court (ICC) undermines peace.
It said turning to international institutions and international law is a legitimate and peaceful means of protecting Palestinian rights and should not be equated with occupation, illegal settlement expansion, annexation, displacement and violence by Israeli illegal settlers.
Ignoring Palestinian reforms
It said turning to international institutions and international law is a legitimate and peaceful means of defending Palestinian rights and should not be equated with occupation, settlement expansion, annexation, displacement or violence by Israeli forces and settlers.
The ministry said international recognition of the State of Palestine is not a substitute for negotiations, but rather recognition of the Palestinian people’s right to self-determination and support for a just peace based on the two-state solution.
It also expressed surprise that the US statement did not acknowledge what it described as substantial Palestinian reforms, including changes to the social protection system and reforms in the financial, administrative, educational and legal sectors.
The ministry said punitive measures and restrictions on Palestinian officials “do not promote peace or combat violence, but instead weaken the Palestinian partner committed to a political solution.”
It also said any restrictions preventing the full participation of the Palestinian delegation in UN meetings would infringe on Palestinian rights and conflict with US obligations as host country under the UN Headquarters Agreement.
Palestinian-US dialogue
The ministry called on the US administration to reconsider the decision, end what it called “a policy of sanctions and restrictions,” and engage in direct Palestinian-US dialogue to address outstanding differences.
On Wednesday, the US State Department said it would extend visa restrictions denying entry to PLO members and PA officials after reporting to Congress that the two bodies had again failed to meet commitments under US law.
The US cited Palestinian actions at international organisations, including what it described as efforts to “internationalise the Israeli-Palestinian conflict” through the ICC and ICJ.
The State Department also accused the PLO and PA of failing to carry out reforms and of continuing activities that Washington says undermine prospects for peace.
The US did not specify which officials are covered, maintaining an exemption for staff of the PLO's UN observer mission. It also cited Palestinian efforts to "bypass negotiations through seeking unilateral recognition," accusing the PLO and PA of continuing stipend payments it says benefit people involved in attacks against Israelis and of glorifying terrorism.
"As a consequence of their failure to reform... the United States will extend sanctions that deny visas to PLO members and PA officials," the department said.
The measures come ahead of the UN General Assembly's 81st session next week, following a similar US move last year when Washington denied or revoked visas for PLO and PA officials, though the PA Mission received waivers under the UN Headquarters Agreement.
President Mahmoud Abbas was unable to attend in person last year and addressed the gathering virtually.

China conducts 2 successful space launches, sends satellites into orbit

Saadet Gokce
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
China conducted two successful space launches Thursday, sending a new batch of low-orbit internet satellites and two commercial interferometric synthetic aperture radar (InSAR) remote-sensing satellites into orbit, state media reported.
The first launch took place at 8.32 a.m. (0032 GMT) from the Hainan commercial spacecraft launch site. A Long March-12 rocket successfully placed the 25th group of low-orbit internet satellites into orbit, according to the Global Times.
It was the 667th launch of the Long March rocket family.
At 10.40 a.m. (0240 GMT), a Kuaizhou-11 Y3 solid-fuel rocket launched from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China, carrying two satellites into preset orbit.
It was the seventh mission of the Kuaizhou-11 rocket and the 40th launch of the Kuaizhou rocket series.

US Democrats look to stop Trump's Saudi nuclear deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:53:12 UTC
01:53:12 KST

US Democrats look to stop Trump's Saudi nuclear deal
WASHINGTON, Sept 17 - US House of Representatives Democrats raised concerns on Thursday about President Donald Trump's civil nuclear agreement with Saudi Arabia, and said they had introduced a resolution of disapproval seeking to block the deal from coming into force.
Trump sent the proposed agreement to Congress in August, opening a 90-day window for lawmakers' review and giving them an opportunity to try to pass a resolution of disapproval.
Democrats and nonproliferation advocates have criticized the nuclear pact for not barring Saudi Arabia from enriching uranium or reprocessing nuclear waste, two potential pathways to a nuclear weapon. The United Arab Emirates agreed to such measures, known as the gold standard, in its 2009 civil nuclear deal with Washington.
"A region already gripped by conflict and escalation does not need another nuclear power," the four Democrats — Representative Gregory Meeks of New York, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee; Brad Sherman and John Garamendi of California, and Don Beyer of Virginia — said in a statement.
The Trump administration says the deal has nonproliferation measures required by law.
It is not clear whether Saudi Arabia will get the deal without normalizing relations with Israel. Trump has said the pact will only go into effect if Riyadh does so, but congressional aides said there is nothing in the agreement addressing that issue.
Members of Congress have also called for all of the agreement — including classified "side letters" reached with Saudi Arabia — to be made public.
The 30-year nuclear deal calls for the construction of AP1000 reactors, a project worth tens of billions of dollars that would benefit Westinghouse, jointly owned by Canada-based Cameco and Brookfield Asset Management.
It is unclear when the House might vote on the resolution. Speaker Mike Johnson on Wednesday sent members home until after the November 3 midterm elections.
Additionally, while Congress has passed dozens of disapproval resolutions over the years, no resolution regarding nuclear power or civil nuclear cooperation has ever successfully passed.
Under Section 123 of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954, agreements for peaceful nuclear cooperation automatically go into effect after 90 days if Congress has not passed a disapproval resolution to block them. REUTERS

Over 116,000 public observers prepared to monitor Russian elections — Civic Chamber
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:52:05 UTC
01:52:05 KST

MOSCOW, September 17. /TASS/. Public activists and experts have trained more than 116,000 observers to monitor the State Duma elections, Alexey Peskov, co-chairman of the coordinating council for public monitoring of voting under Russia’s Civic Chamber, said.
"A total of 2,634 in-person events were held across Russian regions to prepare and train public observers, with more than 116,000 future specialists trained," Peskov said at the opening of the Civic Chamber's Situation Center for election monitoring.
Peskov noted that training seminars were held in all Russian regions from June through early September. "The process of preparing and training public observers was in full swing throughout the summer months. We can now sum up the figures. As of today, the number reflecting the scale of our community's work exceeds what we had planned," Peskov said.
Voting in the elections to the 9th State Duma will take place from September 18 to 20. For the first time ever, residents of the recently incorporated Donetsk and Lugansk People’s Republics, as well as the Kherson and Zaporozhye Regions, will participate in legislative elections for the lower house of the Russian parliament. A total of ten parties are taking part in the election: United Russia, the Communist Party of the Russian Federation (CPRF), the Liberal Democratic Party of the Russian Federation (LDPR), New People, A Just Russia - For Truth, the Party of Pensioners for Social Justice, the Communists of Russia, Rodina, the Party of Direct Democracy, as well as the Greens Ecological Party.
Elections for regional legislative bodies will also be held in 39 Russian constituent entities, alongside elections for regional leaders. In eight regions, the leaders will be elected directly, while in three regions, they will be chosen by the regional parliaments. A total of 23,000 seats will be filled.

Latvia's Saeima backs higher tariffs on grain transit from Russia
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
19:51:26 EEST
01:51:26 KST

Latvia's Saeima on Thursday adopted amendments to the railway law that allow tariffs on the transit of grain from Russia to be revised on an expedited basis, the parliament's website has reported.
"The amendments will make it possible to more quickly review and, if necessary, increase the fee for the transit of grain via the country's public railway infrastructure, if the loading station is located in Russia. This procedure will also apply to cargo brought into Latvian ports for further export. Revenue, if generated from the increased infrastructure fee applied to Russian grain transit, will go toward Ukraine's defense needs," the statement said.
The special procedure will be in effect until December 31, 2026.
The railway law currently provides for a two-month period for publishing changes to infrastructure fees, but the amendments will shorten this to two weeks for Russian grain. The law will take effect the day after publication.
It was noted that in submitting the bill to the Saeima, the country's Cabinet of Ministers called on LatRailNet JSC, which decides on railway infrastructure usage fees, to assess the possibility of setting an increased fee of 300% of the current rate for the transit of grain cargo of Russian origin.
As reported, Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs said in early September that Latvia's government plans to introduce a 300% duty on Russian grain and its processed products. "Latvia is seeking to reach a common position among the Baltic states so that Russian grain does not use the region's infrastructure," Kulbergs said, adding that the restrictions would also apply to grain supplied from Belarus.
According to the Latvian prime minister, he has already held talks on this issue with the prime minister of Estonia and plans similar talks with the head of government of Lithuania.
It was also earlier reported that Lithuanian Agriculture Minister Kęstutis Mažeika had ordered a check into the origin of grain being transported through the country in transit from Russia and Belarus.

Greens push Zack Polanski to take stance on proposed policy declaring ‘Zionism is racism’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:50:05 UTC
01:50:05 KST

The Greens are pushing Zack Polanski to take a stance on a potential party policy stating “Zionism is racism”, with some fearing it could alienate Jewish supporters if it was passed.
Polanski, who leads the Greens in England and Wales, has not spoken publicly about the motion, which came top of a members’ vote of policy motions to be debated at the party conference in Brighton at the start of October, and is thus almost certain to feature.
The Greens make party policy by member votes at conferences. If passed, the motion would equate Zionism – the movement for a Jewish state – with racism, would call for a single Palestinian state, and would risk members who supported Zionism being disciplined for racism.
While Polanski is believed to have reservations about the motion, some in the party believe he is wary of speaking out publicly to avoid angering left-leaning members who have joined the Greens in large numbers under his leadership, a number of whom have strong views on Gaza and Israel.
“Zack can try to be everything to everyone, and that doesn’t always work in politics,” one senior Green said. “But he is in a difficult position. Some of the supporters of the motion can be quite aggressive.”
A motion with the same title was submitted to the Greens’ spring conference but was never debated due to time constraints.
If the motion had been debated, it is understood that the party’s MPs and Polanski would have opposed it.
Polanski has not given a view yet this time but is understood to have concerns about any motion that could leave Jewish members feeling unwelcome in the party, or which could be seen as not helping a peace process.
Some in the party view the coming weeks, and whether Polanski takes a stance or not, as a test of his leadership, and whether he is willing to challenge some of the new Green members, particularly those who were formerly in Jeremy Corbyn’s Labour.
The motion calls for “a single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine with Jerusalem as its capital, equal rights for all, and the right of return for Palestinians and their descendants”, and says the Palestinian people have the full right to “resistance and liberation from Israeli occupation, domination and subjugation” within international law.
If passed, Zionism “will be treated as any other form of racism” by the party, it adds.
Two amendments to tone down the motion have been tabled, which one Green source said Polanski appeared to support.
A Green official said that many activists loyal to the party’s leadership might not be at the autumn conference because it takes place a week before voting in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, in which Polanski hopes to take Keir Starmer’s old seat from Labour, potentially leaving more scope for others to push through the motion.
“The risk is that if it passes as it is we are alienating ourselves from the Jewish community in the UK, a lot of whom are not big fans of the current Israeli government,” a Green source said.
There was, they added, a parallel worry about internal splits, with some Green activists in leaked WhatsApp chats warning that Polanski was “struggling to overcome Zionist indoctrination”.
They said: “In the past, even highly contested policy debates in the Greens have always been conducted in a mature and sensible way, even [a] boring way. Now it’s changed.”

'Fundamental national responsibility’: India's envoy to US strikes defiant note as Trump's 100% tariffs loom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:49:25 UTC
01:49:25 KST

India’s Ambassador to the United States Vinay Mohan Kwatra has defended New Delhi’s energy sourcing policy after the US House of Representatives passed legislation that gives US president Donald Trump the authority to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on countries continuing to buy Russian oil and gas, including India and China. The bill was approved 262-159 after clearing the Senate last month and now goes to Trump for signature.In an X thread titled “People First: What Drives India’s Energy Imperative”, Kwatra said India’s energy choices were driven by development and energy security.“Energy is a vital strategic necessity for 1.4 billion Indians and a foundation of our development….India is the world’s fastest-growing major economy and its third-largest energy consumer. Yet the average Indian consumes less than one-third of the global average and one-tenth of average American. Our energy needs will, and must, grow,” he said.Kwatra said reliable and affordable energy was essential for homes, farms, hospitals, schools, factories and transport.“India imports over 85% of its crude oil and around half its natural gas. Our sourcing reflects a fundamental national responsibility: looking outside our borders to secure adequate, affordable and uninterrupted energy for our people,” he said.
He added that India sources energy from partners across the Middle East, Africa, Latin America, Eurasia and the US, with decisions guided by “availability, affordability, market conditions and commercial viability”.
“When recent conflicts squeezed global supplies, India acted decisively to protect its people from price shocks. That also helped steady global energy markets and prevent a deeper crisis. The energy security of India’s people comes first!” Kwatra said.The Ministry of External Affairs said India had noted the passage of the legislation and was monitoring further developments. It reiterated that New Delhi remained committed to energy security through diversified sourcing and evolving market conditions.
The MEA said, “The Indian side has also made clear its determination to take all necessary measures to protect its trade and economic interests,” adding that the government would work with Indian trade and industry bodies to address the implications.
The legislation comes amid wider trade tensions between India and the US. Further bilateral trade discussions are expected on the sidelines of the G20 Trade Ministers’ meeting in Wisconsin later this month, as negotiations on a broader trade agreement continue.

US passenger duct-taped to plane seat says: ‘I don’t remember any of it’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:49:18 UTC
01:49:18 KST

An American Airlines passenger who was duct-taped to his seat following an alleged outburst including racial and homophobic slurs said that he does not recall the incident.
On 3 September, 67-year old Layne Lundeen was restrained in his first-class seat with duct tape and zip ties over alleged unruly behavior. The American Airline Flight 618 was originally traveling from Dallas, Texas, to Newark, New Jersey, and was diverted to the Baltimore/Washington Thurgood Marshall airport in an emergency landing.
Upon landing, authorities arrested Lundeen and charged him with second-degree assault and disorderly conduct.
In a court hearing the following day, Lundeen said, “I don’t remember any of what happened,” according to a recording recently reviewed by the Baltimore Banner.
The outlet added that after being read his charges, Lundeen said: “I assaulted a police officer? Is that what it says? I don’t have my glasses.”
He added: “Oh my god, what a mess … I don’t remember any of it.”
The Guardian has reached out to Lundeen’s lawyer for comment.
Speaking to ABC following the incident, Juan Mejia, a former law enforcement officer and one of the flight’s passengers who helped restrain Lundeen, said that he had allegedly “made derogatory remarks to the staff of American Airlines and other passengers – racial slurs, vulgar language, very offensive to the women.”
Another passenger, Richard Olenick, told CNN that Lundeen had allegedly also tried to hit the passenger next to him, as well as a woman who tried to intervene. Olenick, who also helped restrain Lundeen in his seat using duct tape, told the outlet: “Physically it lessened his ability to move for sure, but it did not solve the issue. He was still pushing and resisting and trying to get up.”
American Airlines has also issued a statement, saying: “The safety and security of our customers and team members is our top priority and we do not tolerate violence. We thank our team members for their professionalism and our customers for their understanding.”
Meanwhile, Lundeen’s former employer, Long Realty in Tucson, Arizona, said in a Facebook statement that it had “ended its affiliation” with him.
“Long Realty is aware of reports concerning criminal charges filed against a former affiliated real estate agent arising from an incident that allegedly occurred during a commercial flight. Upon learning of the incident, Long Realty promptly ended its affiliation with the individual. The individual is no longer associated with or authorized to represent Long Realty in any capacity,” the company said.

Ed Sheeran music dropped by Irish station amid Macklemore row
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:47:01 UTC
01:47:01 KST

Breadcrumb
Ed Sheeran faces fresh backlash as Irish radio station drops his music
An Irish radio station has dropped British singer-songwriter Ed Sheeran’s music from its playlist amid controversy over rapper Macklemore’s removal from his US tour following his pro-Palestine advocacy.
Classic Hits Radio in Ireland said the singer, known for hits such as ‘Galway Girl’ and 'Thinking Out Loud', would no longer be featured on the station for the "foreseeable future", in response to "reaction from our listeners".
In a statement, Dave Kelly, group programme director at Bay Broadcasting, which runs the station, said: "Our decision to remove Ed Sheeran’s music from the Classic Hits Radio playlist has been carefully considered.
"It is not intended as a personal judgment on Ed Sheeran, and we acknowledge his own explanation of the circumstances surrounding recent events.
"As an independent Irish-owned radio station, however, we believe it is important to listen to our audience and to stand alongside Irish artists who have made what is undoubtedly a significant professional decision based on their own convictions.
"Ultimately, our position is a simple one. We believe in peace, humanity and respect, and in the right of people and artists to express and act upon their sincerely held views.
"In light of the strength of feeling expressed by our listeners and the decisions taken by Irish artists involved in the tour, we believe removing Ed Sheeran’s music from our playlist is the appropriate decision for Classic Hits Radio at this time."
The station added that the decision to drop the British singer’s music would remain “under review”.
The move comes after all support acts on Sheeran’s current Loop Tour, including Irish artist Aaron Rowe and Sheeran’s backing band Beoga, withdrew from the remaining dates in response to Macklemore’s removal from the tour.
Macklemore, whose real name is Ben Haggerty, made comments in support of Palestine while performing as a support act at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey earlier this month.
His subsequent removal from the tour prompted an international backlash, including within the music industry, amid concerns over artistic freedom and the conflation of pro-Palestine advocacy with anti-Jewish sentiment.
The rapper has since announced that he donated his US$1 million (£747,328) in net tour earnings to charities supporting Palestinian people, amid the genocidal war in Gaza and Israeli settler and military violence in the West Bank.
He also challenged US billionaire Robert Kraft, who called for his removal from the tour, to match his donation.
Kraft subsequently said Sheeran had asked him to match a $2 million donation before Macklemore announced his pledge.
On Tuesday, Sheeran defended himself against growing backlash in a lengthy social media post, arguing that Macklemore’s departure from the tour was the promoter’s decision and not his, after a pro-Israel boycott was launched calling for the Grammy Award-winning rapper to be removed.
He said “upcoming tour dates had communicated that they would pull the shows if he was still supporting”, adding that Kraft’s Gillette Stadium was among them.

The global response to the Russia sanctions bill the U.S. Congress approved late Wednesday has been swift and defiant, with Moscow warning it would prolong its war on Ukraine, India vowing to protect its interests, and Beijing pushing back against what it called illegal “long-arm jurisdiction.”

It also empowers Trump to hit the five largest global purchasers of that fuel with 100% sanctions, a cudgel that has U.S. allies worried. China has bought 50% of Russian crude exports since 2022, India 37%, Turkey 5% — and the EU 5%. The bloc has also been the largest buyer of Russian LNG (49%) over that period, as well as the largest buyer of Russian pipeline gas (32%), according to data from the Helsinki-based Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air non-profit.

Ed Sheeran, Macklemore, and the music industry’s habit of choosing white feelings over Black and Brown lives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:44:32 UTC
01:44:32 KST

Ten days after Macklemore stood on the MetLife stage and said “Free Palestine,” which drew vocal backlash from Zionists and artists like P!nk, he was removed from Ed Sheeran’s Loop Tour. According to Macklemore, Sheeran was called by Robert Kraft, a Zionist billionaire and owner of Gillette Stadium, where they were scheduled to play later this month. Kraft had rallied together a group of venue owners and issued an ultimatum: if Sheeran did not drop Macklemore from the supporting slot, the venues would refuse to let them play, and there would be no tour.
Macklemore then recounts that Sheeran told him the words “Free Palestine” and the sight of the Palestinian flag were “hurtful to a lot of people he spoke with,” and concludes that Sheeran couldn’t get past his “public facing, ‘I don’t take sides.'”
It is this second part of Macklemore’s account that makes clear Sheeran’s decision to continue the tour without him was not due to career and financial pressures alone, but by something else just as powerful: white feelings.
And while this exchange is one between friends, one many of us have had, it is also an example of what happens when the illusion of neutrality, upheld for the sake of white comfort, clashes with the real world.
Neutrality is fiction
White feelings are not simply just the feelings of white people. They are those rooted in superiority — the internalized belief that one’s feelings as part of an in-group matter more than those of an out-group. When they meet reality, it is painful, because it exposes the violence that this superiority necessitates. What follows is shame, guilt and discomfort. That is why it is of the utmost importance to create and maintain an illusory world, one of neutrality, to protect white feelings from the truth of their impact.
It is important to note here though, that whiteness is a social construct, one created to uphold a hierarchy of exploitation, including imperialism and colonialism. Therefore people who do not fall squarely into the category of whiteness can still approximate and benefit from whiteness through upholding this hierarchy, and thus harbor white feelings, too.
Before Macklemore was taken off the Loop Tour, The Israeli-American Council petitioned to remove him. Their statement read, “This was an Ed Sheeran concert — not a political rally, not a protest, not an activist event.”
This is storytelling. It is an effort to convey a narrative as if it were reality, and that narrative is: complicity in a genocide is the default, the norm. But staying silent about an ongoing and well documented genocide is in itself a political stance. It is an endorsement of and an investment in the status quo. It is the acceptance of lack of change.
The rhetoric of The Israeli-American Council also serves up another farce: that a stadium itself is a neutral ground. But a stadium is not neutral, it is owned. In this case, owned by billionaires with political agendas. Kraft, for example, is deeply invested in Israel. Not only has he taken NFL players on trips to Israel, but he has financially backed opposition to the BDS Movement. Benjamin Netanyahu has even gone as far as saying “Israel does not have a more loyal friend than Robert Kraft.”
Despite this, succumbing to his demands is what Sheeran considered the neutral act because of what Palestinian-born intellectual Edward Said called “flexible positional superiority.” The West doesn’t need to engage with what Palestinians are actually saying to retain the power to decide whether it’s sayable at all. Kraft, Sheeran, and the venues never had to debate the substance of “Free Palestine.” They just had to exercise the authority to decide it didn’t belong in their room in the first place.
White feelings as facts
Scholar Kyla Schuller has a name for the deeper machinery underneath all of this: sentimental biopower. While her book The Biopolitics of Feeling is written mostly through the lens of Black and white America, the mechanism she describes and their modern impact, help us understand the relationship between white feelings and those of all racialized people.
Schuller traces how, since the founding of the country, the feelings of the “civilized” individual (coded white) have been treated not as a byproduct of American political life, but as its foundation.
In the 1800’s, as race science became more popular, so did the concepts on sentimentalism and impressibility. It was theorized that more evolved beings were capable of a higher degree of impressibility, or the ability to absorb external stimuli, and process it. They could then reflect back on it (sentimentalism). Primitive bodies on the other hand, were only capable of immediate feeling, or reflexes as opposed to reflection.
Race scientists then used this concept to reinforce racial hierarchy: white feelings were so valid, so evolved, that they were almost a logic or a fact. The feelings of Black people as their binary, and particularly Black pain, held no epistemological weight. It was something to be filtered out or made bearable to witness.
We are seeing a similar dynamic at play here with Palestinians as the racialized “other.” The comfort of largely white, largely American audiences is structurally protected by the corporations whose business models rely on that very comfort. The unease of billionaire Robert Kraft is acted on within 10 days. The feelings of those claimed to be hurt by the sight of the Palestinian flag and the call for Palestinian freedom require no evidence that either actually harms their well being or personhood, because their feeling alone is proof.
Meanwhile the mention of Palestinian death and suffering is simply ushered off stage because this suffering is seen as “primitive reflex”. Three years into the live-streamed escalation of the genocide of Palestinians, the actual evidence has not been enough to move Sheeran into any type of outward solidarity, let alone the amorphous pain of Palestinians themselves. Their pain is disputable. Footage, first hand accounts and casualty counts are treated as claims to be weighed rather than facts to be reckoned with. Palestinian feelings are testimonies that must be argued, contextualized and verified.
The historical throughline
This is not the first time that corporations, or in this case, a tour reliant on many of them, calculates that the emotional comfort of a specific audience is worth more than telling the truth about who’s dying and why. The refusal to name state violence in real time, rather than after it is safely historical, is a habit of the American music industry and entertainment industry at large. In fact, one of the most famous records of all time was rejected by a major record label for this same reason.
In 1939 Billie Holiday recorded Strange Fruit. Its lyrics were written two years earlier by Jewish teacher, poet, and member of the American Communist Party, Abel Meeropol. After seeing a disturbing photo of two young Black men hanging from a tree, surrounded by a crowd of white spectators, one looking at the camera while pointing to the corpses, Meeropol penned it in protest of lynchings in the United States. It was put to music and pitched to Holiday.
Holiday’s label Columbia Records refused to release it, not because they disputed the truth of what the song described, but due to concerns it would upset white Southerners. Along with not wanting to alienate Southern record stores, Columbia was co-owned by CBS Radio, and feared backlash on affiliate radio stations. Holiday instead released it through alternative jazz label Commodore records. It would become her most successful record, selling 1 million copies.
After the success of Strange Fruit the U.S. government, led by Federal Bureau of Narcotics Commissioner Harry J. Anslinger, ordered Holiday to stop performing it. The song, turned anthem of a movement, was seen as a direct threat to the status quo. When she refused, government agents framed her by selling her heroin. A decade later when Holiday was hospitalized for health complications due to drug and alcohol abuse, Anslinger sent agents to handcuff her to a gurney and banned doctors from treating her. She died days later.
The parallels to Macklemore are almost exact: The discomfort in 1939 was white Southern audiences confronted with the reality of lynching. The discomfort in 2026 is Zionists being faced with the inherent violence of an ideology hinging on supremacy and ethnonationalism. Columbia Records was the institution capable of putting Holiday’s work in front of the masses. Ed Sheeran’s tour would have put Macklemore on stages in stadiums, larger venues than Macklemore currently sells on his own. Columbia’s fear wasn’t of the song’s lyrics, but of losing business. Sheeran’s fear wasn’t of Macklemore’s words either. We can assume that Sheeran had heard Macklemore shout “Free Palestine” from a stage before. He was afraid of who it made uncomfortable, and what that discomfort might cost him.
As for the future, Strange Fruit became a civil rights standard decades after Columbia refused it. Holiday’s message reached millions despite being distributed independently. This could be the fate of Macklemore, and every artist willing to put humanity before career, too, but that is up to us.
Because while Strange Fruit was vindicated once it was safely historical, these artist don’t get that luxury of hindsight. It’s happening now, while the same institutional reflex that tried to bury Holiday’s hit is still fully operational.
Suddenly everyone was clapping
As much as the story of Strange Fruit should serve as a warning of the lengths institutions will go to suppress the voices of artists who challenge oppressive systems, it should also serve as a testament to the power of art.
In her autobiography, Holiday writes of the first time she sang Strange Fruit live at Cafe Society in Greenwich Village. It is a real account but also serves as a greater metaphor:
“There wasn’t even a patter of applause when I finished. Then a lone person began to clap nervously. Then suddenly everybody was clapping.”
There are rooms in this world, stages, stadiums, classrooms, office buildings, filled with silence. With those like Ed Sheeran who refuse to speak the truth. But once that silence is broken by those with the courage to do so, as Macklemore did at MetLife, it may only be a matter of time before everyone is clapping.
Every remaining opening act of Ed Sheeran’s Loop Tour has dropped out in solidarity with Macklemore and the people of Palestine.

Pakistan's PNS Hunain sustained significant damage after colliding with India's INS Kolkata.
NEW DELHI: When 2600-tonne Pakistan warship PNS Hunain collided with Indian Navy’s 7400-tonne destroyer INS Kolkata, three times its weight, on Tuesday evening, the outcome was known as the Pakistani vessel was no match to India’s big warship. The Pakistan offshore vessel was severely damaged and had to return to the harbour whereas, Indian sources said, the Indian destroyer suffered no damage in the collision.In a statement on Thursday, Pak govt said its “Navy was undertaking its biennial exercise SEASPARK-26 when the Indian vessel carried out aggressive manoeuvres in dangerously close proximity to a Pakistani naval ship, resulting in contact between the two vessels”. Visuals emerging showed PNS Hunain a huge dent on it and the warship had to be sent for repairs. PNS Hunain is aYarmook-class patrol vessel designed for maritime security, surveillance and limited combat capabilities. Commissioned in 2014, PNS Hunain is about 98 metres long.
On the other hand, INS Kolkata is 164 metres long and has a maximum speed of 30 knots and is the lead ship of the indigenously designed and constructed Kolkata-class guided missile destroyers. It carries a heavy mix of surface-to-air missiles, anti-ship cruise missiles, rapid-fire guns, and anti-submarine weapons like BrahMos missiles, Barak 8 missiles and close-in weapon system. For anti-submarine warfare, the Indian warship has torpedo launchers, rocket launchers and a bow-mounted sonar system.PNS Hunain would have sunk if INS Kolkata had taken offensive action. “However, despite extreme provocation, the captain of INS Kolkata “had exercised extreme restraint by taking actions to prevent a severe accident from taking place,” the source told TOI.

Moroccans furious as Rabat deepens diplomatic ties with Israel
Scores of Moroccans and activists have lambasted Rabat's decision to upgrade diplomatic ties with Israel, distancing themselves from their government's decision and expressing their rejection of the move.
The development comes after Tel Aviv and Rabat agreed on Wednesday to open embassies and appoint ambassadors in both countries, following a meeting between their foreign ministers hosted by US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz.
The foreign ministers of both countries, Gideon Sa'ar and Nasser Bourita, also agreed to advance economic and trade relations, with two agreements to be completed by the end of this year focusing on investment protection and preventing double taxation.
Both sides said direct flights operated by carriers from their respective countries would be allowed and that high-level bilateral visits would take place in the coming months.
Many activists said they opposed the expansion of diplomatic relations, noting that it comes as Israel continues to bombard Gaza despite a ceasefire agreed last year. Israel's war on Gaza, which leading scholars and rights groups have described as genocide, has killed over 73,000 civilians in the enclave.

As part of the Morocco agreement, Washington recognised Moroccan sovereignty over the disputed Western Sahara, breaking with decades of previous US policy. Morocco considers the territory part of the kingdom, while the Algeria-backed Polisario Front seeks independence.
The normalisation agreements were strongly opposed by Palestinians, who argued that they undermined a longstanding Arab position linking full diplomatic relations with Israel to the establishment of a Palestinian state and an end to Israel's occupation of Palestinian territory.

A war-fatigued and anxious Russia picks a new parliament
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:42:00 UTC
01:42:00 KST

A war-fatigued and anxious Russia picks a new parliament
September 17, 2026
Russians are increasingly anxious. Nearly half of those surveyed by state pollster FOM say a sense of alarm is the prevailing mood among the people around them.
According to data by independent pollster ExtremeScan, 60% of Russians believe that the war against Ukraine has had negative consequences for their day-to-day lives.
"Anxiety and war fatigue are driven by increasing uncertainty," Margarita Zavadskaya, a sociologist and senior research fellow at the Finnish Institute of International Affairs in Helsinki, told DW.
She says this year has seen a shift in public opinion. Rising prices, internet crackdowns, fuel shortages caused by Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries and rumors of another mobilization drive are making it harder for Russians to plan for the future. Some are even leaving the country, afraid they could be drafted after the elections.
Sociologist and the founder of ExtremeScan Elena Koneva said people were starting to ask the question: "How much does this war cost me and my family? And am I ready to pay this price? "
That could pose a problem for the Kremlin.
From September 18 to 20, Russians are voting for a new parliament (the State Duma) for the first time since 2022. It's the first parliamentary election to take place in Russia during the Ukraine war. And although there are unlikely to be any surprises in the official results, the Kremlin will be closely monitoring turnout.
Why are these elections important for the Kremlin?
"The Kremlin is confident it can fabricate whatever figures it needs. The question is how high of a price it will have to pay," said Zavadskaya.
Although elections in authoritarian systems like that of Russian President Vladimir Putin have little to do with democratic change, they still serve an important purpose. They are a reality check on whether the population remains loyal. And for Putin, that is especially important right now.
"They are crucial for him because they demonstrate that the majority supports the main party, the party of war, and that he has legitimacy for further escalation and the continuation of this war," Russian opposition politician in exile Ilya Yashin told DW.
In the fifth year of the war in Ukraine, there is little sign the Kremlin is willing to end the conflict. United Russia, a party de facto led by Putin, is campaigning on a platform that lists victory in the war among its priorities. Its candidate list is headed by people presented as veterans of the war against Ukraine.
But many Russians appear to want the opposite.
"The silent majority just wants the war to end," opposition politician Yulia Galyamina, who still lives in Russia, said in a recent interview with online media-outlet Bereg. Most of these people still support Putin, but they are becoming increasingly anti-war, she said.
That mood is also reflected in polling. Six in 10 Russians favor peace negotiations with Ukraine, according to independent pollster Levada Center. Recent Kremlin hints at a new round of peace talks in October may be a tactic to calm the electorate, Zavadskaya said.
Support for Yabloko has been rising
One party has sought to capitalize on this anti-war sentiment: Yabloko.
The liberal opposition party is the only registered political force opposing the war in Ukraine.
Although its rating was below 5% in July, the party has seen a surge in popularity since then. Many people, especially younger Russians, are joining Yabloko and volunteering.
According to the independent pollster ExtremeScan, 18% of Russians would have voted for Yabloko. But they will not be able to: In a recent court decision, Yabloko was barred from running in the parliamentary elections.
"This support for Yabloko is, in fact, a demonstration of people's attitude toward the war," Koneva told DW.
What will anti-war voters do?
Now, with Yabloko out of the race, are there still ways for Russians to express that attitude?
Yulia Navalnaya, the widow of Alexei Navalny, and opposition politician in exile Maxim Katz are urging supporters to back any party except United Russia in an effort to reduce the ruling party's result in the election.
Yabloko has taken a different approach, encouraging voters to spoil their ballots.
Yashin says neither choice matters. What matters, he says, is showing up at polling stations at noon on Sept. 20.
"These queues will be a visible expression of public discontent," he said. "No need for flags, banners, or symbols. Everyone will know: the queues at noon are made up of people who do not want the war to continue."
DW Russian asked its readers anonymously whether they plan to vote in the upcoming election. Most of those who responded said they would follow Navalnaya's and Katz's advice.
"Elections have long become a farce and a political spectacle. But I will vote because I want to show that I have a position," one user said.
Others decided to stay away from the elections. One respondent wrote: "I don't want to legitimize Putin's regime."
Sergei Satanovskii contributed reporting.

EDITORIAL: Defense waits for no one
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:41:19 UTC
01:41:19 KST

China’s military activities in the Taiwan Strait and South China Sea are becoming increasingly aggressive and provocative. Retired US admiral James Ellis Jr, who led two US Navy carrier strike groups to stabilize the situation in the waters surrounding Taiwan during the 1996 Taiwan Strait missile crisis, last week warned that the power struggle has not ended, but has significantly intensified and spread to other regions.
Ellis supported the proposal of President William Lai’s (賴清德) administration to increase defense spending and modernize the armed forces, with emphasis on uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAV) and drones.
He also warned that: “If national defense is used as a tool to pursue short-term partisan interests, the only beneficiary is the adversary.”
Although Ellis did not specify a party, his statement highlighted growing international concerns over the opposition-controlled legislature’s obstruction of Taiwan’s defense budgets.
The Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and the Taiwan People’s Party delayed the review of this year’s general budget for more than 300 days and blocked several military procurement funds, severely affecting military planning.
A proposed NT$1.25 trillion (US$39.21 billion), eight-year special defense budget to boost Taiwan’s UAV industry was also slashed; instead, the opposition forced through an act that incorporated drone-related funding into the annual budget, making budget allocation much more time consuming and uncertain.
Although the Cabinet countersigned the act, the change has triggered worries and criticisms that it would undermine Taiwan’s drone development, especially as proposals for this year’s supplementary defense budgets and next year’s general budget are still stuck in the legislature, with further deliberation uncertain.
As China’s escalating military activities threaten stability in the First Island Chain and in the Indo-Pacific region, countries such as Japan, South Korea and the Philippines have raised defense spending.
The Japanese government ordered the rapid enhancement of its asymmetric warfare capabilities; announced an “Interceptor Drone Early Acquisition Program” to speed and scale up mass production of domestic drone airframes; and shortened the timeline of drone procurement and production from years to just 80 days — an astonishingly efficient mechanism and policy shift to upgrade the country’s combat ability.
Meanwhile, Taiwan’s opposition parties are politicizing and blocking defense budgets and military procurements, impeding the armed forces’ modernization, and exacerbating the military imbalance across the Taiwan Strait and raising international allies’ concerns about Taiwan’s resolve to defend itself. Ultimately, such actions benefit only China and its ambition to take Taiwan.
With US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) set to meet for another summit next week, Beijing has been generating media buzz to emphasize that the Taiwan issue is a “red line” and that the meeting could be canceled if Washington approves new arms sales to Taipei. That shows Chinese pressure to weaken Taiwanese defense would continue and intensify.
A nation’s defense and deterrence should not be weakened by political division or party interests. Taiwan’s stability and security should be a common goal among Taiwanese.
US Representative John Moolenaar, who previously warned that “Taiwan’s cuts to its defense budget is sending the wrong message to international allies,” on Tuesday told a delegation of visiting KMT legislators in Washington that “political disputes and delays over higher defense spending had raised concerns among Taiwan’s partners.”
“It will be essential for the KMT to follow through and provide the resources needed to deliver on Taiwan’s plans to build critical defense capabilities,” he said.
Ellis said that in 1996, in the face of China’s missile launches, Taiwan completed its first direct presidential election and showed the world that missiles could not prevent Taiwanese from choosing their own future.
Thirty years on, Ellis believes Taiwan could again counter China’s growing threats with its determination and resilience.
An Institute for National Defense and Security Research survey found that the majority of Taiwanese believe that “investment in defense is an investment in national security.”
The government and political parties should overcome their differences and work together to bolster national defense. Otherwise, the public would again remove obstructions to Taiwan’s defense through ballots, and demonstrate their determination to fight for the nation’s security and sustainability.
Taiwan’s domestic political situation is following recognizable political rhythms, while the international environment surrounding Taiwan is undergoing a major transformation. Central bank keeps key rates unchanged
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:41:17 UTC
01:41:17 KST

The central bank yesterday kept its key interest rates unchanged for a 10th straight quarter while easing housing credit controls, signaling confidence that property lending has cooled enough to allow a targeted relaxation without undermining financial stability.
The central bank left its discount rate at 2 percent, the collateralized lending rate at 2.375 and the short-term lending rate at 4.25 percent.
However, it increased the maximum loan-to-value ratio for people buying a second home to 70 percent from 60 percent and ended a restriction on loans for land purchases.
Photo: CNA
Central bank Governor Yang Chin-long (楊金龍) said that monetary policy has remained relatively tight since 2024, helping stabilize domestic prices and anchor inflation expectations.
“We still have time to observe,” Yang said, adding that two central bank board members dissented, while the majority backed maintaining the current policy stance.
Some members nevertheless warned that inflation still requires close monitoring, he said.
The cautious approach reflects uncertainty over the global economic outlook and the potential effect of conflict in the Middle East on Taiwan’s prices and economy, Yang said.
Domestic inflation is manageable this year and is expected to fall below 2 percent next year, while economic growth is expected to remain solid, he said.
The central bank lifted its forecast for full-year economic growth to 11.48 percent and said it expects the pace to slow to 5.82 percent next year.
It also raised its growth forecasts for this year’s consumer price index (CPI) and core CPI to 2.03 percent and 2.16 percent respectively, putting both above its 2 percent inflation watch level.
The easing in housing comes as property lending has continued to moderate. Real-estate loans accounted for 34.44 percent of total bank lending at the end of July, down from 35.56 percent in March and 37.61 percent in June 2024.
Credit flows into property have dropped, while first-home buyers account for a growing share of residential mortgage borrowers, Yang said.
Lending for urban renewal and reconstruction of aging or unsafe buildings has also taken up a larger share of construction loans, he said.
Housing transactions have cooled, with speculative activity declining and expectations of further home-price gains moderating, Yang said.
The central bank also removed a requirement introduced in December 2021 that land loans be accompanied by a commitment to begin construction within a specified period.
Yang cited labor shortages and difficulties disposing of excavated soil as factors that can delay projects.
Commercial banks have gained more experience managing property-related credit risks after several years of tighter controls, giving the central bank room for a targeted relaxation of land-financing restrictions, Yang said.
The bank also expects growth in broad money supply to exceed its 2.5-to-6.5 percent reference range this year and raised the upper end to 6.75 percent, citing robust artificial intelligence-related exports and investment, buoyant stock-market activity and a low comparison base.
Global stock markets mostly rose yesterday after the US Federal Reserve delivered a widely expected interest rate hike, while falling oil prices and easing bond yields also helped calm inflation fears.
The Fed on Wednesday lifted borrowing costs for the first time since 2023, despite US President Donald Trump’s demand for cuts, as Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh insisted on the need to combat inflation that has been “too high” for “too long.”
Stock markets in Taipei, Tokyo, Sydney, Singapore, Wellington, Mumbai, Bangkok and Jakarta all advanced.
Hong Kong and Shanghai dipped, while Seoul was flat.
Additional reporting by AFP

The Kuma Academy yesterday urged local candidates to propose policies that would improve resilience and the whole-of-society defense system, as Taiwan faces increasing “gray zone” harassment and the threat of “war-related disaster.”
Taiwan’s disaster-preparedness should incorporate the compound threat of natural disasters as well as “gray zone” tactics and a possible Taiwan contingency, the group told a news conference.
It urged local candidates in November’s elections to propose policies that would protect critical infrastructure — including communications, energy and stockpiles of supplies — and strengthen grassroots civil defense capabilities.
Photo: George Tsorng, Taipei Times
Taiwan’s 14 undersea cables are concentrated at eight landing stations, making them vulnerable to physical damage, cyberattacks or cognitive warfare to spread false information, Taiwan National Security Institute deputy secretary-general and Kuma Academy cofounder Ho Cheng-hui (何澄輝) said.
He urged local governments to set up backup noncommercial communications systems that could stabilize public sentiment in a crisis.
To counter energy and supplies vulnerabilities, they should also promote community microgrids and backup power supplies, he said.
Ho further suggested planning a “civil defense fund” and working with convenience stores and logistics operators to increase stockpiles of supplies by 20 to 30 percent.
Kuma Academy chairman Liu Wen (劉文) said that local governments should make use of village and community committee systems to build grassroots defense capabilities.
Liu suggested building “model resilient communities” with incentives to improve.
Moreover, they should deepen cooperation with Taiwan’s strong network of disaster-response nongovernmental organizations, links that could also be incorporated into drills, she said.
Presidential Office Whole-of-Society Defense Resilience Committee member Liu Yu-hsi (劉玉皙) said that the Ministry of Labor and the labor affairs authorities of local governments should jointly formulate provisions to protect small businesses in the event of a crisis, such as work suspension guidelines and regulations governing attendance and wages to avoid labor disputes.
Local governments should also establish reporting channels for industries highly dependent on energy, such as precision manufacturing, to report power and water outages and receive information on service restoration, she said.
Local government funding has increased from NT$433.8 billion (US$13.6 billion) to NT$848.7 billion this year and NT$933.6 billion next year, Taiwan Economic Democracy Union convener Lai Chung-chiang (賴中強) said.
He called on the next local governments to immediately produce a three-year analysis of civil defense budgets covering last year to next year and substantially increase civil defense budgets.
They should submit supplementary budgets on a rolling basis in line with the growth rate of centrally allocated tax revenues, he added.

Unknown Publisher

16:41:14 UTC
01:41:14 KST

An Argentine federal judge on Wednesday ordered British and Israeli companies to stop developing an oilfield off the Falkland Islands, opening a new legal front in the sovereignty dispute between Argentina and Britain.
The injunction by Judge Mariel Borruto targets the Sea Lion oil project 220km north of the British-controlled archipelago in the South Atlantic, barring drilling, offshore installations and port construction until Argentine authorities can conduct an environmental review and issue a decision.
In practice, Wednesday’s order is unlikely to halt progress on the project.
Photo: EPA
Borruto said that enforcement “depends on international cooperation and the conduct” of the two firms, Israel’s Navitas Petroleum and Britain’s Rockhopper Exploration, which have already vowed to press ahead with the project despite Argentine President Javier Milei’s threats of tougher sanctions.
Rockhopper declined to comment and Navitas did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the injunction.
With its commercial oil production expected to start in 2028, Sea Lion has raised the stakes of a territorial dispute that led Britain and Argentina to a short war in 1982.
For the territory’s roughly 3,500 residents, the oilfield promises to transform an economy long dependent on fishing.
For Argentina, which calls the islands the Malvinas, the project would allow foreign companies to extract oil riches it regards as its own.
Its claim to the archipelago, about 480km off its coast, is enshrined in the constitution and woven into national identity, drawing support across the country’s political divisions.

Indonesia scheme turns hunters into protectors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:41:13 UTC
01:41:13 KST

Indonesian villager Octavius wades through the forest in rubber boots and tattered joggers, ears pricked, eyes peeled, a telephoto lens on his phone primed to capture orangutans, monkeys or birds.
The daily photograph hunt earns Octavius and hundreds of others in Borneo cash as part of a conservation program seeking to make animals worth more alive than dead.
Locals on the island have long made money from hunting wild songbirds and selling them, mainly to domestic customers.
Photo: AFP
The KehatiKu project aims to break that cycle by paying people in nine participating villages in West Kalimantan Province for photos or recordings of animals instead.
Payments range from 5,000 rupiah (US$0.30) for observing a common bird, to 130,000 rupiah for an endangered orangutan — the top prize.
The most successful observers earn up to 10 million rupiah a month, several times an average farmworker’s income.
The extra cash “really helps, especially to pay for my children’s college,” said 50-year-old Octavius, who like many Indonesians uses a single name.
The program, run by environmental consultancy Borneo Futures, began two years ago and produces data on wildlife distribution and population changes.
Most participants are small-scale farmers of rice, cacao, durian and the stimulant kratom.
Early signs suggest that the scheme is working.
“People have started to realize that where previously they caught one bird and it was worth 50,000 rupiah, now they just need to take a photo, send it to us, and they can receive a payment of 5,000 to 10,000 rupiah,” Borneo Futures Indonesia director Nardiyono told reporters. “If they take just five photos, they [may] earn 50,000 rupiah, and the bird is still in their environment, still observable, and still able to reproduce, so the potential income from observing birds is far greater than from hunting birds.”
That shifting logic has prompted two participating villages to voluntarily introduce hunting bans since the project started, Nardiyono said.
The program is funded by philanthropic foundations and has received about US$300,000 to date, Borneo Futures said.
Half has gone toward development, including a mobile app for uploading animal sightings and an artificial intelligence system that helps humans verify observations.
So far, users have submitted more than 350,000 observations, about half of which have been validated and paid for.
Invalid entries might include multiple observations of the same animal, or a species that is not on the program’s list.
This month, Octavius and dozens of others gathered at the tiny office in Labian village — population 683 — for their monthly payments.
His share was 4 million rupiah, or nearly US$230.
“This is a side-job; it doesn’t interfere” with farming, he told reporters as he showed off a patch where he grows kratom and cacao. “Sometimes when we’re working, when everyone is gathered to collect kratom leaves, we hear birds calling, so we go over, observe them — if we can take a photo, we take a photo; if not, we just make a sound recording.”
The program’s model is “likely better for both environmental and social impacts than an unincentivized, top-down conservation project design,” said researcher Paul Ferraro of the Baltimore, Maryland-based Johns Hopkins University.
The main challenge will be maintaining funding, Ferraro said.
“People may revert to their prior behavioral patterns because the incentive payments are insufficient when the enthusiasm has waned,” said Ferraro, an expert in human behavior and public policy.
For now, Borneo Futures has funding secured through 2028, and two more villages are to join next month.
It pays for observations of 73 species, including birds, monkeys, wild cats and deer.

Shares of Winbond Electronics Corp (華邦電), the world’s leading NOR flash memory maker, edged up 0.59 percent yesterday, paring a 6 percent intraday rally triggered by its announcement of a US$1.12 billion acquisition of Infineon Technologies AG’s NOR Flash and F-RAM portfolio.
The acquisition comes as the memorychip industry undergoes a supercycle, driven by a supply crunch that Winbond estimated could last through 2028.
Winbond shares closed up at NT$170 yesterday, the highest in four trading days. The deal is expected to solidify its global leadership in NOR flash memory and deepen its penetration into the automotive sector.
Photo: CNA
About 28 percent of the chipmaker’s memorychip revenue last quarter came from the automotive and industrial segment. Winbond last year had about a 23 percent share of the global NOR flash memory market, data compiled by Omdia showed.
The portfolio Winbond is acquiring is NOR Flash and F-RAM products tailored for automotive, industrial and infrastructure markets, Infineon said.
The deal would help bolster Winbond’s research and development efforts and supply chain resilience, as well as enhance customer services, the Kaohsiung-based memory chipmaker said in a statement on Wednesday.
The company plans to operate the portfolio as a standalone entity with headquarters in Silicon Valley, it said.
The new entity would use the legacy “Spansion” name, marking the return of a historical brand to the memorychip industry, Winbond chairman Arthur Chiao (焦佑鈞) said in the statement.
Winbond and Infineon aim to close the transaction in the second half of next year. The deal remains subject to regulatory approval.
Spansion Inc was a California-based memory maker that in 2015 merged with Cypress Semiconductor, which was acquired by Infineon in 2020. Advanced Micro Devices Inc (AMD) and Fujitsu Ltd founded the company in 1993 as Fujitsu AMD Semiconductor Ltd before AMD took full control of the company and renamed it Spansion in 2004.

Paid marriage leave for workers to be extended
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:41:08 UTC
01:41:08 KST

Paid marriage leave for workers is to be extended to 14 days from eight starting on Oct. 1, with foreign workers covered by the Labor Standards Act (勞動基準法) also eligible, the Ministry of Labor said yesterday.
The change was proposed through amendments to the Regulations of Leave-Taking of Workers (勞工請假規則), which are to undergo a seven-day public notice period, Department of Labor Standards and Equal Employment Director-General Huang Chi-ya (黃琦雅) told a news conference in Taipei.
“For the additional days, from the ninth to the 14th day, employers are still required by law to pay wages, but after making the payments, they can apply to the government for subsidies,” Huang said.
Photo: CNA
The new rules are expected to take effect after the public notice period, with details of the wage subsidy to be announced at the same time, she said.
The expanded leave would apply equally to Taiwanese and foreign nationals as long as they are covered by the Labor Standards Act, she said.
That means foreign nationals working in Taiwan, including white-collar workers and migrant workers in sectors such as manufacturing who are covered by the act, would also be entitled to the 14 days of paid marriage leave, she said.
Migrant domestic helpers and live-in caregivers would not be eligible, as they are not covered by the act, Huang said.
Asked after the news conference why foreign workers were included in a policy introduced as part of the government’s efforts to address Taiwan’s low birthrate, Huang said the ministry also had to take “basic human rights principles” into account.
“Although our policy goal is to address the low birthrate, we will not create discriminatory differences in labor laws between local and foreign workers because of that,” she said.
The measure is part of the government’s broader family-support policy announced in May, which also includes plans to extend maternity and paternity leave.
Ministry of the Interior data showed that Taiwan’s fertility rate, the average number of children a woman is expected to have over her lifetime, fell to 0.695 last year, among the lowest in the world.
The number of births also fell for a 10th consecutive year to a record low of 107,812, the data showed.
In terms of marriages, 104,376 couples registered to marry last year, compared with 147,861 in 2016, a decline of 29.4 percent, the data showed.
The crude marriage rate, or the total number of marriages registered in a year divided by the total midyear population, was 4.47 percent last year, down from 6.29 percent a decade earlier, the data showed.
Workers can take paid marriage leave in the 10 days before they register their marriage if they provide “relevant supporting documents,” such as a wedding invitation, the labor ministry said.
All 14 days of leave must be taken within two months and 20 days of registering a marriage, although the period can be extended to a year at the discretion of employers.
Workers who register their marriage before Oct. 1 also qualify for the expanded leave if their eligible leave period extends beyond that date and they have not used all eight days of their entitlement, Huang said.

Shifting dynamics in Ireland should be treated with caution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:41:03 UTC
01:41:03 KST

A decade ago, the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) viewed Brexit as a potential gamechanger in the struggle to resist future pressure for a united Ireland. As the author and journalist Fintan O’Toole wrote in an essay published last year, the DUP hoped that the 2016 referendum would deliver “a double exit. Brexit would not simply mean the UK’s departure from the EU. It would also be an act of separation from the Republic. It would reverse the slow drift towards integration.” That proved to be, to put it mildly, a deeply flawed judgement.
The direction of travel since 2016 has instead been the opposite. Rather than leading to a hard border between Northern Ireland and Ireland, which would have disastrously undermined the Good Friday agreement, the UK’s divorce agreement from Brussels eventually placed one in the Irish Sea. The logic of further economic integration between north and south within the EU’s single market was reinforced.
At the same time, demographic change has meant that people with a Catholic background outnumber those with a Protestant one in Northern Ireland, changing the political calculus. In 2022, Sinn Fein won a historic victory in Stormont elections, leading to Michelle O’Neill’s appointment as the first nationalist first minister. On Monday, during a meeting with the heads of the UK’s other devolved nations, O’Neill welcomed off-the-cuff remarks by US President Donald Trump during an unofficial visit to Ireland, in which he said he would “love” to see unification. The US president’s comments, she claimed, reflected the fact “that there is a growing conversation around constitutional change”.
That is undoubtedly the case, but it is a debate that has barely begun, and one which needs to be conducted with care and caution. The 1998 Good Friday agreement was intentionally vague about the criteria for holding a border poll. Successive governments in London and Dublin have since preferred to concentrate on promoting and developing cross-border cooperation.
Given the history, and the level of political risk involved, that was a sensible strategy. However, the dynamics of the debate have shifted. Trump’s blithe remarks followed hard on the heels of an early spat between O’Neill and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, after the prime minister said during a visit to Belfast that a poll on a united Ireland was “off the table.”
In the short and medium term, Burnham’s position makes sense. Sinn Fein’s commitment to a referendum on Irish unity by 2030 is wildly unrealistic, but for all sides, sleepwalking into a vote without adequate preparation is equally unpalatable. In the absence of a proper debate, commitment to unity in the Irish republic is broadbased, but shallow. In Northern Ireland a disturbing revival of tensions over Orange Order marches in Catholic areas suggests deepening polarization, fueled by ongoing political dysfunction at Stormont.
A sober, lengthy and detailed public conversation is required over what form unification might take, and the possible tradeoffs involved.
In an interview with the Guardian last month, former UK prime minister Gordon Brown suggested that “of course, in the long term, Ireland will be united.” Although, unlike Trump, he added a significant rider. Reaching that outcome would be “a long process where people have got to come together and find a way of agreeing. Basically, that is the issue: whether people can actually agree,” he said. Leaders on all sides of the debate should heed that caveat.

Far right’s influence in Sweden remains despite election setback
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:41:02 UTC
01:41:02 KST

Since the party was founded in 1988, the story of the far-right Sweden Democrats (SD) has been one of such continuous growth that a triumph in Sunday’s general election seemed inevitable.
In 2022, the party capitalized on electoral gains — and the desperation of right-leaning parties to form a minority administration — and almost made its way into government. A supporting role in Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson’s Tido coalition earned the party, which has neo-Nazi roots, huge influence and mainstream acceptance by the political establishment.
This year’s election had been billed as final confirmation they were no longer pariahs, but serious political heavyweights. Early in the campaign, Kristersson announced that, if his coalition were to win, the SD would take key ministerial positions. However, Sunday’s results suggest the march of the far right into the heart of Sweden’s government has been halted — for now.
Illustration: Mountain People
Having fallen from Sweden’s second-biggest party to third place and, with right-leaning parties unlikely to be able to form a coalition, the SD appears to have lost its route into government.
“What we saw yesterday [Sunday] was a historic setback for the Sweden Democrats,” said Niclas Nilsson, a lecturer and researcher at the anti-racism foundation Expo. “The party has grown in every government election since 1988,” he said.
SD leader Jimmie Akesson appeared visibly shocked when he addressed supporters late on election night. He said it was obvious they had lost some percentage points, but claimed they were still “winners.” He appeared to suggest his decision to be a team player and support coalition partner the Liberals might have played a role in their loss of support.
It is perhaps too soon to say why the party shed votes, Nilsson said, but some of its supporters might have gone to the Moderates, who had a good night.
Another factor might have been that, after four years closely involved with the government, the SD is no longer able to claim it is an anti-establishment party. Turnout was about 80 percent, comparatively low for Sweden, which might also have played a role.
There is also the fact that much of what the SD stand for has become part of the Swedish political norm: anti-immigration, harsh approaches to crime and punishment, an attitude to integration that puts the onus on people moving to Sweden to abandon their culture and religion to adapt to “Swedish” norms.
Their influence has spread to the center-left Social Democrats who — after losing the last election — shifted their crime, immigration and integration strategies to the right.
If the Moderates end up joining a coalition government with the Social Democrats, then the SD would be the biggest party in opposition, meaning it would still have a prominent role on the national stage. However, if the Social Democrats are able to form a government without the Moderates, then the SD would again be on the outside looking in, which could help steer national conversation, politics and societal norms away from the right.
How it responds to this moment would be key — to the party’s survival and the tenor of Swedish politics.
However, if, with no center-right parties to answer to, they end up going further right to reinvigorate their base, it could have consequences in the future — and bring Swedish politics to new lows, Nilsson warned.
After all, there is no shortage of far-right support in Sweden. Recruitment, the spread of ideas and mobilization by far right groups known as active clubs continue to grow without regulation or political rules — regardless of what is going on in Sweden’s parliament.

Photo: Wu Meng-ju, Taipei Times

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi yesterday retained her key ministers in a Cabinet reshuffle and made two appointments of Taiwan-friendly politicians.
