They include Kihara, Minister of Finance Satsuki Katayama, Minister of Foreign Affairs Toshimitsu Motegi and Minister of Defense Shinjiro Koizumi.
Photo: AP
The prime minister also made new appointments, with Hisayuki Fujii named minister for internal affairs and communications, and Takashi Yamashita returning as minister of justice.
Fujii and Yamashita have represented the ruling Liberal Democratic Party in the “two-plus-two” policy dialogues with Taiwan.
At the talks between the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) and the LDP, the two have engaged in face-to-face discussions on issues such as Taiwan Strait security.
Fujii participated in the dialogue in 2024, while Yamashita engaged in the seventh, expanded edition of the dialogue on Monday with DPP representatives, including Legislator Puma Shen (沈伯洋), the party’s candidate for Taipei mayor.
During the meeting, the LDP’s Taiwan policy project team identified enhancing deterrence, civil defense, “gray zone” contingencies and economic cooperation as areas for further discussion.
While Fujii has engaged in Taiwan-Japan exchanges through the lens of diplomatic and security policies, Yamashita has been more involved in the internal deliberation of Taiwan policy within the LDP.
The small-scale reshuffle comes as Takaichi navigates rising inflation and a weak yen while pursuing a consumption tax cut on food starting next year.
While Takaichi’s tax cut pledge is popular among voters, economists have criticized the plan, warning that she has failed to identify about ￥5 trillion (US$32 billion) needed annually to fund it.
Takaichi’s policy of expansive government spending has also rattled markets, pushing Japan’s benchmark bond yield to about 3 percent, its highest in three decades.
With Katayama in the finance role, Japan has repeatedly intervened in the foreign exchange market to prop up the falling yen.
On defense, Koizumi remains tasked with updating Japan’s foundational national defense strategy.
“Revising our strategy is something that has a major impact on Japan’s security and on the entire region,” Koizumi told reporters after he was reappointed.
The defense ministry “must marshal all our resources and move forward with a greater speed” with the review with “a strong sense of urgency,” he added.

Groups urge more green energy use at TSMC fabs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:41:00 UTC
01:41:00 KST

Environmental advocates yesterday urged Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC) to promote Taiwan’s green energy supply chain and align its renewable target for plants at Shalun Science Park with its RE100 target.
The Shalun Science Park development project’s scoping meeting is slated to take place at the Ministry of Environment today.
The project site covers 506.9 hectares in Tainan’s Shalun Township (沙崙), of which nearly half is designated as industrial land.
Photo: CNA
The park’s annual power consumption could reach 23.7 terawatt-hours, surpassing New Taipei City’s annual power consumption of 22.4 terawatt-hours, environmental advocates said.
Given such massive additional power consumption and the substantial benefits TSMC would derive, the company should work with government authorities in developing more green power, rather than just being a passive green power consumer, the advocates said.
Citizen of the Earth, Taiwan deputy secretary-general Aries Huang (黃靖庭) said TSMC in its sustainability report pledged to increase its renewable use to 60 percent by 2030 and 100 percent by 2040 after it joined the RE100 initiative.
However, TSMC’s renewable target for its plants at the park is less ambitious, aiming to reach 45 percent renewable use by 2040 and 100 percent by 2050, she said.
TSMC’s sustainability report said the company’s renewable use for plants in Taiwan amounted to only 11.4 percent of its total power consumption last year, Huang said.
Given the anticipated additional power consumption, it would be challenging for TSMC to reach its RE100 target, she said, calling on the company to leverage its capital and market influence to boost green power supply.
Taiwan Climate Action Network director Chao Chia-wei (趙家緯) said that if the park’s renewable energy use reaches only 25 percent instead of TSMC’s RE100 target of 60 percent by 2030, there would be an annual power deficit of about 7.5 billion kilowatt-hours.
Such a deficit is equivalent to the annual power output of a large-scale gas-fired unit with a capacity of 800 megawatts or more, he said, calling on TSMC to incorporate renewable planning into its Shalun construction plans.
Climate Era Catalyst standing director Ko Chien-yu (柯建佑) said solar power generation, storage and charging facilities should be integrated into designs of the residential or commercial buildings, parking lots and other public works in the project site.
More green power should be deployed, given the park’s high power demand, he said.
The National Science and Technology Council’s Southern Taiwan Science Park Bureau yesterday said TSMC’s renewable target of 45 percent by 2040 and 100 percent by 2050 was set in accordance with regulations on strategic environmental assessments.
Renewable energy use would be raised by 25 percent of the previous year’s actual power consumption every year, once the advanced integrated circuit production process at the park becomes scalable, it said.
The bureau would also assist park tenants in installing rooftop solar systems, as well as apply low-carbon, smart power grid to the park’s public facilities, it added.

Exploring the true epicenter of Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:40:56 UTC
01:40:56 KST

The one-day trip begins at the geographical center of Taiwan: Puli Township’s (埔里) Hutou Mountain Geographic Center of Taiwan Monument (臺灣地理中心碑), embedded at the foot of Nantou County’s dense forested slopes.
It sits entrenched in forest vegetation amid the tall, spindly bodies and spiky heads of the betel nut trees; the air is cool, and its surroundings are mostly silent save the sounds of late-season cicadas.
Roughly two minutes from the first destination, and after a bend in Yongfeng Road (永豐路), there’s a glimpse of a resplendent golden dome on the horizon.
Photo: Shane O’Reilly
It’s the cap of the 135m-tall main building of the Chung Tai Chan Monastery (中台禪寺) located north of Puli Township.
Spread across 40 acres, it’s the world’s tallest Buddhist monastery building, serving as the head of the monastic order of Taiwan and a permanent home to a community of over 1,200 monks and nuns.
Within, there are several majestic halls, grand staircases, and a plethora of robust, towering statues, some standing 12m high. However, any in-depth exploration of the monastery requires a guide, and no photography is allowed.
Outside, opulent grounds encompass the Great Luminance Garden & Bell Pavilion, the beautifully landscaped Miaojue Park & Unity Bridge Park and the captivating Wood Sculpture Gallery.
The corresponding Chung Tai World Museum (中台世界博物館), located a 5-minute drive away, is an enormous feast for the senses.
Set across 22 acres, it’s a vast labyrinth of high-ceilinged showcase rooms connected with winding passageways, and enfilade-type layouts displaying over 1,500 religious artifacts.
The complex is so grand, yet it all feels so hidden from casual travellers, tucked away and enshrouded, available only to those who seek it out.
With a far more central location, the Puli Brewery (埔里酒廠) is an impressive multidisciplinary site.
Known for its production of traditional Shaoxing wine, it’s also an interactive exhibition center with a fascinating Liquor Museum & Shaoxing Story Hall featuring chambers and narrow passageways lined floor-to-ceiling with ancient porous earthenware urns.
The wine itself is an acquired taste, but at the sales center you’ll find all manner of locally-crafted goods beyond alcohol, from horse fat soap to shampoos, decorative urns, popsicles, meat products and more.
The nearby Niu Xiang Chu Garden Restaurant (牛相觸庭園餐坊) provides a uniquely playful setting with its Chinese-Style Botanical Gardens replete with wild chickens, ducks and a koi pond.
There’s plenty of children scurrying among a melange of bric-a-brac signposts, totems, props, antiques and giant figurines, while the adults eat at indoor and outdoor tables.
Dessert follows at Feeling18 LAB (烘焙研究所), a popular bakery brand. It specializes in artisanal French pastries that can be paired with internationally sourced coffees or milk teas.
The last stop of the day is as famed for its uniquely jade-green roofing as it is for its anomalous setting on the flank of Jinying Mountain (金鷹).
Dimu Temple (地母廟) is an elaborate, colorfully decorated Taoist temple doused in long strings of spherical golden lanterns.
An unforgettable sight with its back sunk into the mountainside, the structure has formed a mutual architectural and aesthetic symbiosis with its natural surroundings.
A short climb, the steep gradient levels out onto a large tiled forecourt before the main temple hall, adjoined by open balcony wings that allow intoxicating panoramic views of the surrounding basin and mountain range.

The People’s Liberation Army has been increasing its navy and air force activities in the region. The Chinese Coast Guard has likewise been ramping up their activities, and the civilian paramilitary People’s Armed Forces Maritime Militia has been backing up the navy and coast guard with alarming swarming maneuvers. The PRC claims most of the South China Sea through its U-shaped 10-dash

The laughter and indignation that essay generated among Taiwan aficionados is an indicator of how far Western journalism on Taiwan has come. Twenty years ago, it would have been another piece for the pile. Today, it is an obvious outlier. Shuster’s piece was
For a small nation, Taiwan has an unusually long list of territorial disputes. In part or in whole, it has disputes over the Spratly Islands (Nansha Islands, 南沙群島) with Vietnam, the Philippines, Malaysia and Brunei. It also has another territorial dispute with Vietnam over the Paracel Islands, and with Japan over the Senkaku Islands (Diaoyutai Islands, 釣魚台). Of course, the biggest territorial disputes are with the People’s Republic of China (PRC), which not only claims all of the above, but also Pratas Island (Dongsha, 東沙島), Kinmen, Penghu and all of Taiwan itself. More extreme heat days likely by end of century
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:40:54 UTC
01:40:54 KST

Taiwan could see an additional 53 days a year of extreme heat — when temperatures reach 36°C or higher — by the end of this century, Central Weather Administration specialist Chang Wan-yu (張琬玉) said yesterday.
The estimate was based on 100 years of data, which showed that average temperatures have risen by 1.5°C and summers have become longer, she said.
Under the most severe global warming estimates, temperatures could rise by a further 3.4°C by the end of the century, meaning Taiwan could see nearly two additional months per year of extreme heat, she added.
Photo: Liao Chen-huei, Taipei Times
In 2020, the Taipei weather station recorded 46 days in which temperatures surpassed 36°C, she said.
Global warming is directly impacting Taiwan’s weather systems, as the first day of temperatures dipping below 14°C and the first autumn front have steadily arrived later in the year, Chang said.
Rising temperatures also affect rainfall, with years of low rainfall becoming more frequent between 1960 and 2020, compared with before 1960, she said.
From 1990 to 2015, the maximum daily precipitation per year has become more extreme, she added.
The Oceanic Nino Index, a metric for tracking the El Nino phenomenon, has continued to rise from negative values at the start of this year to 1.8 between May and July, she said.
From June 2023 to June 2024, global temperatures rose to unprecedented levels for 13 consecutive months, with 2024 marking the hottest year since records began in 1850, Chang said.
Estimates for global temperature increases range from 1.5°C to 2°C, but a small discrepancy of 0.5°C could have a significant impact on the global climate, as it could raise the proportion of coral reefs experiencing bleaching from 70 percent to 99 percent, she said.
The extra 0.5°C could also mean that the proportion of the population exposed to extreme heat once every five years would rise from 14 percent to 37 percent, she added.
Compound climate events — such as droughts and heat waves occurring simultaneously or consecutively — could amplify their impacts, Chang said.
Meteorological droughts are poised to become more severe, frequent and widespread, while typhoons are expected to become more intense, but less frequent, she added.

Modi draws US chip leaders’ backing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:40:53 UTC
01:40:53 KST

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi yesterday launched a charm offensive for global investors at India’s top chip-industry event, drawing pledges from US firms Applied Materials Inc and Lam Research Corp for billions of dollars in outlays.
Marking India’s audacious bid to win a seat at the global chipmaking table, Modi touted the country’s vast pool of engineering graduates and semiconductor-friendly policies as assets international companies should take advantage of.
“The world urgently needs new and reliable locations for manufacturing,” Modi told the conference in New Delhi. “India is readying itself constantly.”
Photo: AFP
Modi is using the three-day Semicon event to display India’s fledgling chip and electronics industry that barely existed a decade ago. He is courting global semiconductor producers, potential partners and customers for India’s homegrown contenders, as well as equipment makers and parts suppliers all seeking to ride the artificial intelligence investment wave.
The stakes are high for an economy that has outpaced much of the world for years. Modi is trying to prove the nation has what it takes to become a hub in higher value-added industries such as chips, all part of a bid to further modernize the economy and keep it humming by bolstering exports. Expanding manufacturing is crucial for Modi’s vision of moving more workers from farms into better-paying jobs.
“Semicon in New Delhi is Modi’s way of signaling that India has a long-term commitment to growing the chip industry,” said Pranay Kotasthane, deputy director of Bangalore-based think tank Takshashila Institution. “That’s his message to global investors.”
More than 600 exhibitors, more than 150 speakers and 300 global companies are converging on a state-of-the-art convention center in New Delhi. There are to be start-up showcases and a student hackathon.
The event comes just two months after India pledged a further 1.9 trillion rupees (US$19.86 billion) in subsidies to boost local chip and electronics production. The first round of subsidies in 2020 and 2021 helped Apple Inc expand iPhone manufacturing in the South Asian region. It now makes 25 percent of its marquee device there.
India sought to replicate that momentum in semiconductors with an initial US$10 billion fund that helped drive early initiatives. Some of those are starting to bear fruit.
Conglomerates Tata Group and Murugappa Group have begun packaging and assembling chips, while US memory maker Micron Technology Inc has also commenced production. Tata is also building a chip fabrication plant in western Gujarat that is due to become operational in early 2028.
Executives from Micron and Tata spoke ahead of Modi, pledging to forge ahead with their local plans.
Micron plans to test and assemble hundreds of millions of chips in India next year after starting output from its Gujarat plant this year, chief executive officer Sanjay Mehrotra said.
Chip-equipment maker Applied Materials is to invest US$5 billion in India over the next decade, said Prabu Raja, president of the US company’s semiconductor products group.
Competitor Lam Research plans to invest about US$1 billion in a local manufacturing facility, chief operating officer Sesha Varadarajan told the audience.
Germany’s Infineon Technologies AG, known for power and automotive chips, boosted its workforce 28 percent in the country over the past year, chief executive officer Jochen Hanebeck said.
Countries around the world are committing massive budgets to making chips at home as the race for AI supremacy heats up. AI is already becoming ubiquitous in everything from self-driving vehicles and healthcare to finance and fraud detection.
However, as computing resources remain scarce, chips and chipmakers are fast becoming kingmakers in deciding who is winning.
Although India’s push is in early stages, it is accelerating efforts to build a domestic industry spanning the entire supply chain. It is offering seed funding to start-ups working on semiconductor products, support for chip-making gear as well as for new fabs and assembly plants.

Max Verstappen on Wednesday needed about 35 minutes to overcome 100 karting drivers in a Red Bull event at Silverstone.
Organizers had allowed a maximum 30 laps and 75 minutes for the Dutch driver to work his way through the field from the back on a modified kart track at the British Grand Prix circuit, but he needed far less.
Starting 101st, the 28-year-old four-time Formula One champion overtook 64 drivers, who were then eliminated, on the chaotic opening lap, with many of his opponents crashing among themselves.
Photo: AP
Dutch F1 journalist Jacky Martens, who regularly reports on Verstappen’s races, started on pole and was the last driver overtaken in a field that included social media content creators, celebrities and Red Bull athletes.
“When I went to the grid and I saw where I had to start, with 100 karts in front of me, I was a little bit worried,” Verstappen said. “After my first lap with all the carnage, I did think: ‘OK, we have got this under control.’”
Many got blocked on the track after a pileup that prompted a full-course yellow flag. Verstappen went off track, but was able to return.
Verstappen, who finished second in Formula 1’s Spanish Grand Prix on Sunday, was up to 37th two minutes into the race.
He went off track again, but stayed comfortably faster than most drivers, none of them with any significant professional driving experience.
“I think this is the best one yet,” joked Verstappen, winner of 71 grands prix.
“My first lap was quite incredible,” he added. “There was a lot happening and actually a few cars got stuck and I always managed to be on the other side, so didn’t get stuck.”
Verstappen has yet to win a grand prix this season and is sixth in a championship dominated by Mercedes.
“It’s my first win of the year, so I take this one,” he said.

CGA plans a historic 2027 visit to Philippines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:40:51 UTC
01:40:51 KST

Coast Guard Administration (CGA) ships are scheduled to sail to the Philippines bearing the words “Taiwan Coast Guard” in a high-profile visit in October next year, the first such visit by a Taiwanese maritime law enforcement vessel to the Southeast Asian nation, the agency said yesterday.
The CGA also confirmed that it had donated one of its decommissioned patrol vessels to the Philippines in a rare transfer of a retired ship to a nondiplomatic ally.
The Republic of China (ROC) Navy last made such a visit in 1974, shortly before the Philippines switched diplomatic recognition to the People’s Republic of China in 1975.
Photo courtesy of the Coast Guard Administration
Official naval visits between Taiwan and the Philippines have effectively halted for half a century, a senior government official said on condition of anonymity.
Unlike the navy’s goodwill missions, which involve an annual deployment of three ships intended to project force and conduct more sensitive operations, the CGA’s nonmilitary functions make it a more effective tool for overcoming Taiwan’s diplomatic difficulties, the official said.
In September last year, the CGA’s 4,000-tonne Chiayi-class vessel Taipei (台北) visited Palau on a goodwill mission.
The CGA’s planned visit to the Philippines next year would carry considerable geopolitical significance, the official said.
Taiwan and the Philippines are both targets of China’s “gray zone” tactics, prompting the two sides to strengthen cooperation in maritime law enforcement and regional security, the official said.
The efforts include the attendance of a senior Philippine Coast Guard official at Central Police University’s graduation ceremony last year and Taiwan’s donation of a retrofitted 500-tonne disaster relief and rescue vessel to the Philippines on Wednesday.
According to media reports citing information from VesselFinder, a Philippine law enforcement vessel named Bling No. 1 sailed from the Port of Kaohsiung for sea trials before returning.
Although stripped of its armaments and CGA markings, the vessel resembled the Lienchiang (連江), which was decommissioned on Oct. 27, 2023, or the Kinmen (金門).
The CGA said in a statement that the transfer was “handled according to usual practice.”
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs declined to comment on whether it was the first time Taiwan had donated a vessel to the Philippines.
Su Tzu-yu (蘇紫雲), a research fellow at the Institute for National Defense and Security Research, said the donation was part of an international trend to counter China’s “expansionist behavior” at sea.
Japan is to transfer decommissioned Abukuma-class destroyer escorts to the Philippines, while the US has transferred many patrol boats to the country, Su said.
“China’s gray zone threats have prompted collaboration between the ‘white fleets,’” Su said. “This shows that Beijing’s actions have backfired.”
Next year’s eight-day goodwill mission is to reportedly involve celestial navigation training using sextants, maritime operations and law enforcement instruction for 100 CGA personnel and students in Central Police University’s Department of Maritime Police.
The trip is to facilitate exchanges with the Philippines on non-traditional security issues, including maritime humanitarian assistance and combating crime at sea.
The approach would not only help reduce political sensitivities among neighboring countries, but also demonstrate Taiwan’s flexibility and adaptability as a maritime nation, the official said.

Citi supports Taiwanese companies’ growth in central and eastern Europe amid supply-chain shifts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:40:49 UTC
01:40:49 KST

Amid ongoing shifts in global supply chains, Taiwanese companies are increasingly seeking to diversify their operations, move closer to customers and strengthen their presence in key overseas markets. Citi is drawing on its global network and on-the-ground capabilities to help clients assess opportunities and navigate their expansion in Central and Eastern Europe, including Poland, Citi Country Officer for Poland Elzbieta Czetwertynska said on Monday in Taipei.
She told a small group of Taiwanese reporters that the needs of Taiwanese companies in the region span across multiple industries.
Citi supports clients by providing local market insights and solutions tailored to their cross-border business needs.
Photo on courtesy of Citi
A strategic gateway to Europe
The trend reflects the growing importance of “near-shoring” and “friend-shoring,” as companies seek to reduce exposure to geopolitical tensions and supply-chain disruptions by locating production closer to major markets or in countries regarded as strategic partners.
Poland is particularly well positioned because of its location between Western Europe and the wider Central and Eastern European region, Czetwertynska said. Poland’s economy is approaching the US$1 trillion milestone and progressing toward developed market status. GDP growth is projected at approximately 3.5-3.6 percent this year, around three times the EU average, she said.
Its established industrial base and skilled workforce could complement Taiwan’s strength in technology and hardware manufacturing.
Trade and investment ties deepen
The relationship is also being reinforced by rapidly growing trade. Bilateral trade exceeded US$2.5 billion in 2025, according to Taiwan’s Ministry of Economic Affairs, with integrated circuits, semiconductors and LCD panels accounting for about 60 percent of Poland’s imports from Taiwan.
Polish imports of computers, servers and electronic components from Taiwan surged about 500 percent in the first half of 2026 from a year earlier, underscoring the growing role of AI and data-center investment in the bilateral relationship.
Green energy transition, supply chain security and digitalization are among the key investment themes, Czetwertynska said.
AI infrastructure offers opportunities
AI infrastructure is likely to be one of the most promising areas. Taiwanese companies involved in AI servers, GPU systems, server racks, power supplies, liquid cooling, thermal management, networking and data-center power systems could use Poland as a production or service base for the European market.
The opportunity is not limited to final assembly. Taiwanese companies could also establish local operations in testing and packaging, equipment maintenance, precision machinery, automation, vacuum systems, factory infrastructure and semiconductor equipment components, Czetwertynska said.
Poland’s automotive industry offers another potential entry point, providing Taiwanese suppliers with a base from which to serve European automakers and parts manufacturers, she said.
Green energy transition could create opportunities in battery-management systems, power electronics, inverters and energy-management systems as Poland expands renewable power, energy storage and grid infrastructure.
Beyond manufacturing
Another emerging area is drones. Poland accounted for nearly 60 percent of Taiwan’s drone exports in 2025, making it Taiwan’s largest export market for the products. The two markets could deepen cooperation by combining Poland’s system-integration capabilities with Taiwan’s strengths in key drone components, Czetwertynska said.
Poland as a regional platform
The potential extends beyond Poland itself. Its position within the EU means companies establishing operations there can use the country as a base for serving customers across the bloc, while Poland’s proximity to Ukraine could also become strategically important when reconstruction begins.
The reconstruction of Ukraine could eventually generate more than US$500 billion in economic opportunities, with Poland expected to play an important role as a regional gateway.
For Taiwanese companies, however, establishing a European base also means navigating a more complex regulatory environment, Czetwertynska said. A factory in Poland is likely to serve customers across the EU, exposing companies to requirements involving carbon emissions, supply-chain transparency, sustainability and other regulations.
The longer-term opportunity, Czetwertynska said, is therefore not simply to use Poland as a lower-cost production location, but to build a deeper presence that connects Taiwanese technology supply chains with European industrial markets.
Taiwanese companies are increasingly moving beyond exports toward local manufacturing, research and development, industry partnerships and joint ventures.
Citi’s role
Citi has supported clients through changing market environments. With a presence in over 90 markets, Citi helps clients capture cross-border opportunities around the world, said Christie Chang, Citi Country Officer for Taiwan and Chairman of Citibank Taiwan Ltd.
Through close collaboration between its Taiwan and Poland teams, Citi helps companies expand into the European and Central and Eastern European (CEE) markets.
Citi provides insights on the local investment environment, macroeconomic developments, and geopolitical trends, while offering cross-border banking solutions including trade finance, supply chain finance, foreign exchange, cash management, and corporate financing.
Through the One Citi model, clients benefit from a consistent and seamless banking experience across different markets.

Former Kosovar president Hashim Thaci on Wednesday was sentenced to 25 years in prison after being found guilty of war crimes committed during the war for independence from Serbia in 1998 and 1999.
Thaci resigned from office nearly six years ago to face the charges at the EU-backed Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague, Netherlands. He was convicted of four counts of war crimes, including murder, torture, cruel treatment and arbitrary detention.
He and the prosecutors, who had asked for a stricter sentence, can appeal.
Photo: Reuters
The judgement sparked anger among Thaci’s supporters and was a crushing blow for a man who was once embraced by the West, invited to the 1999 peace talks in France and seen as the leader who could guide Kosovo to independence.
Presiding Judge Charles Smith said that Thaci participated in and encouraged crimes, including by promoting individuals involved in crimes, and “showed a ruthless ability to remove and eliminate political impediments” to his and other commanders’ leadership.
Wearing a suit and tie, Thaci stood in silence as Smith read out the sentence.
Kosovar Minister of Foreign Affairs Glauk Konjufca condemned the verdicts as “a terrible judgement for Kosovo, for our people and for our liberation war.”
Hundreds of supporters waited at a park near the courthouse in The Hague and some clashed briefly with Dutch riot police, who said on X that they detained two people.
In Kosovo’s capital, Pristina, thousands of people watched the hearing live on a huge screen and were stunned by the sentence.
Some shouted “UCK,” the Albanian-language acronym for the Kosovo Liberation Army that Thaci once led before entering politics.
One supporter, Bekim Fetahu, said the verdict was “a catastrophic decision.”
“They [judges] have put the victims together with the aggressors,” Fetahu said.
Later, masked protesters threw stones at the wall surrounding the compound of the EU Rule of Law Mission in Kosovo on the outskirts of Pristina, smashing several windows.
Smith said that Thaci “used his position, leadership, authority and standing” to encourage crimes and failed to investigate or punish abuse by UCK fighters.
However, he also stressed that the trial was “not about the legitimacy of the Kosovo Liberation Army” or its ultimate goal of securing independence for Kosovo, which at the time was a province in Serbia.
Specialist Prosecutor Kimberly West applauded the judgement.
“Certain individuals exploited those war circumstances to commit grave crimes and it is to the credit of Kosovo that those individuals are now being held accountable,” West said in a statement.
In Belgrade, Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic said “we have no reason to rejoice” and expressed concern that the verdict would not hold after appeals.
Vucic was critical that multiple other alleged crimes against ethnic Serbian civilians have not been taken into account, claiming anti-Serb bias.
“No responsibility has been established for the toughest crimes,” he said. “Serbs are always [war] criminals, and others are liberators and heroes.”
Thaci was on trial with three other former UCK leaders who fought Serb forces in the 1998-1999 war and are widely regarded as national heroes in Kosovo. They pleaded not guilty to all charges against them.
The four were acquitted on six charges of crimes against humanity because the judges said the prosecutors failed to prove that crimes were committed as part of a widespread and systematic attack on civilians.
They were found guilty of the war crimes of the arbitrary detention of 385 people, cruel treatment of 49, torture of 303 detainees and the murder of 96 people.
Thaci and the other defendants, Kadri Veseli, Rexhep Selimi and Jakup Krasniqi, all maintained their innocence. Veseli was sentenced to 18 years, Selimi to 13 years and Krasniqi to 25 years in prison.

As Pete Crow-Armstrong came up with the bases loaded in the eighth inning, the Wrigley Field crowd chanted “M-V-Pete” — and not for the first time on Wednesday night.
The fans serenaded the Chicago star after his first home run, his 43rd to break Billy Williams’ Cubs record for left-handed hitters. They made their feelings known after his RBI triple and after his 44th home run.
Even when Crow-Armstrong struck out on five pitches in the eighth, he still received a standing ovation on his way back to the dugout at the end of a 3 for 4 night with three RBIs and three runs in an 8-4 victory over the Atlanta Braves, his seventh multi-home-run game of the season.
Photo: AFP
With Shohei Ohtani still on the injured list with right biceps inflammation, Crow-Armstrong keeps hitting homers, closing in on the first 40-40 season in Cubs history, putting the finishing touches on his Most Valuable Player (MVP) case, at least as far as Cubs fans are concerned.
“You’re shaking your head in amazement, sometimes,” Cubs manager Craig Counsell said. “In amazement. You know, you don’t get to see this. That’s what I told Alex [Bregman]: ‘We don’t get to see things like this.’ You spend your whole life in baseball and you just don’t see this happen on a baseball field.”
Yet as he has gone from breakthrough player to MVP candidate to MVP favorite, Crow-Armstrong has been unfazed by the pressure, his performance unwavering as the Cubs chase a wild-card spot.
“I keep it pretty simple,” Crow-Armstrong said. “I enjoy just kind of laying low, as I always do and always will. I’ve got a really nice support system.”
Only one home run behind the Philadelphia Phillies’ Kyle Schwarber for the major league lead, Crow-Armstrong is hitting. 283 with 105 RBIs, 29 doubles and 37 stolen bases to go with Gold Glove-caliber defense in center field.
Crow-Armstrong’s breakthrough season at age 24 has him at or near the top of every offensive metric in the National League while also tapping out the vocabulary of Wednesday’s winning starter, Shota Imanaga.
“We can always say he’s great, or he’s excellent, but really there’s no words to describe him,” Imanaga said through an interpreter. “So I’ll think of a new word in English for that.”
In New York, Pete Alonso’s storybook return to Citi Field continued after he hit another home run against his former team, sparking another important win for the late-charging Baltimore Orioles and earning himself another ovation from Mets fans still smarting over his departure last year.
The slugger’s first-inning drive was the first of four home runs for the Orioles, who beat the Mets 7-1 to finish a three-game sweep and move within 2-1/2 games of the Chicago White Sox for the last American League playoff berth.
Elsewhere, the Cleveland Guardians took sole possession of first place in the American League Central with a 6-3 victory over the White Sox, while the Cincinnati Reds beat the Los Angeles Dodgers 6-2 and the Milwaukee Brewers sank the Pittsburgh Pirates 5-4 to sweep the series.
The San Francisco Giants pipped the St Louis Cardinals 6-5 in 10 innings, the Minnesota Twins outlasted the New York Yankees 5-4 in 13 innings, the Tampa Bay Rays defeated the Athletics 4-3, the Phillies blanked the Nationals 3-0 and the San Diego Padres rocked the Colorado Rockies 9-3.

Realizing Taiwan’s AI ambitions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:40:45 UTC
01:40:45 KST

When Taiwan Power Co (Taipower) vice president Tsai Chih-meng (蔡志孟) visited Paris last week, the discussion was not about another spectacular artificial intelligence (AI) investment announcement. It was about the less visible infrastructure needed to make those investments possible: power grids, transformers, fuel supplies and the ability to deliver electricity where and when industry needs it.
Tsai on Thursday last week cochaired the Taiwan-France Economic Cooperation Conference with MEDEF International Sustainable Cities Task Force chairman Gerard Wolf. The meeting was organized by the Chinese International Economic Cooperation Association and MEDEF International, with the involvement of the Taipei Representative Office in France. Representative to France Hao Pei-chih (郝培芝) also addressed the meeting.
The program showed how much the energy discussion has changed. The three sessions dealt with grid modernization, infrastructure resilience in the AI era, and energy security and geopolitics. For Taiwan, AI policy is becoming electricity policy.
Taipower has already received 75 transmission-level connection requests from data centers, representing 4,523 megawatts of requested capacity by the end of July. However, a request for capacity is not the same thing as a functioning data center.
Of the 47 requests that had received Taipower’s agreement, about 40 percent expired before a formal application was submitted.
Governments and grid operators need to know which projects are likely to happen, where they would be located and when they would need electricity. Otherwise, billions could be committed to infrastructure for projects that remain on paper, while more mature investments wait for connections.
This issue is not unique to Taiwan. France is also changing the way large electricity users are connected, paying more attention to the maturity of projects rather than the date on which a request entered the queue. That creates an obvious field for Taiwan-France cooperation.
Taipower’s Chang Chia-hsi (張家熙) spoke in Paris about grid upgrades in response to the AI wave. Lionel Besombes of EDF International Networks discussed smart metering. Ancillary Power founder and CEO Ivan Cheng (鄭智文) presented a Taiwanese view of grid resilience.
Behind these technical subjects lies a political question: How much infrastructure should be built, for whom and who should pay for it?
A new data center or semiconductor plant can require major upgrades to substations and transmission lines. If a project is delayed by five years, those costs do not disappear. If several very large consumers arrive in the same area, the problem becomes even more acute.
Demand management, storage and better information can reduce some of the pressure, but they do not remove the need for physical infrastructure. The same is true of equipment.
Fortune Electric, whose representatives I met during the conference, manufactures transformers and other power equipment. This is another part of the Taiwan-France relationship that deserves more attention. Taiwan is not simply a market for European energy technology. Taiwanese companies can also contribute to the huge investment now required in European grids.
The wider Taiwanese mission in France reflects this shift. The association’s program included meetings with major energy companies and grid actors, including RTE, TotalEnergies and Hitachi Energy. This is important, because Taiwan’s energy problem does not stop at the grid.
The country remains highly dependent on imported fuels. Taipower Department of Fuels deputy director Chiang Kuan-shen (蔣光聲) spoke in Paris about reserves and diversification at a time of growing geopolitical uncertainty.
For liquefied natural gas, diversification is useful, but has limits. Buying gas from more countries reduces dependence on a single supplier. Yet the gas still has to reach Taiwan by ship.
That is why I said in Paris that Taiwan should look at energy security in terms of different kinds of dependence.
Gas provides useful flexibility, but it requires frequent deliveries. Nuclear power also depends on imported fuel and technical services, but the fuel can be planned over much longer periods. Offshore wind produces electricity locally, but requires a stronger and more flexible grid. Geothermal can provide firm domestic generation, but the first obstacle is finding and proving the resource.
For geothermal, the main risk comes before the plant produces a single kilowatt-hour. Exploration wells are expensive and some will fail. France has experience with mechanisms that share part of that geological risk. This is the kind of practical tool that could be discussed with Taiwanese partners.
The same reasoning applies to nuclear power. A restart of nuclear plants is not simply a decision to turn a reactor back on. Fuel must be procured, maintenance organized, qualified suppliers available and spent-fuel storage managed. If Taiwan chooses that path, these issues have to be planned together.
The objective should not be to choose one technology and expect it to solve every problem.
Taiwan needs technologies with different strengths and weaknesses. Gas, nuclear, offshore wind, solar, storage and geothermal do not create the same vulnerabilities. A more resilient system is one that does not depend too heavily on a single fuel, route or technical solution.
Taiwan’s semiconductor industry is central to global supply chains. Europe has spent several years discussing how to reduce the risks surrounding its semiconductor supply, but chip security also depends on the reliability of the electricity system that produces those chips.
Taiwan and France have a reason to move beyond general discussions about “energy cooperation.” They could compare electricity demand scenarios linked to AI and semiconductor investment, share experience on grid planning and large consumers, work on storage and flexibility, and select a small number of concrete projects where cooperation can actually be measured.
Some cooperation would be French technology moving to Taiwan. Some should also be Taiwanese technology moving to Europe.
The office, the association and MEDEF International have already created the political and business channels. Taipower and French grid companies have technical experience. Taiwanese manufacturers have equipment and industrial capacity. The next stage is to connect these pieces.
The energy transition is often presented as a debate about how electricity is produced. For Taiwan, that is too narrow. The more important question is whether the entire electricity system — generation, fuel, grids, storage and equipment — could support the industrial strategy the country has chosen.
For an economy betting heavily on semiconductors and AI, that might become one of the most important economic questions of the decade.
Romain Blachier is president of Association France-Formosa, an energy and Asia consultant, an associate fellow at the Fondation Jean-Jaures, works in renewable energy, and teaches energy policy and geopolitics.
Taiwan’s domestic political situation is following recognizable political rhythms, while the international environment surrounding Taiwan is undergoing a major transformation. Within Taiwan, there are ongoing battles between the legislative and executive branches over the budget, and between cities and the central government over resources. Tensions between political parties dominate headlines and consume much of the attention of party leaders. Jockeying is underway for local elections this November and national elections in 2028. And the longstanding philosophical debate inside Taiwan over how best to protect Taiwan and promote the good life remains unresolved. Amidst all of this, Taiwan continues to function well. It

At a Frankfurt news conference announcing his first squad as Germany manager, the former Liverpool coach referenced the state election landslide win by the anti-immigration AfD on Sept. 6.
The party won almost 44 percent of the vote in the former East German state of Saxony-Anhalt and expects strong results in elections on Sunday in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
Photo: Reuters
Klopp took over the Germany job in July after the four-time FIFA World Cup winners suffered a third straight early elimination at the tournament. The 59-year-old has often spoke out about social issues during his time as manager of Liverpool, Borussia Dortmund and FSV Mainz 05.
While not mentioning the AfD by name, Klopp advocated for adopting “positive patriotism,” while saying: “I don’t want to entrust national pride to the wrong people.”
“A crazy amount of things have happened not that long ago,” he said. “There was a vote which some people probably found OK, but others would have thought ‘good heavens, what’s going on here?’”
“From the perspective of someone in sport, I’d like to reclaim the flag for myself and for us. When we wave it, I don’t want that someone thinks: ‘what’s going on with you?’ I want that they think you’re happy and you understand how lucky you are to be born in this wonderful country or to have moved here and live here,” he added.
Topics involving patriotism and nationalism are often sensitive in Germany, a country still at pains to atone for its dark history of Nazi rule, World War II and the Holocaust.
Speaking of national pride, Klopp said he was “not even sure if one can — or is allowed to — use that term anymore without it being misunderstood.”
“I can be proud of being German and still be open, diverse, kind and friendly,” he said.
It was more important that the country had enough doctors and caregivers, but soccer can “foster a sense of community here, allowing us to truly feel the power of sport,” the coach said.
Klopp took the unusual step of naming a huge 44-man squad for four upcoming UEFA Nations League matches, despite match day lists being restricted to 23 players.
“It’s very unusual that you’ve got four games in two weeks with the national team,” Klopp said. “I want to get to know as many players as possible in that time.”
Klopp won the UEFA Champions League and Premier League during a trophy-laden nine-year stint at Liverpool.

French presidential hopeful Attal vows to build ‘United States of Europe’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:40:42 UTC
01:40:42 KST

PARIS — French presidential candidate Gabriel Attal laid out an ambitious pro-European platform for his campaign Thursday, vowing to make France part of a powerful, economically muscular “United States of Europe” if he wins next year’s race to succeed President Emmanuel Macron.
“The great mission of my generation is to realize the European dream and to give birth to the United States of Europe,” he said, borrowing language from Victor Hugo. “I don’t want my generation to witness Europe becoming the 51st U.S. state or the 24th Chinese province.”
Speaking to lawmakers, former ministers and employees at an aerospace startup in the heart of Champagne country, Attal laid out a series of proposals that appeared to be drawn straight from the playbooks of Mario Draghi and Enrico Letta, the Italian statesmen who authored two landmark reports on the bloc's economic agenda.
Advertisement
To better compete with the U.S. and China, Attal proposed implementing a two-speed EU so like-minded partners can more quickly merge their economies, regulatory frameworks and labor and capital via a new dedicated treaty to be approved by citizens via referendum. Attal also advocated for joint European debt, removing intra-bloc trade barriers and encouraging bloc-wide mergers, especially in telecoms and financial services.
Attal’s advisers told reporters that the former prime minister is trying to stake out a position as one of the most pro-European options in a crowded field of candidates. The 37-year-old centrist has struggled to break through, and polls have repeatedly shown him lagging behind his main ideological rival, Edouard Philippe, and euroskeptic front-runner Marine Le Pen.
But since launching his campaign in May, Philippe has stayed relatively quiet on matters relating to Brussels — which gives Attal a way to better distinguish his campaign from that of Philippe.
It’s a risky strategy, though. Voters in France are less sanguine about the bloc’s future than other Europeans, with many still frustrated after the Commission last year pushed through a massive trade deal with Latin America that was widely viewed domestically as a threat to the French agriculture industry. The EU is also seen as a source of environmental rules that French farmers consider too strict while business see the bloc as a source of red tape.
Attal in his speech paid tribute to Macron’s European legacy while also criticizing European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, accusing her of overlooking the bloc’s problems in her Wednesday State of the Union speech — which he called “too little, too late.” He also hit out against the trade deal she agreed to with U.S. President Donald Trump last year.
Should Attal win, it will be up to von der Leyen to decide the professional fate of his romantic partner, Industry Commissioner Stéphane Séjourné, given the potential conflict of interest. Séjourné swore an oath upon taking office to prioritize EU interests over national matters, and his term runs beyond the French presidential election in April 2027.
Advertisement
Séjourné said in a recent interview that he did not believe there would be a conflict of interest if Attal won the election but added that it was a “legitimate” question.
Attal campaign director Maxime Cordier said a group of MEPs will endorse the plans in an op-ed in the coming days. MEP Valérie Hayer, who heads the Renew group and backs Attal’s presidential bid, stressed that Attal was the first candidate to pitch a project to reform the bloc and she accused the European Commission and some member countries of “inertia” in implementing the Draghi agenda.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:40:41 UTC
01:40:41 KST

Taiwan yesterday handed Japan more than NT$300 million (US$9.4 million) in public donations to help rebuild communities affected by a magnitude 7.1 earthquake that struck Kumamoto Prefecture in late July.
Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) presented the funds to Kazuyuki Katayama, head of the Taipei Office of the Japan-Taiwan Exchange Association, during a ceremony at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs headquarters in Taipei.
The July 28 earthquake killed 38 people and damaged nearly 43,000 homes.
Photo: George Tsorng, Taipei Times
On Aug. 1, the ministry commissioned the International Cooperation and Development Fund to open and administer a public donation account, marking the first time the ministry had asked the organization to run a public disaster-relief fundraiser.
The account raised more than NT$300 million within a month, with the entire amount to be used for recovery and reconstruction, Lin said.
“Kumamoto’s safety is a shared concern for Taiwan and Japan,” he said, adding that Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC) and members of its supply chain have established operations there, bringing more Taiwanese to the prefecture to work and live.
Lin thanked businesses, civic groups and Taiwanese communities overseas for contributing, saying the response reflected the “family like” bonds between Taiwan and Japan.
Katayama thanked Taiwan’s government and people for the donations, saying that the swift and broad response demonstrated the close friendship between Taiwan and Japan.
Tomoaki Motojima, who heads a Taiwan-based association representing people from Kumamoto, also expressed gratitude to Taiwanese donors and spoke about the earthquake’s impact and the work needed to rebuild affected communities.
Lin said Taiwan and Japan had repeatedly assisted each other following major disasters, including Taiwan’s 1999 Jiji earthquake (also known as the 921 earthquake), Japan’s 2011 Tohoku earthquake and tsunami, the 2016 Kumamoto earthquakes and last year’s Hualien earthquake.
“At the moments when we needed each other most, Taiwan and Japan have never been absent,” he said.
Lin called for deeper bilateral cooperation on disaster prevention, mitigation, relief and post-disaster reconstruction, adding that both sides face frequent earthquakes and typhoons.
Taiwan’s government previously donated NT$5 million for disaster relief, while President William Lai (賴清德), Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim (蕭美琴) and Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) each donated NT$200,000 in a personal capacity.
TSMC, which operates a plant in Kikuyo, Kumamoto, separately pledged ￥250 million (US$1.6 million) for reconstruction.

Be wary of Beijing’s new exit regulations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:40:40 UTC
01:40:40 KST

China’s new entry and exit regulations officially took effect on Tuesday, and the Mainland Affairs Council (MAC) has warned that the new rules expand authorities’ discretion in enforcing entry and exit controls.
Matters such as import and export controls, and national security could serve as grounds for restricting a person’s departure. In certain cases involving national security or investigations, authorities might even withhold from someone the fact that they have been barred from leaving the country, as well as the reasons and avenues for appeal. For Taiwanese businesspeople, high-tech workers and semiconductor professionals who frequently travel across the Taiwan Strait, what they should consider is not whether they can get into the country, but whether they would be allowed to return home.
Every country has the right to control its borders, and national security can be a legitimate reason to restrict freedom of movement. The question is what constraints are placed on that power. Administrative agencies are generally required to justify any unfavorable actions. This is because if the parties involved do not know what conduct was deemed problematic or what legal basis was invoked, it is difficult to present evidence or challenge the application of the law. When the reasons are withheld, avenues for legal recourse become meaningless.
This issue is particularly important for Taiwan’s technology industry. When tech workers cross borders, they carry more than just luggage — they carry smartphones, laptops, cloud accounts, work e-mails and technical documents. When export and import controls, and national security are incorporated into exit restrictions, companies can no longer treat the risk of traveling to China as a mere matter of business trip management. They should first establish what data can be carried across the border, which files cannot be downloaded onto personal devices and how employees should respond if they are asked to provide electronic data.
The government should also provide more detailed risk advisories. Tourists, semiconductor research and development managers, sales staff with access to customer data and civil servants who have handled sensitive government operations face different legal and information security risks. The government could develop specific guidelines based on industry, job responsibilities and sensitivity of information to which people have access — including who should avoid carrying work devices, which data should be removed in advance and where family members and employers can seek assistance when someone is barred from leaving China.
Businesses should also incorporate this issue into their corporate governance frameworks. Semiconductor, artificial intelligence, information and communications technology and precision manufacturing companies should review their policies on business travel to China and assess whether meetings could instead be conducted in a third country or via video conference. If travel to China is absolutely necessary, companies should provide dedicated devices that do not contain sensitive data and establish daily check in and emergency response procedures. This is not a call for companies to halt all cross-strait business dealings, but to assess the risks in light of the changing legal environment.
For cross strait exchanges to be sustainable, participants must be able to reasonably predict their legal situation. Following the implementation of China’s new regulations, the government should continue to issue risk warnings, and companies should re-evaluate their travel and information security policies.
Eason Chen is an engineer.

Houthis’ advance leaves Gulf states with tough choice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:40:40 UTC
01:40:40 KST

The Houthi capture of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline is reshaping the balance of power in the Gulf, strengthening Iran’s hand and confronting Saudi Arabia and its neighbors with a difficult choice: absorb mounting costs or seek accommodation with Tehran.
By securing a position overlooking Bab el-Mandeb, one of the world’s most important shipping arteries, the Iran-aligned group has opened a second pressure point, threatening the Saudi oil exports diverted from the Strait of Hormuz.
The calculation, according to regional officials and analysts, is straightforward: By threatening Red Sea shipping while Iran chokes off Hormuz, Tehran and the Houthis can raise oil prices and fuel inflation while narrowing the region’s prospects of relying on Washington to resolve the crisis.
They said the strategy is designed to force a stark choice on Gulf states: put up with growing economic pain from the squeeze on their oil exports and Iranian strikes or engage with Iran to protect trade, energy flows and economic stability.
“The Houthi capture of strategic islands near Bab el-Mandeb is a game changer,” Middle East analyst Fawaz Gerges said. “It changes the balance of power and gives them far greater geopolitical and geoeconomic leverage over Saudi Arabia, the Gulf, the United States and global trade.”
Riyadh rerouted much of its crude through Red Sea ports since the war effectively closed the strait on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula, but on Friday last week it closed the pipeline that carried the oil after it came under attack.
US President Donald Trump’s reported refusal to agree to a Saudi request for the US to strike the Houthis, combined with mounting economic costs, is reinforcing a view in some Gulf capitals that negotiations with Tehran are no longer a choice, but a necessity for self-preservation, regional sources said.
A meeting in Oman on Monday between Gulf Arab ministers of foreign affairs and their Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araqchi, to discuss a possible arrangement on the Strait of Hormuz has been postponed due to disagreements over the terms of the talks, a Gulf source said.
The gathering was part of an Omani and Iranian push to secure a temporary framework for managing shipping through the waterway, a critical artery for global oil exports.
Omani Minister of Foreign Affairs Badr Albusaidi said the regional meeting scheduled for Monday in Salalah had been postponed “in the interests of consensus.”
“We remain committed to fostering dialogue that supports stability and lasting co-operation in our region,” he wrote on X, without elaborating on the reasons for the delay.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Sunday last week that he had held good talks with United Arab Emirates Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan in New Delhi on the sidelines of the BRICS leaders’ summit.
“We agreed to put the past aside and look forward to the future, and how we can build a future together,” he said.
The dilemma for the Gulf states is that geography is immutable. Decades of confrontation have failed to alter a simple reality: Iran’s position alongside the region’s energy and trade arteries makes it an unavoidable player in any Gulf security equation.
Whatever Gulf leaders think of the Islamic republic, it remains a reality they cannot bypass or simply wish away and the conflict triggered by US and Israeli attacks on Iran has blown apart decades of diplomatic efforts to contain it.
Asked on Sunday if he was concerned about the Gulf states meeting with Iran, Trump said that was up to them.
Alex Vatanka of the Middle East Institute said the question for Gulf states might increasingly be less whether they trust Iran than how to protect their interests and survive hostilities Washington cannot quickly end.
That could push them toward parallel diplomacy with Tehran and, over time, a broader security strategy less dependent on the US alone.
“The Gulf states are contemplating the basic reality that they might have to cut a deal with the Iranians on their own, regardless of whether they hurt American feelings or not, because America can’t get them out of this quagmire,” he said.
The flareup revives a struggle that long predates the US-Iran conflict. The Houthis, drawn from Yemen’s Zaydi Shiite minority, fought a series of wars with Saudi Arabia before seizing Sana’a in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led intervention the following year.
Despite years of air strikes and cross border warfare, they survived, expanded their capabilities and emerged as one of Iran’s most effective regional allies.
The Houthis are pursuing their own longstanding conflict with Riyadh while exploiting a position that gives them leverage far beyond Yemen’s borders to create growing value for Tehran.
“The Houthis are not traditional proxies,” former US negotiator Aaron David Miller said. “They can weaponize geography and have a dramatic impact on the international economy and on the global oil economy.”
One regional official said that the Houthi advance was the latest step in a careful strategy by Tehran.
“For Iran, this is a chess game. They plan what comes next. They don’t push all their buttons at the same time out of panic,” the regional official said.
“The Houthis are the only proxy Iranian ally with formidable operational capabilities left,” the official said.
Washington’s economic squeeze on Iran is having an impact, but the unintended consequence is that it is squeezing the US’ Gulf partners into reconsidering whether confrontation with Tehran is sustainable, a Gulf source said.

Russian academics signed an anti-war letter four years ago. Now the FSB is questioning them again, and universities are refusing to renew some of their contracts.
The FSB and administrators at universities and research institutes are pressuring scholars who signed an anti-war letter in 2022, as well as employees whose names appeared in a leaked database of Smart Voting users, according to T-invariant.
University and research institute employees across Russia told the outlet that scholars are being summoned for questioning or having their employment contracts go unrenewed.
One scholar in the Urals said an FSB officer assigned to his university summoned him to a meeting because he had signed the letter. The officer asked what he thought about the war in 2022 and what he thinks about it now. The scholar said his signature had caused him no problems in the four years since he signed the letter and that removing it now would be pointless — the officer showed him a printout of a spring 2022 archived copy of the webpage containing the letter.
An employee at a Siberian research institute was summoned for questioning by an FSB representative following a request from Moscow. He asked where she had gotten the link to the letter and whom she had forwarded it to.
According to T-invariant, pressure on scholars over their opposition views is especially widespread at St. Petersburg State University. Oleg Shaidulin, who formerly headed the political department at the local Center E anti-extremism unit, serves as deputy to the university’s vice rector for security.
Several former St. Petersburg State University employees said their immediate supervisors told them their contracts had not been renewed because they were on a blacklist. A former employee of one of the university’s IT departments called the system a “traffic light”: Employees are placed on yellow or red lists. She was put on an internal list of employees deemed “politically unreliable” because she had registered on the Smart Voting website.
Employees can get off the St. Petersburg State University blacklist by donating to the Defenders of the Fatherland Foundation, which supports Russian military personnel, or becoming lecturers for the pro-government Znanie Society.
One T-invariant source said HSE University in St. Petersburg and the European University at St. Petersburg had also refused to renew employees’ contracts.

Ireland boycotts the "Eurovision" Song Contest for the second time over Israel's participation and the war in Gaza
Kyiv • UNN
Ireland will not participate in the 2027 "Eurovision" Song Contest due to the humanitarian crisis in Gaza. Four other countries had previously boycotted the contest.
Ireland will boycott the Eurovision Song Contest for the second year in a row because of the "horrific" and ongoing killings in Gaza. The national broadcaster announced this, UNN reports, citing The Guardian.
Details
Ireland was one of five countries — along with Iceland, the Netherlands, Spain and Slovenia — that refused to participate in this year’s contest in protest against Israel’s participation.
On Thursday, broadcaster RTÉ announced that it would not participate in the 2027 contest. Dutch broadcaster Avrotros announced its own boycott last month, calling Eurovision "a platform for division."
In its statement, the Irish broadcaster said: "RTÉ believes that Ireland’s participation cannot be justified in view of the horrific and ongoing loss of human life in Gaza and the humanitarian crisis there, which continues to put the lives of many civilians at risk."
Next year, Eurovision is scheduled to take place in the Bulgarian Black Sea city of Burgas after the country won the contest for the first time in May.
Avrotros said it would not participate, arguing that the contest "can no longer be considered neutral when a participating country is involved in a large-scale military conflict."
Eurovision director Martin Green expressed regret but also respect for RTÉ’s decision. "They remain an important part of our family, and we will miss them," he said.
"This ability to bring people together is at the heart of what makes the contest so special, and it is even more important now, in an increasingly complex and divided world," he added.
"All broadcasters make decisions each year about participating in the following year’s contest. We will continue our dialogue with RTÉ and hope to welcome them back to the contest in the future."
The European Broadcasting Union (EBU), which organizes the event, has twice attempted to respond to broadcasters’ concerns about Israel’s participation.
Last year, it limited the number of votes one person could cast online or by phone amid allegations that Israel had mounted a disproportionately large campaign to win viewers’ votes.
Last month, the EBU announced that broadcasters would no longer be allowed to host the Eurovision Song Contest if their country is involved in an "armed conflict" or is in a "sensitive geopolitical situation." In recent years, the Eurovision Song Contest has been accompanied by protests both at competition venues and outside them over the participation of Israel, which has competed in the contest since 1973.
In 2024, the European Commission took the unusual step of criticizing the organizers’ decision to ban spectators from unfurling the EU flag during the grand final in Sweden; the decision was called "astonishing" and "regrettable."
The Palestinian Authority reports that more than 73,000 people have been killed in Israel’s war in Gaza, which began after Hamas-led militants killed 1,200 people during an attack on southern Israel in October 2023.
A US-mediated ceasefire agreement reached last year provides for the territory’s further reconstruction, but Israeli strikes continue. According to Gaza’s Ministry of Health, 1,369 Palestinians have been killed and 4,627 wounded since the fragile truce took effect on October 11, 2025.

The National Development Council (NDC) yesterday approved a plan to expand Taoyuan’s Longtan Science Park (龍潭科學園區) by 104 hectares, a project expected to create about 4,500 jobs.
The NDC, the policy planning arm of the Executive Yuan, approved the plan submitted by the National Science and Technology Council (NSTC) at a review meeting.
The plan next goes to the Executive Yuan for final approval.
Photo: CNA
The expansion is intended to enhance the semiconductor industry cluster in the Taoyuan-Hsinchu-Miaoli area and further consolidate Taiwan’s competitive advantage in the high-tech sector, the NDC said in a statement.
The NT$95.63 billion (US$2.99 billion) expansion project would be funded through annual budget allocations from the Science Park Bureau’s Operation Fund, it said.
Under the plan, reviews of development permits for nonurban land and an environmental impact assessment are to be completed by the end of 2028.
Following land acquisition, the design and construction of park infrastructure would begin in 2030, with companies allowed to build their facilities concurrently, the NDC said.
The NSTC and Taoyuan City Government selected the 104-hectare site on the eastern side of Longtan Science Park in response to the growing demands of semiconductor firms, it said.
Once the expansion is completed, companies at the site are expected to produce NT$550 billion of goods and services per year and create about 4,500 well-paying jobs, it said.
Longtan Science Park is one of six satellite parks overseen by the Hsinchu Science Park (新竹科學園區).
The Longtan site currently covers 106.94 hectares and employs about 7,000 people, mainly in the integrated circuit, optoelectronics and biotechnology sectors, the Hsinchu Science Park’s Web site says.
In May, local media reported that Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (台積電) was seeking government approval to build an advanced wafer fab at Longtan Science Park following the expansion.

WASHINGTON, September 17. /TASS/. The US administration is ready to authorize the transfer to Ukraine of ten MIM-104E GEM-T guided interceptor missiles, currently in Germany, for the US Patriot air defense missile system, at a cost of $29.6 million, according to a notification from the Department of State published in the Congressional Record.
The document noted that the deal involves transferring ten MIM-104E GEM-T Patriot interceptors to Ukraine that were previously received by Germany. According to the terms of such agreements, a country that purchases US weapons cannot transfer them to a third party without Washington’s consent. "This transfer is consistent with US security assistance objectives. The United States government is prepared to authorize this transfer, having taken into account political, military, economic, human rights, and arms control considerations," the notification said. The State Department listed two reasons for the deal: "Ukraine seeks to acquire these systems to bolster its air defense capability against ongoing Russian attacks," and "Ukraine already possesses munitions of the same type."
At the end of last week, US President Donald Trump stated that Washington and Kiev had discussed the possibility of transferring a license to Ukraine to produce obsolete Patriot interceptors. Moscow has repeatedly stressed that the West's transfer of weapons to Kiev and its contribution to the training of Ukrainian servicemen only prolongs the conflict and does not change the situation on the battlefield.

Researchers breed easier-to-rear cattle with better marbling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:40:36 UTC
01:40:36 KST

The Taiwan Livestock Research Institute has created a new cattle breed with a shorter feeding period and better beef marbling, which is expected to help conserve Taiwan yellow cattle germplasm and boost the nation’s beef self-sufficiency.
The new cattle breed, nicknamed the “Angus-Yellow,” was developed by crossbreeding Taiwanese yellow cattle and Angus cattle from Australia, the institute said on Wednesday, adding that the research took more than eight years.
The institute said it has long been dedicated to developing new cattle breeds for the domestic beef industry, which are primarily sustained by dairy bull cattle and hybrid yellow cattle.
Photo courtesy of the Taiwan Livestock Research Institute
Dairy bull cattle have good beef quality, but require more attentive handling, cooler living environments and more refined feed, it said, adding that they are also less resistant to heat and diseases than Taiwan yellow cattle.
Most cattle breeds that are imported from temperate regions, such as Wagyu or Angus, feature good marbling, but are less resistant to Taiwan’s hot weather and local diseases, the institute said.
Taiwan yellow cattle do not grow as fast as dairy bull cattle, but they adapt much better to local conditions, it said.
As they do not have as much marbling as most cattle breeds from temperate areas, many beef farmers crossbreed them with imported cattle breeds, the institute said.
However, privately developed breeds usually have inconsistent marbling and are prone to diseases, it added.
The research team bred Taiwan yellow cattle with different foreign cattle to create a new breed that maintains the former’s heat and disease-resistant germplasm, but has better market potential — such as shorter feeding periods and better marbling, it said.
Angus-Yellow’s feeding period ranges between 21 and 23 months, about one to two months shorter than dairy bull cattle’s up to 24 months, the institute said.
It is also expected to encourage beef farmers to continue rearing Taiwan yellow cattle to use in crossbreeding Angus-Yellow cattle, which would help preserve the hardy breed’s germplasm, it said.
Angus-Yellow cattle are expected to help boost domestic beef’s market share — which accounts for 5 percent of local beef market, the institute said.
The cost of importing an Angus cattle from abroad is NT$200,000, it said, adding that locally produced Angus-Yellow would eliminate such expenses and could be stably supplied in Taiwan for two years.

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:40:35 UTC
01:40:35 KST

US allies in Asia are growing anxious that US President Donald Trump might be tempted to soften Washington’s support for Taiwan in return for an economic win with Beijing as he prepares to host Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) next week.
Concerns that Trump could make concessions on Taiwan have heightened since he described US arms sales as a “negotiating chip” in May, and as he tries to shore up approval ratings dented by the Iran war.
Xi would likely press Trump on Taiwan during their summit on Thursday next week, and even a subtle change in US rhetoric could embolden Beijing and risk the region’s fragile peace, according to interviews with government officials, lawmakers and analysts in Taipei, Tokyo and Washington.
Photo: Reuters
“There’s a great deal of trepidation, particularly from our allies, about where our China policy is going to land,” said Emma Chanlett-Avery, political-security affairs director for US-based think tank Asia Society Policy Institute.
“Any indication of a softness on Taiwan would be quite alarming,” she added.
The Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the White House did not respond to questions.
Trump has said Xi has personally assured him that China would not attack Taiwan while Trump is in office.
Former US president Joe Biden repeatedly said that the US would defend Taiwan if China attacked, while Trump has declined to say whether he would.
Speaking at a defense forum in Beijing on Tuesday, China’s former envoy to Washington Cui Tiankai (崔天凱) said “reunification” with Taiwan would bring stability that is “in the interest of the United States.”
Ahead of the summit, Taipei has been clearly conveying its positions to the US side, Mainland Affairs Council Deputy Minister Shen Yu-chung (沈有忠) told reporters in Taipei on Monday.
“We hope ... there will be no situation that harms Taiwan,” he said.
Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) on Tuesday said that he expected Xi to bring up Taiwan, but that Washington had repeatedly said its policy had not changed.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi — who angered Beijing by saying last year Tokyo could be drawn into a conflict over Taiwan — has also been trying to get Trump’s ear ahead of his meeting with Xi, two Japanese government sources said.
A senior Japanese foreign ministry official visited Washington last week to help try to secure a meeting, the sources said, requesting anonymity due to the sensitivity of the matter.
The UN General Assembly in New York early next week is the most likely venue for an exchange, they added.
Japan’s foreign ministry declined to comment on trips by working-level officials and said nothing had been decided regarding contact between Takaichi and Trump.
Japan will “closely follow with great interest” the upcoming summit and believes it is important that US-China relations contribute to the “stability of the international community,” it added.
Tokyo wants Trump to stick to established diplomatic language on Taiwan and avoid making it the focus of the summit, as it was when he last met Xi in Beijing in May, one of the sources said.
The biggest fear for Japan is that Trump signals a softer stance on Taiwan to secure Chinese commitments to buy US goods, an economic win he could sell to voters ahead of important midterm elections, two senior Japanese ruling party lawmakers said, requesting anonymity.
While Trump has cast his summitry with Xi as rebalancing trade relations between the two economic superpowers, he said the Chinese leader repeatedly asked him about Taiwan when they met in Beijing in May, including about arms sales and Washington’s resolve to defend the nation.
A US$14 billion US arms package for Taiwan has been awaiting Trump’s approval for months.
After the May summit, Trump said he was holding the package in abeyance and described it as a “very good negotiating chip.”
Washington must take Beijing’s concerns about arms sales seriously after long brushing them off, Wu Xinbo (吳心伯), a professor at Fudan University who advises China’s foreign ministry, told the defense forum in the Chinese capital on Tuesday.
Beyond the arms, experts say that even a slight change of Trump’s wording could embolden Beijing.
The US follows a “one China” policy under which it officially takes no position on Taiwan’s sovereignty and acknowledges, but does not endorse, Beijing’s position that Taiwan is part of China.
Xi asked Biden to clearly denounce Taiwanese independence at a summit in 2023, although Washington refused.
Trump’s propensity to make off-the-cuff remarks is particularly worrisome given the sensitivity of this issue, the two Japanese government sources said.
The US and other Western countries significantly underestimate the importance of Taiwan to Beijing, Malaysia Council Director-General of National Security Raja Nushirwan Zainal Abidin said during a visit to Washington this week.
A Chinese invasion of Taiwan, which produces more than 90 percent of the world’s advanced semiconductors, would roil the global economy.
“It will change the world as we know it, and because of that we have to be very, very careful,” Raja Nushirwan said.
