Nigeria begins trial of five suspected Ansaru members over school kidnapping
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
14:18:10 UTC
23:18:10 KST

Nigeria begins trial of five suspected Ansaru members over school kidnapping
LAGOS, NIGERIA, Sept. 17 - Nigeria's state security service on Thursday opened the trial of five suspected members of Islamist group Ansaru over the abduction of pupils and teachers from schools in southwestern Oyo state.
• The defendants — Mahmud Muhammad, Abubakar Abbas, Abdulrazak Umar, Yunusa Musa and Shamsu Sani — pleaded not guilty to seven terrorism-related counts before Federal High Court Judge Salim Ibrahim in Abuja.
• They face sentences ranging from 20 years to life imprisonment if convicted. If prosecutors prove that deaths resulted from the kidnapping, they could face the death penalty, under Nigeria's 2022 anti-terrorism law.
• The first prosecution witness, identified only as "AAA", told the court that gunmen entered the schools on May 15, firing shots before taking seven teachers and 39 pupils into a forest, where they were held for 56 days.
• Prosecutor Rotimi Oyedepo sought protection for witnesses, citing the case's sensitivity. Defence lawyer Bala Dakum did not object but requested permission to see witnesses during cross-examination. The judge granted both requests.
• Mass kidnappings for ransom have spread across Nigeria, though large school raids have been less common in the southwest.
• In July, the presidency said security forces had rescued 39 pupils and six teachers and arrested eight suspected kidnappers.
• In May, one teacher was killed in captivity and security personnel were wounded by explosives during an attempted rescue. REUTERS

Italy won't wait for EU to ensure its ships can get through Bab el-Mandeb - Crosetto
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:16:37 CEST
23:16:37 KST

Defence Minister Guido Crosetto said Thursday that Italy was willing to go it alone with military operations to ensure its ships can pass the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which Yemen's Houthi rebels have made significant advances around. 
    "Together with the Chief of Staff, we have decided not to wait for (EU's Red Sea operation) Aspides to decide whether ships can pass or not," Crosetto said at the Risorsa Mare Forum in La Spezia. 
    "We will likely take action so that Italian ships can begin passing through (the Bab el-Mandeb Strait) without waiting for European bureaucracy to compound our own, because delaying action in cases like this equals holding back the economy and exacerbating problems. 
    "When we can, we intervene to alleviate crises".
Crosetto added that any decision on sending ships to Bab el-Mandeb would be made with government and Parliament, saying that "if we do send them, it will be to protect merchant vessels" and the priority will be restoring shipping traffic..
"I am not deciding right now" how many Italian naval vessels will be deployed to ensure safe passage through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, he said.
"This is a developing situation; we will assess what needs to be done together with the government and Parliament. The priority is restoring shipping traffic, so if we do send ships, it will be to protect merchant vessels.
"Djibouti is not currently affected by the Houthis' actions; my focus is on restoring the flow of Italian ships through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait," Crosetto reiterated.

studiomateriality translates lucha libre into green-lit, stainless-steel bar in athens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
14:15:14 UTC
23:15:14 KST

studiomateriality designs Mexican-inspired bar in athens
OchoTac is a Mexican-inspired bar in Athens, where architecture, graphic identity, and food culture come together through a bold material and visual language. Designed by Studiomateriality, the project takes its name from its defining offer: eight tacos, alongside a drinks-focused menu, creating a concept built around the number eight. The design draws from the visual culture of Mexico while deliberately avoiding a literal interpretation of Mexican aesthetics. Instead, the project translates references to Mexican wrestling, or lucha libre, into a contemporary spatial and graphic identity.
Wrestling becomes the conceptual thread connecting the interior, the branding, and the experience of the bar. At the heart of the identity is the wrestling ring. Studiomateriality developed a graphic system based on eight wrestling movements and eight distinct masks, creating a visual vocabulary that directly references the eight tacos of the concept. The masks, poses, and ring graphics are translated across the branding and the interior, establishing a playful dialogue between food, movement, and Mexican popular culture.
The material palette is deliberately raw and industrial. Concrete, stainless steel, white tiles, and green glazed tiles form the architectural foundation of the space, while mirrors introduce reflections and depth. Green and white dominate the visual identity, with green extending beyond the surfaces and graphics into the lighting itself. The green illumination gives the bar an atmospheric, almost theatrical quality, reinforcing the connection to the dramatic world of lucha libre. Rather than recreating a Mexican environment, the project works through abstraction and contrast. The coolness of stainless steel and white ceramic surfaces is balanced by the saturated green of the tiles and lighting, while concrete adds a rough, tactile quality. Together, these materials create a space that feels simultaneously utilitarian, playful, and highly constructed.
OchoTac extends its lucha libre identity below the bar
A particularly distinctive element of the project is located below the main bar: the bathroom area, conceived as an independent spatial experience rather than a conventional service zone. The entire basement section is treated in white, with white flooring and white wall tiles, while a mirrored ceiling reflects the space and intensifies its sense of depth. All the doors are made from stainless steel and resemble the heavy doors of commercial refrigeration units. This reference becomes explicit inside the individual toilets. Entering one of the cubicles feels like opening the door of a butcher’s refrigerator: green tiles line the interior, while stainless steel shelves carry sculptural representations of pieces of meat. The familiar language of a professional cold-storage or butcher’s refrigerator is transformed into an unexpected and theatrical bathroom environment.
Outside the individual toilets, a large stainless-steel island accommodates four sinks, functioning almost as a central piece of furniture within the space. A sofa, armchair, and artworks complete the area, turning the bathroom section into a social and visual extension of the bar rather than simply a functional space. The project by Athens-based design practice studiomateriality is ultimately conceived as a continuous identity system in which architecture and branding are inseparable. From the eight tacos to the eight wrestling movements and masks, from the green tiles and lighting to the stainless-steel refrigerator-like bathroom doors, every element contributes to a single narrative. OchoTac uses the language of lucha libre, industrial materials, and a highly controlled palette to create a contemporary Mexican bar that is as much about atmosphere and identity as it is about food and drink.
OchoTac is a Mexican-inspired bar designed by Athens-based Studiomateriality
lucha libre provides the central visual reference for the project
concrete introduces a rough, tactile quality to the space
stainless steel forms part of the bar’s raw, industrial material palette
white tiles establish a clean architectural backdrop
mirrors introduce reflections and visual depth across the space
a sofa, armchair, and artworks turn the bathroom into a social extension of the bar
the combination of green and white defines OchoTac’s visual language
the basement bathroom is conceived as an independent spatial experience
stainless-steel doors reference the heavy doors of commercial refrigeration units
green tiles and sculptural meat forms turn the toilet cubicles into refrigerator-like interiors
green lighting extends the project’s visual identity into the atmosphere

The West turns blind eye on Ukrainian bombing strikes on Russian polling stations — MFA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
14:14:52 UTC
23:14:52 KST

MOSCOW, September 17. /TASS/. The West fails to see that elections in Russia are taking place amidst the bombings of polling stations, Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova has said.
"It is strange that the West do not see that the elections are taking place - among other things - amidst the bombings of polling stations, resulting in casualties," she said.
"It is strange that the West has never seen the killings of children by Ukrainian drones - drones that the West itself supplies," Zakharova emphasized.
The voting period to elect the 9th Russian State Duma is scheduled for September 18-20. For the first time ever, residents of the recently incorporated Donetsk and Lugansk People’s Republics, as well as the Kherson and Zaporozhye Regions, will participate in legislative elections for the lower house of the Russian parliament. A total of ten parties are taking part in the election: United Russia, the Communist Party of the Russian Federation (CPRF), the Liberal Democratic Party of the Russian Federation (LDPR), New People, A Just Russia - For Truth, the Party of Pensioners for Social Justice, the Communists of Russia, Rodina, the Party of Direct Democracy, as well as the Greens Ecological Party.
Elections for regional legislative bodies will also be held in 39 Russian constituent entities, alongside elections for regional leaders. In eight regions, the leaders will be elected directly, while in three regions, they will be chosen by the regional parliaments. A total of 23,000 seats will be filled.

Russia’s electricity exports down slightly in eight months of this year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
14:13:05 UTC
23:13:05 KST

MOSCOW, September 17. /TASS/. The volume of electricity exported by Russia in January-August of 2026 was lower than in the same period last year, Member of the Management Board at Inter RAO (Russia’s sole operator of electricity exports and imports) Alexandra Panina told reporters.
"In the first eight months there was a slight decline compared to last year’s levels," she said.
Inter RAO increased exports by 4% to 3.2 bln kWh and reduced electricity imports by 5.3% to 1.2 bln kWh in the first half of the year. Electricity supplies to Kazakhstan grew by 20.3% to 1.68 bln kWh in the reporting period, which accounted for 53% of the group's total exports. Deliveries to Mongolia fell by 6% to 450 mln kWh (14%). Exports to other countries reached 1.07 bln kWh, down by 11% year-on-year.

Iran’s speaker mocks US interest rates, citing the Taylor equation amidst the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran’s missiles and drones have downed dozens of US aircraft, damaged or destroyed hundreds of the United States’ buildings at its bases in the Middle East, and drained its inventories of military equipment worth billions of dollars, the Pentagon conceded earlier this week.
On Wednesday, Tehran unleashed another unlikely weapon in its war against the US: a maths equation.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4‘They called us’: Has Trump abandoned Bab al-Mandeb to the Houthis?
- list 2 of 4US CENTCOM tells Al Jazeera Hormuz blockade ‘highly effective’
- list 3 of 4Trump claims direct talks with Iran: Is diplomacy picking up again?
- list 4 of 4Why is inflation rising again around the world?
Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who has also been a lead negotiator during talks between Tehran and Washington at different stages during the past six months, typed out a version of the Taylor equation, a formula used by central banks to determine interest rates, in a post on X loaded with a wartime message.
“Let’s see if a hike could open SOH or produce a single barrel,” he wrote, referring to interest rate hikes and the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial waterway Iran has effectively blocked for global shipping.
“You can’t 25bp [basis points] a chokepoint,” he added, seemingly again referring to the strait. “It’s SOH risk premium, and We set it.”
Hours after Ghalibaf’s post, the US Federal Reserve did raise the benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points.
Early in the war, which was launched by the US and Israel against Iran on February 28, Ghalibaf frequently used financial arguments to mock how the conflict was being conducted by the administration of US President Donald Trump, to point to Iran’s ability to hurt Washington economically unless it changed its approach.
Now he’s turned to maths.
“This is a spectacular bit of agitprop from Iran, a country which, if nothing else in 2026, has demonstrated an impressive ability to needle its US opponent,” Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG Group, told Al Jazeera.
But what exactly is Ghalibaf trying to say? What is the Taylor equation, has the Iran war influenced the US interest rate, and does Tehran “set it”, as the parliament speaker has suggested?
What is the Taylor equation that Ghalibaf cited?
The rule is a formula economists use to estimate where a central bank should set interest rates based on inflation and the strength of the economy.
Developed by economist John Taylor in the early 1990s, the rule links the US federal funds rate to inflation and the “output gap” – the difference between actual economic output and its potential.
In its simplest form, the formula is:
Interest rate = inflation + 0.5(output gap) + 0.5(inflation − 2%) + 2%.
This means the recommended interest rate rises when inflation moves above the 2 percent target or when economic output exceeds its potential. It falls when inflation weakens or the economy operates below potential.
However, the equation is a benchmark, not a set rule that is strictly followed. Policymakers at the US Federal Reserve weigh other economic factors when setting interest rates.
Is the Iran war a factor in the US interest rate hike?
Trump’s tariffs, the energy shock following the US-Israeli war with Iran, and heavy investment associated with the artificial intelligence boom, taken together, have kept inflationary pressures strong, experts say.
On Wednesday, when the US Federal Reserve raised interest rates by 25bp, it was the first increase in three years.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh, in his speech following the rate hike, said renewed fighting between the US and Iran, which has pushed up petrol prices, helped convince Fed officials to support higher rates.
“There’s no hiding from hot spots around the world,” Warsh said.
IG Group’s Beauchamp said, “The Iran war, indirectly, is a huge driver of last night’s hike, though no one wants to admit it.”
“The energy spike has combined with the rise in yields to drive the Fed into a corner with no way out,” he said.
Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at the Wealth Club, said there is “no denying” that Iran’s retaliatory action against the US and its allies across the Gulf region has “intensified concerns about energy supplies and led to hotter inflation forecasts”.
“The ongoing geopolitical turmoil and elevated crude prices certainly were key issues behind the Fed’s decision to hike rates,” she said.
Is Iran ‘setting’ the US interest rate?
In short, no.
Wealth Club’s Streeter cautioned that while the war in the Middle East and rising oil prices were certainly an element in the Fed’s decision, they weren’t the “only factors at play”.
“The spending might of AI hyperscalers has also pulsed through the veins of the economy, with strong capital investment and resilient domestic demand adding to inflationary pressures, so policymakers will have been looking at the whole picture,” she noted.
“So, while Tehran has arguably had an influence on some of the forces feeding into US monetary policy, particularly through the impact of the conflict on oil supplies and prices, it is not ‘setting’ US interest rates.”
Streeter said the US Federal Reserve was responding to a much broader set of economic conditions.
“Iran’s actions have affected the inflation outlook, but the decision on where to set interest rates ultimately rests with the Federal Reserve, and there are plenty of other data points policymakers use,” she noted.
What’s behind Ghalibaf’s maths mocking?
In March, Iran’s parliamentary speaker repeatedly used social media to comment on markets and energy prices, including mocking efforts by the Trump administration to influence oil futures and arguing that financial manoeuvring could not create “actual fuel” at petrol stations.
Last month, Ghalibaf posted a graphic bearing the phrase “Make America Hungry Again” – a play on Trump’s slogan “Make America Great Again” – together with statistics on food insecurity and hunger in the US. “You can’t cover up defeats with false claims,” he said.
“Ghalibaf’s point is that a US interest rate increase cannot reopen the Strait of Hormuz or replace disrupted oil supplies,” Negar Mortazavi, a senior fellow at the Center for International Policy in Washington, DC, said. “His altered Taylor rule adds Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb to a formula normally concerned with inflation and economic output. He is using the Fed’s own language to argue that the war’s economic costs depend partly on maritime security, which Tehran can affect.”
That is a statement about Iran’s leverage rather than a serious proposal for setting interest rates, she added.
“The timing matters: he posted it as the Fed raised rates by a quarter point. His repeated financial posts are aimed at making the war’s costs legible to a US audience through prices, markets and monetary policy.”

Ukrainian forces struck two Russian S-400 launchers in Russia’s Bryansk Oblast on 16–17 September, Ukraine’s General Staff reported. These same systems were used to launch missiles at Kyiv last night.
Ukraine faces severe shortages of high-end air-defense interceptors capable of countering Russia’s ballistic missiles, making strikes on the launchers themselves increasingly important. Russia has used S-400 systems to launch missiles at Ukrainian cities, including Kyiv, so destroying these systems can reduce Russia’s ability to carry out future attacks.
S-400 missile systems hit
The General Staff said Ukrainian Defense Forces struck two S-400 launchers near Vygonichi in Bryansk Oblast as part of a series of attacks on Russian military targets.
The strikes took place as Russia launched another major overnight attack against Ukraine. According to Ukraine’s Air Force, Russian forces used S-400, Iskander-M and KN-23 ballistic missiles launched from Bryansk and Voronezh oblasts, among other weapons.
The S-400 is a Russian long-range surface-to-air missile system designed to detect and engage aircraft and missiles. It was originally designed for air defense, but Russia has also used S-400 systems to launch ballistic missiles for strikes against Ukrainian cities, including Kyiv.
Kyiv Oblast was among the main targets of last night’s Russian attack.
One alternative to air defense: Ukraine strikes Russian Bastion system used to attack Ukrainian cities from Crimea
Ukraine targets Russian military infrastructure
The S-400 launchers were among several Russian military targets struck by Ukrainian forces on 16–17 September, the General Staff reported.
Near occupied Donetsk, Ukrainian forces hit a Russian site used to store, prepare, and launch attack drones. They also struck Russian logistics warehouses in Kurakhivka, Nova Mariivka, and Luhansk.
Ukrainian forces additionally hit Russian personnel concentration areas near Strilkove in occupied Kherson Oblast and Druzhne in occupied Luhansk Oblast.
The General Staff said operations against key Russian military targets are continuing.

Kyiv’s arms industry wants to kill the export fee. Parliament just refused to route that money to the army

23:09:39 KST

Ukraine's arms industry wants the government to scrap a steep fee on weapons exports, warning it undercuts their prices just as Europe's defense market opens, RBC-Ukraine reported. The same fee has opened a second fight in Kyiv, where parliament this week declined to turn its revenue into money for the army.
Russia's war on Ukraine has pushed Europe into rearming, and Ukraine's battle-tested arms makers are among the few that can deliver at scale right now—an opening that domestic red tape could blunt, handing the advantage to competitors just as the market grows.
A €60 billion European window—and a fee in the way
The push comes as Europe opens a major market for Ukrainian weapons. The EU's €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan for 2026-2027 reserves €60 billion for defense purchases, and partners increasingly want weapons built on their own soil. International partners report more than 200 cooperation approaches to Ukrainian firms still without a decision, according to the industry's press release. Producers link the fee fix to Build with Ukraine, a co-production push they consider strategically significant.
Ukraine’s Build with Ukraine has 200-plus foreign cooperation bids pending decision. Its arms industry, representing 400-plus firms, wants to help fix mechanism
Parliament won't route the money to the army
On 15 September, the Verkhovna Rada—Ukraine's parliament—rejected a bill in first reading that would have sent fee revenue collected from 1 August 2026 into a special budget fund for the Defense Ministry, half for buying, modernizing, and repairing weapons, half for soldiers' pay. The vote left the fee itself untouched, since it rests on the Cabinet resolution, and settled only that its revenue will not be earmarked for the army.
The fee producers want gone
The Ukrainian Council of Arms Manufacturers, joined by other defense and employer groups, prepared proposals to rework the July government resolution, No. 875. They want the fee—20% on finished goods and technologies, 30% on parts—cut to zero, or capped at 5%. Firms must also pay upfront, before any foreign payment lands, with no refund guaranteed if a deal collapses. A UAH 15 million (about $337,000) threshold shuts out the small test shipments new clients often begin with.
Ukraine put an Italian-Swiss Skyguard into combat duty. The missile inside is a Cold War design derived from the American Sparrow
The fee has drawn complaints since the resolution took effect in early July. Ihor Fedirko, the council's executive director, earlier said the 30-day review window was welcome but warned it could clog into a bureaucratic queue as staff leave the agencies running it. One of the associations behind the submission calls the 30% rate on parts prohibitive, since Europe is where Ukrainian firms would undercut Chinese suppliers on price.
Ukraine has swung from banning weapons sales abroad to courting foreign buyers, and its defense sector now ranks among the country's fastest-growing industries. Wartime certification to NATO standards is turning that output into something European militaries can actually buy.

Scientists discover a mysterious new frog hiding in the Amazon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
14:08:44 UTC
23:08:44 KST

Scientists discover a mysterious new frog hiding in the Amazon
A newly discovered frog hiding in the Amazon’s flooded forests reveals just how much biodiversity scientists may still be missing.
- Date:
- September 17, 2026
- Source:
- Fundação de Amparo à Pesquisa do Estado de São Paulo
- Summary:
- Scientists discovered a new frog species in the flooded forests of the western Amazon, distinguishing it from nearly identical relatives through DNA and its unique call. Adenomera varcena highlights how much Amazonian biodiversity remains hidden even as habitat loss and climate change threaten these poorly understood species.
- Share:
Scientists have identified a previously unknown frog species living in the seasonally flooded forests of the western Amazon. Named Adenomera varcena, the species adds to growing evidence that Amazonian biodiversity is even richer than it appears.
The discovery also highlights the importance of cryptic diversity, in which animals that look nearly identical can actually belong to separate species. Researchers distinguished the new frog by combining several lines of evidence, including its DNA and distinctive call.
The findings were published in the journal Ichthyology & Herpetology. The research team includes Célio F. B. Haddad, a professor at São Paulo State University (UNESP), and Thiago R. Carvalho, a professor at the Federal University of Minas Gerais (UFMG). Both are part of the Center for Research on Biodiversity Dynamics and Climate Change (CBioClima), a Research, Innovation, and Dissemination Center (RIDC) funded by FAPESP.
A New Frog From the Western Amazon
The discovery grew out of field expeditions in the Upper Juruá River region of western Acre. Scientists surveyed forest fragments near the Moa and Crôa rivers, close to Cruzeiro do Sul.
Confirming that the frog represented a new species required far more than simply examining its appearance. The team compared DNA data, recordings of its calls, body shape (morphology), habitat information, and specimens preserved in scientific collections.
The name varcena refers specifically to Amazonian floodplain forests, ecosystems that are submerged during certain parts of the year. That is the environment where the newly described frog was found.
Its habitat is particularly notable because members of the genus Adenomera are generally associated with dryland forests. Finding Adenomera varcena in seasonally flooded forest therefore reveals a previously unknown habitat association for the genus.
DNA and a Distinctive Call Reveal Its Identity
Although Adenomera varcena closely resembles related frogs, researchers found physical and acoustic features that set it apart. One visible difference is the absence of a dark spot on the underside of its forearm.
Its mating call also has a distinctive signature. The frog produces a short sound at a slow rhythm, along with other specific acoustic characteristics that helped researchers separate it from closely related species.
The discovery offers another example of how much Amazonian biodiversity remains undocumented, particularly among animals that appear almost identical on the outside. This type of hidden variation is known as cryptic diversity.
Researchers also found evidence that numerous Adenomera lineages have still not been formally described. That suggests scientists have much more work to do to understand how these amphibians diversified throughout the Amazon.
Climate Change Could Alter Its Flooded Habitat
Scientists do not yet know enough about the ecology and life history of Adenomera varcena to determine how environmental changes could affect it.
"Since we don't yet know in detail the species' ecological requirements and its natural history [reproductive period and mode], it's difficult to predict the impacts of climate change, which may alter the seasonal flooding patterns of the floodplain forest ecosystem in this region of the Amazon," says Carvalho. "Since the species has a preference for this specific ecosystem, it's possible to suggest that these changes in flood dynamics may influence - though we don't know to what extent - the species' reproductive behavior. In a scenario of accelerated loss of natural areas, the formal description of a new species underscores how much more effort we still need to make to advance studies on our biodiversity. Species may become locally extinct even before they're formally recognized as species through their naming and description."
Because the frog appears to favor this particular floodplain ecosystem, shifts in the timing or extent of seasonal flooding could potentially affect its reproduction. However, researchers do not yet know how large that effect might be.
A Race to Catalog Brazil's Biodiversity
Haddad notes that new amphibian species are still being discovered regularly, but scientists face increasing pressure to document Brazil's biodiversity as natural habitats continue to disappear.
"Currently, the pace of ecosystem destruction outpaces the capacity of taxonomic studies to keep up. Consequently, species that haven't yet been described are omitted from lists of threatened fauna and remain legally and environmentally vulnerable. Thus, describing new species serves as a tool that aids in their protection. Furthermore, deepening our knowledge of actual biodiversity expands our understanding of the evolution of organisms, consolidating an essential pillar for both pure science and conservation strategies," he says.
Formally identifying a species can therefore have practical consequences for conservation. Animals that have not yet been recognized scientifically may be absent from threatened species lists, environmental policies, and extinction risk assessments.
The identification of Adenomera varcena expands scientific knowledge of Neotropical amphibians while also illustrating why taxonomy matters for conservation. Rare species and those restricted to highly specific environments can be especially easy to overlook if they have not been formally described.
The project brought together researchers from Brazilian and international institutions, including UFMG, UNESP, the University of São Paulo (USP), the Federal University of Uberlândia (UFU), and the University of Ecuador (PUCE-Quito).

Brazil's Lula raises welfare benefit ahead of October election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
14:08:10 UTC
23:08:10 KST

Brazil's Lula boosts welfare payments, eyes new debt-relief push ahead of election
BRASILIA, Sept 17 - Brazil's leftist government on Thursday announced a 15% increase in benefits under the country's flagship welfare program, which supports tens of millions of low-income people, and signaled a new initiative to help indebted households clear negative credit listings ahead of next month's general election.
The measures aim to boost disposable income among Brazilians, whose finances have been strained by record levels of debt servicing, a vulnerability widely seen as weighing on President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's prospects of winning a fourth non-consecutive term.
Opinion polls show the leftist leader losing ground among low-income Brazilians and running neck-and-neck with his main challenger, right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, in a potential runoff election.
The government says the move does not violate electoral law because it simply restores purchasing power lost to inflation. Flavio Bolsonaro, however, called it illegal.
"He knows he can't do that, but it's an act of desperation because he knows he has already lost," the senator said at a campaign event.
Brazilian assets came under pressure after the announcements, with the benchmark Bovespa stock index falling more than 1% before erasing losses.
Speaking alongside Lula at the presidential palace, Planning Minister Bruno Moretti said the boost to the "Bolsa Familia" welfare program, a cornerstone of the social agenda of Lula's Workers' Party, would cost the government 5.8 billion reais ($1.13 billion) in 2026 and 22 billion reais in 2027.
The minimum monthly benefit will rise to 691 reais ($134.02) next month, from 600 reais.
Finance Minister Dario Durigan said the additional spending would be absorbed within existing budget allocations and would not represent a new expenditure, "so that we maintain our fiscal targets and fiscal results trajectory for the country."
He added that spending tied to the program will amount to around 1.25% of gross domestic product in 2027 after the adjustment.
The increase will be implemented by presidential decree.
NEW DEBT-RELIEF INITIATIVE
In an interview published on Thursday by Extra, a Brazilian newspaper, Durigan also signaled that the government is designing a new program to help heavily indebted consumers and to feature in Lula's presidential campaign.
Under the proposal being studied, the government could purchase debt at steep discounts to allow borrowers to clear overdue obligations, particularly older debts that creditors have largely written off, he said.
"It is about making it possible for people who today have more jobs, more income and greater access to quality services to start over," Durigan was quoted as saying.
The Finance Ministry confirmed to Reuters that the debt-relief initiative is being designed. Officials, however, are still assessing which categories of debt would be eligible.
This effort would effectively represent another debt-relief measure only months after Lula relaunched "Desenrola," a broad government-backed debt renegotiation program that uses state guarantees to help reduce borrowing costs.
Critics say the measures fail to tackle the root causes of rising household debt and risk encouraging borrowers to expect future government-backed debt relief, weakening incentives to remain current on their obligations.
Delinquency rates in Brazil have continued to climb to record levels as consumers grapple with high borrowing costs in an environment of elevated interest rates.
Investors have also demanded hefty risk premiums to finance the government, reflecting persistent concerns about its commitment to containing public spending growth.
POLITICAL PUSHBACK
A senior Bolsonaro campaign adviser, who asked to remain anonymous to discuss private deliberations, told Reuters a legal challenge to the Bolsa Familia increase is under consideration, either directly by the campaign or through allies in Congress.
Guilherme Augusto Mota, an electoral law specialist, said the measures could face scrutiny because they were announced so close to the election, but would not automatically violate election rules.
Brazil's electoral court would have to examine "whether the increase stems from a regular and justifiable public policy or whether the policy was exceptionally altered to confer an advantage in the election," he said.
There is a precedent. Jair Bolsonaro's administration increased the value of the same cash transfer program months before the 2022 election, which Bolsonaro lost to Lula.
Lula administration officials had previously said no benefit adjustment was under consideration, and the 2027 budget proposal sent to Congress in August did not include funding for the increase. REUTERS

The West’s pretend outrage won’t save Palestinians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
14:07:49 UTC
23:07:49 KST

The West’s pretend outrage won’t save Palestinians
On September 2, without warning, Israeli bulldozers destroyed the homes of 12 Palestinian families in Khirbet al-Tabban, a herding community in Masafer Yatta, south of Hebron, leaving 70 people homeless, nearly half of them children.
RT’s Charlotte Dubenskij visited the community soon after, interviewing the families and the head of Masafer Yatta council, Nidal Younis. Younis described the demolition as the erasure of this village. He said that in addition to the destroyed homes, “water sources were also targeted, including rainwater collection wells and the families’ small water tanks.” They also destroyed the ten pens housing their 600 animals.
Terrain in the South Hebron Hills is desert-like, dry and hot, and the families’ livelihoods mainly depend on the sheep, goats and chickens they raise and the vegetables they grow – all of which requires water.
According to Israeli rights group B’Tselem, in the 1980s, around 3,000 hectares of the South Hebron Hills were declared a “restricted military zone.” It notes that the expulsion of the roughly 700 residents of 12 villages occurred in 1999, “on the official grounds that they were ‘illegally living in a firing zone’. This flimsy argument blatantly ignored the fact that the families had been living in the area for many years, since before Israel occupied the West Bank and afterwards, with the full knowledge of Israeli authorities … These are false claims, meant to conceal Israel’s aspirations to take over the land for its own purposes and use it to benefit the Jewish population only.”
Just days after razing Khirbet al-Tabban homes, Israeli bulldozers erased another Masafer Yatta community, Khirbet al-Fakhit, leaving 32 more people homeless, and also demolished the home of seven people in still another community, Khirbet Khallet a-Dabe’.
The UN reports that between January 2023 and 31 August 2026, “130 Palestinian communities experienced full or partial displacement. Of these, 48 communities have been fully displaced, including 12 so far in 2026. Overall, more than 6,400 Palestinians, including over 3,100 children, have been displaced in this context since January 2023. Of them, more than 2,500 people, including over 1,200 children, were displaced in 2026 alone.”
All the while Palestinians are being forcibly displaced from their homes, there are upwards of 800,000 Israeli settlers, internationally recognized as illegal, in ever-expanding colonies throughout the West Bank.
Siege as a tool of forced displacement
These colonists further aid in Israel’s ethnic cleansing project by surrounding, blockading, and starving Palestinians. And they do so with the help of the Israeli army and government.
Take the case of Qusra, a village south of Nablus, where Palestinian homes have been cut off and besieged by colonists since August 9.
When activists or others try to bring food, water, medicine and other vital basics to the besieged families, the settlers and the Israeli army usually prevent them from entering, often detaining those trying to help. On September 4, Israeli soldiers blocked a group of around 100 peace activists trying to deliver humanitarian aid to the families.
TRT’s Zena Tahhan reported on September 7 on the twelve Palestinians trapped inside their homes in Qusra. She explained, “The illegal Israeli settlement outpost at Qusra was established in January when settlers took over a nearby building under construction. In August, illegal settlers erected an outpost directly outside one family’s home, blocking the only road, cutting off their electricity and water.”
According to TRT, the families have received some food and basic necessities on several occasions through rights groups. “The army has said they can leave, but have given no guarantee they will be allowed to return to their home.”
Palestinians know that if they do succumb and leave their homes, they almost certainly will never be allowed to return. “In July, a Palestinian family in the neighboring village of Jalud was forced from their home after a similar three-month siege.”
This siege is not only fully allowed by the Israeli government, but also assisted by Israeli soldiers and police. In effect, the fanatical settlers are doing the work for the Israeli authorities, setting the stage for still further forced expulsion of Palestinians.
Colonists continue deadly attacks
On August 6, a Palestinian activist posted of an attack just two hours prior by settlers who “launched a pogrom on the village of Tuba in my community Masafer Yatta, attempting to burn a family alive in their home. At least six people were injured, including two children.”
Almost every day and night there are new attacks by colonists who maim and kill Palestinian civilians by any means possible, from point-blank shooting to burning Palestinians alive. The ferocity and frequency of these attacks is so immense that it is difficult to keep up with their endless terrorism.
And terrorism it is, not only in the opinion myself and others who have watched the abuse of Palestinians for years, but even of one Israel’s own military chiefs, who earlier this year described settler violence as “Jewish terrorism.”
I’ve written countless times over many years on this insane violence. While there has been a dramatic increase in attacks in the past few years, they have been ongoing for decades, aided and abetted by the Israeli military, police and government.
The UN’s OCHA reported that as ofAugust 31, “82 Palestinians, including 19 children, have been killed and about 1,900 injured by Israeli forces or settlers in the West Bank,” since the start of 2026. It notes, “Of these, 23 Palestinians were killed and over 1,100 injured in the context of settler attacks.”
By September 9, the number of Palestinians reported killed by armed colonists and Israeli forces since the start of the year had risen to 100. This is in the West Bank alone, and does not include the over 1,355 Palestinians killed in Gaza by Israeli forces since October 2025, in violation of a ceasefire that the Israelis never intended to adhere to.
Far from the front pages of Western media who are always ready with a story about alleged human rights violations in Iran or North Korea, over three hundred Palestinian children from the West Bank languish in Israeli military detention – “the highest number in eight years,” according to UNICEF, which notes, “Nearly half – 164 – are held under administrative detention without charge or trial.”
They are among the nearly 10,000 Palestinian hostages ignored by Western media and rights groups, many being starved, beaten, tortured, denied medical care, and nearly 3,200 of who were never actually charged with any crime but are being held under administrative detention.
These are the brutal realities of daily life for Palestinians in the West Bank undergoing Israel’s ethnic cleansing project of depopulating Palestinians from their homeland by any means possible. In full sight, for the world to see.
Once again, it is useful to ask the rhetorical question: What would the reaction be by global media and politicians if this scenario was playing out over and over again in Iran, China, or another state vilified and targeted by the West?
The UK ban on illegal colony goods is mere lip service
When British foreign minister Ed Miliband on September 8 announced plans to ban imports from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, it was wrongly perceived by some as concrete action, solidarity, or even a victory.
Reports citing Bloomberg say Miliband assured Washington that the measures would be “largely symbolic.” This is the only truth in the charade: It would put absolutely no pressure on Israel to stop expanding the colonies, and would not cause Israel to prevent the colonists from continuing their attacks on Palestinian civilians.
As Palestinian author and writer, Ali Abunimah, noted, Miliband’s statements in Parliament and on X, “reveal that Britain’s overriding priority remains protecting Israel as a racist Jewish state...This ‘solution’ offers Palestinians disconnected enclaves under permanent Israeli military, economic and political domination – the equivalent of apartheid South Africa’s Bantustans. They would be expected to call these fragments a state, renounce their right to return and accept Israel’s permanent existence as a Jewish supremacist entity.”
Back in 2007, after my eight months in different West Bank communities afflicted with near-daily violence from the Israeli army and from colonists, I understood the notion of a two-state solution has long been dead and has never been just.
Abunimah argues, and I agree, that the joint official statement which Canada, France and several other European countries support explicitly says the objective is to “protect” the two-state solution. “This is coordinated action to rescue a segregation plan, not end Israel’s racism. This is not solidarity with Palestinians. It is just the latest Western attempt to rescue the genocidal Jewish supremacist state that Britain created.”

Baby found wrapped in 1910 newspaper was killed with twine, UK inquest concludes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
14:06:48 UTC
23:06:48 KST

A baby boy who was found with twine looped and knotted round his neck and wrapped in a 116-year-old newspaper was unlawfully killed, a coroner has concluded.
Crispin Oliver on Thursday said the child, known only as Baby Auckland, had been garotted by an unknown person.
He said it was an “unusual case, legally and evidentially”. The whole story, he added, was “very sad and singular”.
Oliver said: “Clearly, this was a terrible thing that happened to a defenceless infant. It happened in our community. But it happened over a century ago, and it is heartwarming how the public and individuals in this community have stepped up to do the right thing by Baby Auckland.”
The inquest heard that the skeletal remains of the baby had been found during renovations on the second floor of a late 19th-century house in Bishop Auckland, County Durham, on 29 July 2024.
They were found by the house owner, Peter Moody, while he was laying a new floor. In a statement he said he had made the discovery when he lifted up a floorboard. He contacted the county council, unsure of whether he needed to call the police.
DCI Mel Sutherland told the inquest he had been on duty in Bishop Auckland when he was alerted to the discovery of skeletal remains in a town centre house.
After they were confirmed as human, he supervised the sealing of the house to keep it forensically sterile, while a forensic anthropologist was contacted. That scientist, Dr Micol Zuppello, travelled up that evening and spent two days at the house investigating.
The baby’s skeleton was mostly complete, the inquest in Crook heard, bar a missing toe tip. The remains were partly mummified. Carbon dating could conclusively establish only that the baby died between the 17th century and 1955.
A postmortem of the skeleton was carried out by Zupello and Dr Louise Mulcahy, a Home Office pathologist for north-east England based at the Royal Victoria Infirmary in Newcastle.
Mulcahy said the baby had been 38-40 weeks, with no signs of traumatic injury, and had twine looped around his neck. She said it had been looped around the neck three times, knotted, and then looped again.
It was not possible to say, she added, if it had been tight or loose. The medical cause of death, she said, was “unascertained”.
The skeleton was too old to be able to confirm or refute the presence of natural disease, she said. In the absence of soft tissue it was not possible, the inquest heard, to say if there had been any assault or trauma. Equally, it was not possible to say with any certainty if the baby had been stillborn or not.
Oliver said police had “had to think laterally” during their investigation. He praised Sutherland for “leaving no stone unturned”.
Sutherland described some of the techniques they had used to investigate further, including DNA testing. All were inconclusive.
He said the newspaper was very brown, but articles could be seen. It was called The Umpire and dated June 1910.
Sutherland said that in 1911 census data, the building was described as dining rooms, meaning “a cafe-type establishment”.
A public appeal was made for people who thought they might be related to come forward. Two sisters came forward who believed they were related to a servant at the house, but DNA testing revealed no match.
During the whole investigation, Sutherland said, there had been “very little to go on”.
Oliver asked if the twine might have been used for a religious artefact, but nothing like that had been found, Sutherland said. There was also no evidence to suggest any link to midwifery practices of the time.
A knot specialist could not be used, the inquest heard, because the nearest person was in the Netherlands and would have been too expensive for this type of investigation.
Baby Auckland was laid to rest at Bishop Auckland cemetery in April this year, with professionals involved giving their services for free.
Sutherland said it had been two years of investigating, “challenging and frustrating at times, but heartwarming to see the send-off he got at the end”.

The fight to preserve Lebanon's history before it's lost
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
14:06:08 UTC
23:06:08 KST

Breadcrumb
A war of narratives: Why these archivists are fighting to preserve Lebanon's history before it's too late
When Monika Borgmann heard about Israel’s evacuation orders for Tyre in June 2026, she decided she couldn’t wait any longer.
As the co-founder of UMAM Documentation and Research, one of Lebanon’s largest private citizen archives based in Beirut’s southern suburbs of Dahiye, she feared the project she had spent decades working on could be at risk.
"I was afraid that if they could call for the whole evacuation of Tyre, they could call for the whole evacuation of Dahiye," she tells The New Arab.
Despite withstanding previous wars and near misses, Monika mobilised her network and made the difficult decision to relocate tens of thousands of books, records, photographs, audiovisual materials, and periodicals that chronicle Lebanon’s complex modern social, cultural, and political history.
"I'm glad I took this decision because ten days later a building next to us was bombarded without any warning," she continues. "Also, I feel that the war is maybe not finished."
Monika now sits in a small office spanning two floors in Beirut’s Badaro neighbourhood, stacked with boxes overflowing with Lebanon's cultural history. It’s a temporary home.
Each day, a team of dedicated archivists meticulously sorts through the records, preserving fragments of a past that might otherwise disappear — while the other half of the collection sits elsewhere in a metal container.
Like other private archives in the country, UMAM remains displaced by the risk of war and uncertainty about the future.
It’s a poignant reminder of the fragility surrounding Lebanon’s relationship with history — and the emotional weight that comes with the responsibility of preserving memory.
"We are going around with our history on our backs in the boxes… waiting until they can go back home," says Chaza Charafeddine, the founder of Athar, an archive containing 2,624 artefacts documenting public life in Tyre that was similarly evacuated from southern Lebanon this year and is now being stored at her home in Beirut.
"It's a difficult situation," she adds.
Lebanon lacks a complete record of its national history, and private archives play a vital role in filling the gaps — often remaining independent of political influence and powerful actors.
Through decades of instability, archives in Lebanon have been targets of looting, destruction, deliberate erasure, as well as underfunding and age-related deterioration. And this ultimately limits memory itself.
During Lebanon’s civil war — an era of history that still isn’t spoken about in some history books — some 1,200 precious manuscripts reportedly “disappeared” from Lebanon’s National Library, while cultural centre Dar el Fan wa-l-Adab was completely looted.
In 1982, Israel also seized the Palestinian Liberation Organisation archives in Beirut, confiscating crucial photographs and documents.
More recently, in 2023, unknown assailants stole a server from Lebanon's state-run National News Agency containing historical records dating back to 1961.
"What Lebanon is living today is a war of narratives, and in this sense, archives have a major role to play," Monika adds. "They should be even more present in the public discourse than they are today."
At UMAM, the work is also personal. Monika’s husband Lokman Slim — a prominent activist, publisher, and UMAM co-founder — was assassinated in 2021 in a case that remains unsolved now, five years on.
At the Badaro office, research and archiving continue, even as questions remain about its future home.
Incredible daily discoveries, tiny threads unravelling a moment of Lebanese citizens' history, are deeply exciting for those at the heart of this work.
Ayman Nahle, for example, focuses on audiovisual archives, including decades of moving images and Lebanese cinema from Baalbeck Studios — work full of discoveries. Sometimes the delicate film is impossible to restore, but other times, the results are breathtaking.
He tells The New Arab that through his work, which includes reactivating old footage, he encounters ‘wow’ moments "each hour, each minute."
"It's just the role of the archivist," he adds. "It's become a kind of lifestyle. What is so beautiful here about the historical construction, how we construct history from the fragment itself."
Beyond the visuals, countless audio recordings also share intimate portraits of Lebanese life.
"You have this huge Lebanese diaspora, and a lot of families, instead of sending letters, they were sending tapes," Monika says. "I was listening to some, and it really was a beautiful experience."
Marie-Claude Souaid, another member of the team, has been working on a special archive from the Carlton Hotel, a legendary Beirut hub and site of memory with decades of prominent guests and events from the 1960s until the 2000s.
"These archives are confronting me with two contradictory things," the anthropologist tells The New Arab. "The prestige of the country in one hand and the collapse of the country in the other."
Such history, in many ways, offers a window not just into the past but into the essence of Lebanese identity itself.
"Lebanon was already prestigious in the Golden Age and now… we are collapsing. But in between, in some qualitative approach, the archives of UMAM… are the citizen archives that can enlighten the citizen story of this country," says Marie-Claude.
These days, people are racing to preserve the documents and history, particularly in southern Lebanon, where conflict continues, as a way to remember and learn from the past.
More broadly, efforts are also underway to digitise the archival material at UMAM and in other private archives across Lebanon.
Many feel it’s more important than ever to hold on to physical copies — especially given the rise of AI.
"The originals and not only the digital copies are becoming more and more important," Monika says.
Chaza explains that many of the women in her archives from Jaafaria College in the south aren’t veiled, and physical photos cannot be doctored in the way digital files can.
"This is my only security, my only evidence that this era existed in this way," she says. "These people were doing these things at the time in the 40s, in the 50s. This is the only real, real evidence. So that's why absolutely, it's very, very important."
Efforts and conversations have been underway, most recently involving Lebanon’s Ministry of Culture, to try to find a home for some of Lebanon’s displaced archives.
But hopes of a collective, creative space remain uncertain for now.
Yet amid another period of uncertainty, the mission to preserve Lebanon’s history has become increasingly tied to the meaning of identity.
"There are a thousand Lebanons," Chaza adds. "Shias have their Lebanon, the Sunnis have their Lebanon, the Christians have their Lebanon. And all of a sudden, the idea of unity, the idea of Lebanon, of this one country, was completely blurry."
She adds, "I think that's why many people started to grasp moments in history because they want to understand who they are."
Tamara Davison is a British freelance journalist reporting across the Middle East on humanitarian issues, post-conflict resolution and migration
Follow her on Instagram: @tamaradavison_

Jetten refuses to pick a side as opposition warns of drama
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
14:06:04 UTC
23:06:04 KST

Jetten refuses to pick a side as opposition warns of drama
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Prime minister Rob Jetten has declined to say whether his minority coalition will seek support from the left or right to pass its first budget, telling MPs on the second day of debates that making that choice now would be “short-changing the country”.
Instead of committing one way or the other, Jetten said the cabinet would send invitations on Thursday evening to seven opposition parties – Pro, JA21, ChristenUnie, SGP, BBB, Volt and 50PLUS – for a new round of talks on support for the current budget and tax plan.
But the two parties whose votes matter most, which are pulling left and right, have said they see little point in such talks. Opposition party Pro leader Jesse Klaver said more discussions would be a repeat of the ones that collapsed in the summer.
Far-right JA21 leader Joost Eerdmans said the cabinet had to choose. “Broad isn’t going to work,” he told Jetten. “Which way are you going?”
Jetten admitted the cabinet had underestimated how much time it needed in August to work opposition demands into the budget, and said it wanted to keep talking in the coming weeks. He again said a broad agreement was his preference, but did not rule out seeking support for individual budgets if needed.
“A drama for the Netherlands”
 Klaver said the coalition is “divided to the bone”, and told Jetten “lock yourself in a room,” because “if you don’t make the choice, it will grind to a halt and this autumn will be a drama for the Netherlands.”
ChristenUnie leader Mirjam Bikker said it was “hard for us to talk” to a cabinet that could not agree with itself.
On the first day of the debates yesterday, Eerdmans said a total deal with the cabinet was no longer realistic and JA21 would judge each departmental budget separately, ruling out support for the climate budget and probably the asylum budget so long as the spreading law for asylum seekers remains in force.
Klaver responded that Pro would withhold support from every budget if the cabinet struck separate deals with JA21. The coalition of D66, VVD and CDA has 66 of the 150 seats in parliament and needs 16 extra votes in the senate.
Siding with Pro would give it the easiest chance of a majority, but the right-wing VVD does not want to concede to them on many issues.
Stabs in the back 
 PVV leader Geert Wilders opened the day by confronting Jetten with an article in the newspaper AD, in which unnamed ministers criticised the prime minister for failing to take charge, one saying the only direction he took was the visual direction””, managing the image.
Wilders said Jetten’s colleagues had “stuck three daggers in your back” and asked what he thought of not being trusted by his own party.
Jetten said he was proud of his team and “we are making the best of it”.
Tax plans
 In mid-November parliament will vote on the tax plan. Pro and ChristenUnie have both said they will not back it as it stands, because the burden falls largely on people in work, and Eerdmans said there is no way the plan can satisfy both JA21 and Pro at the same time.
The Council of State, the government’s main advisory body, said this week that €5.8 billion of the €6 billion in tax rises planned for 2027 would be paid by workers, while the burden on companies and wealth falls slightly. A decision on the tax on savings and investments, known as Box 3, has been postponed until next year.
Jetten said the cabinet would spend an extra €10 billion on infrastructure in the coming years and told Pro that the nitrogen plans would not be watered down, though “improvements” were possible provided they delivered the same reduction in emissions.
MPs will vote on motions, including a motion of no confidence tabled by Wilders, at the end of the debate on Thursday night.

Türkiye slams Houthi attacks, hails steps against illegal Israeli settlements

2026-09-17
14:05:55 UTC
23:05:55 KST

Türkiye has condemned a drone attack targeting Saudi Arabia last weekend and actions carried out by the Houthis, while welcoming steps by 12 countries to restrict trade and business ties with illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
Speaking at the National Defence Ministry’s weekly press briefing in Ankara, ministry spokesperson Zeki Akturk said on Thursday that Ankara condemns the drone attack targeting Saudi Arabia, as well as actions carried out by the Houthis.
He said such actions threatening regional stability should end as soon as possible, warning that the continued Houthi threat in the Red Sea and Bab al Mandab Strait adversely affects not only regional security but also international maritime trade and global stability.
Turning to Israel’s actions in the region, Akturk said Israel was further deepening instability by continuing simultaneous attacks on Lebanon, Syria, and Palestine.
He welcomed steps taken by 12 countries, led by the UK, France, and Canada, to prohibit trade and business relations with illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
Akturk also called on the international community to go beyond statements and take “concrete and deterrent measures” in response to Israeli attacks targeting camps sheltering displaced Palestinians in Gaza and residential areas in southern Lebanon.
“We once again emphasise that Israel must immediately end its actions that violate international law in order to ensure peace and stability in the region,” he said.
Mecca defence alliance
Responding to questions following the briefing, the ministry said the Mecca defence alliance between Türkiye, Pakistan, and Saudi Arabia was based on the countries’ longstanding relations and defence cooperation, as well as the principles of defence and collective deterrence.
“The agreement is not directed against any country, nor does it constitute an alternative to the parties’ existing relations with third countries,” the ministry said.
It added that activities aimed at enhancing military cooperation, increasing interoperability, and strengthening defence capabilities were being carried out in coordination among the three countries, while efforts to institutionalise the alliance were continuing.
Greek premier's Meis (Kastellorizo) visit
The ministry also criticised Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis’ visit to Meis (Kastellorizo), saying Ankara had closely followed his contacts with military personnel stationed on the island.
It said the presence of military personnel and a warship on Meis, which was transferred to Greece under the 1947 Paris Peace Treaty on condition that it remain demilitarised, was incompatible with the island’s status and did not contribute to peace and stability.
Türkiye urged Greece “to comply with its obligations arising from international treaties and refrain from activities incompatible with the demilitarised status of the islands.”
The ministry said Ankara supports developing relations with Greece on the basis of good neighbourliness and dialogue, while remaining determined to protect its rights and interests under international law.
US arms embargo decision
On Washington’s decision to extend the lifting of its arms embargo on the Greek Cypriot Administration for another year, until September 30, 2027, the ministry said the move could negatively affect the “sensitive balances and environment of trust” on the island.
The ministry urged third parties to avoid actions that could undermine the delicate balance on the island and to abandon practices that disregard the Turkish Cypriot people.
“Türkiye, as a guarantor country, will continue, as it has in the past, to take the necessary measures in cooperation with the TRNC (Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus) authorities for the security, peace and prosperity of the Turkish Cypriots,” it added.

Up to 12 years behind bars for creating “call centers” — the law will take effect on Friday
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
17:05:41 EEST
23:05:41 KST

Up to 12 years behind bars for creating “call centers” — the law will take effect on Friday
Kyiv • UNN
The law toughens punishment for electronic communications fraud and call center activities to up to 12 years in prison. It will take effect on September 18.
The law strengthening liability for electronic communications fraud and the activities of fraudulent "call centers," which will provide for punishment of up to 12 years in prison, will enter into force on Friday, September 18. This was reported by UNN, citing "Holos Ukrainy."
"This law shall enter into force on the day following the day of its publication," the transitional provisions of the bill state.
The bill was published today, September 17, in the parliamentary newspaper "Holos Ukrainy," and therefore will enter into force on Friday, September 18.
According to the bill, which was signed by President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Wednesday, September 16, and adopted by the Verkhovna Rada on the same day, liability for electronic communications fraud and the activities of fraudulent call centers will be strengthened.
Under the document, the creation of an electronic communications fraud organized group or leadership of such an organized group or its structural part shall be punishable by imprisonment for a term of 7 to 12 years, with confiscation of property.
Participation in an electronic communications fraud organized group by a person who was aware of the unlawful nature of the activities of such an organized group shall be punishable by imprisonment for a term of 5 to 10 years, with or without confiscation of property.
Providing means, services, information, or other assistance to the activities of an electronic communications fraud organized group by a person who was aware of the unlawful nature of the activities of such an organized group but is not its member shall be punishable by imprisonment for a term of 5 to 10 years, with or without confiscation of property.
The intentional recruitment of another person to participate in an electronic communications fraud organized group or to assist its activities by offering employment, remuneration, providing services, or in another manner, as well as the dissemination of information for the purpose of such recruitment, committed by a person who was aware of the unlawful nature of the activities of such an organized group, shall be punishable by imprisonment for a term of 3 to 5 years, with or without confiscation of property.
It is proposed to establish that persons who, before being notified of suspicion of committing this criminal offense, voluntarily reported the creation or activities of such an organized group to a law enforcement agency and actively assisted in exposing the persons who created, led, or participated in the activities of the group, or in terminating the activities of such an organized group, shall be exempt from criminal liability.
The law states that an electronic communications fraud organized group means an association of three or more persons previously organized for the systematic taking of another person's property or acquisition of rights to property through deception or abuse of trust using electronic communications, whose members act in accordance with an agreed plan and distribution of functions.
The activities of an electronic communications fraud organized group may include, among other things, the collection, storage, processing, or use of personal data; information constituting bank secrecy; payment instrument details; individual account information; authentication codes; or other information used to commit fraud.
Recall
The Verkhovna Rada adopted as a basis draft law No. 16013 to strengthen the protection of citizens' bank accounts against cyberfraud. The document provides for criminal liability for transferring cards and access to accounts.

'Powerful explosion' occurs near Polish border amid Russian drone attack on western Ukraine, Tusk says
A Russian jet-powered drone crashed or struck a target about 4 kilometers (2.5 miles) from the Polish border during a Russian attack on western Ukraine, Polish authorities said on Sept. 17.
Ukrainian monitoring channels and the Air Force reported at around 12:45 p.m. local time that the jet-powered drone was flying from Rivne Oblast toward Volyn Oblast, which borders Poland to the west.
The threat of another Russian incursion into Polish airspace prompted the Polish Air Force to scramble fighter jets.
Residents of counties in the Lublin and Podkarpackie districts received government alerts warning of a potential air attack, Polish media RMF24 reported. Airports in Lublin and Rzeszow also temporarily suspended flight operations.
"I received another message: The Russian attack on the western part of Ukraine has ended," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said during a Polish government meeting on Sept. 17.
"Very close to the Polish border, not far from Dorohusk, a gas station was probably attacked again," Tusk said. "There was a very powerful explosion. Our planes took off. This Sept. 17 is an exceptional day, including from the point of view of today's security."
Sept. 17 is a significant date in Poland, marking the anniversary of the Soviet invasion of Poland in 1939. The invasion, launched without a formal declaration of war, came 16 days after Nazi Germany invaded Poland from the west.
The State Border Guard Service of Ukraine denied reports that a Russian drone struck a border crossing with Poland during the attack. Polish authorities, meanwhile, said that the country's airspace was not violated during the Russian attack.
Incursions by Russian munitions into Polish airspace have become increasingly frequent as Russia's war in Ukraine continues, while Russian strikes on Ukrainian targets near the Polish border have intensified in recent weeks.
On Sept. 13, a Russian drone struck a truck about 800 meters (0.5 miles) from the Polish border near the Yahodyn border crossing. The same day, Russian forces struck the locomotive of a passenger train traveling to Warsaw.
Polish President Karol Nawrocki will convene a meeting on Sept. 18 to discuss the country's security situation, Bartosz Grodecki, head of the National Security Bureau, said on Sept. 16, amid heightened tensions between Russia and Poland.

Australia considers smart glasses ban for federal government workplaces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
14:02:07 UTC
23:02:07 KST

Faisal Mahmud
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
Australia is considering banning the use of smart glasses that can record from federal government workplaces amid growing privacy and security concerns, media reports said Thursday.
Finance Minister Katy Gallagher asked the Australian Public Service Commission for advice on the use of smart glasses in Commonwealth workplaces, including whether the devices should be prohibited and what exemptions may be needed, according to ABC News.
"Smart glasses can raise legitimate privacy and security concerns, particularly because of their ability to record and capture information," said Gallagher. "We need clear and consistent guidance for public servants.”
The proposal concerns Commonwealth workplaces and is not a nationwide ban on the possession or use of smart glasses.
It comes as several Australian local councils have separately restricted the technology in public facilities because of concerns that camera-equipped glasses can record discreetly.
Yarra City Council in Melbourne has restricted smart glasses in facilities, including playgrounds, childcare centers and gyms. Brisbane City Council has prohibited non-consensual recording using camera-enabled wearable devices at public swimming pools.
Other councils are considering similar measures.
The federal government has stopped short of pursuing a broader ban on importing smart glasses.
Attorney General Michelle Rowland said last month that an import ban was not currently being considered, although the government was examining privacy issues surrounding wearable technologies.
The privacy commissioner has also been asked to give smart glasses "priority consideration" amid their growing availability and privacy implications.

Switzerland returns ancient golden mask to Egypt (PHOTOS)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
14:01:37 UTC
23:01:37 KST

Switzerland returns ancient golden mask to Egypt (PHOTOS)
Switzerland has returned a more than 2,000-year-old funerary mask to Egypt after it was intercepted by Swiss customs four years ago, the Swiss Embassy in Cairo said on Wednesday.
The ancient mask dates back to Egypt’s Ptolemaic period and was seized by the Swiss customs authorities in 2022. It was subsequently examined and authenticated as an Egyptian artifact. Egypt’s Foreign Ministry described the artifact as “a golden mummy mask.”
The artifact was formally handed over in Bern by Swiss Federal Councilor Elisabeth Baume-Schneider to Egypt’s ambassador to Switzerland, Mohamed Negm.
“This return is another milestone in the longstanding cooperation between Switzerland and Egypt to protect cultural heritage and fight the illicit trafficking of cultural property,” the embassy said. Bern has returned around 80 cultural objects to Egypt since 2011, according to the statement.
It comes as the North African country steps up efforts to recover antiquities taken abroad illegally. On Thursday, the Egyptian Embassy in Beirut received 74 archaeological artifacts from various historical periods from the Lebanese authorities ahead of their repatriation to Egypt. Cairo said the handover was part of work with Lebanon to protect cultural heritage and combat the illicit trafficking of antiquities.
Egypt has also recovered antiquities from the US as part of its repatriation drive. In April, the country retrieved 13 artifacts that were illegally smuggled abroad, following work with the authorities in New York. The objects included an alabaster jar for oils and perfumes from the 7th century BC, as well as cosmetic containers shaped like animals from the Middle and New Kingdoms of Ancient Egypt.
Also last year, Egyptian officials said 13 artifacts were returned from the UK and Germany. The items include a mummy’s skull and hand, ankh and baboon-shaped amulets, a bronze Osiris crown, and a beaded funerary mask.
