South Korea and France held their first joint air drills in three years this week to strengthen their ability to operate together, Yonhap News Agency reported on Thursday.
The three-day exercise began on Tuesday at an air base in Cheongju, about 110 kilometres (68 miles) south of Seoul, the agency reported, citing the South Korean Air Force.
South Korea deployed F-35A stealth fighters and KC-330 Cygnus aerial refueling tankers. France sent two Rafale fighter jets and an A330 aerial refueling tanker.
The French deployment was part of the Pegase mission, which aims to test France’s ability to operate with partner forces and strengthen deterrence across nine countries, including Canada, the US and Japan.
During Wednesday’s drills, the two air forces practiced refueling each other’s aircraft and conducted tactical flights, dividing aircraft into allied and opposing forces. Pilots also exchanged views on flight tactics and aircraft operations.
South Korean and French aircraft separately performed over a memorial cemetery in the southeastern city of Busan to commemorate UN troops killed during the 1950-53 Korean War.
French Space Command chief Maj. Gen. Vincent Chusseau told Yonhap the deployment was a "stepping stone" toward greater operational interoperability.
He said the Pegase mission also sought to examine France’s role as a partner to South Korea in addressing regional challenges.

MOSCOW, September 18. /TASS/. During a Russian Security Council scientific advisory board meeting, Secretary Sergey Shoigu pointed to Yerevan’s blatant intention to strengthen cooperation with NATO and its openly "consumerist attitude" towards the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) and the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO).
He also noted that Western countries are only out to tap the resources of the South Caucasus.
TASS has compiled the top Russian security official’s statements.
Western policies on South Caucasus
The West only wants to take advantage of the South Caucasus prime location and resources: "What they need is control over the region’s resources and logistics capabilities as it has historically been the link connecting Central Asia and Europe, the Caspian and Black Sea, North and South, East and West."
The West wants to isolate Russia from global processes and reduce its cooperation with the Global South: "That is why our strategic adversaries spare no effort or resource to sever the South Caucasus states' ties with us and create hotbeds of tension on our borders."
Western countries have always sought to minimize Russia’s influence in the South Caucasus, and that's still the case today: "The South Caucasus has historically been in focus for Western countries. That's because of its geographic position and resource base. For centuries, Europeans have tried to establish an anti-Russian foothold there, a buffer zone and a corridor to their Asian colonies, while doing their utmost to minimize Russia’s influence by any means necessary. They have fanned the flames of anti-Russian sentiment by condoning contraband, separatism, and flooding the region with weapons to provoke war and conflict."
The West is carrying out unprecedented interference in the politics of Armenia and Georgia: "The Westerners are openly and brazenly seeking to interfere in the political situation. In the South Caucasus, we can see that not only in Armenia, but also in Georgia."
The US and Europe "are strategically interested in maximally weakening Russia’s and Iran’s positions and establishing their own rules in the South Caucasus."
Necessity of regional peace
Russia is interested in peace in the South Caucasus, ridding it of threats, and being able to communicate uninterruptedly with southern partners: "Russia has its own strategic and historical interests in the South Caucasus. We primarily need peace and stability in the region, as well as the absence of direct or indirect threats to security and national interests, and also quality and uninterrupted communication with our partners to the south - Iran, India, Pakistan, Turkey and Arab nations."
Relations with Azerbaijan
Russia and Azerbaijan have overcome the crisis in their relations; now is the time to develop bilateral cooperation: "We note with satisfaction that the recent crisis period in the bilateral relations has been successfully overcome thanks to the efforts of Moscow and Baku. The joint task now is to ensure that Russia-Azerbaijan cooperation gradually develops in accordance with the leaders’ agreements."
Russia proceeds from the fact that relations with Azerbaijan should develop based on bilateral agreements and laws, including the Declaration on Allied Interaction signed at the highest level, as well as on the principles of good neighborliness and partnership: "Russian President [Vladimir Putin] has repeatedly advocated for the joint work in this area."
Armenia’s consumerist attitude
The current situation with Armenia is indicative: "I would like to remind you that in the 1990s, Russia saved this country from economic and energy collapse. In the ten years of its EAEU membership, its economy has almost tripled. At the same time, the current authorities have adopted a course toward severing ties with Russia and strengthening cooperation with the West."
Armenia’s intention "to strengthen its ties with NATO and its blatantly consumerist attitude toward regional integration mechanisms, primarily the EAEU and the CSTO" are quite evident.
Armenia's unfriendly stance toward businesses in which Russia has invested billions is nothing but a hostile takeover: "An unfriendly line and blatant 'double standards' are clear in the treatment of Russian businesses operating in Armenia. What is happening to enterprises and entire industries in which Russia has invested billions can hardly be called anything other than a 'hostile takeover.' "
"At the same time, they are putting forward obsolete arguments, such as the idea that Armenia cannot integrate into the international railway system if Russia continues to manage its railways."
Russia does not intend to fund Armenia’s European integration, and every step Yerevan takes in this regard will have objective consequences: "Russian President Vladimir Putin has quite unequivocally stated our position on this: Yerevan needs to set a course for itself and hold a referendum on whether to pursue the EU path or remain in the EAEU. I would like to stress that Russia is not ready to fund Armenia’s European integration, and every step in this direction will have objective consequences."
Relations with Georgia
"Russia ranks second among Georgia’s largest trading partners, and our cooperation continues to expand. We are ready to facilitate the development of Russian-Georgian economic and humanitarian ties."

Young kids can safely drink 6dl of oat milk a day, food authority says
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:18:26 EEST
22:18:26 KST

A broad Finnish study has resulted in new safety recommendations for plant-based drinks and snacks, with guidelines particularly directed at young children.
The Vegeturva project, by the Finnish Food Authority and VTT Technical Research Centre, found that products sold in Finland are generally safe, though some risks require clearer guidance.
The authority issued recommendations on Thursday for plant-based drink consumption, mainly targeting children aged 1-6 years.
Regarding preschool-age children, it said oat drinks and fermented oat-based snacks should be limited to six decilitres daily. Soy drinks and fermented soy products have a lower limit of three decilitres per day.
"If you eat or drink slightly more on some days, there's no harm. Average intake is what matters," Food Authority specialist Kaisa Kukkonen said.
The new limits address cadmium and nickel content in oats and soy. Whilst small amounts pose no danger, large quantities increase health risks.
The recommendations don't mean young children should avoid these products entirely.
"Oat and soy drinks and snacks made from them suit preschoolers well as part of their daily diet, provided usage limits are observed," Kukkonen said.
Almond drinks are recommended only for occasional use by young children due to risks including the liver-toxic mould aflatoxin. Rice drinks should also be used only occasionally at all ages due to cancer-risk-increasing arsenic.
Oat drink healthiest plant-based option
Researchers ranked four plant-based drinks by health benefits and risks. The ranking was: Oat, soy, almond and rice. The study did not compare cow's milk with plant alternatives.
"Based on current assessment, differences are so minor that neither can be clearly called better or worse for health," researcher Johanna Suomi said, citing previous research.
A Vegeturva survey revealed some Finns worry about the health effects of the processing involved — and additives in — plant-based products.
Suomi said the research doesn't support such concerns. Previous studies show that long ingredient lists don't necessarily make products unhealthy.
"Some factors added to plant drinks directly benefit health. Drinks fortified with iodine, vitamin D and calcium are the most recommended option," Suomi said.
Moderate consumption of plant-based drinks sold in Finland is safe, particularly when chosen as part of a varied diet and fortified with essential nutrients.

AI generated
WASHINGTON – The Pennsylvania health department said it was requesting emergency support from the US CDC as it grapples with one of the country’s largest and most deadly measles outbreaks, according to a document reviewed by Reuters on Sept 17.
The request comes on condition that the federal agency recognise four measles-associated deaths reported by the state, raising the stakes in a dispute with the Trump administration.
The state’s measles outbreak has become the focus of a stand-off between US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr and Governor Josh Shapiro, a Democrat. Kennedy has cast doubt on whether deaths reported in US measles outbreaks since he took office were due to the virus or another cause, and instructed the CDC not to include the Pennsylvania fatalities in a national tally.
Disease experts say the move represented highly unusual interference by a health secretary in the determination by state health officials and could minimise the risks of measles in the eyes of the public. Kennedy has accused Shapiro of politicising the outbreak in his state and of failing to request federal help.
CDC officials were not immediately available for comment.
In a letter sent to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention director Erica Schwartz on the evening of Sept 16, reviewed by Reuters, Pennsylvania secretary of health Debra Bogen said the state had begun the process to request emergency assistance from the CDC, known as Epi-Aid.
“The CDC’s choice not to publicly recognise the deaths undermines our response,” Bogen wrote. “For this reason, if CDC is unable to transparently and accurately communicate information about those measles-associated deaths, the Department will respectfully rescind our request for a CDC Epi-Aid.”

Pennsylvania’s outbreak has since ballooned, growing to more than 700 confirmed cases across 37 counties and four measles-associated deaths, according to the state health department.
It is the latest state to grapple with the worst US resurgence of measles in more than three decades, fuelled by rising vaccine hesitancy, and coincides with US President Donald Trump’s return to office in early 2025. REUTERS

Smuggling suspected as more rare animals seen in India
September 17, 2026
Five infant orangutans, a species found only on the Indonesian island of Sumatra and on Borneo, were found in a forest by rangers patrolling in the Balasore district of India's eastern Odisha state last week.
Indonesia's Forestry Ministry has asked India to establish the origin of the abandoned orangutans, known for their shaggy red fur, and return them if they are found to have come from their usual habitat abroad.
The rescue of the rare apes has raised fresh questions about how exotic animals enter India and how the country is used in the illegal wildlife trade.
How did five baby orangutans end up in India?
"The discovery on the eastern coast of India is a bit mind-boggling. It's like that time a few years ago when live kangaroos were found wandering along the highways of West Bengal," Kanitha Krishnasamy, Southeast Asia director at wildlife trade monitoring network TRAFFIC, told DW.
"What are orangutans doing in India? Were they smuggled from their native Malaysia or Indonesia or did they come from a facility?" she asked.
The Odisha government has asked the Wildlife Crime Control Bureau to investigate how the critically endangered animals reached the state.
"These animals are not found in India and are mostly seen in the rainforests of Malaysia, Indonesia, Borneo and Sumatra in Southeast Asia," said Odisha's Forest and Environment Minister Ganesh Ram Singh Khuntia.
"We suspect that they might have been released in the Balasore district forest… by an international wildlife smuggling racket."
Indian officials seize pythons, parrots, giant tortoises
The orangutans are the latest in a series of exotic wildlife being seized in India.
In November 2024, authorities in the Indian city of Bengaluru seized 40 rare animals arriving from the Malaysian capital, Kuala Lumpur, including Aldabra giant tortoises, gibbons, American alligators and iguanas.
In June 2025, Mumbai Customs seized 284 exotic animals arriving in four consignments from the Thai capital, Bangkok, including snakes and tortoises.
In July 2025, customs officials in the Indian city of Pune intercepted 20 exotic animals from passengers arriving from Bangkok. They included 14 green tree pythons, four double-eyed fig parrots and two Sumatran striped rabbits.
'Shocking' volume of trafficked wildlife found in India
According to figures from TRAFFIC, 7,272 individual animals, alive and dead, were seized from passenger baggage in smuggling attempts between Thailand and India between January 2022 and May 2025, with more than 80% of interceptions taking place in India.
The animals included reptiles, birds and mammals — many apparently destined for the exotic pet trade.
"We have found hundreds of species and thousands of individuals being trafficked into India through air and land routes. This changed drastically from around 2020," conservation researcher and practitioner Uttara Mendiratta told DW.
"Both the volume of this trafficking, and the number of species involved, many of which are endangered, have been shocking."
Law enforcement lagging behind smugglers
TRAFFIC says India and Malaysia were the countries most implicated in an illegal gibbon trade chain identified in 2025, with gibbons being moved from Malaysia to India.
Trishala Ashok, a conservation filmmaker and science communicator, says the scale of the trade remains difficult to establish.
"Our enforcement systems haven't evolved at the same speed as the trade," Ashok told DW. "We are still reacting to individual seizures rather than mapping the networks, financiers, suppliers and buyers behind them."
Tito Joseph of the Wildlife Protection Society of India says the situation is escalating.
"Smuggling of exotic species was always there in India," Joseph told DW.
At the same time, he noted that it has increased significantly since 2018.
He identifies routes running from Myanmar through northeast India into other parts of the country, as well as movement from Bangladesh into India. By air, Thailand and Malaysia are important sources of trafficked wildlife.
The routes into India also extend beyond airports. Exotic animals are also reaching India through its northeastern land borders.
"What is new is the large volume of incoming live wildlife. There are indications that some of the traders who were involved in smuggling live animals like star tortoises out are now also involved in sourcing [other] exotic wildlife," said Mendiratta, the conservation researcher.
Social media fans illegal animal trade
Demand is being fueled by growing ownership of exotic pets and unregulated digital marketplaces, according to a June 2026 analysis of India's exotic pet trade by Humane World for Animals India, an NGO that works to tackle the root causes of animal cruelty.
"Internationally, social media platforms have aided and abetted the growth of illegal trade in wild animals by providing a platform for people to display and boast about the animals they collect," wildlife biologist and conservation scientist Ravi Chellam told DW. "These platforms are also serving as an online marketplace for the illegal trade to flourish."
"The problem is exacerbated by the senseless and obscenely huge personal collections of animals from around the world by the rich and the famous," Chellam noted.
Establishing where an animal came from can become particularly difficult once it has crossed several borders.
"A seizure cannot be the end of the investigation. It should be the beginning," said Ashok, the conservation filmmaker.
"Who supplied the animals? Who arranged the movement? Who paid? Who was waiting for them?" she asks. "Until we start following those links, we will keep catching consignments without dismantling the networks behind them."
Edited by: Keith Walker

Baby orangutans are adorable, but five in a forest in India is a telltale sign of animal trafficking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:18:00 UTC
22:18:00 KST

Smuggling suspected as more rare animals seen in India
September 17, 2026
Five infant orangutans, a species found only on the Indonesian island of Sumatra and on Borneo, were found in a forest by rangers patrolling in the Balasore district of India's eastern Odisha state last week.
Indonesia's Forestry Ministry has asked India to establish the origin of the abandoned orangutans, known for their shaggy red fur, and return them if they are found to have come from their usual habitat abroad.
The rescue of the rare apes has raised fresh questions about how exotic animals enter India and how the country is used in the illegal wildlife trade.
How did five baby orangutans end up in India?
"The discovery on the eastern coast of India is a bit mind-boggling. It's like that time a few years ago when live kangaroos were found wandering along the highways of West Bengal," Kanitha Krishnasamy, Southeast Asia director at wildlife trade monitoring network TRAFFIC, told DW.
"What are orangutans doing in India? Were they smuggled from their native Malaysia or Indonesia or did they come from a facility?" she asked.
The Odisha government has asked the Wildlife Crime Control Bureau to investigate how the critically endangered animals reached the state.
"These animals are not found in India and are mostly seen in the rainforests of Malaysia, Indonesia, Borneo and Sumatra in Southeast Asia," said Odisha's Forest and Environment Minister Ganesh Ram Singh Khuntia.
"We suspect that they might have been released in the Balasore district forest… by an international wildlife smuggling racket."

A Drunk Passenger Brutally Beat an Airport Employee in Berlin After Being Denied Boarding
Kyiv • UNN
In Berlin, a passenger who was denied boarding on an airBaltic flight beat a ground services employee for several minutes. The police detained the attacker.
At Berlin Airport, a passenger beat a ground services employee after being denied boarding on an airBaltic flight to Tallinn, UNN reports, citing Bild.
Details
The incident occurred on the evening of September 6, but it became known only now. Surveillance footage shows a man beating the employee for several minutes, including after he falls to the floor. The victim was later taken to hospital.
According to BILD, the attacker was drunk and was with another man. Other passengers tried to intervene, and eventually one of them managed to grab the attacker from behind, after which several people restrained him.
At the same time, the footage shows neither airport security personnel nor federal police for at least three and a half minutes.
The airport told BILD that the police and security service arrived "within a short time," after which the man was detained.

====================================================================================================

Plan to limit NHS diagnoses of ADHD attacked as ‘rationing’ healthcare
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:14:43 UTC
22:14:43 KST

Proposals to limit the number of patients being formally diagnosed with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder have been attacked as “rationing” healthcare and pushing children and adults to self-diagnosis via social media.
The comments came before a government review due next week, which is expected to say that patients with ADHD symptoms should not automatically be formally diagnosed, but should be “triaged” and offered support without the need for a formal diagnosis.
Details of this “needs-based” system, first revealed in the Times, would mean NHS services target those most acutely affected by ADHD, such as those at risk of self-harm or unable to work.
Less severely affected people may not be referred for a formal diagnosis to NHS clinics but would be offered help according to a “holistic” assessment of their needs, the report will say.
The government’s independent review of mental health conditions, autism and ADHD was commissioned in December by the then health secretary, Wes Streeting, amid concerns over the sharp rise of people making sickness benefit claims due to mental health, autism and ADHD diagnoses.
Led by Prof Peter Fonagy, a clinical psychologist and psychoanalyst at University College London, the interim review concluded that the system forces children and adults to obtain a formal diagnosis in order to get support.
Official figures show that patients are waiting years to be assessed, with 800,000 on NHS waiting lists. Meanwhile, complaints about autism and ADHD services in England have more than tripled in five years.
As a result, growing numbers of adults and young people with ADHD are not in education, training or work, of whom about 100,000 are on health-related benefits due to their condition. The ADHD taskforce calculated that the cost of undiagnosed, untreated ADHD was £17bn.
Fonagy’s review will recommend that only patients who would benefit from a formal diagnosis, such as those needing medication, would be referred to ADHD clinics.
Under the proposed holistic needs-based assessment, patients would be triaged according to their difficulties and ability to cope at school, college, work or other settings. They would be offered targeted early support, regardless of whether they had a diagnosis or not.
Experts said such support could include one-to-one help for children to cope with lessons, quiet rooms in schools, classes to help parents support children with ADHD symptoms, and encouraging employers to offer staff with ADHD flexible hours.
The final report is expected to propose a similarly holistic approach to supporting people with autism, and to mental health more widely.
But experts said the proposals would in effect introduce rationing of health services and that schools and workplaces were already able to offer early support without a formal diagnosis.
Henry Shelford, the chief executive of ADHD UK, said the review proposed “rationing”.
“There is no ‘mild’ ADHD. Diagnosis requires evidence of a debilitating impact on your life. We already have a clinically drawn line of need.
“Without a formal diagnosis, it appears we will be left to self-diagnose via social media. Schools and businesses shouldn’t be forced to rely on TikTok to know when to put in adjustments and support.”
Shelford said that, on average, a woman with ADHD would die nine years younger than her peers and a man seven years younger.
“In almost any other area, those numbers would have this treated as a health emergency, but the stigma and misunderstanding around ADHD means instead we’re treated as an inconvenience and proposed to be ‘disappeared’, untreated, from the waiting lists.
“Diagnosis means people turning their lives around, more people in employment and succeeding in careers.”
Investing in ADHD services, he said, offered a high return on investment to the country, noting that last year, the NHS spent £574m on a single weight-loss drug because treating people meant they could get back to work. “The same is true of ADHD, with cheaper medication and better evidence.”
Mel Merritt, the head of policy and influencing at the National Autistic Society, said: “Denying people a diagnosis will only worsen inequalities experienced by people who are autistic and autistic people with ADHD.”
Andy Bell, the chief executive of the Centre for Mental Health, said: “People seeking support for their mental health need speedy access to effective help. Getting a diagnosis can be helpful for people to understand the nature of their distress and to get the right treatment for a mental illness.
“But effective help can also be provided without the need for a diagnosis – for example in schools, workplaces and young people’s hubs. No one should be left without the right mental health support, or made to wait for many months for essential services, at risk of getting worse while they’re waiting.”
A government spokesperson would not comment on the forthcoming report, but said: “Last December, we asked clinical psychologist Prof Peter Fonagy to lead an independent review, examining the prevalence of – and support for – ADHD, autism, and mental health conditions. Prof Fonagy’s final report will be published shortly and will inform our new national approach in this area.”

US bars Palestinian president from UN trip
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:14:25 UTC
22:14:25 KST

US bars Palestinian president from UN trip
The US has denied Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas a visa to attend the UN General Assembly in New York for a second year in a row.
The ban comes as Washington continues to hold direct talks with Hamas and imposes no comparable restrictions on Israeli leaders.
The US State Department said the Palestinian Authority (PA) and Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) had failed to reform and were taking steps that “undermine the prospects for peace.” Washington specifically objected to Palestinian efforts to pursue Israel at international courts, seek wider recognition of statehood, and continue payments to Palestinians jailed or killed by Israel.
The decision has again put Washington at odds with the UN. Last year, after the US imposed the same ban, the General Assembly voted 145-5 to allow Abbas to speak by video, with Washington and Israel opposing. UN experts said the US was violating its obligations as host of UN headquarters by preventing invited Palestinian officials from reaching New York.
The PA remains the internationally recognized Palestinian administration, although Hamas has de facto ruled Gaza since 2007. The State of Palestine is recognized by 160 of the UN’s 193 members, including Moscow. Russian President Vladimir Putin received Abbas at the Kremlin in January and has argued that Gaza should ultimately be returned to Palestinian administration.
Washington, however, has increasingly sidelined Abbas and the PA while senior US officials have met with Hamas leaders several times since 2025, despite shunning the militant group for years and designating it as a terrorist organization.
The contrast has further been sharpened by Israel’s own role in sustaining Hamas-run Gaza before the October 7 attack. Successive governments under Benjamin Netanyahu approved and encouraged hundreds of millions of dollars in Qatari funding for the enclave. Critics in Israel have long argued that the policy strengthened Hamas at the expense of the PA.
Nevertheless, Washington has continued to shield Israel from international pressure and has fought the International Criminal Court over its pursuit of Israeli officials.
At the same time, the UN says Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank has reached record levels, with more than 1,600 attacks causing casualties or property damage recorded in the first eight months of 2026.
Abbas and Netanyahu are both scheduled to address the General Assembly on September 24. Unless the visa decision changes, Abbas will once again appear on a screen while Netanyahu will take the podium in New York in person.

Okinawa’s election reshapes Taiwan security outlook
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:14:24 UTC
22:14:24 KST

Okinawa is Japan’s prefecture closest to Taiwan and has elected a new governor backed by Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae: Koga Genta.
His victory ends 12 years of local governance defined by opposition to US bases and skepticism toward Japan’s Self-Defense Forces. The conservative-leaning candidate was supported by the ruling Liberal Democratic Party and a broad coalition of parties spanning the ideological spectrum but united on defense.
Koga’s win is more than a local political shift; it removes domestic bottlenecks hampering Takaichi’s regional deterrence agenda and opens the door for closer Okinawa–Taiwan cooperation against Chinese coercion.
Koga defeated two-term incumbent governor Tamaki Denny by a historic margin, winning roughly 60% of the vote. He captured about three times as many votes as Tamaki among voters ages 18 to 39 and carried 40 of Okinawa’s 41 municipalities. His support was decisive among all voters under 60.
When Koga takes office on Sept. 30, it will mark a turning point not only for Taiwan–Okinawa ties but also for Tokyo’s push to advance long-overdue defense reforms. Tamaki, who repeatedly refused to link Taiwan’s security with Japan’s, famously dismissed the late Prime Minister Abe Shinzo’s dictum that “a Taiwan contingency is a Japan contingency.”
He argued that an armed attack on Taiwan was not inextricably tied to Japan’s survival and spent much of his tenure opposing the US military presence on the islands, routinely calling for the complete removal of US bases to “prevent Okinawa from ever becoming a battlefield again.” Koga’s victory removes active local administrative resistance, paving the way for Tokyo to move forward with military upgrades in the prefecture.
Cultural ties?
Beyond his anti-base stance, Tamaki actively cultivated closer ties with Beijing. He declined to publicly call out the Chinese military’s routine intimidation maneuvers around Japan and Taiwan. In July 2023, Tamaki led an 80-person political and business delegation to Beijing, where he met extensively with senior Chinese Communist Party officials, including a reception hosted by Chinese Premier Li Qiang.
During their talks, Li and Tamaki emphasized boosting economic cooperation and highlighted more than 600 years of cultural ties between China and Okinawa. That narrative is a staple of Chinese disinformation campaigns targeting Okinawa.
Beijing has repeatedly pushed false claims questioning Okinawa’s sovereignty, arguing that the former Ryukyu Kingdom, which ruled Okinawa until the late 19th century, was a Chinese vassal state.
Tamaki’s overtures to Beijing went further. Ahead of his trip, Chinese leader Xi Jinping made a rare comment in the People’s Daily stressing the deep historical and cultural links between Fujian Province and the Ryukyu Kingdom. During his visit, Tamaki paid respects at a historic Ryukyu burial site in Beijing and told Chinese state media that his trip aimed to “unswervingly maintain” the links created by his Ryukyu ancestors.
In stark contrast, Koga has explicitly acknowledged the worsening regional security threat posed by China around Taiwan. He has stressed the importance of working closely with Tokyo, aligning with the Takaichi administration’s security outlook.
Koga has publicly stated, “The security environment surrounding Okinawa is becoming increasingly severe. This is a fact.” That marks a significant departure from Tamaki, who routinely downplayed the risk of armed regional conflict.
Geopolitical hotspot
With aligned security and economic objectives, Tokyo and Okinawa can now work hand in hand to bolster regional deterrence and better counter Chinese malign influence. Koga is expected to advance the Gateway 2050 projects, a massive public–private initiative endorsed by Tokyo to transform returned US military base land along Okinawa’s west coast into commercial and economic hubs.
A thriving Okinawan economy would leave China less room to influence local public opinion or argue that cooperation with Beijing is inevitable, while also reducing the impact of Chinese economic coercion.
Koga’s campaign focus on reviving the economy and improving livelihoods closely mirrored Takaichi’s own platform, which resonated with Okinawan voters and, earlier this year, with much of the Japanese electorate in Takaichi’s decisive national election victory. By dedicating resources to improving lives and securing the future near one of the region’s most volatile geopolitical hotspots, Okinawans will be less susceptible to deceptive Chinese narratives.
On security, Koga supports resolving the long-standing deadlock over relocating the US airbase at Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in Ginowan to the Henoko area in Nago. The move would allow Japan and the US to build upgraded infrastructure and expand dual-use access to key transport hubs across the Okinawan islands.
New dawn
Tokyo can now accelerate deployments of missile batteries, electronic warfare units and ammunition storage facilities across Japan’s southwestern island chain without debilitating local administrative hurdles.
Taiwan’s closest international neighbor is Okinawa’s Yonaguni Island, just 111 kilometers away. A pro-alliance, pro-security local government under Koga would enable greater defense planning and coordination for a Taiwan contingency.
It would boost allied readiness among Japan’s closest security partners — the US, the Philippines and Australia. Japan Self-Defense Forces facilities on Yonaguni could be expanded into dual-use hubs where allied forces train to rapidly respond to a Chinese blockade or armed invasion of Taiwan, demonstrating to Beijing the combined capabilities of a fully functioning US–Japan alliance and raising the cost of any aggressive move against Taiwan.
Moreover, Koga opens new opportunities for Taiwan to work directly with the Okinawan local government across multiple fronts — from boosting trade to practical security cooperation. Potential areas include integrating radar and military data, countering disinformation and other forms of electronic warfare, and surveilling Chinese PLA and coast guard movements, alongside other informal and structural synergies that elevate Taiwan and Okinawa’s security.
By bridging the long-standing rift between Tokyo and Okinawa, Japan is no longer boosting deterrence over a Taiwan contingency with a local barrier at the epicenter of potential conflict on Japanese borders. This new dawn could help forge a collective defensive shield against China’s primary expansionist target: Taiwan.
Rath Wang is a political commentator based in Taipei focusing on Taiwan’s politics, media, civil society and key issues influencing Taiwan’s future.

Government working on incentives for veteran employment - Kim

2026-09-17

The government is working on incentives for businesses to hire veterans that are not linked to tax breaks, Veterans Affairs Minister Vitalii Kim said.
"Right now veterans make up 6-7% of all people working in Ukraine. When the guys and girls come back from the battlefield, plus all their families, that will be up to 10 million people. That's a third of the economy. This isn't a separate category of people, this isn't about creating separate jobs for them. That's impossible. We have a program to create 100,000 jobs. But I know it's impossible to create 100,000 jobs all at once, so businesses can be adapted to take veterans on. Documents on this have already been signed, and the fund is working on it. About 120 companies have already signed up," Kim said at a news conference in Kyiv on Thursday, commenting on the issue of veteran employment.
He said that, among other things, there is a program for veterans to move into the police force, since there is currently a shortage of about 10,000 vacancies there.
"Separately, the government is working on creating incentives. I won't say whether that's tax-related or something else - that's not what this is about. But additional incentives for businesses to hire veterans are being worked out. The groundwork is there, because businesses want this, they're grateful to our military, and they want to respond and create jobs. This process is already underway and the program has been developed," the minister said.
He said that large enterprises and businesses already have separate professions and retraining programs for veterans, as well as jobs, including for people with disabilities.
Kim noted that 330,000 veterans are currently registered in Ukraine as unemployed, but he believes about 200,000 of them are working "in the shadows."
"One of the tasks is to pull veterans from the gray zone into the white zone. I think if veterans get additional payments - not to reveal too much - or incentives, that will push their employer to move to the 'white side' and pay taxes," the minister said.

Bab al-Mandeb Strait’s shipping traffic comes to halt amid conflict in Yemen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:13:37 UTC
22:13:37 KST

Bahattin Gonultas and Emir Yildirim
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
Escalating conflict off Yemen’s western coast brought shipping traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to a standstill, threatening a critical chokepoint for global logistics.
The waterway is facing its quietest days ever, coupled with the crisis in global trade and energy supply due to the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.
The Bab el-Mandeb Strait carries 10% of global maritime trade and accounts for 12% of crude oil shipments. It has become a weak point in the global supply chain due to the military developments in the region.
The resurgence of conflict in Yemen since July altered the map of control of the region, as the Houthis secured the entire province of Hodeidah and advanced westward to Taiz, seizing Red Sea coastal cities like Mokha and the routes providing access to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
After taking over Mokha, the Houthis captured the Hanish archipelago, the Mayun island, and the town of Dhubab, all located around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The capture of the Mayun island, located at the entrance to the western channel, raised security risks to the highest level.
An average of 33 ships transit the waterway each day, but traffic fell 88%, with only four vessels passing through in the past 24 hours, according to International Monetary Fund (IMF) PortWatch data.
The passage of oil and chemical tankers fell 91%, while only one ship passed in the last 24 hours.
Container ship traffic declined 86% below the average at the same time.
The few ships that were able to transit the waterway were flying the flags of Panama, Singapore, Liberia, and Ethiopia.
The Bab al-Mandeb Strait serves as the most critical southern gateway for goods and oil traveling from Asia to Europe via the Suez Canal, as well as for commodities bound for Asia.
Global shippers and energy firms are losing this safe passage amid escalating military tensions and continue to reroute their vessels around the southern tip of Africa’s Cape of Good Hope.
Circumventing the African continent extends voyage durations by weeks and causes freight and insurance costs to surge.
The Houthis’ intensifying pressure on the strait could lead to a new wave of global oil shocks, analysts say.
The bottleneck in the region is affecting alternative bypass plans for global energy routes.
Saudi Arabia is able to transport its crude oil directly to Red Sea ports by relying on its East-West Crude Pipeline, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz, but oil tankers loading cargo at these ports and heading south toward global markets have to transit the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
Blockading the strait would threaten the viability of the route that bypasses the already conflict-ridden Strait of Hormuz.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Central Bank on Thursday kept its key interest rates unchanged for the 10th consecutive meeting while raising its economic growth forecast to 11.48%.
The bank left its discount, collateralized loan, and short-term accommodation rate at 2%, 2.375%, and 4.25%, per CNA. Central Bank Governor Yang Chin-long (楊金龍) said the bank must consider uneven economic conditions when setting monetary policy.
Yang said international oil prices remain elevated due to the Iran war, adding to inflationary pressure. He said major forecasters expect inflation to fall below 2% in 2027, giving the Central Bank time to monitor economic and price trends.
Yang said the bank’s decision to hold rates does not mean monetary policy has been loose in recent years. Instead, he said the bank has maintained a tight stance by managing the amount of money in the financial system through open-market operations.
Yang said banks have ample liquidity, with average excess reserves above NT$52 billion (US$1.63 billion) from June to August, but funds remain unevenly distributed. He said the bank also considered difficulties facing traditional industries, mortgage costs for first-time buyers, and export-driven growth that has yet to fully boost domestic demand.
When the economy is relatively uneven, implementing policy is a challenge, Yang said. He said widening income and wealth gaps make the bank more cautious about raising rates despite strong growth.

Germany turns on Brussels as Chinese car sales on track to exceed 1m in 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:12:31 UTC
22:12:31 KST

Germany's finance minister demanded tougher EU tariffs on Chinese carmakers during a visit to Volkswagen's crisis-hit headquarters, as Chinese brands head toward selling more than a million cars on the continent in 2026.
When Germany's finance minister chose Volkswagen's headquarters to deliver a warning about China, the symbolism wasn't subtle. Standing in the shadow of the carmaker's flagship plant on Thursday, Lars Klingbeil told Brussels it was time to stop pulling punches with Beijing — a message aimed less at EU trade officials than at the tens of thousands of German autoworkers watching their jobs disappear.
"We cannot, when all is said and done, be naive in our dealings with China," Klingbeil said, fresh from meetings with VW staff representatives and local politicians. Germany, he added, needs "a different, more robust approach toward countries that threaten our industry."
It's a striking shift in tone from Europe's largest economy, one that reflects just how existential the crisis at its iconic industry has become. Volkswagen — still Europe's biggest carmaker and long a symbol of German industrial might — is in the middle of what it has itself called the deepest restructuring in its 89-year history, with cumulative job cuts now approaching 100,000.
Mercedes-Benz and BMW are trimming their own workforces too, as all three grapple with a common enemy: Chinese manufacturers that are out-producing, out-pricing, and increasingly out-selling them, especially in electric vehicles.
A crisis Brussels can no longer ignore
Klingbeil's visit lands at a delicate moment for the EU's trade relationship with Beijing. The bloc has imposed elevated tariffs on Chinese-built EVs, arguing they're propped up by state subsidies that give them an artificial cost advantage. But those tariffs stop short of hybrid vehicles which have become one of the fastest-growing categories for Chinese exporters looking to sidestep the existing barriers.
That loophole is now squarely in Berlin's sights. Klingbeil said Germany would push Brussels for "concrete measures" covering both plug-in hybrids and local content requirements — rules that would force manufacturers selling into Europe to source a greater share of parts from European suppliers.
He wasn't alone in making the case. Daniela Cavallo, who chairs Volkswagen's supervisory board and has long been one of the company's most influential labor voices, appeared alongside the minister to back an extension of tariffs to Chinese hybrids. "We find ourselves in enormously tough, difficult and unfair competition with China," she said.
The numbers behind the alarm
The scale of the shift explains why a finance minister is now weighing in on car tariffs. Five years ago, Chinese-brand vehicles barely registered in Europe selling 66,000 units out of a market of more than 11 million new cars. By 2023 that share had climbed to roughly 3%. Then it kept climbing: 6.1% in 2025, and 9.2% in the first half of 2026 alone, with Chinese manufacturers now regularly outselling established names like Ford, Audi and Mercedes-Benz in individual months.
Chinese brands are on track to sell more than 1 million cars in Europe in 2026 for the first time — a threshold that would have seemed implausible just three years ago, when sales were smaller than what a single mid-size European manufacturer might convert in a good quarter.
Much of that growth has come through a route the existing tariffs don't cover. The EU's elevated duties on Chinese EVs, in place since 2024, briefly slowed the pace that year — but manufacturers pivoted hard into plug-in hybrids, a category exempt from the levies. Chinese brands' share of European PHEV sales jumped from 2.5% to 13.7% in just twelve months.
The workers aren't waiting quietly
The politics here are inseparable from the shop floor. IG Metall, Germany's largest industrial union and a powerful presence on VW's supervisory board, has spent much of the past year locked in an increasingly bitter standoff with management over the pace and scale of job losses.
The union has organized repeated walkouts and protests at VW plants from Zwickau to Hanover, and it's planning another round of nationwide demonstrations at car plants and suppliers on Monday — a pointed reminder to Berlin that patience is running out.

Erdogan to sidestep Turkey’s constitutional term limits in early 2028 vote, adviser says
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan intends to run in an early election in 2028 in order to circumvent the constitutional term limits he would face if he serves out his full current term, a top adviser said Thursday. Under Turkey's constitution, parliament can trigger early elections given the support of 360 lawmakers, meaning the ruling AKP and its nationalist ally MHP will need support of at least 34 more lawmakers.
A top adviser to Recep Tayyip Erdogan said the Turkish leader would run again in an early election likely to be held in April 2028, media outlets reported on Thursday.
It was the first official confirmation that the 72-year-old leader would run again for president.
"If 360 lawmakers back a decision to call a new election, it will be held on April 16, 2028," the president's chief adviser Mehmet Ucum said in remarks cited by private NTV broadcaster and the Cumhuriyet newspaper.
Under Turkish law, an election would normally be held in May that year.
Read moreTurkey detains dozens in raids of bars, homes in crackdown on LGBTQ community
By bringing the election forward by one month however, the Turkish leader is able to sidestep a constitutional provision limiting a president from serving more than two five-year terms in office.
Under the constitution, parliament can trigger early elections if such a move has the support of 360 of the chamber's 600 lawmakers.
Erdogan's ruling Islamo-conservative AKP and its nationalist ally MHP hold 326 seats in parliament, meaning to trigger the election, they will need the support of at least 34 other lawmakers.

Erdogan, who came to power as prime minister in 2003, served three terms as premier before being elected president in 2014.
Following a referendum three years later, Turkey switched to an executive presidential system, which took effect when Erdogan was re-elected in 2018.
He was re-elected for the third time in 2023.
'I won't run again'
Until now, the government has repeatedly insisted elections will be held on schedule.
During a weekend visit to his Black Sea home province of Rize, Erdogan spoke to supporters of "the upcoming elections" in remarks seen by observers as signalling an early vote.
"Within this unity and solidarity, I renew my belief that we will, God willing, successfully get through the upcoming elections," he said.
But party spokesman Omer Celik dismissed the suggestion, telling reporters: "It was not a signal of an early election. There is no election on our agenda."
After he was re-elected in May 2023 following a devastating earthquake and as concerns grew over Turkey's economic outlook, Erdogan said it would be his final term in office.
And last year, during discussions about updating Turkey's constitution, Erdogan said: "I have no intention of being re-elected or running for president again."

Opposition leader Ozgur Ozel has repeatedly called for an early election since the March 2025 jailing of Istanbul Mayor Ekrem Imamoglu, widely regarded as Erdogan's main rival, over what critics have said is a politically motivated graft probe.
Imamoglu was jailed on the same day he was named the 2028 presidential candidate for the main opposition CHP.
But following a court ruling that reshaped the CHP leadership earlier this year, Ozel left to set up the Yeni Parti (New Party) drawing support from enough MPs to take over as Turkey's main opposition force.
It remains unclear who would be the main opposition's challenger to Erdogan, with Imamoglu unlikely to be able to run from behind bars.
Erdogan has been frequently accused by critics of authoritarian tendencies, particularly after the failed July 2016 coup and the sweeping purges that followed.
But he remains popular among his supporters, who see him as the only leader capable of resisting Western pressure and steering Turkey through regional and international crises.

Berry Sakharof's New Album Dances With Zionism, Faith and the Abyss
For years, you could tell if Berry Sakharof was in the zone by his hair. If his brown-then-silver forelock was swaying during a performance, it was clear the rock musician was in that place of ecstatic joy sought by musicians everywhere. But sometime in the early aughts, they found a new sign: his legs would begin to move too. Unlike the Sakharof of the '80s and '90s, who would stand on stage, feet together, this one loves to dance, with or without guitar.
Dance is a core action, a generative act, in Sakharof's new album, "The Ladder of Love" ("Sulam Ha'ahava"). Its presence is woven in and felt throughout it. In "Dancing," written and composed by Nadav Hollander, Sakharof sings: "So I dance/ I now dance the demons," later adding: "Even if the abyss seems near, I dance all the way to the brink."
And in "Night Bonfires," written in the early 20th century by poet Yitzhak Lamdan as part of his epic "Masada," Sakharof sings – less in his modern voice than that of the ecstasy of early Zionism – "Our fathers when they danced/ Closed well, closed their eyes… So too shall we dance/ And our eyes are thus closed."
The moment our eyes close, especially on the brink of the abyss, dance becomes more than an act of enjoyment and liberation – it becomes the physical expression of devotion and surrender. "They knew, our fathers then knew/ That over abysses they would dance/ And if they opened their eyes/ The springs of joy would be sealed," Sakharof sings.

INTERVIEW – How is the race for power and profit reshaping space?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:09:42 UTC
22:09:42 KST

For decades, the space race was about getting there first.
The Soviet Union put the first satellite and first human into orbit. The US put the first humans on the moon. Mars then emerged as the distant destination that could define the next generation of exploration.
Today, the competition is becoming much more complicated.
In a wide-ranging conversation with Anadolu, Fabrizio Pinto, an Italian astrophysicist, former NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory navigation specialist and founding director of the EKOSPACE Aerospace Research Center at Izmir University of Economics, explained how space is becoming an increasingly crowded economic frontier.
Where the Cold War space race was an ideological duel between two superpowers, today’s competition involves a growing number of countries and private companies pursuing commercial opportunities alongside scientific and strategic goals.
And as global space leaders prepare to convene at the 77th International Astronautical Congress in Türkiye’s Antalya, the conversation is shifting from how we explore space to how we govern, commercialize and protect it.
The moon, rather than Mars, has become the primary short-term objective of the international space race, according to Pinto.
"A few years ago, the answer would have been colonization of Mars," he told Anadolu. "In more recent years, due to competition with China, that goal has been reset to the moon, which is achievable in the shorter term."
The epicenter of this race is the lunar south pole, where permanently shadowed craters are believed to hold vast reservoirs of water ice. If extracted, that ice could provide drinking water and be processed into oxygen and rocket fuel, reducing the supplies that must be shipped from Earth.
NASA’s Artemis program aims to return astronauts to the moon and build the capabilities for a longer-term human presence, with the first crewed lunar landing now targeted for 2028.
China is pursuing a parallel program, targeting a crewed lunar landing before 2030 and developing the Chang’e-7 and Chang’e-8 missions as steps toward its planned International Lunar Research Station, which is expected to take shape in the 2030s.
In 2023, India made history by becoming the first country to land a spacecraft near the lunar south pole with Chandrayaan-3.
Yet, the push to control cislunar space – the region between Earth and the lunar orbit – is as much about terrestrial security as it is about science.
"The states are competing because, politically speaking ... the conquest of cislunar space is basically the strategic height to be conquered in order to dominate the Earth," he said.
"There is a fear on the part of some that the moon will become territory from which the Earth can be controlled, attacked or influenced."
Asked about establishing a sustained human and commercial presence beyond Earth rather than simply visiting the moon or Mars, Pinto called it “the central task.”
"To sustain life on a different planet – even on the International Space Station – is a huge enterprise, because the human body cannot operate above seven or eight miles of altitude from the surface of the Earth."
Keeping a functioning outpost running, he said, means treating it like an industrial supply chain.
Pinto said the current race is being fought simultaneously by governments and private companies, and the two are increasingly impossible to separate.
"When we say the United States, we cannot mean NASA anymore," he said. "Right now, what we mean is SpaceX, maybe Blue Origin, Virgin Galactic."
Modern space architecture relies heavily on commercial subcontracting. NASA, for instance, has contracted SpaceX and Blue Origin to build human landing systems that will carry astronauts from lunar orbit to the moon's surface.
According to analytics firm BryceTech, commercial providers accounted for 87% of the world's orbital launches in 2025.
At the same time, rapid technological growth has outpaced international law.
The foundation of space governance – the United Nations' 1967 Outer Space Treaty – banned the placement of nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction in orbit and declared that no nation could claim sovereignty over celestial bodies.
But the treaty was written for an era when only a few nations had demonstrated independent launcher capabilities.
"The existing laws cannot be enforced," Pinto argued, pointing to modern military discussions surrounding orbital maneuvering, counter-space capabilities and even nuclear-powered space hardware.
"If China lands on the moon and claims an immediate area for exploration, can China actively do anything in order to avoid the Americans landing in the same area or vice versa? Nobody has ever been in that situation."
The issue moved from hypothetical to headline news this week.
On Monday, US Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink publicly confirmed for the first time that the US has deployed on-orbit "space control weapons" to protect American satellite architecture from adversary interference.
China subsequently called on Washington to "stop preparing for war in outer space" and avoid triggering a new arms race.
The growing energy and environmental footprint of AI data centers on Earth has sparked proposals to move massive server farms directly into space.
"Clearly here, there is another mechanism to generate revenue," Pinto said.
A US startup called Starcloud has already run an AI model on an Nvidia chip aboard a satellite, Google is building solar-powered satellites for AI processing and SpaceX has proposed a constellation of up to 1 million satellites for orbital computing.
China is developing its own space-based AI computing network, having already launched a cluster of satellites designed to process data in orbit.
Yet, Pinto cautioned, orbital data centers carry hidden environmental costs on Earth.
“If those things are in space, you could argue that the impact is lessened. However, you must not forget that the spacecraft eventually needs to reenter the atmosphere. And when they reenter, we're talking about millions of these vehicles, we are going to have some kind of chemical pollution and thermal effects,” he said.
At the same time, low-Earth orbit is undergoing a quiet traffic crisis. Where space once held a few thousand active payloads, commercial satellite constellations are scaling into the tens of thousands.
As orbits become more crowded, relying on ground teams to guide individual spacecraft becomes harder to manage, he said.
Historically, satellites relied on Earth-based radio dishes, like NASA's Deep Space Network, to determine their position and guide adjustments to their course.
Pinto, who worked on NASA's landmark Deep Space 1 mission, the first probe to test autonomous spacecraft navigation in deep space, explained that traditional manual guidance cannot scale to meet modern orbital density.
Autonomous navigation – allowing spacecraft to make navigation decisions onboard – is becoming essential rather than experimental, he said.
Many of these issues will be on the agenda when the international space community gathers in the Turkish resort city of Antalya next month.
The 77th International Astronautical Congress will take place from Oct. 5 to 9, marking the first time Türkiye has hosted the annual event.
Organized by the International Astronautical Federation and hosted by the Turkish Space Agency, the congress is expected to bring together 10,000 attendees, including leaders from NASA, the European Space Agency, China’s and India’s space programs and other agencies, under the theme “The World Needs More Space.”
Pinto has watched Türkiye’s space ambitions develop since arriving in the country in 2017, a year before the Turkish Space Agency was established.
He pointed to Türkiye's first astronaut mission to the International Space Station, its communications satellites and its lunar ambitions as milestones in the country's development as a spacefaring nation.
Drawing a parallel to Türkiye’s rapid rise over the last decade into a global exporter of uncrewed aerial vehicles, Pinto sees space as the natural next frontier for developing industrial ecosystems.
"I expect that Türkiye will be able to do the same in space, but it takes time and investment,” he said. “A deal in aerospace has a multiplier effect – it isn't just one spacecraft, everybody benefits."

The Space Security Landscape Is Deteriorating Rapidly
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:08:00 UTC
22:08:00 KST

There is little doubt that great power competition is ramping up. Now, another front has opened, with the United States announcing that it has deployed a space weapon. China, and subsequently Russia, had been pushing the limits in space, testing advanced technologies with possible offensive uses in outer space, including cyber weapons, ground-based lasers, and artificial robotic arms that could be used for repairing satellites but also have obvious military and intelligence uses. Now the U.S. has responded by joining the developing arms race, which is likely to spur further competition.
The space arms race now appears to be fully underway.
The acknowledgement of U.S. space weapons was made by U.S. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink. He revealed that the U.S. Space Force has launched “space control weapons” into orbit. Delivering a keynote address at a recent Air and Space Forces Association (AFA) conference, Meink said that “the United States now has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action.”
Not surprisingly, he justified this step with reference to the threats from China and Russia, both of which “continue to demonstrate aggressive maneuvers and are developing – and demonstrating – space weapons of their own.”
Meink is not the only U.S. official who has talked about these new space weapons.
Addressing the “State of the Space Force” at the AFA conference, Chief of Space Operations Gen. Douglas Schiess made an unequivocal claim that the U.S. Space Force “uses active space-based weaponry to support United States national defense.” He noted the “increasingly contested” space domain where adversaries have technologies that are meant to disrupt or destroy satellites in orbit. He also made a mention of hypersonic weapons that pose a threat to the United States and its allies and partners.
While details are scanty and there has been no elaboration of the weapon systems that have been launched, this is clearly a recognition of and a response to what Russia and China have been doing in terms of their own space weapons. In fact, Meink dismissed ideas from journalists that the U.S. announcement of developing space control weapons could give permission to its adversaries pursuing space weapons. The race is already on.
Space is central to U.S. national security and war fighting efforts. The domain represents essential eyes and ears for military operations, which meant that the United States could not afford to ignore China and Russia’s threats and advancements.
Threats to national assets in outer space have grown rapidly and are very diverse today. Just as the world seemed as if it was outgrowing fears about nuclear weapons, it was revealed that Russia was developing and potentially deploying nuclear anti-satellite (ASAT) weapons. If used, such weapons can result in the indiscriminate destruction of entire satellite orbits. These developments were revealed in February 2024 by U.S. intelligence officials.
Kinetic anti-satellite (ASAT) weapons have also made a comeback since the first successful ASAT test by China in January 2007. China in effect broke an unwritten moratorium that had been in place since the 1980s. Since the Chinese ASAT test, others followed: the U.S. (2008), India (2019), and Russia (2021). The Russian ASAT test, using the A-235 / PL-19 Nudol kinetic interceptor missile system, resulted in the creation of “more than 1,500 pieces of trackable orbital debris” according to a statement from U.S. Space Command. The United States saw this as a direct effort to target it.
Gen. James Dickinson, commander of the U.S. Space Command, stated that “Russia is developing and deploying capabilities to actively deny access to and use of space by the United States and its allies and partners.” He added that the test was a clear demonstration of the Russian pursuit of counterspace weapons that “undermine strategic stability and pose a threat to all nations.”
Both the Chinese and Russian ASAT tests were also conducted at a higher altitude – 865 km and 480 km respectively – which would mean that the debris generated as a result would stay afloat in space orbits for decades because the atmosphere drag at that altitude is lower.
In addition, there is an entire range of non-kinetic counterspace weapons that have been deployed in space, causing innumerable incidents of interference, disruptions, and destruction of space assets. Non-kinetic weapons include electromagnetic pulses, high-powered lasers, and high-powered microwaves, in addition to electronic and cyber options including jamming and spoofing as well as data interception and/or corruption and taking full control of data. All of these weapons have been employed and there have been growing incidents of space interference as far back as 2008. Attribution is difficult but many of these threats are thought to be sourced from Russia and China.
Therefore, while the open U.S. claim about deployment of space weapons have made headlines everywhere, with many even suggesting that this will push Russia and China to develop such weapons, the reality is that Beijing and Moscow have been developing and employing these weapons, all while using the rhetoric of non-weaponization and peaceful use of space. Calls for non-weaponization and getting more countries to see the benefits of keeping space safe, secure, and sustainable are important, but this effort is increasingly being overtaken by a space arms race that now appears inevitable.

ISTANBUL, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- Diesel prices in Türkiye rose by another 4.68 Turkish liras (about 0.10 U.S. dollars) per liter from Thursday, pushing pump prices above 100 liras for the first time as the country faced its second major diesel price hike in two days.
The latest increase followed a rise of about 6.5 liras per liter on Tuesday, according to fuel retailer Petrol Ofisi.
Following the two consecutive hikes, diesel prices rose to about 100.3 liras per liter in Istanbul, while prices exceeded 101 liras in Ankara and Izmir. In some provinces, prices climbed above 102 liras, according to nationwide pump price data.
The successive increases came as global oil prices remained elevated amid heightened geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and concerns over disruptions to regional energy supplies.
Fuel stations across the country began replacing their price displays with three-digit figures ahead of the latest increase, reflecting the sharp rise in diesel prices.
Diesel prices in Türkiye have risen sharply over the past year. They stood at around 54 liras per liter in September 2025, meaning prices have increased by more than 85 percent over the period.
On Wednesday, Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Simsek said the government has temporarily given up additional tax revenue through a sliding-scale fuel tax to cushion pump prices against surging global oil prices.
"While diesel exceeds 150 liras per liter in many European countries, it is hovering around 100 liras here. We have truly given up significant tax revenue to achieve this," Simsek said in a televised interview on Wednesday.
Simsek noted that keeping diesel prices temporarily contained is crucial for easing cost pressures on the country's vital agricultural and transportation sectors, which heavily influence inflation. (1 U.S. dollar = 48.68 Turkish liras) ■

EU proposes social media ban for children under 13
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
21:06:43 CST
22:06:43 KST

BRUSSELS, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- The European Commission on Thursday proposed new EU-wide restrictions on children's access to social media, including a ban for those under 13 and a minimum age of 15 for minors to open their own accounts.
Under the proposed EU KIDS Act, children under 13 would be barred from social media, and children aged between 13 and 15 would only be allowed to use limited social media accounts set up through a parent or guardian's account. Such accounts would include restrictions on social contacts and screen time of up to one hour per day.
The proposal would also require social media platforms, video-sharing services, online video games, AI companions and chatbots used by minors to be "safe by design."
Addictive features, including infinite scrolling, certain reward mechanisms and push notifications during sleeping hours, would be restricted. Profiles of minors would have to be private by default, with geolocation, camera and microphone access switched off.
AI companions and chatbots would also be disabled by default for minors and prohibited from simulating interpersonal relationships in ways that could create emotional dependency.
The proposal requires online services and app stores to introduce age-assurance mechanisms. The Commission said its EU age-verification app could be used without retaining identity documents or biometric data.
The act would also reverse the burden of proof for very large online platforms, requiring providers to demonstrate that their services are safe for children. They would have to submit compliance plans for independent auditing before introducing relevant services or features.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the proposal was intended to put parents "back in the driving seat" and require platforms to prove their services are safe by design.
The proposal has been submitted to the European Parliament and the Council of the EU for consideration and approval. Enforcement would build on existing mechanisms under the Digital Services Act and the Artificial Intelligence Act, with fines for violations potentially reaching 6 percent of a company's total worldwide annual turnover. ■

1 killed, 2 injured by falling Houthi drone debris in western Saudi Arabia

There was no immediate comment from the Houthis on the Saudi statement.
Saudi Arabia said Tuesday that its air defenses intercepted and destroyed a drone allegedly launched by the Houthis toward Mecca before it entered the holy city’s restricted airspace. The Yemeni group denied responsibility.
The Saudi-led coalition said it was the second attempt to target Mecca since 2017.
Saudi Arabia has faced a series of missile and drone attacks attributed to the Houthis in recent days amid escalating regional tensions.
Fighting between Yemeni government forces and the Houthis has also intensified since early July.
The renewed clashes have ended a period of relative calm that had largely held since a UN-brokered truce took effect in April 2022.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and several provinces in September 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.

Japan PM Takaichi reshuffles cabinet, retains key ministers, taps first JIP member
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
21:06:19 CST
22:06:19 KST

TOKYO, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi reshuffled her cabinet on Thursday, retaining most key ministers while bringing in a newcomer from the Japan Innovation Party (JIP), the junior coalition partner of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP).
It is Takaichi's first cabinet reshuffle since she took office last October.
According to the new lineup, Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara, Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi, Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi and Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama all remained in their respective posts.
Among those entering the cabinet for the first time, House of Representatives members Kazuo Yana and Yoshihiro Seki had previously been disciplined by the LDP over a high-profile political slush fund scandal. They were named agriculture minister and education minister, respectively. This marked the first time since the scandal came to light that lawmakers disciplined by the party over the affair had received cabinet positions.
Hiroshi Nakatsuka, formerly secretary general of the JIP, was appointed minister in charge of regulatory reform, making him the first JIP member to serve as a cabinet minister. The move marked a shift from the LDP and JIP cooperating outside the cabinet to cooperation within the cabinet.
Shigeaki Koga, a former official at Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, said that on foreign and security policies, the JIP is even more hawkish than Takaichi and could potentially encourage the prime minister to pursue more hawkish policies.
Another focus of the reshuffle is the absence of former Internal Affairs and Communications Minister Yoshimasa Hayashi from the new cabinet. Hayashi was Takaichi's rival in last year's LDP presidential election.
Analysts said the personnel changes indicate, on the one hand, that the Takaichi administration will press ahead with its established military buildup, proactive fiscal policy, and diplomatic agenda.
The Takaichi government is set to revise Japan's three key security documents by the end of this year, potentially including plans to acquire large numbers of unmanned systems and move toward mass production of hypersonic missiles.
On the other hand, Takaichi's latest cabinet reshuffle is also aimed at consolidating her administration's power base and paving the way for her to secure another term as LDP president in next autumn's party leadership race. ■

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17

This photo taken on Sept. 10, 2026 shows ceramic products made by an intelligent workshop in Jingdezhen, east China's Jiangxi Province.
Jingdezhen, known worldwide as China's "porcelain capital," is revitalizing its centuries-old ceramics industry through digitalization and smart manufacturing.
Once reliant on 72 intricate steps and skilled craftsmanship, porcelain production process at the intelligent workshop is now increasingly automated with smart production lines, AGV robots and intelligent kilns, resulting in higher efficiency and precision.

U.S. faces global criticism after deploying weapons in space
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
21:06:13 CST
22:06:13 KST

WASHINGTON, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- The United States faces global doubts and criticism after announcing for the first time that it has deployed weapons in space, with countries warning against an "arms race" in space.
U.S. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said Monday that the United States has fielded "on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action," but declined to disclose the types of weapons deployed or whether they were designed to target objects in space or on Earth.
Back in March, Chief of Space Operations Gen. Chance Saltzman said that the U.S. Space Force was tasked "to contest and control the space domain" to ensure U.S. forces could operate freely while "denying the same to our adversaries."
Established as a separate military branch by U.S. President Donald Trump in 2019, the Space Force was the first new branch of the U.S. military in more than seven decades. It carries out both offensive and defensive operations aimed at affecting adversary capabilities, from disruption to degradation to destruction, including "orbital warfare and electromagnetic warfare," Saltzman said.
Trump is further stepping up the militarization of space in his second term.
Ordering the Pentagon to pursue space-based interceptors during the first week of his presidency, he announced in January 2025 the "Golden Dome" missile defense system with space-based capabilities as a crucial component.
The Congressional Budget Office estimated that space-based components of the Golden Dome system alone could cost as much as 542 billion U.S. dollars over the next 20 years.
Astronomer Jonathan McDowell, who has spent decades compiling a list of rocket launches, told The Guardian, a British daily, that it was reasonable to assume Washington had such weapons in space, likely jammers, as it had already deployed several satellites with secret payloads.
McDowell said the United States was moving away from the idea that space should be used solely for peaceful purposes. The United States "sees conflict in space as something that is conceptually normalised, whereas 20 years ago it was 'no, we will never want to do that'," he said.
"I think this is wrong," he added. "I also think it is still not too late to change course on this."
Similarly, Lemmy Nyongesa Mulaku, a scholar of international affairs at the University of Nairobi, said Washington's secret deployment of space weapons has undermined the international legal framework established by the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which bans weapons of mass destruction in orbit but does not prohibit conventional weapons in space or ground-based weapons against assets in space, leaving room for interpretation.
"The dangers associated with Washington's actions include triggering an arms race in space, which would pose dangers to civilians in terms of increasing the probability of debris falling; interference with civilian communications networks; and increase an erosion of trust in international treaties," Mulaku said. "An arms race in outer space will make it a contested sphere with consequences for the whole world."
Russia's Foreign Ministry said Tuesday that Washington's deployment of orbital weapons ignored the possible consequences of a conflict and threatened long-term stability in space-based activity.
"In pursuit of its narrow self-interests, Washington is ready to completely ignore the catastrophic consequences for humanity of any armed conflict in orbit," Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said in a commentary on the ministry website.
The country has long argued that the United States and its allies opposed a ban on all weapons in outer space because they planned to deploy weapons there.
Meanwhile, China urged the United States to stop expanding military build-up in outer space and uphold global strategic stability with concrete actions, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Tuesday.
Guo added that China stands for peaceful use of outer space and keeping it safe, and opposes any arms race in outer space or any attempt to weaponize it and turn it into a war zone. ■
