From Syria to France, how soaring fuel costs inflame protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:14:18 UTC
19:14:18 KST

Breadcrumb
From Syria to France, how soaring fuel costs are inflaming protests
Protests over soaring fuel prices and rising energy costs have recently erupted across several continents as regional conflicts push up oil prices and put greater pressure on households and businesses.
Oil prices climbed back above $100 a barrel last week after new US strikes on Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf, while renewed fighting in Yemen has raised fresh concerns over shipping through the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
In the US, rising fuel costs have also prompted warnings that households reliant on heating oil could face price increases of as much as 40% this winter.
The impact is being felt well beyond the cost of filling up a car. More expensive diesel and petrol feed into transport, food deliveries, manufacturing, construction, agriculture and electricity generation, meaning a shock at the pump can quickly become a wider cost-of-living crisis.
Here are some of the countries where fuel and energy costs have triggered protests, strikes or growing public anger.
Syria
A sharp increase in fuel prices over the weekend sparked protests across Syria, marking the largest demonstrations the country has seen since the fall of Bashar al-Assad two years ago.
The government temporarily raised the price of a litre of diesel to 175 Syrian pounds ($1.43), an increase of around 40%, while petrol prices rose by more than 25%, according to the state-run SANA news agency. The Energy Ministry blamed the increases on the global rise in fuel prices and ongoing maintenance at the Baniyas refinery, the country's largest refinery, which has increased Syria's reliance on imports.
Most demonstrations were peaceful, but protesters on Sunday blocked the highway linking Hasakah and Deir Ezzor, burned tyres and stopped oil trucks, according to conflict-monitoring organisation ACLED.
Diesel is particularly important in Syria because it is used for far more than transport. It is also widely relied on for heating and power generation, meaning higher diesel prices can affect households both on the road and at home as winter approaches.
The same is true across neighbouring Lebanon, where diesel is widely used by private generators as well as for heating. A rise in the cost of diesel can therefore hit households through electricity and heating bills as well as transport and other everyday costs.
Iran
Iran is facing a different but closely related fuel crisis, with long queues at petrol stations and strikes by truck drivers adding to growing economic pressure.
The government has been struggling to maintain fuel subsidies, while cuts to subsidised fuel allocations have angered drivers. Taxi drivers in particular have been affected by reductions in their subsidised fuel allocation, according to the Union of Truckers and Drivers.
The economic fallout from the Israel-US war and an American blockade has added to problems already facing ordinary Iranians, including a plunging currency, worsening joblessness and rising prices for everyday goods.
Portugal
In the coastal Portuguese city of Espinho, around 80 people protested on Saturday over rising fuel and living costs.
The demonstration was organised by local business leaders and workers seeking government action. Protesters marched towards the home of Prime Minister Luís Montenegro in the city, according to Portuguese news agency Lusa.
The Portuguese Association of Firefighters has also warned that rising fuel prices are placing a heavy burden on fire services, particularly volunteer organisations. The government announced a package of measures on Monday aimed at easing the impact on freight companies, taxi drivers, firefighters and social-sector organisations.
France
In southern France, around 50 fishermen blocked a major fuel depot in the coastal town of Fos-sur-Mer on Tuesday in protest at rising prices.
The blockade lasted several hours and included brief clashes between protesters and police, according to local broadcaster BFMTV.
The mayor of Fos-sur-Mer, Philippe Maurizot, described the fishing sector as facing a "deep crisis" requiring an urgent state response. He also warned that rising costs, higher fuel prices, restrictions, insufficient incomes and a lack of future prospects had left some workers in an "unbearable" situation.
Guatemala
Truck drivers and other protesters blocked highways in several parts of Guatemala last week in response to rising fuel prices, causing disruption in different areas, according to the Associated Press.
Peaceful demonstrations were also held in the capital, with protesters demanding immediate government action.
Guatemala's Congress is considering legislation that would cap fuel prices until the end of the year. Under the proposed measure, the government would provide support to fuel importers if international prices rise above the ceiling.
Philippines
Transport workers from the Manibela group went on strike on Monday over rising fuel prices, calling for government support and the abolition of taxes on fuel.
The strike coincided with another round of price increases that took effect on Tuesday, raising the price of petrol by 5.68 pesos, alongside further increases in diesel and kerosene prices, according to the Philippine News Agency.
Bus and other public transport drivers have been dealing with higher operating costs for months, with prices having risen sharply in March and remaining above levels seen before the war.
In Manila, protests also took place near the presidential palace during the peak of the earlier price shock, as transport workers and others voiced anger over the rising cost of energy.
Sudan
Sudan illustrates how fuel shortages can become catastrophic even when the immediate trigger is not global oil prices.
In Khartoum, the price of a gallon of fuel has climbed to around 55,000 Sudanese pounds (US$92) on the black market, while shortages have left hundreds of vehicles queuing at petrol stations.
But the roots of Sudan's crisis lie primarily in the country's internal war, which began in April 2023, and its consequences, including the collapse in the value of the Sudanese pound and the disruption of domestic supply and distribution networks.
The situation shows that energy security depends not only on global prices or oil production, but also on whether countries can transport, distribute and sell fuel reliably inside their own borders.
Why fuel prices trigger wider crises
Fuel costs affect far more than transport. Higher diesel and petrol prices raise the cost of food, goods, manufacturing, construction and agriculture. In countries such as Lebanon and Iraq, expensive diesel can also drive up electricity costs because of reliance on private generators.
The impact is particularly severe where people already face weak currencies, unemployment, unreliable electricity and high food prices.
The latest protests across the Middle East, Europe, Latin America and Asia show how quickly an energy shock can spread through economies. With regional conflicts threatening shipping through Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb and winter approaching, further price rises could increase pressure on households and governments.

Hong Kong will lack 130,000 workers by 2028, fewer than projected due to talent policies

Hong Kong will lack 130,000 workers by 2028, fewer than projected due to talent policies
Shortage mitigated by AI development and talent import policies, labour chief says, as top talent visa renewal to be relaxed for tech founders
Hong Kong will be short of 130,000 workers by 2028, about a third less than originally projected, a reduction the city’s labour chief attributed to the development of artificial intelligence (AI) and government policies to import labour and top talent.
A day after the release of the city’s first five-year plan and annual policy address, Secretary for Labour and Welfare Chris Sun Yuk-han said on Thursday that authorities would exempt start-up founders approved under the Top Talent Pass Scheme from needing to provide proof of company income when renewing their visas to better support these entrepreneurs.
“Our previous manpower projection found that we will be short of 180,000 workers by 2028, but in the latest study, to be announced in detail next week, the shortfall will be reduced to 130,000,” he said.

In Silicon Valley, AI data center boom meets local resistance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:13:22 UTC
19:13:22 KST

In Silicon Valley, AI data centre boom meets local resistance
- Silicon Valley's San Jose is promoting AI data centre growth for economic benefits but faces local resistance over concerns about energy, water use, and pollution impacts.
- Residents and groups demand stricter reviews, transparency, and environmental studies before approving new data centre projects, while city officials advocate responsible development.
- California lawmakers propose bills to ensure large energy users pay fair costs and increase transparency, with industry warning of potential negative effects on investment and jobs.
AI generated
SAN JOSE, California – In Silicon Valley’s biggest city, residents and environmental groups are organising against a wave of proposed data centre projects that officials have courted in a bid to position the city as a hub for AI infrastructure.
The clash highlights a challenge confronting policymakers nationwide: how to support an industry viewed by government and business leaders as critical to economic competitiveness while responding to growing public concerns about the electricity, water and pollution impacts of the infrastructure required to power it.
In California, that debate is particularly fraught because the state is home to many of the companies driving the AI boom, including Google, Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic.
San Jose, a city of nearly one million and California’s third-largest, has embraced the industry’s growth. In 2025, city leaders announced an agreement with utility PG&E to speed delivery of power to large energy users such as data centres.
The city estimates each new facility could generate between US$3 million (S$3.8 million) and US$6 million in tax income annually for services such as police, fire protection, libraries, roads and parks.
Despite Silicon Valley’s wealth, however, many residents remain unconvinced that the benefits of the wave of tech-driven growth tied to AI-focused facilities will be broadly shared.
“The companies have to prove to us why they deserve our resources and how they’re going to give back to the community,” said Ellina Yin, a leader of the grassroots I Love San Jose coalition.
Yin and others are pushing for stricter public review, more transparency around energy and water use and studies of health and environmental impacts before more projects are approved.
Mayor Matt Mahan says the answer is not to halt data centre development but to ensure it is done responsibly.
“People are right to question, ‘Is this pushing up my energy costs? Is it using our clean water supplies? Will it degrade quality of life in my city?’” Mahan told Reuters. “These are very fair questions.”
The fight comes as California Governor Gavin Newsom weighs a package of Bills intended to protect state residents from the costs of powering data centres and increase transparency around their energy and water use.
PG&E said new large customers can help spread fixed grid costs across a broader customer base and help lower bills.
Air quality is a particular concern. In April, a coalition led by the Center for Biological Diversity petitioned the Bay Area Air Quality Management District to strengthen oversight of diesel backup generators used at data centres, arguing that existing regulations predate the recent expansion of AI-related facilities.
The district said it is exploring whether stronger protections are warranted.
New legislation pending
The concerns raised in San Jose have increasingly made their way to Sacramento, California’s capital.
Lawmakers recently gave final approval in both the state Senate and Assembly to several Bills addressing data centres, including measures intended to ensure large electricity users pay their share of grid-related costs and requirements aimed at increasing transparency around energy and water consumption.
State Senator Steve Padilla, who authored several of the measures, said California has an obligation to lead because it is home to many of the world’s largest technology companies.
The Data Center Coalition, an industry trade group whose members include Google, Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic, said it supports responsible growth but argued the Bills unfairly single out data centres rather than other large industrial and commercial electricity users. The group warned the measures could discourage investment and push jobs, tax revenue and projects to other states.
Newsom has until the end of September to either sign or veto the legislation. His office declined to comment because the Bills are pending before the governor. REUTERS

Russia says new US sanctions, if signed by Trump, would make Ukraine peace deal harder
MOSCOW, Sept 17 - The Kremlin said on Thursday that further U.S. sanctions against Russia would make it harder to reach a peace deal in Ukraine.
On Wednesday, the U.S. House of Representatives passed a sweeping sanctions package intended to increase economic pressure on Russia over its war in Ukraine, sending the bill to President Donald Trump to sign into law.
"We are, of course, monitoring the progress of this document. It falls under the category of unfriendly actions, and of course the imposition of any additional sanctions by the U.S. would certainly complicate efforts to find a peace settlement in Ukraine," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
U.S.-mediated efforts to end the 4-1/2-year Ukraine war have been stalled for months, but President Donald Trump sent two envoys to Moscow and Kyiv earlier this month in an effort to get the process moving again.
The U.S. sanctions bill targets Russia's energy and defence industries, as well as its "shadow fleet" of tankers that evade existing sanctions, in order to deprive Moscow of revenues to finance the war with Ukraine.
It also authorises Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on China, India and other countries to reduce their dependence on Russian oil and gas.
India has warned Washington that new measures to levy tariffs over the purchase of Russian oil could impact bilateral ties. REUTERS

Handcuffed runners cross Tallinn half marathon finish line in record time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:13:00 UTC
19:13:00 KST

Handcuffed runners cross Tallinn half marathon finish line in record time
Four friends from England ran the Tallinn half marathon handcuffed together last Saturday, setting a world record for the fastest half marathon by a group of four in restraints.
This was no jog around the course in fancy dress though – the quartet finished the 21-kilometer course in just under 90 minutes: 1:29:29, a well above average time even for an unshackled runner.
Meanwhile, the attempt now awaits confirmation that it is an official record, while the tale of how they got to the event is worth telling.
"We actually didn't practice with the handcuffs on," Joshua Lally, one of the four that pulled off the feat, told ERR News. "We had planned to, but rather embarrassingly the handcuffs were confiscated at the airport. So we had to buy some more on arrival and only got chance to warm up together with them all locked, so we were very unsure whether it was possible."
The group had trained together, including interval running but without using the arms – among other things these are usually central in counterbalancing leg rotation, maintaining balance, and saving energy.
Even with the training, coordination on the day proved challenging. "We didn't want to get in anyone's way so we started quite far back, and going in and out and avoiding obstacles was challenging," Lally explained. "Not having any arm movement meant the arms and upper body quickly tired."
The four were also decked out in stripy "prisoner" outfits, which drew attention along the route.
"I've run a lot of different races and it's the most cheers I've ever heard," Lally said. "The spectators seemed to find it quite funny — a lot were recording and shouting things like 'the police are chasing you.' Even other runners were giving support."
In fact spectators on the day can help with the record ratification process, too. To secure it, the group needs as much footage as possible. Lally recorded every two kilometres, but said the quality of the clips isn't sufficient on its own. Anyone who took photos or video on race day, Saturday, September 12, can send them to Joshua Lally here or to ERR News here.
Estonian records topple
Race weekend in Tallinn saw more conventional records falling too, in both the full and half-marathons. This included several Estonian veterans' records getting broken. Aleksandr Kuleshov ran a marathon in under two and a half hours for the first time, setting a new Estonian record in the M45–49 age group with a time of 2:29.29 — breaking his own record in the process.
Among the women, Siiri Kaaver set a new Estonian record in the W60–64 age group with 3:30.30, more than five minutes faster than the previous mark.
Aimi Pihel also set what should be a new Estonian record in the W75–79 half marathon category with 2:09.03. However, as Marathon100 does not have access to runners' dates of birth, there is some ambiguity over whether Pihel is in that age group or is still competing in the W70–74 category. Esmeralda Lille, also born in 1951, was a couple of minutes faster at 2:07.09, but her 75th birthday was reportedly still a few days away at the time of the event.
Evans Kimtai Kiprono and Vivian Cherotich, both of Kenya, won Sunday's marathon, while two Kenyans, Vincent Kiptoo and Regina Wambui Ndungu, also took victory in the men's and women's half marathon the day before.

Lithuanian drone maker plans up to €50 million defence factory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:12:00 UTC
19:12:00 KST

Lithuanian drone maker RSI Europe plans to invest up to 50 million euros in a new factory in central Lithuania, shifting its focus from developing defence technology to industrial-scale production, the company’s chief executive said Thursday.
RSI Europe and Lithuania’s Ministry of Economy and Innovation signed an investment agreement for the facility, which will develop and manufacture defence systems in Panevėžys district.
“This is a major step for RSI Europe from technology development toward industrialisation and rapid capacity expansion,” CEO Tomas Milašauskas said at the signing ceremony.
The factory is expected to create up to 40 jobs, with about 35% of them for highly qualified engineering and technical specialists, Economy Minister Edvinas Grikšas said.
The facility is expected to begin construction early next year, with most of the work completed by the end of 2027, Milašauskas said.
“The war in Ukraine has shown that armies need not only the best technologies, but also mass production, industrial scale and, above all, secure supply chains,” he said.
The factory will produce complete attack drone systems, including first-person-view, or FPV, drones and about 20 different system elements, according to Milašauskas.
RSI Europe already operates a factory in Vilnius with annual production capacity of about 120,000 drone systems. The new facility will not increase that overall capacity, but will allow the company to manufacture more components in Lithuania.
The company currently uses more than 400 components and subcomponents in its systems and manufactures only some of them domestically. It imports components from more than 30 countries.
“Our total capacity will remain at 120,000, but the range of what we supply will expand,” Milašauskas said.
The equipment will meet the needs of the Lithuanian military, although most production will be exported, he said. Current commercial contracts and production plans are primarily based on demand from foreign buyers, while demand in Lithuania is also developing.
Milašauskas said speed is critical in the defence industry: “Those defence companies that can quickly make decisions, turn decisions into projects and projects into production are the ones that succeed.”
The Panevėžys district site was selected because military manufacturing requires large safety zones, he said. The precise location has not been disclosed.
Šarūnas Genys, head of Invest Lithuania’s manufacturing team, said the factory will be built on a state-owned plot reserved for investment. Four such plots, ranging from 42 to 125 hectares, are currently reserved in Panevėžys and Upytė municipalities.

France can provide defense aid to Ukraine but should scale back financial support, Le Pen says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:11:02 UTC
19:11:02 KST

France can provide defense aid to Ukraine but should scale back financial support, Le Pen says
France cannot continue supporting Ukraine at the current level due to its own financial constraints, the co-leader of the French far-right National Rally (RN) party, Marine Le Pen, said on Sept. 16.
"This is not an act of hostility towards Ukraine. We can continue to train their soldiers, their armies; we can continue to provide them with equipment so they can defend themselves," Le Pen told the French media.
However, France "cannot continue" providing the same financial aid "given the considerable amount we have done so far," the Euroskeptic leader added.
The comments come less than a year before the French presidential election, with surveys putting Le Pen far ahead of any other candidate at 33-34%, making her the most likely successor to pro-European President Emmanuel Macron.
Le Pen argued that France cannot keep spending money abroad while "there isn't a single euro... to index pensions."
Her views echo those of her party's co-leader, Jordan Bardella, who said earlier in September that France should not "abandon" Ukraine completely but cannot continue financing the war-torn country indefinitely and without any guarantees.
The RN has come under criticism from other French parties over its Ukraine policy after Louis Aliot, the RN's vice-president, suggested "turning off the tap" on support for Kyiv.
France has been one of Kyiv's most strategically important allies amid Russia's full-scale war, spearheading pro-Ukrainian initiatives and providing the country with jets, long-range missiles, intelligence support, and other aid.
Macron has also been one of the leading voices in the Coalition of the Willing, a group of over 30 nations coordinating assistance for Ukraine and preparing post-war security guarantees, including a potential deployment of a European-led peacekeeping force.
However, the Kiel Institute's Ukraine Support Tracker says that France lags behind in support provided to Kyiv relative to its economic strength, especially compared to Germany, the Nordics, or the Baltic countries.
As of June 2026, Paris devoted a little over 1% of its GDP to bilateral and EU support for Ukraine, while much less populous countries like Denmark, Estonia, and Lithuania contributed over 3%, Kiel Institute researchers say.
Before Russia's all-out invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Le Pen openly expressed her admiration for Russian President Vladimir Putin, said she did not believe Russia's annexation of Crimea was illegal, and her party took a 9-billion-euro loan from a Russian bank in 2014 despite sanctions.
Le Pen and her party sought to cast away their pro-Kremlin rhetoric after 2022, denouncing Russian aggression and praising Ukrainian defenders. At the same time, Le Pen has opposed more decisive support for Kyiv, such as the deployment of French peacekeepers on the ground.
The nationalist leader has made three unsuccessful runs for the French presidency and was thought to have lost the chance for a fourth attempt when she was convicted of embezzling EU funds and banned from running for public office last March.
However, a Paris appeals court in June 2026 shortened the ban, clearing her path for the presidential run.

====================================================================================================

'I'm not a doomer': US Senator Mark Warner makes the case for acting fast on AI guardrails
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:08:54 UTC
19:08:54 KST

'I'm not a doomer': US Senator Mark Warner makes the case for acting fast on AI guardrails
WASHINGTON, Sept 17 - The U.S. Congress should pass legislation by the year-end setting AI safety standards, as an immediate first step toward broad guardrails for an industry whose rapid development has alarmed tech CEOs and the public alike, U.S. Senator Mark Warner told Reuters in an interview.
Warner, vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee and a leading congressional voice on technology and national security, dismissed much of the doomsday talk surrounding AI but said the time is ripe politically for legislative action, with worries over AI "now at tipping point for Americans."
"I'm not a doomer," the Virginia Democrat said in the interview on Wednesday. "This talk about human extinction is over the top."
He warned, however, of possible trouble ahead, raising "the idea that these swarms of AI agents might jump the fence and take over a banking system or take over a water system or, God forbid, take over a hospital."
A sudden groundswell has risen in favor of federal intervention after OpenAI said in July that an autonomous AI agent went rogue during a security test and hacked into another company, subverting human control.
Warner, who invested in startup companies in wireless telecommunications and other tech sectors before entering politics, said there is an opening for acting before a new Congress is sworn in next January.
"In the short term, I think the only thing we can actually ... get done is a set of safety protocols," he said, adding that UK protocols could be a template for the United States, as could programs that other nations, including China, are pursuing.
TRUMP, REPUBLICANS WARY OVER AI REGULATION
Even that short-term goal, though, is likely to be a heavy lift.
Many Republicans, following the lead of President Donald Trump, are hesitant to thrust the federal government into the AI industry, which is powering U.S. investment and stock market gains.
"I think we need to be careful that we don't get too much government drama," Republican Representative Roger Williams of Texas said in a sidewalk interview near the Capitol on Tuesday. "I think you start out by letting the private sector see how they can compete and make it grow," Williams added.
Republican Representative Ralph Norman of South Carolina, a member of the hard-right House Freedom Caucus, said that while voters want guardrails, "that's going to take a lot of time to work through that." He added: "I'm for limited government."
A bipartisan bill, whose backers range from Democratic Senator Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota to Republican Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, is being refined and Warner said he is reviewing it.
But he stopped short of backing that bill as a first step.
"I think it's well-intentioned, but a lot of it's focused on after-action report, or incident disclosure after action," he said, adding: "We can't wait to have an incident and then look back and see how do we fix it."
TRUMP-XI MEETING PUTS FOCUS ON GLOBAL COLLABORATION
While Trump has taken a hands-off stance toward AI regulation, Washington will be watching closely whether he maintains that position when he meets Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House on September 24.
U.S. opponents of domestic regulation of AI say any government restrictions would simply give China the upper hand in the AI revolution.
But for many Democrats, including Warner, the U.S. must work together with China, France, the UAE and other nations that are developing AI industries, as the world tries to thwart bad actors.
"This is really one where we have to go back to a level of international collaboration," Warner said, at a time when Trump has been pulling away from such cooperation.
Doing so would benefit U.S. industry, he said.
"It would be in their best interest to have an outside, independent, international veteran in this room."
FEDERAL ROLE FOR AI SAFETY
Warner said eventual legislation could include the creation of a new federal agency overseeing AI.
"Nobody would climb on an airplane or drive a car without some level of outside safety reviews. And the industry would need something like potentially even an antitrust exemption to talk to each other."
With the 100 senators pushing for varying provisions, it could make for a prolonged battle — one that Warner said the country cannot risk.
"I don't think whether we call it a pause or pacing means that we're going to stop innovation" in the AI industry, he said.
One relatively easy provision to legislate, Warner said, would be to impose safety standards as a prerequisite for corporate tax breaks, such as the bonus depreciation.
For the economy, he said there were downsides to AI advancements, such as rising unemployment in some sectors that he said the industry has not addressed while the economy transitions.
But "there will be enormous growth" around blue-collar jobs, such as electricians and welders and healthcare advances. "Everyday Americans and not just a bunch of tech guys out in San Francisco" will benefit, he said.
As he campaigns for a fourth Senate term in this November's midterm election, Warner, 71, warned that Congress often waits for a disaster before addressing problems.
Asked to predict the likelihood of AI safety legislation happening in 2026, Warner said he is not good at making predictions, but made one exception.
"If we don't do something and something happens, there's a 95%-plus probability that Americans are going to be even more pissed off at Congress than at President Trump." REUTERS

Is NATO ready to fight? The Ukraine war is raising doubts among military analysts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:08:43 UTC
19:08:43 KST

Is NATO ready to fight? The Ukraine war is raising doubts among military analysts
KYIV, Sept 17 - Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine has killed hundreds of thousands of people. It has also served as a proving ground for new weapons systems and raised an uncomfortable question for the North Atlantic Treaty Organization: Is the alliance prepared for the next war it might have to fight?
Five Ukrainian and Western defense officials told Reuters that developments on the battlefield are moving so quickly that some NATO weapons and tactics risk becoming outdated. While Ukraine – which is not an alliance member – adapts in weeks, NATO buys and develops systems over years, sometimes decades.
The Ukraine war and U.S. President Donald Trump’s haranguing of European allies have prompted many NATO members to dramatically increase their defense spending. The Pentagon is currently reviewing its military presence in European countries, which Trump has accused of sponging off U.S. protection and refusing to help prosecute his unpopular war against Iran.
Denys Shtilerman, the co-owner and chief designer of Fire Point, a leading Ukrainian missile and drone builder, told Reuters that tanks are now “worthless” because a drone costing about $5,000 can destroy one. Yet Europe still spends heavily on tanks – which, say many military analysts, still have a key role to play in future battles.
Cheap drones have also transformed warfare in other ways. Troops gathering in groups or large vehicle convoys all become far easier targets.
“They are good at storming positions,” Oleksandr Pivnenko, Commander of the National Guard of Ukraine, said of the international troops his units trained with last year. “But if there’s a drone overhead and you don’t even look up, what do you think will happen to your squad?”
In June, Reuters attended a NATO military exercise near Paldiski in Estonia – a small Baltic country now fortifying its 210-mile border with Russia – in which American and European troops treated dozens of simulated casualties at wartime field hospitals. But the exercise took place with the assumption that NATO would command the airspace above the hospitals – no longer a given in the age of cheap, stealthy, long-distance drones.
Rather than simply receiving NATO training and assistance, Ukrainian officials described a growing role for Ukraine in teaching the alliance lessons drawn from the war with Russia. Yet they also said NATO’s military bureaucracy struggles to absorb those lessons. A Ukrainian officer who underwent NATO psychological operations training in Romania told Reuters that some alliance training materials still relied on case studies from World War Two. NATO didn’t respond to questions about the officials’ criticism of its training and bureaucracy.
The Ukraine war has also exposed a vulnerability that NATO officials say is far harder to solve: air and missile defense. Russia’s relentless barrages against Ukrainian cities have highlighted Europe's dependence on sophisticated U.S. anti-missile systems such as the Patriot, first used in the 1991 Gulf War. Ukraine has a critical shortage of Patriot interceptors – the missiles fired to destroy incoming threats.
Fearing that its reliance on Patriots might become a strategic vulnerability, Europe is building non-U.S. alternatives. Ukraine is awaiting delivery of the new French-Italian SAMP/T-NG air-defense system, designed to intercept ballistic missiles. France has promised to accelerate its deployment to Ukraine, and European diplomats previously told Reuters it was expected to arrive by next spring.
In a statement, the Ukrainian defense ministry said its soldiers and NATO’s had much to learn from each other, hailing Ukraine’s use of drones and radioelectronic warfare as “globally unmatched" and praising European efforts to help tackle Russia’s drone and missile bombardments.
In July, Ukraine and nine European allies launched an air-defense coalition that includes plans to jointly develop a new anti-ballistic missile system. Known as Freyja, the project is a consortium of about a dozen companies with Fire Point as the lead private-sector partner. The goal is to build a system that is cheaper and faster to produce than the Patriot, while ensuring that Europe, not the U.S., controls its manufacture.
“If you spend $20 billion on your air defense system, you must be independent in your security,” said Fire Point’s Shtilerman. REUTERS

Nigeria sends state police amendment bill to state assemblies for ratification
ABUJA, Sept 17 - Nigeria's parliament has sent a constitutional amendment bill that would establish state police forces to the country's 36 state assemblies for ratification, advancing a key security overhaul by President Bola Tinubu as he faces mounting pressure over worsening insecurity ahead of January elections.
• National Assembly clerk Kamoru Ogunlana said the Constitution (Sixth Alteration) Bill, 2026, which contains provisions for state police, has been cleared by federal lawmakers and sent to Nigeria's 36 state assemblies for consideration.
• Ogunlana said the National Assembly had asked states to return their resolutions within 30 days, but added that the timeframe was administrative and not constitutionally binding.
• The bill must be approved by at least two-thirds of state assemblies, or 24 of the 36 states, before it can become law.
• Supporters say state police would improve responses to local security threats by decentralising policing powers from the federal government.
• Other constitutional amendment proposals still awaiting final approval include local government autonomy, independent candidacy, reserved legislative seats for women and citizenship by investment.
• If ratified by the required number of state assemblies, it would be one of the most sweeping changes to Nigeria's security and governance framework since the country returned to civilian rule in 1999. REUTERS

At least 19 injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine
The missile and drone strikes targeted Ukraine’s capital Kyiv as well as the Zaporizhzhia and Odesa regions.
Ukrainian officials say at least 19 people have been injured in Russian missile and drone strikes targeting Kyiv and surrounding areas.
Ukraine’s Air Force said on Thursday that it destroyed or suppressed 131 Russian aerial targets during the overnight attacks, adding that the main areas targeted were the Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia and Odesa regions.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items

- list 2 of 3Why is Trump warning Zelenskyy not to hit Russian diesel refineries?
- list 3 of 3NATO pledges more Ukraine support after Russia strikes near Poland
Strikes were recorded at 36 locations, while debris from intercepted targets fell at five sites.
Russia’s Defence Ministry said its forces hit metallurgical and electronics plants, factories of the military-industrial complex, energy and transport facilities in the three regions.
Three bulk carriers and a ferry used to carry supplies for the Ukrainian military were hit in the port of Chornomorsk, added the ministry.
In Odesa, seven people were injured, including two children, according to Ukraine’s State Emergency Service. High-rise apartments in a residential building were damaged.
A private residential building in Odesa was destroyed, while warehouses, a nursery school, cars and garages were damaged at other locations, the service said on Telegram.
In Kyiv’s Dniprovsky district, a warehouse, office building, residential buildings and cars were damaged, according to local authorities. A warehouse was damaged in the Solomyansky district, while a warehouse and cars were damaged in the Darnitsky district.
In the Podilsky district, the roof of a non-residential building was damaged, authorities said.
In the Kyiv region, civilian areas and infrastructure were targeted in the Obukhiv, Brovary, Fastiv and Bucha districts, according to Tymur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv Regional Administration.
A total of 33 sites were damaged, with the worst reported in the Brovary district, where 14 sites were hit, and the Fastiv district, where 10 were damaged, Tkachenko said in a statement on Telegram.
The damaged sites included homes, warehouses, production facilities and vehicles. No casualties or injuries were reported, he said.
Al Jazeera’s Rory Challands, reporting from Kyiv, said the strikes come days after United States President Donald Trump announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to suspend attacks on energy facilities.
“We have a situation where just a few days ago, [US President] Donald Trump announced that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop hitting each other’s energy targets,” as Trump has blamed the Russia-Ukraine war for the rising cost of diesel around the world, said Challands.
However, “neither Russia nor Ukraine have agreed to this and they are continuing to hit each other’s energy targets”, said Challands, with Russia promising to increase its “mass attacks on the Ukrainian energy grid going into the winter months”.
Russian attacks “almost collapsed the Ukrainian energy grid” last winter, with Ukraine’s energy providers now saying that they are “expecting another very tough winter” but hoping that it will be better than the previous one, said Challands.
A Ukrainian drone attack hit an oil refinery in the Russian city of Yaroslavl, northeast of Moscow, said President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
The resulting fire from the attack had been extinguished, announced regional governor Mikhail Yevrayev.
Zelenskyy also reported damage to Russian warplanes and helicopters in a strike on a military base in the southern city of Rostov.
“There have also been good results in the Black Sea,” the president said on social media, without giving further details.
Meanwhile, Russia and Ukraine exchanged the bodies of their war dead, with Moscow handing over the remains of 252 people and receiving 23 bodies in the swap at the Belarusian-Ukrainian border, Belarusian state news agency BELTA reported.

FvD refuses to remove racist podcast episode amid outcry

FvD refuses to remove racist podcast episode amid outcry
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
An English language podcast broadcast aired by the far-right FvD party’s international arm, Forum & Friends, has sparked an outcry after guests described African people as “pack animals”, discussed racial IQ theories and described Black people as genetically inferior.
The podcast is a weekly show which, like other party operations, is funded through the interior ministry’s subsidy for political parties.
The August 26 episode was hosted by John Laughland, a British party staffer who has run FvD International since 2022 and is a mentor to party founder Thierry Baudet.
Laughland’s guest was British author Simon Elmer, who had posted a series of messages on X about Jason Arday, a Black Cambridge professor who took his own life earlier this year following plagiarism accusations.
Elmer went on to describe the “genetically determined culture and mentality of African people” and said their only use was “to destroy us and breed us out of existence”. He called people from 10 African countries “feeble-minded”. Laughland nodded along and said at the end that it was “hard to disagree” with the analysis.
“Outlandish”
 FvD parliamentary leader Ralf Dekker told Volkskrant he had not heard the episode. The podcast gives a platform to voices that “provoke thought”, he said, “and then it can sometimes be outlandish. But if this was said literally, I do not agree with it.” He said there was no reason to remove it: “You should never take anything offline.”
Laughland and the FvD press office have not responded to questions from Volkskrant since Friday.
Léonie de Jonge, a political scientist who researches the far right, told the paper the English-language format was no accident: the podcast is aimed at international far-right networks, not Dutch voters. Anthropologist Amade M’charek said “feeble-minded” is a eugenics term used to justify mass sterilisation in the 20th century.
Earlier episodes have featured guests defending the “great replacement” conspiracy theory, and Laughland himself has spoken of a “horrible cabal” transferring wealth to a small elite, a phrase closely tied to antisemitic conspiracy theories, Volkskrant said.
Laughland, who taught Baudet at Oxford, worked from 2008 to 2015 for a Russian-funded think tank in Paris. Investigative platform Follow the Money reported last year that he spoke at four Russian government-linked conferences between June 2024 and May 2025, with his travel and accommodation paid by his Russian hosts, which the FvD confirmed. He has described Ukraine as “a fiction”.

Lithuania Plans to Use Its Defense Industry to Supply Ukrainian Forces With Advanced Drones
Lithuania is planning to use its domestic defense manufacturing capacity to produce unmanned aerial vehicles for Ukraine in cooperation with Ukrainian partners.
Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda announced the initiative following a meeting of the State Defense Council, as reported by Delfi on September 16.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Each year, the Baltic nation directs over 0.25% of its gross domestic product to assist Ukraine, an amount that exceeds €230 million ($265 million).
Officials propose utilizing a significant portion of these annual funds to manufacture drones on Lithuanian territory.
The manufacturing initiative relies on integrating Ukrainian technology into production lines, with the resulting equipment to be supplied directly to the Ukrainian Defense Forces.
Two agreements covering this cooperative effort have already been signed between the two nations. However, actual production volume at facilities in Lithuania has not yet reached expected levels.
Delays were initially attributed to lengthy licensing procedures required on the Ukrainian side.
President Nausėda acknowledged that domestic factors in Lithuania have also contributed to the slow ramp-up, specifically citing delays in selecting participating manufacturing companies and a small volume of initial orders.
Ukrainian FP-1 long-range drones, meanwhile, have recently set a new distance record by traveling over 3,200 kilometers to strike a Gazprom processing plant in Russia’s Yamalo-Nenets region.
The strike targeted a specific gas treatment unit, which, as estimated, could disrupt roughly 10 percent of Russia’s combined polyethylene and polypropylene production capacity.

The EU Wants to Break Up Kids and Their Chatbots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:06:50 UTC
19:06:50 KST

The EU plans to ban chatbots from simulating emotions or interpersonal relationships in interactions with anyone under the age of 18 as the bloc tries to stop children from developing emotional dependencies on the technology.
The rules will be part of the EU Kids Act, proposed on Thursday, which includes similar restrictions on minors’ access to social media and video-sharing platforms. Children under 13 will be banned from accessing chatbots without their guardians’ supervision, and digital platforms will have to build child-safety protections into their products or face fines of up to 6 percent of total worldwide turnover, according to a draft of the legislation seen by WIRED.
Chatbots operating in the EU will also not be allowed to retain memory of interactions between separate conversations under the new rules, since the Commission worries this could lead to systems accumulating sensitive data of minors over time and potentially reinforcing harmful interaction patterns.
Providers of online social networking sites, video-sharing platforms, and games should not automatically activate or encourage the use of AI chatbots on their services, the proposed law will also stipulate. That includes not pinning AI companions and general conversational chatbots at the top of a minor’s contacts list, it says—as had been done by Snapchat.
The proposal is limited to AI companions and general conversational chatbots seen by the Commission to pose serious risks to minors’ health, safety, and well-being. Simeon de Brouwer, a policy adviser at the Brussels-based advocacy group European Digital Rights, welcomes the chatbot measures, but tells WIRED it doesn’t make sense to restrict them to young people only. “Don’t we all deserve to be protected from AIs designed to be addictive, from AIs which create emotional dependencies, or from AI features which are activated and pushed by default onto users?” The EU says its Digital Fairness Act, due to be unveiled later this year, is expected to propose clampdowns on addictive design more widely.
In documents seen by WIRED, the European Commission says it is worried that dependency on chatbots may negatively impact a child’s development and its relationships with other humans. It’s also concerned by chatbots giving minors dangerous advice, including on their mental health and personal development, which it said can shape and encourage risky behavior.
“Platforms have been playing fast and loose with children’s mental health,” President Ursula von der Leyen said in a press conference on Thursday. Around half of Europeans aged 11 to 25 have discussed intimate or personal matters with AI chatbots, according to an Ipsos BVA survey across France, Germany, Sweden, and Ireland. Australia and the UK are both attempting to restrict minors’ access to chatbots through their social media bans.
It also highlighted the harms of deepfakes generated by chatbots, which von der Leyen nodded at in Wednesday’s State of the Union speech: “We do not have to accept that girls have their photos used for AI-generated sexualised images … Europe has the power to act.” While the EU AI Act has required synthetic content to be labeled as AI-generated since August, the rules currently only apply to deepfakes generated for commercial use.
The Commission also blames digital distraction for a decline in basic skills in young people. Children who say they use AI chatbots for schoolwork get lower test scores than those who don’t, according to research spanning 91 countries by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. Concerns about cognitive impacts and deskilling “expose the absence of children’s rights from the design of GenAI’s tools,” researchers from the independent network EU Kids Online wrote in a report.

Founded by chef Michele Pascarella, London's 'Napoli on the Road' took the top spot ahead of the reigning champ 'Una Pizza Napoletana'.
London has officially got the world's best pizza. Napoli on the Road, the Chiswick pizzeria founded by chef Michele Pascarella, has taken the top spot at the 50 Top Pizza World Awards 2026, beating out hundreds of contenders from around the globe.
The win was announced in Naples – the original birthplace of pizza – where Pascarella celebrated a remarkable journey. He launched Napoli on the Road in 2016 from a three-wheeled Piaggio Ape fitted with a wood-fired oven, serving pizzas at London’s streets and farmers’ markets.
A decade later, the business has grown into restaurants in Chiswick, Richmond and Soho, with the latter branch offering a pizza tasting menu inspired by Pascarella’s childhood in Caserta in the south of Italy.
"I’m in shock. I probably need to have a few drinks and a sit down to process this. I can’t explain how big this is. It’s like the Oscars but for pizza," Pascarella said at the ceremony in Naples.
After two consecutive years at number one, Anthony Mangieri’s Una Pizza Napoletana in New York has dropped to second place. In third is Milan's Confine, ran by Francesco Capece and Mario Ventura.
The results of the competition, now in its tenth year, are based on almost 1,000 anonymous inspectors, with each restaurant visited twice and judged on its pizza, ingredients, service and hospitality.

To take stock of the artistic and cultural collaboration between Italy and Armenia and to explore prospects for further cooperation between the Armenian theater and Italian institutions in the sector, the Italian ambassador to Yerevan,Alessandro Ferranti, paid a visit to the Armenian National Academic Opera and Ballet Theater. US Senate blocks AI ‘kill switch’ bill amid debate over superintelligence risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:05:43 UTC
19:05:43 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
The US Senate on Wednesday blocked an effort by Sen. John Kennedy to fast-track legislation requiring developers of advanced artificial intelligence systems to install an emergency “kill switch,” amid growing debate in Washington over the potential risks posed by increasingly autonomous AI.
Kennedy, a Republican from Louisiana, sought unanimous consent to advance his AI Emergency Button Act, arguing that humans must retain the ability to shut down an AI system if it becomes uncontrollable, according to The Hill.
“Well, I’ve got a bill, and it basically says that if you’re going to sell an advanced AI model in the United States of America, it has got to have a kill switch,” Kennedy said.
He said the legislation would leave responsibility for activating the switch with the companies developing the systems rather than the federal government.
Kennedy warned that advances such as recursive self-improvement could, in a worst-case scenario, allow an AI model to operate beyond effective human control.
“What I would like to see us do is to figure out a way to strike a balance between innovation and public safety,” Kennedy said.
Sen. Rand Paul, a Republican from Kentucky, objected to the request, saying Congress should seek a better understand of the technology before imposing broad requirements.
Paul warned that an open-ended mandate could affect AI systems used throughout the economy, including search engines and medical applications.
“AI is going to be throughout the economy and so many facets. Are doctors going to have to build a kill switch into drug prescription analysis?” Paul said.
Paul proposed establishing a bipartisan committee to study the risks posed by superintelligent AI and possible safeguards. Kennedy rejected the proposal, arguing that another congressional study could further delay action.

President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelensky believes that China could exert pressure on the Russian leadership to end the war, but refrains from doing so for its own reasons, he stated in an interview with Japan's public broadcaster NHK.
"I have seen a real North Korean-made missile in Ukraine. I have not seen Chinese missiles. But I know that their technologies find their way to Russia. The equipment they use comes from China, presumably along with specialists and technologies. I do not see China pressing Russia to end the war. I have never seen this. Perhaps they do it during some of their bilateral meetings, I do not know," Zelensky said.
He noted that China wields enormous influence over Russia, especially now amid extensive sanctions, the shadow fleet, and severed energy and banking systems. He expressed confidence that Beijing could find a way to push Vladimir Putin toward negotiations, adding that its failure to act amounts to support.
Zelensky called it regrettable that China is political on the side of Russia, clarifying that it is not about weapons, but political will. He stated that the war could be stopped instantly by strong leaders, including China, and expressed disappointment that Beijing is not on Ukraine's side, describing its stance as leaning closer to Russia through openness and readiness to help.
Regarding North Korea, the president reported that Pyongyang has deployed between 30,000 and 50,000 soldiers to Russia, while Moscow has provided them with real combat experience and training. He added that North Korean troops are learning, working with drones, and training, which poses a major security concern, particularly for the Pacific region.
Addressing bilateral ties, Zelensky emphasized that Ukraine is eager to build military-technology cooperation with Japan, noting that there are no neutral countries when it comes to defense. Revolut hack: criminals steal data of 700 European clients, demand $3m ransom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:05:14 UTC
19:05:14 KST

Prosecutors in Reggio Calabria have opened an inquiry into a scam against banking app Revolut, after hackers stole data via an Italian PEC and demanded a 3 million dollar ransom.
The public prosecutor's office in Reggio Calabria has opened an investigation into a case involving the banking services company Revolut, founded in London, which is now reportedly being blackmailed.
A group of hackers requested sensitive data from the bank using a compromised institutional email account belonging to the Reggio Calabria prefecture.
The digital bank has confirmed that data belonging to around 680 European customers has been affected, but that their funds have not been touched.
According to the Financial Times, which contacted the cybercriminals via Telegram, the group calls itself "iamnotavillain" and posted on its website on Wednesday afternoon a ransom demand for 3 million dollars, equivalent to 2.61 million euros.
If they do not receive the money within 24 hours, the hackers are threatening to sell the sensitive data to other criminal organisations.
The National Anti-Mafia and Counter-Terrorism Directorate is also working on the case, as it concerns a government body. The cybercrime division of the police says it was a highly sophisticated operation, but several points still need to be clarified.
An unusual ransom demand
The group posted the ransom demand on its site on the dark web. The Financial Times (source in Italian) notes that making such a demand public is unusual; typically, ransom and extortion attempts are made privately at first and only made public if the targets refuse to pay.
In this case, however, the British newspaper received a message demanding that Revolut transfer "6,000 XMR / 3,000,000 $… otherwise all the data will be sold and you will have blood on your hands".
XMR is the ticker symbol for the cryptocurrency Monero, often used in illegal contexts because it is difficult to trace.
The criminal group also told the newspaper that this was the first time it had used its site for a ransom demand and that it had not yet contacted the bank to open negotiations.
After making the ransom demand public, the hackers sent the Financial Times a 60-second screen recording showing an unidentified user scrolling through a collection of documents, possibly belonging to Revolut.
The information contained in the documents taken from Revolut is said to include passport details, driving licence data, other identity documents and photographs. The hackers claim to hold a total of 147 gigabytes of data.
How far the investigation has progressed
Prosecutors are considering the offence of intrusion into an IT system of public interest. An initial report from the cybercrime police indicates that the operation, which lasted for months, was highly sophisticated, and it is still not certain whether a computer at the Reggio Calabria prefecture or at Italy's Interior Ministry was compromised.
Experts are also trying to establish whether the institutional email account from which the requests originated was infiltrated or cloned.
Alongside the national Anti-Mafia and Counter-Terrorism Prosecutor's Office, the Italian data protection authority has also stepped in, immediately launching checks for possible security breaches at Italian banks and urging data-protection officers to carry out a "prompt review" and, if any vulnerabilities are found, to notify the authority immediately.
The Italian privacy watchdog has also contacted its counterpart in Lithuania, where Revolut's registered office is located, starting an exchange of information to strengthen efforts to counter the threat.
The investigation will determine how the offence was carried out and whether other public bodies were also affected.

Fiji declares national HIV crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:05:06 UTC
19:05:06 KST

This file photo taken on April 20, 2026 shows an HIV awareness poster displayed along a main road in Suva, as health authorities and aid agencies step up public messaging amid a surge in HIV cases in Fiji. (AFP Photo)
Fiji has declared a national HIV crisis as sexual transmission and illicit drug use help to spread the virus, now infecting an estimated one in 60 adults in the Pacific nation.
New HIV diagnoses surged to 2,016 cases in 2025, 16 times the level recorded in 2019, authorities said, vowing a “whole of government” response.
“I am formally declaring a national HIV emergency in Fiji,” Health Minister Atonio Lalabalavu told reporters on Sept. 16.
“This decision recognizes the seriousness of the epidemic and the urgent, coordinated response our country now needs.”
An estimated one in 60 adults in Fiji have HIV, up from one in 167 five years earlier, the government said.
Two in every 100 pregnant women carry the virus, it said. Of the 59 babies born with HIV in 2025, 18 died before their first birthday.
The government said it was expanding access to free HIV testing, prevention services and treatment.
“This includes rapid testing, prevention medicine for people at higher risk, harm-reduction measures for people who inject drugs, and free treatment for people diagnosed with HIV.”
Among HIV cases with a known mode of transmission, more than half were linked to sexual transmission and more than 42 percent to injecting drug use, UNAIDS said.
The U.N. agency welcomed Fiji’s plans to introduce legislation for a needle and syringe program.
“Fiji still has an opportunity to change the course of this epidemic,” said Eamonn Murphy, UNAIDS director for regions including Asia and the Pacific.

A bear killed two men who were gathering wild berries in Siberia’s Irkutsk region, police said Thursday, coming amid a reported rise in deadly encounters between humans and bears since the spring.
Law enforcement said the bear attacked three people who were foraging in the Taiga, killing a 55-year-old and a 65-year-old on Wednesday in a remote forest on the banks of the Lena River, located around 4,200 kilometers (2,610 miles) east of Moscow.
“One person managed to escape and report the incident,” the regional branch of Russia’s Interior Ministry said.
A search team of police officers and hunters located the bodies of the two men in the forest and opened fire after the bear was said to have appeared and behaved aggressively. The bear fled the area, and authorities are trying to track it down.
At least 14 people are now reported to have been killed in bear attacks across Russia since the start of the year, according to a tally by The Moscow Times. The number of non-fatal incidents is higher, experts say.
In the neighboring Krasnoyarsk region, investigators said Wednesday that a bear killed a 66-year-old woman in her remote village home.
The Natural Resources and Environment Ministry has dismissed reports of an uptick in bear attacks this year, noting that the annual figure tends to hover between 20 and 30, which includes both fatal and non-fatal incidents. In 2014, Russia saw a record 166 bear attacks.
Russia’s brown bear population has more than doubled since 1990 and now stands at 307,000. Authorities have reportedly killed more than 530 aggressive bears across the country since the spring

On October 28, 2026, the Italian Cultural Institute in Pretoria will host an exclusive literary event at the Italian Embassy to mark the publication in Italian of Etienne van Heerden’s acclaimed novel *The Long Silence of Mario Salviati*.
                                    
                                       
				Joining Etienne van Heerden—one of South Africa’s most prominent novelists—will be Dr. Raphael d’Abdon, writer, scholar, and translator of the new Italian edition, for a special discussion.
                                    
                                       
				Originally published in Afrikaans in 2000 under the title *Die swye van Mario Salviati*, the novel is now available to Italian readers in a new translation published by CH3 Press. The book received the M-Net Prize in 2001.
                                    
                                       
				Set against the spectacular landscape of the Great Karoo, in the fictional town of Yearsonend, “The Long Silence of Mario Salviati” is a rich and layered novel in which history, memory, myth, and magical realism intertwine.
                                    
                                       
				   At the heart of the novel is Mario Salviati, an Italian prisoner of war during World War II, who was interned at the Zondewater camp before arriving in the Karoo, where he became a stonemason. Now deaf, mute, and blind, Mario has remained silent for decades; his silence, however, conceals crucial knowledge about the town’s past.
                                    
                                       
				Van Heerden explores the themes of memory, uprooting, identity, and silence, as well as the way in which the past continues to shape the present. The novel intertwines South African history with the experience of an Italian prisoner of war, creating a fascinating literary bridge between South Africa and Italy.
                                    
                                       
				This special event will offer the public the opportunity to meet Etienne van Heerden and Dr. Raphael d’Abdon and to hear them discuss the novel, its themes, the South African context, and the challenges involved in translating this important work of Afrikaans literature into Italian.
                                    
                                       
				Copies of both the Italian and English editions will be available for purchase during the presentation.

mushlume co-creates with living organisms to grow design objects at MADE: bush terminal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:00:50 UTC
19:00:50 KST

MUSHLUME RETHINKS MATERIAL APPROACH INSIDE MADE: BUSH TERMINAL
MADE: Bush Terminal, a revitalized public landmark, reopens its historic doors as a productive workspace designed to fuel local innovation and economic growth. Inside the renewed space, designboom speaks with Danielle Trofe, founder of MushLume, one of the resident studios shaping the hub, who combines a biofabrication laboratory and production. Awarded for its sustainable lighting and acoustic panels, MushLume grows its collection using living mycelium and agricultural hemp, pioneering a design approach that treats nature as a true partner rather than a simple material resource.
‘The story of how I came across this material really shaped my relationship with this living organism. I began my design studio in 2011 and was working mainly in hydroponics. Then, I found this material in a materials library that was grown using living mycelium and hemp. Just that concept alone was so intriguing: that I didn’t have to take an inert material and shape it into something; I could actually co-create with a living organism to grow an object. It really changed my whole design approach,’ Danielle Trofe starts the exclusive interview with designboom.
MushLume sound-absorbing lighting fixtures | image © Rob Frost, Chance Productions
LEARNING FROM NATURE, NOT EXTRACTING FROM IT
Grounded in the philosophy of learning from nature instead of extracting from it, MushLume applies biomimicry by studying biological processes rather than simply copying their visual forms. Fostering optimal conditions for organisms to thrive, the studio cultivates the growth of living materials and collaborates directly with biological systems to create sustainable design solutions.
‘It’s really about understanding these intricate relationships, whether on an ecosystem level or on the organism level of how it functions. Nature has evolved over millions, if not billions, of years. The species that exist today have the solutions for surviving and thriving in this world. We are looking at nature as a source of information rather than just a source of material,’ says Danielle.
MushLume leverages biomimicry, integrating biological functions into design
Ditching traditional manufacturing norms, MushLume develops products designed to return safely to the earth at the end of their life cycle. Instead of competing with mass production materials like plastic, the studio engages directly with architects and interior designers seeking healthy, low-embodied-carbon alternatives. This material focus results in bio-based lighting and acoustic solutions that support both planetary health and indoor well-being.
‘There aren’t many architects or designers who don’t want to use healthy materials that have low embodied carbon or energy impact. We are all trying to specify products that are good for both the planet and the people using those spaces. What we need now is more investment and specification of biomaterials that are proving themselves. We differentiate ourselves by showing the true benefits of a compostable, non-toxic material that doesn’t off-gas,’ Trofe affirms.
partnering with architects and designers, the practice delivers sustainable solutions for contemporary interiors | image courtesy of Starwood Capital Group
SCALing HANDCRAFTED BIOMATERIALS FOR COMMERCIAL spaces
In the crafting process, agricultural and fiber hemp waste is upcycled and combined with living mycelium, the underground root network of mushrooms. Utilizing the full organism instead of its fruiting body, the studio does not take it directly from nature, but grows its material in lab or farm environments.
‘We inoculate the substrate and pack it into custom molds that hold the shape of this loose, mulch-like material. Then, we create the conditions for the living organism to grow by controlling humidity, temperature, and light, allowing it to do what it does best: grow. This happens in days. Most of our lampshades are grown within 7 to 10 days,’ Danielle declares.
hemp waste is upcycled and bound with living mycelium, transforming raw byproduct into bio-based material
Managed entirely in-house, inventory is constantly rotated through a strict production schedule to maximize output within a minimal footprint. ‘We’re growing, drying, storing, and then shipping — trying to do this in the least amount of space. We understand that scale is crucial for a biomaterial like this to compete in a commercial marketplace, so we need to prove that a handcraft can still compete on cost as well,’ says the designer.
Whether crafting lighting fixtures, acoustic panels, or custom sculptures, MushLume scales its bio-fabricated designs to meet the demands of commercial, workplace, and residential spaces. The studio leverages the inherent performance qualities of its two core ingredients: mycelium and hemp. Achieving a Class A fire rating required for commercial lighting standards, the material relies entirely on mycelium’s natural fire resistance without synthetic chemical retardants. Additionally, the porous fibrous matrix naturally absorbs sound, delivering dual-function performance that combines high-efficiency acoustic dampening directly within illuminated elements.
‘Instead of just single lamps, we are creating integrated acoustic lighting systems that feel like art on your wall while silently performing by adding light and sound absorption to the space,’ Trofe tells designboom.
mushlume bio-fabricated fixtures secure a class a fire rating through mycelium’s natural flame resistance
The new MushLume lab at MADE: Bush Terminal opens a pivotal chapter for the studio, consolidating design, cultivation, and production under one roof. Bringing these operations together in a single facility enables the studio to transition from an innovative experimental lab into a fully scaled commercial producer of bio-fabricated lighting and acoustic systems.
‘Now, we can combine everything under one roof. Beyond achieving a higher scale of production, we chose this space because we wanted a public-facing side. It allows us to bring in designers, architects, and clients to visualize the process and the end product in space. It also lets us engage with the public — students, designers interested in biomaterials, or anyone curious about the field — by hosting workshops for hands-on experience with biomaterials,’ Trofe notes.
unifying research, growth, and production under one roof accelerates the studio’s evolution
Embedded in the vibrant maker community of Sunset Park, South Brooklyn, the studio benefits from a unique creative ecosystem. Proximity to diverse fabricators, materials, and production methods encourages spontaneous cross-pollination and collaborative innovation.
‘As we expand into new product categories, being able to consult with fabricators working in metal, wood, or digital fabrication is so important. Just like nature operates better through shared resources in an ecosystem, the new lab allows designers and artists to collaborate by sharing resources and intelligence,’ concludes Danielle Trofe.
the studio’s proximity to diverse creators at sunset park fuels continuous collaborative design

name: MADE: Bush Terminal
organizer: New York City Economic Development Corporation (NYCEDC) | @nycedc
design studio: MushLume | @mushlume_lighting
location: Sunset Park, Brooklyn, New York

Moeve starts building Europe's largest green hydrogen project in Huelva
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:00:26 UTC
19:00:26 KST

The first phase of the Andalusian Green Hydrogen Valley will include 300 MW of electrolysis and require investment of over €1 billion. Moeve expects to create more than 8,000 jobs during its development.
Moeve has begun construction in Palos de la Frontera, Huelva, on the first phase of the Andalusian Green Hydrogen Valley, a project the company presents as the largest of its kind in Europe and which aims to place Spain in a central position in the development of this new energy industry.
The first phase, called 'Onuba', will initially have 300 MW of electrolysis capacity, with the option of adding a further 105 MW, and will involve a total investment of more than €1 billion, including the associated infrastructure and a photovoltaic plant for self-consumption.
During the development, construction and commissioning phases, Moeve estimates that the project will create more than 8,000 direct jobs, as well as indirect and induced employment along the entire value chain, and will support activity at more than 400 small and medium-sized enterprises and local self-employed workers.
"Once again, we are turning ambition into a tangible reality", said Moeve's chief executive, Maarten Wetselaar, quoted in a statement. "Today we are turning the page on green hydrogen pilot projects and moving into the chapter of large-scale construction."
In comments to 'Euronews', Wetselaar argued that 'Onuba' can help reinforce Spain's role in Europe's energy transition and reduce external dependence. "We need European energy that is decarbonised and produced by us, and that is exactly what this project delivers," he explained.
The company expects the facility to produce around 45,000 tonnes of renewable hydrogen a year, avoiding some 250,000 tonnes of CO₂ emissions annually. The hydrogen will be used to support more sustainable production of fuels for road, air and maritime transport, as well as contributing to the decarbonisation of other industries.
Sánchez hails construction of the plant
The start of construction was marked on Thursday in Palos de la Frontera at an event bringing together representatives of the Spanish government, the European Commission, the regional government of Andalusia and the town councils of Palos de la Frontera and Huelva, along with executives from the companies involved in the project.
Among those attending were the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, the president of the regional government of Andalusia, Juanma Moreno, the third deputy prime minister and minister for the Ecological Transition, Sara Aagesen, and the European Commission's executive vice-president for a Clean, Fair and Competitive Transition, Teresa Ribera.
The prime minister welcomed what he described as a "huge industrial opportunity" which, in addition to creating jobs, shows that "the energy transition is already driving investment", both public and private.
"For decades, Spain and Europe have depended too heavily on energy coming from elsewhere. We still do. Unfortunately, every international crisis reminds us of the huge price we are paying for that dependence," he said at the event. "We cannot leave our supply at the mercy of unjustified wars, of tensions elsewhere, of the legitimate geopolitical interests of other powers that are not our own, nor, of course, keep picking up the tab for those who turn energy into just another piece in their power games."
Spain at the heart of production
For Moeve, Spain's conditions, and those of Andalusia in particular, offer an advantage for the development of green hydrogen. The company highlights the availability of solar and wind power, land for large renewable facilities and conditions that make it possible to produce renewable electricity at competitive cost.
"Spain has abundant solar energy, very good wind power and space to build large renewable parks," Wetselaar said. In his view, given that renewable electricity accounts for a large share of the cost of producing green hydrogen, the availability of renewable resources could make the country one of Europe's leading producers.
The 'Onuba' project is led by Moeve, which holds a 51% stake in the initiative. Hy24 and Cofides together hold 29%, while Enagás Renovable and Alter Enersun control the remaining 20%.
The project has been recognised by the European Union as a Project of Common Interest and has received €304 million in funding from the Spanish government through the Recovery, Transformation and Resilience Plan, financed by the European Union via NextGenerationEU.
A 2 GW project
'Onuba' is the first phase of the Andalusian Green Hydrogen Valley, which Moeve plans to develop to reach a total electrolysis capacity of 2 GW at its energy parks in Palos de la Frontera and San Roque, in the province of Cadiz.
The company also intends to connect production in Huelva with other European industrial hubs through pipeline or maritime transport solutions. "We want to scale up this plant and connect Huelva with other industrial centres in Europe," Wetselaar explained.
The development of hydrogen is part of a broader transformation of Moeve's facilities in Andalusia. The company plans to invest a total of €2.4 billion in energy transition projects in the region, including 'Onuba' and a second-generation biofuels plant that will produce sustainable aviation fuel and renewable diesel.
For Wetselaar, rolling out these projects could have effects that go well beyond energy production. "If Spain scales up, we are talking about thousands of jobs, a significant impact on GDP and, of course, political clout," he said. In his view, the ability to produce and export renewable energy could reshape Spain's energy relationship with the rest of Europe.
