09:43:50 UTC
18:43:50 KST

The Palestinian Authority has condemned a US decision to deny visas to President Mahmoud Abbas and dozens of officials ahead of next week's UN General Assembly, marking the second consecutive year Washington has blocked his attendance.
The Palestinian Authority on Thursday sharply criticised a decision by the United States to deny visas to its officials ahead of next week's UN General Assembly in New York, a measure that also affects its president Mahmoud Abbas.
In a statement, the Palestinian foreign ministry called it "an unjustified measure that runs counter to efforts to rebuild trust, develop Palestinian–US relations, and create the necessary political climate for implementing the two-state solution and achieving peace and stability".
The decision marks the second consecutive year in which Abbas has been prevented from traveling to New York for the General Assembly, after a similar visa denial last year forced him to address the meeting by video instead.
The State Department said Palestinian officials, including Abbas, had failed to live up to their commitments under previous agreements to seek peace with Israel. In its statement, the department said that "as a consequence of their failure to reform, contrary to their commitments to the United States, and their ongoing activities that undermine the prospects for peace, the United States will extend sanctions that deny visas to PLO members and PA officials."
The restrictions extend beyond Abbas himself. Similar rejections were issued to dozens of other Palestinian Authority officials who had hoped to travel with him. According to the Times of Israel, one notice seen by a Palestinian official cited Section 212(a)(3)(B) of US immigration law, which prohibits issuing a visa to anyone who has engaged in terrorist activities or been associated with a terrorist organisation.
Despite the ban, Palestinian representation at the summit will not disappear entirely. The Palestinians will still be represented at next week's high-level meeting by diplomats already accredited to the United Nations, and Abbas is expected to again appear by video.
The US State Department's statement also noted that it would maintain a waiver allowing members of the Palestinian Mission to the UN to continue operating from New York.
The UN General Assembly is expected to vote on a measure that would once again allow Abbas to participate remotely, a mechanism it first used last year.
The renewed visa denial comes at a politically sensitive moment as a number of key members are expected to recognise a Palestinian state at this year's General Assembly.
In 2025 France officially recognised the State of Palestine, joined by the United Kingdom, Australia, Luxembourg, Belgium, Portugal, Malta and Canada. Four of the five permament UN Security Council members now recognise Palestine.
When Washington first imposed the restriction last year, the move drew criticism from European governments including Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez who described the visa decision as "unjust", writing on X that "Palestine has the right to make its voice heard at the United Nations and in all international forums".

SINGAPORE, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- Singapore on Thursday called for stronger international cooperation to expand access to sustainable cooling as rising temperatures drive greater demand for cooling.
"At a time of geopolitical tension and shifting global priorities, international cooperation on cooling matters more -- not less. Now is the time to turn the Global Cooling Pledge into action," Minister for Sustainability and the Environment Grace Fu said during the Global Cooling Pledge Assembly 2026 held in Singapore.
Fu said Asia is warming nearly twice as fast as the global average, while Singapore's annual mean temperatures could rise by up to 5 degrees Celsius by the end of this century.

Fu outlined three priorities for addressing the challenge: planning for adaptation, supporting planning with policy and legislation, and building partnerships across government, business and communities.
For heat resilience, Singapore has introduced measures including a 40 million Singapore dollars (31.35 million U.S. dollars) "Adapting to Heat Impacts" research program, she said.
During heatwaves, more than 300 cooling centers will also be opened islandwide to provide residents with relief from extreme heat.
Singapore's Heat Resilience Policy Office also coordinates efforts across government and supports a national action plan covering infrastructure, health, economic and social needs, she added. ■

Is curtailing AI an illusion for the EU, despite von der Leyen's pledge?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
09:43:08 UTC
18:43:08 KST

The European Commission president's vision of Europe shaping the AI race has drawn a mixed response from MEPs, with sceptics noting that most of the world's leading AI developers are based outside Europe.
Ursula von der Leyen wants the world to believe Brussels will set the pace of the rapid AI development that is threatening to reshape economies and labour markets, as well as security infrastructures, faster than governments can respond.
The trouble is, the EU is barely part of the race.
In her State of the European Union address this week, the European Commission president vowed that Europe would help write the rules for artificial intelligence, positioning the bloc as a rule-setter on a par with Washington and Beijing.
But the EU has no dominant model, no equivalent to OpenAI, Claude or DeepSeek, and precious little leverage over the companies actually building the technology.
Michael McNamara, an independent Irish MEP from the Renew group says Von der Leyen's pledge is little more than "lip-service" at the moment.
"Many of the most significant AI developers are outside of Europe, and will have little regard whatsoever to her comments," the MEP, who is co-chair of the European Parliament's working group on the implementation and enforcement of the AI Act, said.
McNamara pointed to what he calls a wildly inconsistent record from von der Leyen's Commission on AI safety.
It championed the AI Act, the bloc's risk-based rulebook for AI systems, and an AI Liability Directive, which would have made it easier to sue over AI-caused harm, in the last mandate, then withdrew the liability proposal in this one.
Later, it pushed to strip safeguards and pressured the Council and Parliament to carve entire sectors out of the AI Act during the recent Omnibus trilogues, only to reverse course again in the State of the European Union speech.
"Given the contradictory positions she has advanced in quick step, it’s hard to expect AI developers to pay much regard to her latest position," McNamara continued.
He did however agree with Von der Leyen's pledge to work with "like-minded partners like Canada, the United Kingdom and others, particularly on model evaluation, verification and security."
Meanwhile, Italian MEP Brando Benifei, who also co-chairs Parliament's AI working group and was co-rapporteur of the AI Act, praised von der Leyen, saying she is right to claim "the AI Act positions Europe to lead on AI safety".
"It binds every frontier model offered here, American or Chinese. Allied cooperation with Canada and the UK on safety is a welcome step that must be backed by sovereign capacity: European cloud, chips, unified capital, and a public CERN for AI to turn regulatory leadership into technological power."
Is the EU even part of the race?
In yesterday’s State of the European Union speech, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen set out EU plans for the AI industry and called for a slowdown in the development of AI models to “pace the frontier".
Her wording on the issue matches pleas issued by Anthropic’s Dario Amodei in an essay published earlier this week.
“If the people developing the technology are clear, then we should be too,” she told the European Parliament.
Europe currently lags behind the US and China in the AI race and in a number of ways.
The continent captures less than 5% of the estimated $1 trillion (€871.6tn) global AI investment, compared to 75-80% going to the US and another 10-14% to China.
Its only significant AI company, Mistral AI, is valued at just $24 billion (€20.9bn), a figure dwarfed by US firms OpenAI and Anthropic, each valued at $852 billion (€741.2bn) and $965 billion (€839.6bn) respectively.
Even China’s AI scene, which is more pluralistic than America’s, has market leaders such as DeepSeek, valued at $52 billion (€45.2bn), Moonshot AI, at $31.5 billion (€27.4bn) and Zhipu AI at $141 billion (€122.7bn).
The only area it can reasonably be argued that the EU is leading is regulation, with the introduction of the EU AI Act in 2024 and transparency and governance rules coming into effect in August this year.
The Commission president, however, believes the EU AI Act is “a crucial piece to putting guardrails in place” that “puts Europe in the position to shape global efforts on how to tackle this”.
She also announced that the EU would seek to work with its allies, including Canada, the United Kingdom and others. “We want to team up on model evaluation, verification, early warning, AI security and much more.”
Plans for talks in November with industry leaders, entrepreneurs and government officials to see how AI can be implemented in key sectors including health, transport, agri-food, advanced manufacturing and defence and space were also mentioned.
Von der Leyen also promised to table a "Quality Jobs Act" by the end of 2026, to "help develop skills, improve the quality of jobs and give workers a fair chance".

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
17:42:52 CST
18:42:52 KST

VIENTIANE, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- Laos' government continues efforts to clear contaminated land, reduce casualties and support affected communities in collaboration with international partners, local media reported on Thursday.
Lao News Agency quoted Bounpheng Sisavath, head of the National Regulatory Authority for UXO/Mine Action Sector in Laos, as saying that UXO clearance operations are currently carried out in 13 provinces. He made the remarks while speaking to journalists on the sidelines of the third Review Conference of the Convention on Cluster Munitions.
The operations focus on four main areas, including risk education, survey and clearance, victim assistance, and information management. Risk education programs target local communities, particularly children, by raising awareness of UXO dangers and promoting safer behavior.
The government is also working to keep annual UXO-related casualties below the strategic target of 38 people.
To date, clearance teams have safely cleared and destroyed UXO across 105,909 hectares, including 86,222 hectares of agricultural land and 19,686 hectares of land designated for development.
A total of 2,133,952 UXO items have been destroyed, comprising 5,239 large aerial bombs, 1,286,042 cluster submunitions (bombies), 2,954 landmines, and 841,717 other munitions and artillery shells.
Alongside clearance efforts, victim assistance programs have supported 1,928 survivors through medical treatment, physical rehabilitation, vocational training, employment assistance and psychological counselling for survivors and affected families.
Laos became a state party to the Convention on Cluster Munitions in 2009. The treaty promotes international cooperation and assistance to affected countries in clearing contaminated areas and supporting victims, survivors and persons with disabilities.
Bounpheng stressed the importance of continued national and international cooperation to accelerate UXO clearance, reduce casualties, support survivors and affected families, and return contaminated land to safe and productive use.
These efforts are expected to improve safety and support socio-economic development in UXO-affected communities across the country. ■

"We're very confident we can win the group. We believe in ourselves. Recovery is going to be important now, and then make a good preparation for the Philippines, and we expect to put on a good performance," he added. ■

From Yanbu to Sohar: Tracking Saudi Arabia’s alternative oil routes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
09:42:49 UTC
18:42:49 KST

From Yanbu to Sohar: Tracking Saudi Arabia’s alternative oil routes
The world’s second-largest crude exporter is rerouting crude via dark shipments and ship-to-ship transfers off Oman.
Saudi Arabia’s oil exports took another blow last week when drone attacks knocked out part of the country’s East-West pipeline, halting oil flow and removing 4-5 million barrels per day (bpd) of oil from global supply.
It is unclear how long repairs will take, although The Associated Press estimates three to five weeks, citing two regional officials.
The 1,200km (746-mile) pipeline connects the kingdom’s main oil-producing fields in the east of the country with Yanbu port on the Red Sea coast in the west, allowing Saudi crude to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, which has largely remained closed since the United States-Israel war on Iran began on February 28.
As the world’s second-largest oil producer, Saudi Arabia’s ability to keep crude flowing has significant consequences for global energy markets. Al Jazeera asked experts what alternatives remain, how the disruption could affect buyers worldwide, and what it means for the kingdom’s revenues.
Exports down more than 70 percent
Total Saudi crude loadings, which topped 7.5 million bpd in January and February, had fallen to about 2.3 million bpd in August and roughly 2.1 million bpd in the first half of September – a drop of more than 70 percent.
Analysts caution the real loadings figure may run somewhat higher, since shuttle tankers crossing Hormuz with tracking switched off aren’t always captured in vessel data.
How can Saudi Arabia export its oil?
Saudi exports are built around two coastal passages – the Gulf in the east, where crude moves out through the Strait of Hormuz, and the Red Sea in the west, where it can travel either north through the Suez Canal and Sumed Pipeline, or south through the Bab al-Mandeb strait.
Route one: The Strait of Hormuz
Before the crisis, most Saudi crude left on ships through the Strait of Hormuz, the 39km (24-mile) shipping choke point connecting the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman, and the open sea beyond.
Saudi Arabia was exporting about 7-8 million bpd of oil, with most seaborne volumes loading at the terminals of Ras Tanura and Ras al-Ju’aymah, and the former averaging about 5.4 million bpd in 2025.
The route is the most direct and economical way to reach Asia, which buys the bulk of Saudi crude exports.
Dark ships and ship-to-ship transfers
With the western pipeline route closed and the Red Sea’s southern route hostile, Saudi Arabia has little choice but to push exports back through the Gulf – despite the restrictions, higher costs, and physical risk of attack that come with transiting Hormuz, experts say.
“With the East-West pipeline offline, Saudi’s options are limited. The first is shipping more crude from its Gulf terminals through the Strait of Hormuz, including ship-to-ship transfers outside the strait, such as off Sohar in Oman,” according to Rishi Rajanala, research specialist in Oil Americas at LSEG Data & Analytics.
“Gulf producers have already been moving part of their exports this way, but volumes depend on tanker availability, insurance and freight costs, and remain well below pre-war levels.
“The second is drawing on crude already stored on the west coast and at Egypt’s Ain Sukhna and Sidi Kerir terminals, which can continue to supply Europe through the Sumed Pipeline, but only for as long as stored volumes last. The third is a phased restart of the pipeline itself, depending on the extent of the damage.”
Richard Matthews, director of consultancy and research at Gibson Shipbrokers, a London-based shipping services company, said transiting back through Hormuz will “further fuel higher freight costs for Middle East exports and create additional inefficiencies”, adding, “we do not know how long Yanbu loadings will be suspended for, but it doesn’t look to be a quick fix.”
One way to reduce that risk is for tankers to go “dark” by switching off their AIS transponders – used in maritime navigation to identify and track vessels – as they transit Omani coastal waters. “They will transit with transponders off and likely coordinate with the US Navy but still face the risk of attack as everyone else does,” Matthews said.
If the outage extends beyond a few weeks, the balance shifts further: Stored volumes would run down, and any crude that cannot move through the Gulf would have to be stored or left unproduced, adding pressure to production levels already well below pre-war volumes in August.
Rahul Choudhary, vice president of Upstream Research at Rystad Energy, an independent energy research company, said Hormuz-route exports increased in September to more than two million bpd in the first two weeks, roughly one million bpd above August.
“We expect Strait of Hormuz exports to rise further in the second half of the month, already evident in Aramco offering additional loadings to Asian refiners out of Sohar. Saudi Arabia can lean further on dark tanker activity in the coming days to offset Yanbu losses,” he added.
Route two: The East-West pipeline to Yanbu
Most of Saudi Arabia’s crude is produced in the east, and Aramco’s East-West pipeline links the Ghawar and Abqaiq processing facilities there to Yanbu port on the opposite side of the country.
It was built in 1981, during the Iran-Iraq war, precisely to reduce reliance on the Strait of Hormuz in a crisis of the kind Saudi Arabia and other Gulf exporters are now facing.
It runs at a maximum capacity of about 7 million bpd.
Crude shipped from Yanbu has two ways to travel onward through the Red Sea – south via Bab al-Mandeb or north via Suez.
South, via Bab al-Mandeb
Shipments heading south to Asia must pass through the Bab al-Mandeb strait – the second-best route after Hormuz.
But Iran-backed Houthi forces launched a rapid military offensive in September, seizing the Yemeni port of Mocha, the coastal town of Dhubab, and Mayyun Island, and now control the strait. They have also declared a maritime embargo on Saudi Arabia, prohibiting vessels from loading or discharging cargo at Saudi ports.
North, via the Suez Canal
With the southern exit blocked, tankers wishing to reach Asia must instead travel north.
Oil tankers can pass through the Suez Canal directly, or discharge their cargo at Egypt’s Ain Sokhna terminal on the Red Sea into the Sumed pipeline, which carries it overland across Egypt to a Mediterranean port near Alexandria, where it is reloaded onto tankers bound for Europe.
Very Large Crude Carriers (VLCCs) are too large to transit the canal at full draft – the maximum safe depth when fully loaded – so they instead partially discharge at Ain Sokhna and reload the remaining volume at the Mediterranean terminal before continuing.
According to HSBC Global Investment Research, Aramco had planned a similar “shuttling” operation before Yanbu was suspended, using smaller Suezmax tankers to move crude between Yanbu and Ain Sokhna.
From there, reaching Asian buyers means sailing west through the Strait of Gibraltar and around the Cape of Good Hope – a journey of about 13,140 nautical miles (equivalent to about 24,335km) that dwarfs the roughly 3,370 nautical miles (6,241km), 10-day journey via Hormuz, adding almost a month to the voyage and making shipping far more expensive while tying up tankers for longer.
But some experts expect the East-West pipeline to resume operations sooner, offering hope that Saudi oil exports could return to more sustainable levels.
Choudhary said: “We expect the pipeline to restart within a couple of weeks at a reduced 40-60 percent capacity, flowing around 2.5-3 million bpd. With Saudi likely to prioritise refinery runs, only about 0.5-1 million bpd would be left for export, meaning Yanbu crude exports fall by 2.5-3 million bpd even after a partial restart.
“Part of that gap can be covered by higher Hormuz liftings and increased dark-fleet activity, bringing the net impact on Saudi crude exports down to roughly 1.5-2 million bpd.”
Why trucking is not a viable option
One option conspicuously absent from Saudi planning is trucking – and the maths explains why. The kingdom typically exports 5-7 million bpd. Replacing even a single day’s volume by road would require roughly 25,000 to 35,000 fully loaded tanker trucks, each carrying about 200 barrels.
Lined up bumper-to-bumper, that convoy would stretch nearly 500km (310 miles) – roughly the distance from Riyadh to the nearest coast.
A single VLCC, by comparison, carries about 2 million barrels in one voyage, and the pipeline itself moves millions of barrels daily with minimal manpower – which is why, even with its main export arteries compromised, Saudi Arabia’s fallback plan runs through ships, not roads.
The impact on global markets
Oil prices have so far been cushioned by stockpiles and releases from strategic reserves, with Brent crude trading at about $70-$90 a barrel in recent months. But the longer regional disruptions continue, the more we may see prices rise, with Brent crude currently trading above $105 a barrel.
“The market is pricing a significant loss of supply, with the length of the outage as the main uncertainty. Saudi authorities have not given a timeline for the repair, and estimates reported so far range from a few days to eight weeks for a full recovery,” Rajanala, the research specialist at LSEG, said.
What does this mean for buyers of Saudi oil?
Saudi Arabia was, until recently, the world’s largest oil exporter.
Its main buyers are Asian and European refiners, including China, which bought 22 percent of Saudi Arabia’s oil, followed by South Korea (14 percent), Japan (13 percent), India (10 percent) and the US (5 percent).
Those buyers are already feeling the shutdown. Cargoes scheduled for European refiners are being cancelled, forcing many companies to look elsewhere for their oil, including turning to the US, North Sea and West Africa.
“Some European refiners with cancelled Saudi cargoes are already sourcing crude from the North Sea and seeking cargoes from the Americas and Central Asia, while Asian buyers are being offered alternative loadings from the Gulf,” Rajanala said.
“The missing barrels are also higher sulphur crude. Saudi grades such as Arab Light and Arab Medium are difficult to replace, like-for-like, because the alternatives available from the US, Kazakhstan and much of the North Sea are generally lower in sulphur content. That puts particular pressure on refiners configured for Middle East crude, many of them in Asia, which takes the largest share of Saudi exports.”
What does this mean for Saudi Arabia’s revenues?
Despite higher oil prices benefitting Saudi Arabia, they are being offset by an inability to physically export at normal volumes.
The government depends heavily on dividends, royalties and taxes from Aramco, with its crude and petroleum products sales accounting for more than half of government revenues, generating 606.5 billion riyals ($162bn) for state coffers in 2025.
Sustained disruption would cut deep into public finances. UBS Research now forecasts the 2026 budget deficit reaching 5 percent of gross domestic product against an original target of 3.3 percent.
Louis Vincent-Gave, from Gavekal Research, an independent research firm, noted that “the bombing of Yanbu, combined with the bombing of the East-West pipeline, and the Houthi takeover of the Bab el-Mandab sea passage, suddenly places large question marks on the ability of Saudi oil to keep flowing through the Red Sea to the rest of the world. And if Saudi Arabia cannot keep pumping oil to the rest of the world, the Saudi government could end up selling assets – US treasuries? Stakes in private equity funds? Artificial intelligence investments? – to pay its immediate bills.”

'It can't be that Hindi will not be taught in Tamil Nadu', SC tells state during hearing on Navodaya schools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
09:41:36 UTC
18:41:36 KST

‘Chennai shouldn’t alienate Delhi’: SC tells Tamil Nadu to reconsider opposition to Navodaya schools
NEW DELHI: Supreme Court on Thursday directed the Tamil Nadu government to comply with its December 15, 2025 order to identify land in every district for establishing Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalayas, while urging the state and Centre to resolve their differences over the schools through dialogue.A bench of Justices BV Nagarathna and Augustine George Masih also questioned Tamil Nadu's opposition to the three-language policy followed by Navodaya schools and said the state should not view the establishment of the centrally funded institutions as a threat to its existing education system.
"You have to change your mindset, it can’t be that Hindi will not be taught in the soil of Tamil Nadu," Justice Nagarathna observed during the hearing.The bench also said the people in Chennai should not alienate those in Delhi while stressing the need for cooperative federalism."We are saying in addition to all the good things you’re doing in your State, having something in addition will not bring down your standards. Coming from Delhi, will not lower the standards of Chennai. People in Chennai should not alienate Delhi and vice versa," the Court said.The court granted Tamil Nadu three more months to identify suitable land in each district and directed representatives of the state and Central governments to hold further discussions on the policy for establishing the schools.
The matter has been posted for December 14.
Tamil Nadu raises language concerns
The case relates to Tamil Nadu's challenge to a Madras High Court direction to establish Navodaya Vidyalayas in every district.Navodaya schools are centrally funded, co-educational residential schools run by the Navodaya Vidyalaya Samiti under the Union Ministry of Education. Tamil Nadu has opposed their establishment, among other reasons, because the schools follow a three-language policy that includes Hindi, while the state follows a two-language policy.Senior Advocate Jaideep Gupta, appearing for Tamil Nadu, told the court that the state's objection was not to schools or the teaching of Hindi as such, but to the language policy associated with the Navodaya scheme."It is against the State policy. It supersedes Tamil. This kind of unification is not the purport of the Constitution. It is not a Central government school. It is a school run by a society. There is an adamancy that Hindi must predominate."Justice Nagarathna said the language issue could be discussed between the Centre and the state."If you want Tamil as a second language, it is a matter which can be considered," the Judge said, asking the state Secretary to speak to the corresponding Central government Secretary.Gupta said discussions had already taken place but the Centre had remained adamant about Hindi. He nevertheless agreed to another round of consultations.
Court stresses cooperative federalism
Tamil Nadu also argued that the judiciary could not compel a state to adopt an optional Central government policy through a mandamus.Gupta submitted that education is in the Concurrent List and that Tamil Nadu has constitutional authority to frame its own education policy. He also argued that the Navodaya scheme was not compulsory.Justice Nagarathna questioned the consequences of individual states refusing to accept Central policies."Education is in the Concurrent List. There has to be cooperative federalism. If each State says that I don't accept your policy, what will happen?" the Judge asked.The bench said Tamil Nadu could continue running its own institutions and following its own syllabus, while Navodaya schools would provide an additional educational option.The court also rejected the argument that the establishment of Navodaya schools would lower Tamil Nadu's educational standards."We are not alienating you and we are not alienating them. Some more type of schools come in your state also which will only enhance the high standard which we are aware of. This is not going to lower your standards. If Navodaya schools were going to lower the standard of education in Tamil Nadu we would have said that irrespective of what you would have said. That is not the case here. It will provide more opportunity," Justice Nagarathna told Gupta."Ultimately everybody must work together," Justice Nagarathna said.
State raises financial concerns
Tamil Nadu also raised financial concerns, submitting that the Centre had promised to release Rs 5,000 crore for education but had not done so.Gupta argued that the state could not take on additional financial liabilities when funds under existing schemes had allegedly not been released.Additional Solicitor General KM Nataraj, appearing for the Centre, submitted that the state's primary requirement under the scheme was to provide land, while construction and other expenses would be borne by the Central government.Nataraj said the scheme was at an early stage and construction would take several years, during which the language-related differences could be addressed through discussions.Gupta, however, said around 30 acres of land would be required in each district and that identifying land before deciding whether to accept the policy would create difficulties.The bench clarified that it was not directing the state to acquire land immediately, but only to identify suitable land in its government plan.
Supreme Court refuses to recall land direction
The Supreme Court had in December 2025 directed Tamil Nadu to identify land required for establishing Navodaya Vidyalayas in every district within six weeks. The state subsequently sought recall of the order.On Thursday, the bench declined to recall the direction and instead granted the state three months to comply.
In its order, the bench recorded that Tamil Nadu had cited the change in government and lack of material progress in discussions with the Centre as reasons for non-compliance."Be that as it may, we direct the petitioner to comply with our order of 15.12.2025 in so far as identification of the land necessary to establish the school in each district," the order stated.The bench also directed the Centre and Tamil Nadu to continue discussions on the policy while the state works on identifying the land.Advocates G Priyadarshini and Rahul Shyam Bhandari, appearing for Kumari Maha Sabha, the petitioner before the High Court, argued that Tamil Nadu could not deny students access to free education through Navodaya schools."The Court should not get into this debate," Gupta said during the hearing.Justice Nagarathna responded: "That perception that you are surrendering to the central govt should not be there."
Ayush Pandey is a journalist at The Times of India, covering breaking news, politics, defence, and major legal and policy developments across India and the world. His reporting focuses on elections, national security, and institutional affairs, tracking the decisions and conflicts that shape public life.
He specialises in sharp explainers and in-depth feature stories that go beyond headlines to decode political shifts, defence strategy, geopolitical flashpoints, and changing public sentiment. His work combines speed, clarity, and depth for a fast-moving digital audience.

Poll gauges Zelenskyy's approval after anti-corruption investigations
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
12:40:00 EEST
18:40:00 KST

Poll gauges Zelenskyy's approval after anti-corruption investigations
A poll conducted following investigations by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) and the Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) has found that 54% of Ukrainians said they trust President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, compared with 41% who said they do not. This gives him a trust balance of +13 percentage points.
Source: the survey by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS), conducted from 21 August to 10 September 2026
Quote: "The field phase of this survey began immediately after the NABU and SAPO investigation Forrest Gump, which resulted in the dismissal of Iryna Mudra, Deputy Head of the President's Office. About half of the interviews were conducted from 4 September onwards, after the new Carthage investigation into the Prosecutor General's Office, but the survey did not cover any further developments after 14 September, when former prosecutor general [Ruslan Kravchenko] attempted to move against NABU and SAPO."
Details: Of the 54% who trust Zelenskyy, 18% said they trust him "completely", while 36% said they somewhat trust him. Among those who do not trust Zelenskyy, 25% said they do not trust him "at all", while 16% said they somewhat distrust him.
For reference: The nationwide KIIS survey was conducted from 21 August to 10 September 2026 using a random sample of mobile phone numbers across all oblasts of Ukraine in the government-controlled territories. A total of 1,003 respondents were interviewed.
The survey covered Ukrainian citizens aged 18 and over who were living in government-controlled territory at the time of the poll.
Under normal conditions, the margin of error of such a sample (with a probability of 0.95 and taking into account the design effect of 1.3) did not exceed 4.1% for indicators close to 50%, 3.5% for indicators close to 25%, 2.5% for indicators close to 10%, 1.8% for indicators close to 5%.
KIIS noted that, under wartime conditions, some additional systematic bias may also affect the results.

The summit on connectivity that Bulgaria will host is an expression of confidence in the Bulgarian government, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said at the beginning of a cabinet meeting.
A day earlier, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced the initiative for intercontinental connectivity and named Bulgaria as the host of the future summit that will launch its implementation, Radev said. He noted that, despite attempts by certain domestic circles to suggest that the government’s foreign policy would leave Bulgaria on the periphery of Europe, the country is not isolated. Instead, it is at the centre of the political debate, and not as an observer, but as a country generating decisions of strategic significance, the Prime Minister stressed.
“Bulgaria is Europe’s gateway to connectivity, and I believe it will successfully host the summit,” European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos said in Strasbourg, BTA reported. She added that €12 billion had been earmarked for the connectivity programme and that funding would also be included in the EU’s next budget.

Designer Ivan Donev weaves human stories into Bulgaria's largest dress
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
09:39:43 UTC
18:39:43 KST

News
Designer Ivan Donev weaves human stories into Bulgaria's largest dress
Thursday 17 September 2026 10:59
Thursday, 17 September 2026, 10:59
Designer Ivan Donev
PHOTO Ivan Donev's private archive
Font size
On Bulgaria's Unification Day, September 6, the ancient stage of Plovdiv’s Ancient Theatre was transformed into a bridge between generations, draped in the most delicate creation of women’s hands: lace. Bulgaria’s largest dress, assembled from hand-crocheted lace squares contributed by people from 194 towns and villages across the country and by Bulgarian communities around the world, became the centrepiece of a concert performance featuring a musical and visual spectacle created by the Plovdiv Opera Orchestra, the Academic Folk Choir, the VAYA Quartet and 3D mapping by Petko Tanchev. In this timeless stage experience, the audience embarked on a journey from outer space to planet Earth, immersed in a story of memory, continuity and indomitable spirit.
The idea for “Bulgaria’s Largest Dress”, an art installation made from thousands of crocheted pieces, was conceived about two years ago. At its heart is award-winning designer Ivan Donev, recipient of a fashion “Oscar” and numerous other Bulgarian and international distinctions. He called on people to donate handmade crochet pieces that had been carefully preserved in Bulgarian families for decades.
Fashion Oscar laureate Ivan Donev follows no trends, but creates them
Ivan Donev - the Bulgarian connection in The Children of Maam
PHOTO Ivan Donev's private archive
“The idea was to create a Bulgarian dress, but not a traditional costume, and to make it using a Bulgarian craft, the art of Kalofer lace-making. Rather than allowing the treasures created by the golden hands of our mothers and grandmothers to gather dust in mothball bags, we decided to give them new life, to show them to younger generations and bring them back into the light and before people’s eyes, so that we could admire them in the form of one great Bulgarian dress. This dress will continue to grow, and anyone who wishes to send in materials can continue to do so. It will grow every year and at any time,” Ivan Donev told BNR’s Radio Plovdiv.
Hundreds of volunteers took part in creating the dress. United under the motto “All of Bulgaria in One Dress”, they crafted its panels with care and dedication. The dress weighs 215 kilograms and covers approximately 300 square metres. “But behind these figures are not simply scale and a record. There are 513 human stories. Hundreds of hands and thousands of hours of work. Memories passed down from mother to daughter and from grandmother to granddaughter,” the designer emphasises.
PHOTO Ivan Donev's private archive
According to Ivan Donev, every crocheted piece represents a small fragment of the Bulgarian soul, and when brought together, these fragments become one whole, a symbol of Bulgaria created by Bulgarian women, in a white thread that unites generations. This is why he pays tribute to every woman who, in the solitude of her home, wove into her work a fragment of her own destiny, as well as the marks left by her time.
PHOTO BNT
“Many of these women are no longer among us, so I decided that illuminating the names of every single one of them with light and stars would be the most dignified way to honour their memory, their work and their legacy,” Ivan Donev says.
Thus, amid stirring music and golden glimmers illuminating Plovdiv’s ancient amphitheatre, the co-creators of Bulgaria’s largest dress emerged from anonymity. With its beauty and encoded messages, the dress is only beginning its journey, with plans to travel the world.

Fact check: Will Marine Le Pen hold a Frexit referendum if she becomes president of France?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
09:38:25 UTC
18:38:25 KST

The National Rally politician was once a keen proponent of a vote for France to leave the EU, following in the UK's footsteps.
A number of social media posts claim that Marine Le Pen, the far-right candidate in France's 2027 presidential election, is promising a referendum on the country's EU membership if she wins the keys to the Élysée Palace next year.
The posts, primarily in Spanish, provide no further detail, and that's our first clue that the claims are false: Le Pen is not calling for a Frexit referendum if she becomes president.
It is true that the National Rally politician is a harsh critic of the EU and once championed the idea of France leaving the bloc.
She celebrated the Brexit result when the UK voted to leave the EU in 2016. She made leaving the bloc and giving up the euro two of her flagship proposals in her 2012 and 2017 presidential campaigns.
But she has since abandoned these proposals. During the 2022 election, she instead advocated radically reforming the EU from within, stripping Brussels of most of its power and transforming the bloc into a looser alliance of nations.
Le Pen's change in position reflects a wider trend among far-right parties across Europe. Before the Brexit vote, far-right politicians in the Netherlands and Italy, among others, regularly pushed for their own referenda, but now those calls have generally quietened.
Nevertheless, Geert Wilders, leader of the far-right Party for Freedom, revived his call to reconsider the Netherlands' EU membership on Wednesday, telling Dutch MPs that "Nexit" was necessary to stop migrants and asylum seekers from entering the country.
Even if Le Pen did become president and held a Frexit referendum, she'd be unlikely to win: a study by Pew Research earlier this year showed that support for the EU in France has risen from 38% in 2016 to 52% in 2026. Similar increases were recorded elsewhere in Europe, including in the UK.
A YouGov poll from late 2025, meanwhile, found that 49% of French respondents would vote to remain in the EU, compared with 27% who would vote to leave.
While a Frexit referendum is currently not on the cards, Le Pen, who's currently leading in first-round polling with roughly 33 to 36%, has suggested putting other issues to a public vote if she wins the presidency next year. This may have fuelled some of the online rumours about an alleged EU referendum.
Her proposals include a referendum on combating so-called "Islamist ideologies", including banning the wearing of the veil in public, and a vote on amending France's constitution to restrict immigration.
The National Rally did not respond to a request for comment.

Swiss parliament allocates CHF20 million for Crans-Montana victims
The Swiss parliament has approved a maximum of CHF20 million ($24 million) for settlement arrangements in favour of the victims of the Crans-Montana fire disaster.
On Thursday, the Swiss House of Representatives approved the relevant clause in the Federal Act by 106 votes to 87, with 4 abstentions. The clause had previously been passed by the Senate. To resolve a single point of disagreement, the matter will now return to the Senate.
Under the bill, the Swiss government may contribute a supplementary amount of up to CHF20 million towards any settlements arising from round-table discussions. These discussions are intended to support victims, their relatives, insurance companies and other liable parties and authorities in reaching a settlement.
+ Crans-Montana victims’ foundation seeking more funds
The aim is to reach out-of-court settlements. This would help to avoid protracted civil proceedings.

The Verkhovna Rada refused to appeal to Zelenskyy regarding the removal of Potap’s title of Honored Artist
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
12:37:10 EEST
18:37:10 KST

The Verkhovna Rada refused to appeal to Zelenskyy regarding the removal of Potap’s title of Honored Artist
Kyiv • UNN
The lawmakers failed to secure the 226 votes needed to appeal to Zelenskyy regarding the removal of Potap’s title of Honored Artist of Ukraine. A total of 198 parliamentarians voted in favor of the proposal.
The Verkhovna Rada failed to submit a request to President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy seeking to strip singer Oleksii Potapenko (Potap) of the title "Honored Artist of Ukraine," reports UNN.
I am putting to a vote the proposal to preliminarily support the parliamentary request of a group of people's deputies… to the President of Ukraine regarding the deprivation of Oleksii Andriiovych Potapenko of the honorary Ukrainian title "Honored Artist of Ukraine"
Only 198 deputies supported the request, while 226 votes were required.
Update
A petition was recently published on the website of the Office of the President which, within several days, garnered the required 25,000 votes regarding the initiation of the procedure to strip Oleksii Potapenko ("Potap") of the honorary title "Honored Artist of Ukraine".
The grounds for this appeal are Oleksii Potapenko's public activities, which, in the opinion of the petition's authors, do not correspond to the status of a person awarded a state honor of Ukraine and contain signs of promoting the Russian cultural and linguistic environment and public interaction with representatives of the aggressor state
In particular, this concerns:
-  the public use and promotion of Russian-language cultural products at a time when the Russian Federation is waging armed aggression against Ukraine, while the Russian language and culture are systematically used by the aggressor state as tools of informational and cultural influence; 
-  public statements and actions regarding the Ukrainian language that may be perceived as devaluing or mocking it, or as opposing it to Ukrainian national identity. Such actions are particularly sensitive to society given the person's status as a holder of an honorary Ukrainian title in the field of culture; 
-  public cooperation and the creation of joint media content with citizens of the Russian Federation and representatives of the Russian show business, which requires proper legal assessment in view of Ukraine's current legislation on countering the promotion of the aggressor state; 
-  actual residence and professional activities outside Ukraine, which in themselves do not constitute an offense and cannot serve as an independent ground for stripping someone of a state award, but, taken together with other public actions by the person, should be taken into account when assessing their continued compliance with the status of an award recipient. 
The President has not yet responded to the petition.
Potap himself responded to the petition, saying that he calmly accepts the possibility of being stripped of the title.
If my title helps Ukraine win, take it away. If it makes someone feel better, please do. I do not need an ID card to remain an artist and communicate with people who have been listening to my music for more than twenty years
He added that, for him, knowledge of languages had never meant renouncing his country or culture.
We speak different languages. Ukrainian, Russian, English, Spanish. We write music in different languages and create different projects for different countries and audiences. The more languages you know, the more people you can hear and understand, and the more people you can tell about yourself and your country
Recently, in an interview, answering a question about whether he was subject to mobilization and why he was not fighting, Potap also said: "I am subject to mobilization. If they tell me to leave, I will leave. But someone in this life has to be Potap, and I decided to be Potap".
His wife, Nastia Kamenskykh, also "distinguished herself". In the same interview, she stated that the language issue in Ukraine had allegedly "been taken to the absurd", that it was being "manipulated very heavily", and that she herself considered it "pure politics". At the same time, the singer said that Ukraine should speak Ukrainian, but that she wanted to decide for herself which language to speak and sing in.
In addition, during the interview, Kamenskykh stated that she did not consider herself a patriot of Ukraine because she placed personal interests above the public good. When asked what the homeland meant to her, the singer was unable to answer.
Kamenskikh's statements sparked a wave of criticism and jokes on social media, while the story about the "bone" after switching to Ukrainian became the subject of numerous memes.
According to the law "On State Awards," the title "Honored Artist of Ukraine" is awarded to individuals who work in the relevant sector of the economic and socio-cultural sphere, as a rule, for at least ten years, and who have achieved high professional results and demonstrated professional excellence.
In 2020, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy awarded Potap the title "Honored Artist of Ukraine".
In November 2024, the Verkhovna Rada adopted a law on stripping state awards for propaganda on behalf of the aggressor state.
Under the law, state awards may be revoked: pursuant to a court verdict by which a person is convicted of a serious or particularly serious crime, a criminal offense against the foundations of Ukraine's national security, or against peace, human security, and the international legal order; as well as by a decision of the National Security and Defense Council imposing sanctions.

The EU has billions in unspent defense funds. It wants to use them for projects with Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
09:37:04 UTC
18:37:04 KST

The EU plans to use money remaining under its €150 billion Security Action for Europe (SAFE) program to create a new program for joint projects with Ukrainian companies, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on 16 September. She announced the plan during her State of the Union address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg.
Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine has pushed the EU to spend more on defense and build up its own weapons industry. SAFE was created as part of that effort, giving EU member states €150 billion in loans for defense spending. Ukraine is also facing heavy defense costs, with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy putting its additional defense funding gap for 2026 at $27 billion.
"Using the remaining funds from SAFE, we will be setting up a new programme for joint projects with Ukrainian companies," von der Leyen told the European Parliament.
EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius estimated that the unused portion of SAFE could amount to €10 billion to €20 billion, UNN reported. The exact sum will be known only after member states report on their SAFE projects by the end of October. The announcement caught several governments off guard: Poland and other capitals say the Commission never discussed it with them, and Warsaw had been counting on taking up the funds other countries declined for its own projects.
The proposal would allow unused money from member states' SAFE allocations to be redirected to joint projects with Ukrainian firms. One likely destination is Freya, the joint European-Ukrainian air and missile defense system meant as a cheaper answer to the American Patriot, which von der Leyen described as the start of the collaboration rather than the end of it.
In 2025, Ukraine gained associate partner status in SAFE and access to the EU's European Defense Fund, allowing Ukrainian companies to compete for contracts and co-develop military systems with European firms.
Fifteen member states have since said they plan to buy Ukrainian weapons through the program, and Canada joined it in December 2025 as the first non-European partner. Bulgaria agreed SAFE-funded joint weapons production with Ukraine in March 2026.
The war is costing Ukraine more every year, the government says. Its draft 2027 budget proposes ₴4.885 trillion ($110 billion) for defense needs, nearly 44% of GDP.

BRICS rejects US exclusion of South Africa from G20

BRICS rejects US exclusion of South Africa from G20
BRICS countries have rejected any arbitrary attempt by the US to exclude South Africa from the G20, reaffirming its status as a founding and full member of the group.
The US, which holds this year’s G20 presidency, has barred South Africa from the group’s meetings and has not invited it to the leaders’ summit in Miami in December.
In a declaration adopted at their summit in New Delhi on Saturday, BRICS leaders described any arbitrary revision of the G20’s membership as “inadmissible.” The declaration said any membership change requires the consensus of all G20 members and should reflect geographical balance and the growing economic weight of the Global South.
Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov said the statement addressed the “unilateral, politically motivated attempts” to sideline South Africa, African Initiative reported.
US President Donald Trump announced the exclusion of South Africa after boycotting the G20 summit in Johannesburg last November. He accused the South African government of mistreating the country’s white minority and unlawfully confiscating land – allegations which Pretoria has denied.
Relations between the two countries have been strained over South Africa’s land reform policies, its alleged close ties with Russia and China, and its genocide case against Israel at the International Court of Justice.
Washington suspended aid to Pretoria last year and established a program to resettle Afrikaners and other members of South Africa’s white minority as refugees in the US.
The Trump administration also imposed a 30% tariff on most South African imports. Pretoria has made several efforts to secure a reduction, including submitting a revised trade proposal, but the talks have produced no negotiated tariff relief, and Washington has since increased pressure on the country.
On Tuesday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced new visa restrictions targeting South African officials and other foreign nationals who the administration accuses of enacting or enabling “race-based discrimination”, “uncompensated land seizures”, and incitement to violence against minority groups.
Pretoria condemned the measure as a unilateral act based on a misrepresentation of its domestic policies. “It is our sovereign right to put in place laws that address the nation’s concern over centuries of racial injustice,” the Foreign Ministry said in a statement.

Report: US intelligence fears China could access F-35 technology in $24B Saudi deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
09:33:50 UTC
18:33:50 KST

U.S. intelligence officials have raised concerns that a proposed $24 billion sale of F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia could expose some of the aircraft’s most sensitive technology to Chinese espionage, The New York Times reported, citing American officials familiar with internal assessments.
The planned package includes 48 F-35s and a spare engine. President Donald Trump announced the sale in November 2025, a day before hosting Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman at the White House. The deal has since moved forward, with the State Department sending it to two congressional committees in June for informal approval.
According to the Times, intelligence analysts have warned that China could potentially gain access to F-35 technology through espionage in Saudi Arabia or through the kingdom’s expanding military and security relationship with Beijing.
A recent Defense Intelligence Agency report examined Chinese military access to Saudi bases and the kingdom’s use of Chinese telecommunications equipment. It also questioned whether U.S. and Saudi officials could adequately secure sites housing sensitive F-35 systems.
Pentagon officials are particularly concerned about protecting the jet’s advanced radar and surveillance technology. The report also raised questions over whether Riyadh would agree to limit contact between Chinese military or intelligence personnel and facilities connected to the aircraft.
Another concern is the presence of equipment made by Chinese telecommunications giants Huawei and ZTE. U.S. intelligence officials have asked whether Saudi Arabia would be willing to remove such technology from communications infrastructure and defense installations tied to the F-35 program.
The warnings echo concerns raised during Trump’s first term, when Washington agreed to sell F-35s to the United Arab Emirates after Abu Dhabi normalized relations with Israel in 2020. That deal was later reviewed as the UAE strengthened military, intelligence and technology ties with China, and the sales process was ultimately halted.
Saudi Arabia has long been one of the largest buyers of U.S. weapons, but it also maintains significant defense ties with Beijing. The kingdom purchases ballistic missiles from China, while the Chinese military has helped Saudi Arabia develop missile production facilities and improve its missile capabilities, according to the Times.
The proposed F-35 sale has also raised concerns in Israel, the only country in the Middle East that currently operates the aircraft. U.S. law requires Washington to preserve Israel’s qualitative military edge in the region when approving major weapons sales to neighboring states.
Previous U.S. administrations conducted lengthy classified reviews to determine whether arms sales could undermine that advantage. Some Israeli officials have expressed reservations about the Saudi deal, as they did over the proposed sale to the UAE.
The Saudi military, meanwhile, has faced growing pressure to improve its capabilities. Crown Prince Mohammed has sought for years to acquire F-35s, and the kingdom’s armed forces have struggled to defend against attacks from Iran during the current U.S.-Israeli war with Tehran, the Times reported. Fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthis has also resumed.
Congress could still complicate the deal. Lawmakers and aides have been pressing the administration over the intelligence warnings, according to the report.
The sale also comes as Trump has agreed to help Saudi Arabia develop a civilian nuclear program, another initiative that has prompted security concerns because the crown prince has said Riyadh would seek nuclear weapons if Iran obtained them.

Russia resumed its missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian cities on September 17, hours after the US Congress passed a sanctions package that supporters say will increase pressure on Moscow and countries that help it finance its war against Ukraine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said it was "symbolic" that the US House of Representatives passed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 amid another Russian ballistic missile and drone attack on Ukraine.
He said Russian strikes hit civilian and energy infrastructure in eight regions, damaging homes in the capital, Kyiv, and the major southern port city of Odesa and injuring dozens of people, including children.
"The Lindsey Graham bill, along with other strong sanctions steps by our partners against the source of this war -- against Russia -- is an extremely powerful tool that can stop this terrorist war and bring Russia to the point where it has to make peace," Zelenskyy wrote in a post on X.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha welcomed the passage of the Russia sanctions bill, calling it a strong response to Moscow's continued attacks on Ukraine.
However, he also urged further sanctions, including a full embargo, restrictions on Russia's so-called shadow fleet, and blocking sanctions targeting its military-industrial complex.
"We can stop Putin by depriving him of the resources to continue this war," Sybiha wrote on X.
Following the latest Russian attack, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said 18 people, including children, had been injured in the city, while a repeat drone strike sparked a fire in an administrative building.
In Odesa, regional authorities said a Russian overnight strike injured six people, including two children, and damaged residential buildings, a private home, and infrastructure.
Zaporizhzhya, in southeastern Ukraine, was also hit by a Russian missile strike that injured three people and damaged industrial facilities, according to regional authorities.
Later in the day, regional Governor Mykhaylo Semikin said at least five more people were injured when a Russian first-person-view (FPV) drone hit a bus carrying civilians.
Meanwhile, Russian officials reported that a Ukrainian drone attack damaged an oil refinery in the Russian city of Yaroslavl.
Authorities in Russia's Krasnodar region said drone debris sparked a fire at an oil refinery, which was quickly extinguished. No injuries reported.
The refinery, located about 250 kilometers northeast of Moscow, had previously been targeted by Ukrainian drones and halted processing at two of its three crude distillation units following the August attack.
Zelenskyy confirmed the attack on the Yaroslavl oil refinery, adding that Ukraine's Security Service had carried out a strike on a military airfield in Rostov, in southern Russia near the Ukrainian border, damaging three planes and three helicopters.
The attacks that targeted energy facilities in Russia and Ukraine followed US President Donald Trump's announcement of an energy truce between the two countries on September 14, although neither side has confirmed such an agreement.
Trump had earlier urged Zelenskyy to stop targeting Russian diesel infrastructure, saying the attacks had caused a diesel shortage that was “hurting the world.”
Since the beginning of the summer, Ukrainian drone strikes have caused nationwide fuel shortages in Russia and stoked discontent among citizens who had previously been largely insulated from the war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year.

Barclays is facing a growing backlash over return-to-office plans, with thousands of staff calling for payouts to help cover travel costs and an exemption for those living more than 40 minutes from work.
Unionised staff represented by Unite are pushing back against plans announced by the bank earlier this summer to get staff back into the office at least three days a week from October, with more senior employees expected to come in at least four days a week.
The current policy requires full-time Barclays staff to be in at least two days a week.
Unite, which represents nearly 80% of Barclays’ 45,000 UK staff, says thousands of employees have now signed an open letter – first reported by the Financial Times – that has been sent to the bank’s bosses and widely circulated across its UK offices.
The union plans to speak to Barclays about staff concerns in the coming days.
A Unite national officer, Rick Coyle, said: “One of the issues that has caused consternation is that most employers in banking and financial services are generally embracing greater flexibility. Our members think that Barclays is trying to fix a problem that doesn’t exist.
“Thousands of employees have signed the letter and the figure continues to rise. Unite will be speaking to Barclays about the strength of feeling in the days ahead.”
Barclays’ return-to-office order echoes those imposed by other large banks, which tightened their work-from-home policies after the Covid pandemic, particularly for younger staff.
That includes JP Morgan, whose chief executive, Jamie Dimon, told Bloomberg last year: “It is an apprenticeship system … you can’t learn working from your basement.”
A Barclays spokesperson said: “We recognise the benefits of balancing flexibility for colleagues with the importance of working together in our physical locations. Our minimum time-in-office requirements vary by business area, reflecting the nature of the work and the needs of the business.
“This means that most of our colleagues who are not already working in the office three days [per week] will align with our broader approach across the bank. Alongside this, our most senior leaders will spend an additional day in the office to support collaboration, decision-making and leadership visibility.”

The Trump Administration Sends a New Signal to Alien Disclosure Whistleblowers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Just over a year ago, Dylan Borland—a former Air Force geospatial intelligence specialist—told a House Oversight task force that he'd watched a roughly 100-foot triangular craft lift silently off the flight line at Langley Air Force Base in 2012. But there were some questions he couldn’t answer.
Nearly half a dozen times during the hearing, he told members of Congress he could only answer their questions, such as whether a private company he worked for was reverse engineering nonhuman technology, inside a Sensitive Compartmented Information Facility, or SCIF. He said he was concerned whether he was “legally even allowed to answer” some questions and at one point cited a fear of being charged under the Espionage Act.
A year later, on September 14, the Defense Department announced it had lowered that risk, though it falls short of what some in the unidentified anomalous phenomena research community say is needed to achieve broad transparency.
The Pentagon said on Monday that it had issued a "targeted legal waiver" allowing all current and former “service members, civilian personnel, and contractors" holding UAP-related national defense information to disclose it to the White House–directed effort that has been dumping UFO files on war.gov since May.
The waiver, which hasn’t been made public, "supersedes civil and administrative enforcement provisions" of NDAs and special access program agreements, "strictly for communications directed to the PURSUE team," a reference to the White House program. Basically, if you signed a secrecy agreement and know something about UFOs, you can now tell PURSUE without being sued or losing your clearance, though the same protections don’t extend to speaking with Congress, the press, or the public. The release announcing the waiver says nothing about criminal law, and only covers agreements "previously executed within the United States."
President Donald Trump telegraphed the move over the summer when he reportedly directed the Defense Department and the intelligence community to waive UAP-related NDAs. It was reinforced on July 31 when Principal Deputy Director of National Intelligence Aaron Lukas sent a memo to 18 intelligence chiefs declaring that any NDAs “prohibiting disclosure to the President, or designees like PURSUE, are no longer in force.” The memo cited a “Presidential Direction” it never quotes and gave the intelligence community 30 days to set up its own procedures. That deadline passed in August. The White House directed a request for comment to the Defense Department. An agency spokesperson said it had no additional comment outside the press release and referred further questions to the White House.
Borland, the kind of person all of this was written for, is unmoved.
“Bad-faith actors are talking about, ‘Oh, this allows whistleblowers to go and talk to the public.’ No, it doesn't. It changes nothing,” he tells WIRED. “It's one more place to go.
“Those of us who already became whistleblowers, we already were told that our NDAs were waived. We were legally allowed to talk to AARO,” he says, referring to the Pentagon's All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office, created in 2022 to investigate UAP reports and serve as the official channel for whistleblowers. He adds that the new directive essentially “just repeated what we've been told for three, four years.”
A provision Congress passed in December 2022 already states that an authorized UAP disclosure—meaning one made through AARO—"shall not be subject to a nondisclosure agreement," complies with classification rules, and "is not a violation" of the relevant section of the Espionage Act. The channel was AARO and Borland used it.
But AARO has little credibility with the people it was built to hear from, especially after its former director publicly questioned the credibility of whistleblowers, and its March 2024 historical report found no evidence the government had ever recovered alien technology. Borland told Congress that he met with AARO in March 2023, but that he withheld sources and methods because he considered the agency's public assessments up until then, "a misrepresentation of the truth." That August, after a former intelligence officer testified about an alleged decades-long crash-retrieval program, Borland filed a complaint with the intelligence community's inspector general over what he says he knew and the retaliation he says he’d faced.
Since then, he wrote in his statement to Congress, he has "been prevented from resuming my prior employment" and remains “blacklisted from certain agencies within the Intelligence Community.”
Other UAP whistleblowers have faced similar issues after coming forward, from break-ins at their homes to leaked personal details.
The new waiver also only covers those who have worked with the Pentagon, leaving a CIA-sized hole in it.
“I'm glad that they're waiving NDAs for everybody who was on the [Defense Department] side,” Borland says. “It doesn't change the [Intelligence Community] side.”
He pointed to the need to offer similar protections to the alphabet soup of intelligence agencies beyond just the CIA, including the National Security Agency, FBI, and others, as well as science agencies like NASA.
Marik von Rennenkampff, a former State Department analyst and Obama-era Pentagon appointee now at the Sol Foundation, a UAP research nonprofit, agrees with that sentiment because of where whistleblowers say the secrets about nonhuman technology are kept. He points to a specific unit in the CIA that’s “allegedly—allegedly, allegedly, allegedly, I can't stress that enough—the quarterback for this alleged legacy effort.”
“What has been announced publicly does not cover the core of the alleged legacy program yet,” von Rennenkampff tells WIRED.
There's a second gap that no memo can close. Many of the people alleged to hold this information work for private contractors, and the government can't waive an NDA it isn't party to. Only the 2022 statute addresses those types of agreements, and only for disclosures made through the official AARO channel.
Despite these shortcomings, UAP researchers and whistleblowers point to, von Rennenkampff argues this week’s announcement is still important.
“After 80 years of government denial, obfuscation, and ridicule on this topic, there's now true political capital invested in this,” he says. Unlike AARO, PURSUE is a “presidentially directed initiative” that is reporting ultimately to political appointees in the White House, “versus career bureaucrats.”
“It shows that the Trump administration is taking extraordinary claims about retrievals of a craft of nonhuman origins seriously,” he says. There’s a phrase in the release that von Rennenkampff says is another curious detail, particularly given how “wordsmithed to hell” government statements about UAP generally are. The Pentagon wrote that “individuals with direct knowledge of UAP-related programs” have historically feared legal liability for speaking.
“It doesn't say people with partial knowledge, half knowledge, alleging knowledge,” he says. “It says people with direct knowledge.”
Borland's hope is that PURSUE answers to someone with the power to act on what it hears. He points to White House deputy chief of staff for policy Stephen Miller—who Secretary of State Marco Rubio recently confirmed is working on the UAP portfolio—as someone who would signal the White House is doing more than paying lip service to the topic.
Beyond that, Borland has an offer.
“There's enough smoke, and there's enough people behind the scenes,” he says, referring to himself and other whistleblowers. “If Stephen Miller and Trump wanted to actually know some stuff, they could call us into the White House right now, and I can throw down, and so can the rest of them.”
