US judge dismisses oil trader's Swiss smears complaint
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:04:00 UTC
17:04:00 KST

US judge dismisses oil trader’s Swiss smears complaint
The United Arab Emirates won dismissal of a lawsuit by an oil trader who alleged the state directed a smear campaign that pushed his company into bankruptcy.
The lawsuit, filed in January 2024 by oil trader Hazim Nada, claimed that his company, Lord Energy, was targeted by a misinformation campaign orchestrated by Swiss private investigative firm Alp Services, and ultimately directed by the UAE and its president, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed.
United States District Judge Amy Berman Jackson ruled that the UAE is immune from the suit under the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act. She also dismissed other defendants, including Alp, on various legal grounds.
“Notwithstanding its length and unnecessary detail, the amended complaint is nothing more than a defamation case in search of a legal theory,” Jackson wrote Tuesday in Washington federal court. “It is also an action in search of a basis to require a foreign sovereign and other foreign entities and individuals to defend themselves in the United States.”
The complaint, based on more than 8,000 hacked documents, shone light on the world of private intelligence agencies for hire. Nada alleged that Alp hired journalists and academics to write articles falsely accusing Lord Energy of being a front company to fund terrorist organizations, which led its banks to stop working with it. The company declared bankruptcy in April 2019.
Nada, a 43-year-old citizen of Italy and the US, said he was disappointed by the ruling and is considering an appeal.
“We’re basically telling foreign governments that it’s OK to work in a way where you appoint a third party to do the dirty work for you,” Nada said in an interview. “It’s become a modus operandi for all these states to do the dirty job by hiding behind consultants and mercenaries, so where are we going?”
Nada said he is trying to restart Lord Energy, but he said “it’s tricky with all the things that have happened.”
The UAE embassy in Washington and Alp didn’t respond to requests for comment.
Nada formed Lord Energy in 2008 to trade coal, grain, cement and steel, and he expanded into oil in 2014. His lawsuit claims that the business was seen as a threat by the UAE and its state oil company, Abu Dhabi National Oil, in the spot market for light crude oil in Asia. He sought $2.8 billion in damages.
The lawsuit claimed Nada didn’t know the “scope and scale” of the campaign against him and his company until hackers “obtained tens of thousands of documents from Alp’s servers and shared some of them” with him in April 2021, according to the opinion.
The story of the smear campaign against Nada and Lord Energy was the subject of a New Yorker article in 2023.
The case is Nada v. United Arab Emirates, 24-cv-00206, US District Court, District of Columbia.
(Updates in sixth paragraph with Nada comments.)

More controversially, the legislation allows Trump to impose secondary sanctions on countries that rely on Russian oil and gas, in the form of tariffs. Beijing and New Delhi are expected to be the main targets of such measures.
The bill would also extend sanctions on Iran.
To learn more about the bill passed by the US Congress, click here.

Switzerland raises economic growth forecast significantly
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:02:58 UTC
17:02:58 KST

Switzerland raises economic growth forecast significantly
According to the federal government’s economists, the Swiss economy is likely to perform significantly better than previously expected. They are therefore raising their forecast substantially.
The federal government’s expert group has revised its forecast for 2026 to predict growth in real gross domestic product (GDP, adjusted for sporting events) of 1.7%, up from the previous estimate of 0.9%, as announced by the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO) on Thursday. The forecast for 2027 of 1.6% has been confirmed.
According to the statement, the reason for the revision is the latest data from the Swiss economy, which showed surprisingly high growth. GDP grew exceptionally strongly in the second quarter.
+ Swiss economy grows surprisingly fast in Q2
‘A certain counter-movement’
However, according to federal experts, this growth is unlikely to continue unchecked. On the contrary, a “certain counter-movement” is expected in the second half of the year.
This is because, according to the press release, almost half of the strong growth in the second quarter was attributable to the highly volatile value added in the chemical and pharmaceutical industry. “This is likely to have overstated the underlying economic momentum,” the statement continues.
Weakening of the franc helps
Nevertheless, the Swiss economy remains fundamentally on a path to recovery. The recent depreciation of the franc is also helping in this regard, as it benefits the export sector.
As for inflation, the federal government’s economists continue to forecast a rate of 0.6% for both 2026 and 2027. The unemployment rate is forecast at 3.1% for 2026 and 3.0% for 2027.
The expert group emphasised that the conflict with Iran, high energy prices and ongoing trade policy uncertainty pose significant risks to the economy. Persistently high oil prices could therefore place a significant strain on the global economy, and according to the statement, inflation in Switzerland would also be higher as a result.

Unknown

2026-09-17
08:02:26 UTC
17:02:26 KST

Türkiye’s Financial Stability Committee said on Thursday that recent market volatility does not pose a fundamental or structural threat to Borsa Istanbul or the country’s capital markets, while pledging swift measures to ease liquidity pressures and prevent contagion.
The committee, chaired by Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Simsek, met to assess recent developments in the financial markets and concluded that the turbulence was linked to credit and liquidity problems at certain funds managed by a limited number of portfolio management companies.
“There is no fundamental or structural risk concerning the functioning of Borsa Istanbul and our capital markets,” the committee said in a statement.
It described the issue as concentrated in a specific segment of the fund market and said the problems were temporary and manageable.
Authorities prepare measures to ease liquidity pressures
The committee reviewed potential measures to preserve the healthy functioning of financial markets and protect macrofinancial stability.
“All necessary measures within this scope will be swiftly implemented by our relevant institutions,” it said.
The measures will focus primarily on easing liquidity constraints and preventing problems in the affected funds from spreading to other parts of the financial system.
The committee also said regulatory and supervisory authorities would continue using their powers “with determination” against individuals or entities found to have engaged in activities that disrupted market functioning.
Officials urge public to rely on official information
The committee urged investors and the public to rely only on statements issued by official institutions as authorities respond to the recent volatility.
It said it would continue to closely monitor developments and provide regular updates.

Netballer cops fine after unprecedented assault charge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:00:53 UTC
17:00:53 KST

Netball's unprecedented suspension as Diamond pleads guilty to assault
Australian netballer Sarah Klau has been sanctioned by the sport's governing body after pleading guilty to assault and failing to disclose the matter prior to the Commonwealth Games.
Following an investigation into the incident over the past couple of weeks, Netball Australia has handed Klau a $5,000 fine and a two-game ban that is wholly suspended for 12 months.
The goal keeper will also be required to complete additional education.
Klau breached the sport's code of conduct by failing to behave in a professional manner while in public and engaging in conduct that could bring the game into disrepute.
In a statement, Netball Australia said it took into consideration Klau's "individual circumstances and her otherwise exemplary personal history", as well as her apology to the victim and venue, but the seriousness of the charge and breach of standards warranted formal disciplinary action.
Chief executive Mark Falvo described it as "a significant but momentary lapse in judgement … that has been mitigated by her otherwise excellent character".
This means Klau will still be eligible for selection in the Constellation Cup.
The Australian squad set to face New Zealand in a four-game bilateral series in October will be announced in the coming days.
This is believed to be the first time a Super Netballer and national team member has been in trouble with the law, and the decision now sets a precedent for the sport at the elite level.
Klau fronted Sydney's Downing Centre Courthouse in early September facing a common assault charge from June 7, when she allegedly kicked a security guard in the back outside a pub.
The 31-year-old reportedly attended a Sydney Swans AFL match before arriving at the Paddington Inn and retaliated when she was denied entry due to being too intoxicated.
This took place a day after Klau was ruled out of the NSW Swifts' penultimate game of the Super Netball season to manage an ongoing leg injury.
The assault shocked the netball community and was dubbed "out of character" by many who know Klau.
The charges were laid five weeks after the incident, ahead of Klau's departure with the national team for the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.
Netball Australia's investigation aimed to determine whether the veteran knew about the charges before she left.
There is a possibility that she was notified in writing at her Sydney address while in camp in Melbourne, then flew straight to Scotland to compete completely unaware.
Klau has played 67 caps for her country and has been a mainstay in the squad since her international debut in 2019.
Despite being hampered by injury throughout the recent Super Netball season, Klau was still named and made her second appearance at the tournament, albeit with limited court time.
The Diamonds won bronze after defeating England 68-50 in the medal matches.
Klau then spent time abroad on holiday before returning home and fronting court.
Following the investigation, Netball Australia would not disclose the timeline of events but confirmed it did not find out about the incident until a week before the court appearance on September 3.
Commonwealth Games Australia's (CGA) athletes must agree to their ethical by-laws, which state that an athlete cannot engage in any conduct — whether publicly known or not — that brings the relevant person's sport into disrepute.
The behaviour policies also outline that an athlete must not deliberately withhold information in relation to any possible prohibited conduct and is expected to notify the CEO or CGA President of any potential breach.
When contacted by ABC Sport, CGA said it was aware of the court proceedings but was waiting on the findings of Netball Australia's investigation before determining any impact they may have on Klau's relationship with the Australian CGA team.
Up and coming defender Jessie Grenvold earned her first call-up for the side and travelled as a reserve. Had all of this come to light, Grenvold could have taken Klau's place.
Importantly, Klau has avoided a conviction, likely due to her status as a Diamonds player, as the judge said it would be a "terrible setback" to "everything you have achieved".
"It's always such a shame to see fabulous sports men and women compromise themselves, really, on nights out," the judge said during sentencing according to NewsCorp.
"In any event alcohol and violence tend to be a great leveller, it doesn't matter who you are.
"This is an opportunity that is being offered to you once."
Speaking in a statement issued via the Australian Netball Players' Association, Klau expressed deep regret.
"I am incredibly sorry for my actions and the impact they have had on everyone involved and the wider netball community.
"I take full responsibility for my behaviour and accept the consequences that follow.
"I am committed to learning from this and ensuring my actions reflect the standards expected of me and our sport.
"I am grateful for the support I have received, I care deeply about netball and the values it represents."
Two years ago, the Swifts parted ways mid-season with long-time player Sam Wallace-Joseph due to behavioural issues that happened internally and were never publicly disclosed.
Considering the nature of these charges, the guilty plea and the timing of the incident while Klau was in season and supposed to be resting a leg injury, fans thought the club might also make an example of this incident.
Instead, Klau has missed out on a penalty entirely in club land.
The Swifts re-signed their two-time premiership player for a fifth Super Netball season before the trial and later defended her integrity, confirming no further action will be taken.
"Netball NSW can confirm that Sarah Klau has had a matter heard before the local court dismissed without conviction," a spokesperson said.
"Netball NSW takes the behavioural standards of its athletes and staff seriously.
"Sarah has been an exemplary role model in the NSW Swifts environment for 10 years and the club will continue to provide her with support."

====================================================================================================

‘It’s beautiful when it’s clean’: the Argentine neighbourhood saving a contaminated river
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:00:44 UTC
17:00:44 KST

Twenty-three years ago, María Monges looked around her flooded neighbourhood and knew something had to be done.
Founded in 1998 in Buenos Aires province’s San Martín district, the community of Costa Esperanza sits on the banks of the Reconquista, Argentina’s second most-polluted river and owes its name to the fictional location of a hit Argentine youth telenovela of the time, Verano del 98. But the real place is very different from the idyllic coastal city where the protagonists of Argentina’s answer to Dawson’s Creek met their first loves or sang around bonfires.
“You don’t know what it was like – when we started cleaning up, all the streams were blocked up everywhere: rubbish, dead dogs … a bit of everything. It was unsanitary, but we carried on working anyway,” says Monges, now 61. She started knocking on doors, getting people out to work with her, and in 2005 got the provincial administration to give them tools, uniforms and training. Now Monges leads 9 de julio, a workers’ cooperative that, from Monday to Friday, cleans up streams flowing from the river. “Every day, we will find rubbish,” says Monges. “It’s like people don’t understand.”
The Reconquista is 51 miles (82km) long, located in the north-east of the province of Buenos Aires and flows through 18 municipalities. About 4-5 million people live in its basin. It flows into the Luján River, which then connects with the Río de la Plata estuary.
Since at least the 1970s, the river has been a dumping ground for untreated sewage, industrial waste and landfill leachate. It has the state sewage company on its banks, along with homes that lack adequate infrastructure, residents connecting their drainpipes so that waste is discharged directly into the water. Several factories located in the district of San Martín, known as “the Industrial Capital”, also throw their waste into the river.
“All of this not only pollutes the water, but also the soil and the air. In this area there’s no access to drinking water … all the aquifers are contaminated,” says Natalia Gavazzo, an anthropologist and researcher at the National Scientific and Technical Research Council. Gavazzo directs the Migrantas en Reconquista project, which conducts research and carries out initiatives in the region to strengthen the socio-environmental strategies employed by women in the neighbourhoods of the Reconquista river basin. She adds that the environmental activism in Costa Esperanza is carried out primarily by women. “They are not just victims,” she says. “They are also the key agents of mitigation and adaptation; they possess a wealth of knowledge that is central to the survival of their communities.”
But the Reconquista is just one of the troubled rivers in La Plata, the giant system that connects multiple waterways across Uruguay and Argentina. According to the World Meteorological Organization State of Global Water Resources report, out on Thursday, major parts of La Plata river basins have experienced recurring below-normal water levels between 2021 and 2025, caused by persistent multi-year drought conditions.
La Plata basin includes the Paraguay River, which has consistently recorded water levels at their lowest since 2020. Analysis of WMO data shows that the Paraguay River’s water levels have been consistently below normal for the last six years, with its 25 driest months since 1991 registered after 2020.
The drought and pollution issues plaguing La Plata and the Reconquista are affecting many more of the world’s rivers. As Gavazzo puts it, “climate change has an uneven impact around the world – the north produces the emissions, but we in the south foot the bill.” For the anthropologist, the same is true at a local scale. “People in gated communities throw out rubbish, but it ends up here,” she added.
Juan Borús, who recently retired from the National Water Institute and is one of the country’s leading hydrologists, says that governments should “tackle every one of these sources of pollution individually, which is an extremely costly, painstaking task that requires regulation”, but that “companies that discharge complex effluents evade the rules … They’ve been doing it all their lives.”
In 2001, the Buenos Aires province created the Reconquista River Basin Committee (Comirec) to clean it up, but it had limited impact, and parts of the river where Costa Esperanza is located still exhibit “severe deterioration”, according to its early 2026 reports. High levels of E coli (a bacterium that indicates the presence of fecal matter) and low levels of oxygen make it “not a suitable environment for aquatic life” and “a risk to the population”, according to Patricio Carmona, a biochemist specialising in environmental analysis.
“The smell is like an acid,” says Lorena Batista, 47, a neighbour who works at the National Institute of Industrial Technology. “It is nauseating,” adds Zulma Monges, María’s daughter. The stench, they agree, becomes unbearable in summer, and when the wind blows they have to close their windows. It is not only the smell – neighbours have suffered from skin conditions such as hives, rashes, sores and scars, respiratory and lung problems, and gastrointestinal diseases, although Zulma says the skin conditions have become somewhat rarer since her mother’s community squad started picking up the rubbish.
Once a month, residents meet to discuss problems and contact representatives from the local government, to whom they address their concerns – accumulated rubbish or water cuts, for example. “It’s very much a part of our lives; it’s already become an integral part of the neighbourhood’s culture,” says grocer Rosa Valencia in her shop, laden with coconuts, plantains and yerba mate.
And there are other efforts under way to clean up the river. The San Martín University’s School of Habitat and Sustainability is developing artificial wetlands – a nature-inspired method that could be installed on site to help filter out persistent pollutants and restore the area’s biodiversity. A group of several local organisations, Foro por la Recuperación del Río Reconquista, is campaigning for the creation of an ecological preserve. “Many years ago, before the landfill was built, that area was a large marshland with beaches,” they claim in their petition.
“Older folks used to tell us: ‘we’d go fishing there, we’d spend our weekends there; there were always, always, always lots of animals’,” says Zulma Monges. The area, she says, is overpopulated, and “the few green spaces we do have, we’re maintaining them as a community”. Then she pulls out her phone and shows a picture of one of the streams, just after it was cleaned by her mother’s squad.
“It’s beautiful when it’s clean,” she says. “The thing is, you have to stop the rubbish from reaching the neighbourhood. But this whole area … look, it’s beautiful.”
- 
  Over the next year, in the Our Rivers series, we’ll be focusing on the environmental challenges facing the world’s rivers, looking at the waterways around the planet that are overengineered or suffocating and drying up, and those that are being opened up again and given new life.

How’s your apocalypse stockpiling coming on? Three weeks in, mine has hit a few snags | Emma Brockes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:00:43 UTC
17:00:43 KST

It’s been three weeks since the government advisory urging us to start stockpiling in case of emergency – how’s your prep coming along? The Prepare campaign, backed by Wes Streeting, who one imagines gliding through the apocalypse, quiff undisturbed, listed nine essential items, among them wet wipes, first-aid kits and batteries. The World Health Organization, meanwhile, suggests budgeting for 15 litres of water per person per day, so a family of four will need to store upwards of 180 litres to cover the recommended period of three days. The chances of this actually happening seem to me, intuitively, to be considerably lower than the disaster they’re supposed to forestall. But hope springs, so let’s see.
The first step towards stockpiling is stocktaking. This is where I’m at: one mega-torch (uncharged), which I bought in prepper mode after surviving the terrifying New York blackout of 2019 when for about an hour we couldn’t charge our phones; lots of very large sticking plasters and a handful of small round ones, the normal sizes having long been used up; two cans of tuna, which will go down to one after lunch; two litres of sparkling water, so for the first hour or so after a nuclear strike, assuming it happens this afternoon, we’ll at least be able to enjoy some bubbles; and three OxyContin saved from my c-section almost 12 years ago, which are probably less powerful than homeopathy at this point but I retain a vague hope I can use for barter when money breaks down.
In other words, I’m not really prepared and the biggest deficit in my unpreparedness is, evidently, my attitude. On the evidence of what appeared to be a collective shrug, recently, when we were informed of the threats posed by AI, it’s an attitude problem that’s widely shared. It’s not that we don’t care, perhaps, but that it is hard to know what to do. By which I mean, it’s hard to know what to do that doesn’t involve giving over precious closet space to 40 two-litre bottles of water or disrupting our thought patterns to accommodate large, uncomfortable truths.
In other words, if this is a collective failure of imagination, then what’s needed is some rigorous thought experiments that address our inability to imagine the worst. It’s wild that this should be necessary six years after a global pandemic, but of course, if there’s one thing to be said about humankind, it’s our ability to go scorched earth on recent trauma and pretend like nothing ever happened. This is called resilience – and there are, I’m sure, good evolutionary reasons for it, yet in this case it’s unhelpful. From scratch, then, we must develop what the government calls “household resilience”, which in my house means learning not to go into meltdown when someone can’t find their favourite hoodie or we run out of Nutella, or the Russians aim a missile towards our area.
With this in mind, I would recommend browsing something called the local resilience forum, made up of regional lists of potential threats starting with “nuclear attack by a state on the UK mainland”, working down through pandemics, biblical droughts, floods, and the collapse of the National Grid, all the way to the threat posed by “space weather”. It’s very When the Wind Blows, and if it’s hard to square with real world scenarios, I suspect it’s because when you put something in local government language and stick it in a table, any sense of threat collapses beneath the sheer weight of boredom.
For real imaginative engagement, we must turn to the fiction writers. The scene I go to in my head is the opening pages of Emily St John Mandel’s Station Eleven, in which a character called Jeevan, tipped off by a doctor friend that a pandemic is coming that will kill 99% of the world’s population, runs to a supermarket, shackles seven big shopping carts together and buys enough food and water to barricade himself in his apartment for 58 days, until the first panic has passed.
So, as long as Tesco is open and I can beat the rush, perhaps things will work out just fine? I know there are some walnuts at the back of the cupboard. We could take the batteries out of the remote to use in the torch. Per The Day After Tomorrow, I have plenty of books for firewood, and worst-case scenario, can wear the cats for extra warmth. And while water is a problem, I think about that couple who survived in a tiny boat in the middle of the Pacific for 118 days, and imagine we will figure it out. I can catch the drips from the freezer as it defrosts and suck the gel from the aloe vera. See? Already thinking like a survivor. We’ve got this!
- 
  Emma Brockes is a Guardian columnist

2026-09-17

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – The Aerospace Industry Development Corporation and Acer's Altos unveiled an AI production enterprise resource management system at a trade show on Wednesday.
Traditional manufacturing industries use up to 60 different systems that are incompatible with each other, with scattered data that are difficult to retrieve, a press release said. The co-developed solution connects these systems, allowing management to organize data for making informed decisions to improve efficiency.
The platform combines AIDC's management software with Altos' high-performance server to accelerate data processing. Both firms aim to introduce it to small and medium enterprises.
AIDC Vice President Louis Tseng (曾國益) and Altos CEO Li Chan-chieh (李占傑) signed the agreement. Tseng said that the system marks the firm's expansion into industry digital transformation. Li said AIDC's software and Altos' server will make AI accessible to domestic firms.
The technology is developed in Taiwan using non-China parts, with data processed internally to protect sensitive information, making it suitable for defense, finance, and government work. AIDC is also the first to pass advanced data security certification in the US, making it a qualified defense department vendor.
The platform will first be deployed in AIDC's production lines for demonstration. It aims to standardize the manufacturing of plastics and other materials.
AIDC AIxWare's core applications:
- It allows decades-old data to be shared between different platforms
- It can update production volume and report errors
- It can synchronize orders, detail tasks, and track product origins
- It can merge order lead times and prioritize urgent orders
- It can suggest power-saving measures while monitoring power consumption
- It compiles retrieved data for management reference, adding transparency to corporate decision-making

Taiwan, US push ahead with ‘Hellscape’ drone strategy to deter China attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:00:11 UTC
17:00:11 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan and the US military are continuing to advance a “Hellscape” defense strategy that would deploy large numbers of drones to disrupt a Chinese invasion fleet.
The strategy, conceived during former US President Joe Biden's administration, draws on battlefield lessons from Ukraine and Iran, per The Economist. It combines relatively inexpensive aerial, surface, and underwater drones with artificial intelligence to exhaust Chinese interceptor missiles and damage invasion ships.
The drones can use inertial guidance, image recognition, and onboard AI to identify and prioritize targets, and coordinate swarm attacks, even if Chinese forces disrupt communications. The strategy is not expected to prevent an invasion entirely, but could increase the cost and create time and space for US reinforcements to reach Taiwan.
Whether the US would intervene remains an open question, particularly under President Donald Trump, The Economist said. He has treated arms sales to Taiwan as a bargaining chip in negotiations with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and has yet to approve a US$14 billion (NT$446.23 billion) arms package that Congress cleared in January.
Taiwanese officials worry Washington could make concessions to China to secure trade and technology agreements, The Economist reported. They also fear that shortages caused by the war with Iran could delay previously approved US arms deliveries and take years to replenish American weapons stockpiles.
Taiwan’s limited capacity to produce unmanned systems is another challenge. The country plans to procure 208,000 locally produced aerial attack drones and 1,320 unmanned surface vessels by 2032, but funding disputes delayed the program until it was approved in August with an annual funding cap.
Production and exports have grown over the past two years, but the KMT was the main obstacle to funding approval, raising concerns about further delays if it returns to power in 2028. National Taiwan University Professor Chen Ping-hei (陳炳煇) told The Economist that Taiwan lacks sufficient manpower and funding, estimating that it needs 4 million unmanned aerial vehicles and 10,000 marine drones.
Some military officials remain skeptical, fearing drone investments could divert resources from larger weapons systems, including Patriot missiles. Others emphasize the need for fighter jets and warships to counter Chinese actions short of an invasion, such as a blockade.
Supporters argue that Taiwan and the US do not need to demonstrate that they could defeat China outright. Instead, they need to convince Xi that an invasion would not deliver the quick, relatively low-cost victory he seeks, thereby strengthening deterrence.

Liu said local governments should give businesses preparedness information before a crisis, rather than relying mainly on financial assistance afterward. They should also help companies plan for labor shortages, utility outages, transportation restrictions, and logistics disruptions.
Economic Democracy Union think tank convener Lai Chung-chiang (賴中強) called on newly elected mayors and county commissioners to review civil defense spending after taking office. He said the review should cover training, information systems, exercises, public communication, supplies, and disaster response facilities, per Liberty Times.

Brutalist Asia: A New Publication Reframing the History of Brutalism, from Japan to Lebanon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

The history of Brutalism has largely been written from a Western perspective. Brutalist Asia by Blue Crow Media offers a different view, examining how architects across Asia adopted, questioned, and transformed the architectural language associated with the movement in response to radically different political, climatic, and cultural conditions. Spanning 28 countries, from Japan and Southeast Asia through South and Central Asia to the Middle East, Iran, and Lebanon, the book brings together 140 buildings and more than 150 photographs, placing internationally recognized works by architects including Kenzo Tange, Paul Rudolph, Balkrishna V. Doshi, Raj Rewal, Charles Correa, Kim Swoo Geun, Leandro V. Locsin, and Le Corbusier alongside important but lesser-known works that expand our understanding of post-war architecture across the continent.
Within this broader geography, one particular history unfolds in Lebanon, where the ambitions of Modernism became inseparable from a country undergoing profound social, political, and urban transformation. Read on for an excerpt from ArchDaily Editor-in-Chief Christele Harrouk's chapter in Brutalist Asia, tracing the rise of Brutalism in Lebanon, the architects and buildings that gave it a particular local expression, and the rupture that left this Modernist project unfinished.
Khalil Khoury's Interdesign Building and Brutalism in Lebanon
Long before I knew what Brutalism was, I was drawn, as a child, to the immovable concrete brutes that surrounded me. Often overlooked, they stood apart, not only for their massing, but for their poetic composition and sculptural presence. They carried an intricate, almost vulnerable truth. They revealed an unexpected lyrical dimension. And ultimately, they paradoxically invited me to engage with their surfaces, to touch, explore and discover.
Brutalism in Lebanon
Emerging in the mid-20th century through the works of Le Corbusier and Alison and Peter Smithson, Brutalism spread globally, reaching its peak in the mid-1970s. From Europe to India, Japan, the United States and Latin America, it evolved into diverse contextual interpretations, becoming more than a European export. Through this shared architectural language, different regions negotiated their own paths towards modernity, development, governance and identity. In the Arab world in particular, this architectural evolution was inseparable from its political context, closely aligned with the ambitions of newly formed states and processes of nation-building.
In Lebanon, this Modernist landscape was shaped by local architects and engineers, grounded in practical responses to the local built environment. It became especially visible in the 1960s, an era often described as the golden age of the nation-state project. Architecture at the time was largely institutional, socially engaged and politically driven, embodying a collective vision of modernization. Brutalism emerged within this context, relatively later than elsewhere. Inspired by Le Corbusier and the Brazilian Modernist movement, Lebanese architects such as Joseph Philippe Karam, Khalil Khoury, Georges Khoury, Antoine Romanos and Grégoire Serof adopted exposed concrete as a medium for new architectural expression, transforming it from structure into a symbol of progress and modernity.
Introduced earlier during the French Mandate in the 1920s through engineers and urban planning initiatives, reinforced concrete gradually replaced traditional stone construction. By the 1950s and 1960s, amid rapid urban growth, it had become the dominant building material. Architects like Jacques Liger-Belair reframed it as a continuation of local tradition. He famously stated that 'concrete is our equivalent of stone' and often described it as a kind of 'liquid stone'.
Taking on a more hybrid character, Brutalism in Lebanon combines Modernist ideals with regional identity, climate responsiveness and a deeply expressive, sculptural approach to form. It was not simply an imported style, but a localized evolution shaped by cultural, climatic and political conditions.
This trajectory, however, was abruptly interrupted. The outbreak of the Lebanese Civil War in 1975 marked the collapse of the nation-state project and, with it, the decline of the Modernist movement that had accompanied it. Within a few years, this rupture became visible in the built environment. Today, Beirut stands as a city of contrasts, its skyline marked by bullet-ridden structures, Ottoman and French colonial remnants, post-war developments, and, in between, monolithic concrete buildings dating back to an earlier era. These Brutalist structures remain as fragments of a moment of cultural ambition, revealing both the ambitions of modernity and their eventual unravelling.
The Interdesign building
One cannot speak of Brutalism in Lebanon without addressing the Interdesign Building. Exemplifying many of the movement's defining characteristics, it was conceived by Khalil Khoury in 1973. In 2024, during Bernard Khoury's exhibition dedicated to his father's work, I had the opportunity to speak with him about this enigmatic project, and its story proved as fascinating as the building itself.
While often situated within the broader Modernist movement, the Interdesign Building can be understood as distinctly Brutalist in its material presence and spatial organization. Whether Khalil Khoury himself would have embraced this label, or any label, remains uncertain, yet its use of exposed concrete, monumental massing and uncompromising structural clarity aligns it closely with the core principles of Brutalism. Its strong geometric composition and repetitive structural rhythm reinforce this reading, allowing the building to be understood through its own logic of construction. Its inward, almost defensive configuration, absence of ornament and emphasis on raw material further reinforce this interpretation. It asserts itself as a singular, monolithic object, embodying the tension between function, form and material that defines Brutalist architecture.
The Interdesign Building was conceived at the peak of Khalil Khoury's career, at a time when he was both an architect and a successful industrialist. By the 1960s, he had developed one of the region's most advanced furniture production industries, designing, manufacturing and distributing modern pieces locally, expanding access beyond elite markets. As the company grew, so did its technical sophistication: when imported machinery proved insufficient, Khoury began developing his own technologies, producing custom equipment to bend wood in-house. Within this context, the Interdesign Building emerged as the culmination of an integrated system, a showroom for furniture created and manufactured in Lebanon. Khoury was, in effect, shaping the final stage of a process in which architecture, design and industry converged, embodying the optimism of a time when Lebanon saw itself as a center of production, innovation and export.
Construction began in 1974, but by April 1975, as the project had just reached ground level, the Civil War erupted and brought everything to a halt. Attempts to resume construction during the war were unsuccessful, leaving the building suspended for years. When the war ended in the early 1990s, the context that had given rise to the project had fundamentally changed. Beirut's economy had shifted away from production towards banking, tourism and speculation, making the idea of a large-scale furniture showroom increasingly irrelevant.
Despite financial difficulties and the collapse of his industrial enterprise, Khoury chose to complete the building. By the late 1990s, it was finished but unused, a structure conceived for a reality that no longer existed. In the years that followed, it was seized by banks, briefly repurposed and then abandoned for decades. Its rigid spatial configuration and lack of adaptability made it difficult to occupy. Today, the Interdesign Building stands as more than just an object in the city; it is a physical manifestation of an interrupted modern project. Its story mirrors both Khoury's personal trajectory and the broader transformation of Lebanon.
Explore the wider story in Brutalist Asia, bringing together 140 buildings across 28 countries, more than 150 photographs, and 8 original essays by Bob Pang, John Barr, Bhawna Dandona, Christele Harrouk, Kyung Taek Lee, Caryn Paredes-Santillan, Pinai Sirikiatikul, Soroush Mohajery, and Amirhosein Rad. Together, they trace how Brutalism was interpreted and transformed across distinct political, climatic, and cultural contexts throughout Asia.

Taiwan chip IP firms target AI security at chip level
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
07:59:42 UTC
16:59:42 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s chip intellectual property firms are moving into the AI cybersecurity market by building security features directly into chip designs, UDN Money reported Monday.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang (黃仁勳) said recently that cybersecurity will be one of the next major applications for AI. As AI accelerates software development, it also creates a need for stronger security and faster responses to vulnerabilities.
As chip-level security gains importance, Ememory Technology Inc. and Andes Technology Corp. are developing technologies that build security into chips at the hardware level.
Ememory has expanded beyond its traditional non-volatile memory IP business with its NeoPUF technology, which uses tiny variations created during chip manufacturing to give each chip a unique digital fingerprint. The physically unclonable function makes the fingerprint difficult to predict or reproduce.
NeoPUF can be used for device authentication, encryption key generation, and secure boot. Unlike conventional methods that store keys directly in memory, the technology can reduce the risk of sensitive keys being extracted through physical attacks or reverse engineering.
Andes has incorporated several security features into its RISC-V processor architecture. Secure boot verifies that software has not been tampered with when a device starts, while a trusted execution environment creates an isolated area within the processor for sensitive information such as encryption keys and AI models.
Input-Output Physical Memory Protection controls access to peripheral devices and areas of memory. Andes has combined these capabilities in its AndeSentry framework, which connects with security partners across the RISC-V ecosystem.
Chip IP firms develop reusable technology designs that other companies can license and use when developing chips. This allows chipmakers to add specific functions without developing every part of a chip from scratch, saving time and development costs, according to Sinotrade.

He said the operation also produced unspecified results in the Black Sea.
Rostov Oblast Governor Yury Slyusar confirmed a fire broke out at the site after falling drone debris damaged a transformer substation, cutting power in four districts of Rostov-on-Don. He said preliminary information showed no deaths or injuries, and that the fire was extinguished. NASA’s FIRMS satellite fire-detection service recorded a fire in the area of the airfield’s aircraft parking apron, and the independent Russian monitoring channel Astra separately identified the blaze as occurring on the grounds of the Rostov-on-Don Central military airfield, near the same parking area where military aircraft and helicopters are typically stationed.
The Rostov-on-Don airfield has been a recurring target for Ukraine this year. Fires have been reported there at least eight times in 2026, including strikes on March 28, April 26, May 8, May 22, July 6, July 16, Aug. 6 and Aug. 28. Ukraine’s General Staff also said it struck the same airfield on Sept. 6, along with a Podlet radar station and two Pantsir-S1 air defense systems elsewhere in Rostov Oblast.
“Thanks to our soldiers, who make war tangible for Russia every day,” Zelensky said. “Tonight, thanks to a joint operation by the SBU, GUR and SZR, the Yaroslavl oil refinery was hit. The Security Service also worked precisely against the military airfield in Rostov: the destruction of one An-12, two An-26s and three more helicopters has been confirmed. There are good results in the Black Sea too. We respond to aggression every day. Russia must choose peace.”
Russia’s Defense Ministry had not issued its own damage assessment or confirmed how many drones were involved in the overnight attack as of publication. The exact condition of the aircraft Zelensky named, and whether any were airworthy at the time of the strike, has not been independently verified beyond the fire confirmed by Slyusar, NASA’s satellite detection, and Astra’s analysis.

The government has announced £30m in funding to support the rollout of more than 1,000 community-led clean energy projects across the country.

Means-testing personal independence payment (Pip) would save £8bn without behavioural change, says IFS thinktank
At his press conference this morning Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, was asked if he backed means-testing the personal independence payment (Pip), a disability benefit. (See 12.03pm.) The question was prompted by a report from the Institute for Fiscal Studies. Griffith said he had not read the IFS report and he ducked the question about means testing.
The IFS does not explicitly propose means-testing Pip. But it says the government should have a clear sense of what it wants Pip to achieve, and it considers the pros and cons of seven potential reforms.
On the need for more clarity of purpose, it says:
When designing reforms to Pip, the government needs to decide what it is trying to achieve. What outcome arising from disability is the government attempting to address? Does it want to target resources towards those whose living standards are lower because they face the additional disability-related costs? If so, this would justify a benefit that provides financial support such as Pip. Alternatively, does it want to improve overall well-being? In which case, it is possible that it is more effective to subsidise particular goods and services, which could be achieved by providing vouchers or in-kind support.
The government must also decide on the distributional outcomes it would like to achieve. Does it want to reduce inequalities caused by disability even if this means providing additional money to people on high incomes? If so, then this would justify the current non-means-tested structure of Pip. Alternatively, does it want to focus resources on those most likely to have poor outcomes? In that case, it should consider means-testing support, as those with disabilities and on low incomes are more likely to report not being able to afford essentials and more likely to report low life satisfaction.
A report from the Re:State thinktank published yesterday made similar arguments about the structure of the benefit.
On means-testing Pip, the IFS says:
One unusual feature of Pip relative to other benefits is that it is not means-tested, so high-income households can claim it. If the main goal of the benefit is to reduce inequalities arising from disability, there is a good case for keeping PIP as a non-means-tested benefit. Alternatively, if greater weight is placed on ensuring that disabled people can obtain a minimum standard of living, there is a stronger argument for means-testing PIP – something recently proposed by Reform UK, though the [review of Pip led by Stephen Timms on behalf of the government] has indicated it will recommend keeping PIP non-means-tested. Means-testing Pip, by integrating it into universal credit, would deliver a saving of £8.2bn (33% of PIP spending) if claimant behaviour did not respond to the change. However, in reality, the saving will be somewhat smaller due to behavioural responses.

Local authorities spent a net total of £467.5m on this kind of accommodation in the year to March, up from an inflation-adjusted £383.6m in 2024/25 – an increase of £83.8m.
Andy Burnham has made tackling homelessness – which comes in many forms including people living in temporary accommodation – one of his priority areas since becoming prime minister in the summer.
Figures published today by the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) showed net spending by councils on all types of temporary accommodation for the homeless plus administration costs rose by 2% year-on-year.
Net spending – which is the difference between the total outgoings for local authorities and their income – in the year to March was £1.47bn, an increase from an inflation-adjusted £1.44bn the year before.
Spending on nightly paid, privately managed accommodation fell by a fifth to £494.3m from £622.6m, while spending on hostels, which can include refuges, was down by almost a third to £26.2m from £37.8m.
But figures for private sector accommodation, which is leased by a local authority or registered provider, and for bed and breakfasts both rose by more than a fifth.
The former went from £220.3m to £271.2m – a 23% increase.

The Taxpayers Association calls on the Ministry of Finance to promptly resolve the issue of aviation leasing taxation
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:56:44 EEST
16:56:44 KST

The Taxpayers Association calls on the Ministry of Finance to promptly resolve the issue of aviation leasing taxation
Kyiv • UNN
The Taxpayers Association called on the Ministry of Finance to unify the taxation of aviation leasing payments to non-residents as soon as possible. The uncertainty has led to criminal cases and risks for the industry.
The Ministry of Finance of Ukraine should establish a unified approach to the taxation of airline leasing payments to non-residents of Ukraine as soon as possible. Further uncertainty on this issue creates serious risks for the aviation business, which is facing fiscal and criminal pressure due to differing interpretations of the legislation by government agencies. Hryhoriy Katamadze, President of the Association of Taxpayers of Ukraine, expressed this view in an exclusive comment to UNN.
Criminal cases over the interpretation of aviation leasing as royalties
As UNN previously reported, since 2024 the Economic Security Bureau has begun interpreting transactions involving the leasing of air transport from non-residents of Ukraine as the use of equipment. According to the investigators' version, Ukrainian air carriers should have paid royalties for leasing airplanes and helicopters. Based on this approach, the ESB opened criminal proceedings against at least five air carriers, including Ukraine International Airlines, Constanta Airline, Windrose, N3Operations, and Skyline Express. According to UNN, another airline, Urga, may also be involved in a similar case.
The criminal cases were opened despite the fact that almost all the air carriers had successfully passed tax audits, and the tax authorities' leasing-related objections concerned only one company.
Representatives of the aviation industry insist that the problem arose because of an ambiguous interpretation of the legislation and requires the establishment of a unified state approach.
In response to a request from UNN, the Ministry of Finance reported that the taxation of transactions involving the leasing of aircraft is carried out in accordance with the Tax Code and Ukraine's international treaties. At the same time, the Tax Code of Ukraine does not provide for the possibility of taxing aviation leasing as royalties. Therefore, the Bureau's approach to interpreting aviation leasing without amending the tax legislation is described as pressure that could destroy an entire sector of passenger and transport services. After all, according to data from the State Register of Civil Aircraft of Ukraine, 86% of the aircraft fleet of Ukrainian companies is leased.
That is why the issue of aviation leasing was brought before the Tax Committee of the Public Council under the Ministry of Finance. Following the first meeting, it was decided to initiate the establishment of a working group under the Ministry of Finance, which is to develop a draft generalized tax consultation on the taxation of leasing payments to non-residents.
Businesses need legal certainty
Hryhoriy Katamadze, President of the Association of Taxpayers of Ukraine, emphasizes that when government agencies interpret the same business transactions differently, this deprives businesses of the ability to forecast tax consequences and properly plan their activities.
The Ministry of Finance should consider the issue of taxing Ukrainian airlines' leasing payments to non-residents as soon as possible and put an end to the divergent interpretations that are currently creating serious risks for the aviation business. When government agencies interpret the same transactions differently, and such interpretations result in multimillion-hryvnia tax claims and criminal proceedings, businesses cannot properly plan their activities. And amid a full-scale war and constant Russian strikes, it is already difficult for businesses to operate in Ukraine
He believes that the development of a unified approach to the taxation of aviation leasing must not be delayed. Above all, this concerns ensuring the principle of legal certainty, under which companies can understand their tax obligations in advance rather than learn of a new interpretation only after claims have been raised by government agencies.
Airlines simply need legal certainty: they must understand which tax obligations they are required to fulfill. Resolving this issue is important not only for individual carriers. It concerns preserving Ukraine’s aviation industry and creating normal conditions for its recovery after the war ends
The President of the Ukrainian Taxpayers Association believes that all parties, including representatives of the aviation industry, should be involved in the Finance Ministry’s development of a unified approach that will be mandatory for state bodies to apply.
I hope that the Ministry of Finance will carry out the necessary work as quickly as possible, involving all parties, and formulate a unified approach that both tax and law enforcement authorities will subsequently follow. Businesses should not become hostages to contradictory interpretations of legislation by state bodies. Pressure on business will certainly not produce a positive result for the state

A quarter of Finns have less than €770 in the bank, report finds
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:56:08 EEST
16:56:08 KST

A report by Statistics Finland has revealed a big gap in how much money Finns have in the bank.
A quarter of adults had less than 770 euros in their accounts, while one in ten had more than 60,000 euros in deposits.
The median balance was just under 5,000 euros last year. Men had, on average, just over 800 euros more in deposits than women.
But the median tells a different story — women held about 1,300 euros more than men.
The median is the middle value in a set of numbers arranged in order from smallest to biggest, and provides a better indictor of wealth disparities than the average figure.
"This shows that deposits are distributed more unevenly among men. At the top end of the distribution, among those with the largest deposits, men outnumber women," said Veli-Matti Törmälehto, a senior researcher at Statistics Finland, in a press release.
Older Finns had the most money in their accounts. Half of those aged 85 and over had more than 31,460 euros in their accounts. Among 18–24-year-olds, half had less than 1,240 euros.
The statistics also show that more than a third of Finns own funds or shares. The number rose by almost 100,000 from the previous year and by around 680,000 over the past decade.
Women are slightly more likely than men to own mutual funds, while men are more likely to own listed shares.

China pushes back against US’ Russia sanctions bill, says bilateral ties should not be disrupted
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
07:55:46 UTC
16:55:46 KST

Riyaz ul Khaliq
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
China on Thursday pushed back on the US Congress passing a major sanctions bill targeting Russia, stressing bilateral trade ties should “not be disrupted” by any third party.
“China carries out economic and trade cooperation with countries on the basis of equality and mutual benefit," Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told reporters in Beijing.
He was responding to questions on a US Congress bill that imposes mandatory sanctions on senior Russian officials, including President Vladimir Putin, as well as oligarchs, state-owned companies, and foreign businesses supporting Russia’s defense industry.
Guo, however, said China’s “cooperation does not target any third party and it should not be disrupted under the coercion of any third party.”
“We always oppose long-arm jurisdiction that has no basis in international law or authority of UN Security Council,” he stressed.
Chinese and Russian bilateral trade has grown over the years, surging over $240 billion in 2024, and most of the trade is conducted in national currencies.
The US House of Representatives approved the bill Wednesday by a 262-159 vote, with dozens of Democrats joining Republicans.
The measure now goes to US President Donald Trump for his signature.
The legislation would allow the Trump administration to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries purchasing Russian oil and gas, including China and India.

European markets open higher after Fed hike as US dollar hits seven-week high
Unknown

2026-09-17
07:55:44 UTC
16:55:44 KST

European stock markets opened in positive territory on Thursday morning, shrugging off Wall Street's decline after the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in more than three years and signalled that further hikes are likely.
Investors in Europe took the Federal Reserve rate hike in their stride.
Both the Euro Stoxx 50 and the broader pan-European Stoxx 600 traded over 0.6% higher at the start of Thursday's session.
France's CAC 40, Germany's DAX 30, Italy’s FTSE MIB, Spain's IBEX 35, the Netherlands' AEX and Switzerland's CH20, all traded between 0.2% and 0.7% higher than their Wednesday close.
The UK's FTSE 100 led the pack and rose more than 1%.
Carmakers and industrials led the Paris index, with Renault gaining more than 2%, Stellantis 1.6% and Schneider Electric 1.3%. Technology went the other way, with Dassault Systèmes falling 2.4%.
The calm followed a rougher session in New York, where the Dow Jones Industrial Average closed 1.2% lower on Wednesday and the S&P 500 fell 0.4%, while the Nasdaq was broadly flat.
Asian markets were mixed overnight with Tokyo's Nikkei 225 rising 0.2%, Seoul's Kospi gaining 0.9%, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng lost 0.7% and the Shanghai Composite 0.4%.
Reactions were "pretty much expected since the rate hike was also in line with market expectations", said Lorraine Tan, director of equity research for Asia at Morningstar, adding that the Iran war is likely to keep pressure on inflation.
A stronger US dollar and higher yields
The more consequential moves were in currencies and bonds.
The US dollar climbed to its highest in seven weeks against a basket of major currencies, lifted by the jump in short-dated Treasury yields that followed the decision.
The euro was trading around $1.146, down 0.5% from Wednesday's open.
A stronger US dollar makes European exports more competitive in American markets, but it also raises the cost of anything priced in dollars, which includes oil and gas, which compounds Europe's energy bill at a difficult moment.
In bond markets, the two-year Treasury yield, the maturity most sensitive to rate expectations, jumped to around 4.72% from 4.67% before the decision, holding near that level on Thursday.
The 10-year sat close to 5%, reflecting both the war-driven energy shock and mounting investor concern about American government debt.
Traders now fully expect another rate hike by December and put the odds of a move as soon as October at around 50%. Goldman Sachs became one of the first major Wall Street banks to forecast consecutive hikes, reversing its previous view that this month's move would be the only one.
Attention turns next to the Bank of England, which announces its decision later on Thursday and is expected to hold rates steady, and to the Bank of Japan on Friday, where a hike is anticipated.

Europe and Canada are 'strong, even stronger together', Carney tells European Parliament
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney addressed the European Parliament on Thursday, welcoming the ambition for Canada to become an EU associate member. "Canada and Europe are stronger, even stronger together," he said, a day after US President Donald Trump threatened new tariffs and to cut trade ties with the EU if Canada's bid succeeds.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Thursday embraced the prospect of his country becoming the European Union’s first associate member, saying closer ties with the continent would ensure no country could control Canada’s markets or undermine its sovereignty.
Carney’s speech to the European Parliament repeatedly extolled cooperation between Europe and Canada – but the relationship with the US, which has defined Canada’s economy for decades and has increasingly soured, hung over the address.
Trump’s tariffs, demands for economic concessions and repeated talk of making Canada the 51st state have pushed Ottawa to reduce its dependence on its neighbour and seek a far deeper economic, security and political relationship with Europe.
Carney told the parliament that he welcomed European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s proposal, unveiled Wednesday, though he acknowledged that “associate membership” remains to be defined.
He outlined what he was proposing: deeper integration across trade, defence, critical minerals, artificial intelligence, energy, space, research and financial services to make both sides less vulnerable to economic and geopolitical pressure. He later told reporters he was not pursuing full membership of the EU.
Read moreCanada vows to match US tariffs 'dollar for dollar' after failed trade negotiations
“We do not seek power to dominate others," he said. "On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience so that no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity, or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law.”
The prime minister received an ebullient welcome when he walked into the chamber in Strasbourg, France, with many lawmakers approaching him to shake his hand and ask for selfies – and giving a standing ovation after he spoke. One parliamentarian had donned a Canadian hockey jersey.
On Wednesday, von der Leyen proposed making Canada the EU’s first associate member – a status that does not currently exist in the bloc’s treaties and would have to be created. She said Europe wants to take its relationship with Canada to “the highest level possible".
Carney, sitting in the front row of the European Parliament chamber, nodded and rose to embrace von der Leyen as lawmakers gave the proposal a standing ovation.
Von der Leyen said Canada and the EU should move beyond their existing free trade agreement and create an “Alliance for the Future” encompassing a “common prosperity and economic security space".
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Carney will host EU leaders for a Canada-EU summit in Montreal on Oct. 29-30, when the two sides are expected to discuss the proposed new relationship in more detail.
Canada sends roughly 70% of its exports to the United States, making it highly exposed to Trump’s tariffs. Ottawa has retaliated and rejected demands Carney says threaten Canadian sovereignty.
Europe took a different path, shelving retaliation and accepting tariffs of up to 15% on most EU exports to the U.S.
Trump suggested the proposed arrangement could be a “hostile act” and threatened heavy tariffs on Europe if he judged its intentions to be unfriendly – raising the stakes for the speech.
Asked about Trump’s comments, Carney said Canadians were united in rejecting outside attempts to dictate the country’s choices.
“Canadians are united that nobody is going to tell us what language we speak. No one is going to dictate our culture or with whom we can strike agreements internationally,” Carney said.
Carney has repeatedly urged what he calls middle powers to resist economic coercion. At the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, he warned that when countries negotiate alone with a dominant power, “we negotiate from weakness. We accept what is offered.”
Trump rebuked him the next day.
Jonathan Wilkinson, Canada’s ambassador-designate to the EU, said Ottawa wants “to get as close as we possibly can” to Europe while increasing Canada’s independence.
While associate membership remains to be negotiated, Canada has already taken a major step. This year it became the first non-European country to join the EU’s 150-billion-euro ($173-billion) SAFE defence procurement programme, giving Canadian companies access to joint procurement as Europe increases defence spending.
The two sides have also discussed closer cooperation on energy, critical minerals, artificial intelligence and digital trade.
“The policies and rhetoric of the Trump administration are clearly pushing both Canada and the EU to imagine a world without strong US leadership and to act accordingly,” said Daniel Béland, a political-science professor at McGill University in Montreal.
Nelson Wiseman, a professor emeritus at the University of Toronto, said Carney’s handling of Trump has heightened European interest in the Canadian leader.
Europeans have long regarded Canada as a country that understands the United States particularly well because of their deep economic and political ties. Carney’s willingness to resist Trump rather than quickly accept Washington’s demands has reinforced that perception, he said.
“Carney’s shrewdness in dealing with Trump has captured Europe’s attention,” Wiseman said.

MOSCOW, September 17. TASS/. Russian air defenses intercepted and destroyed 641 Ukrainian unmanned aerial vehicles over Russian regions and the waters of the Black, Caspian and Azov seas overnight, the Russian defense ministry reported.
A fire erupted at an oil refinery in the Yaroslavl Region due to a drone attack. An electrical substation was damaged by falling debris, causing power outages in four districts of Rostov-on-Don.
TASS has compiled the key points on the aftermath.
Scale
- Over the past night, air defense forces on duty intercepted and destroyed 641 Ukrainian fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles over the territories of the Astrakhan, Belgorod, Bryansk, Vladimir, Voronezh, Kaluga, Kostroma, Kransdonar, Kursk, Lipetsk, Nizhny Novgorod, Moscow, Oryol, Rostov, Ryazan, Smolensk, Tambov, Tver, Tula and Yaroslavl Regions, as well as the Republic of Crimea and over the waters of the Azov, Caspian and Black seas, the Russian defense ministry reported.
- Air defenses shot down 65 drones over the Yaroslavl Region, Governor Mikhail Yevrayev said on his Max channel.
- At least 43 unmanned aerial vehicles were intercepted in the Nizhny Novgorod Region overnight and in the morning, Governor Gleb Nikitin said on his channel on Max.
- Air defenses intercepted 23 drones over the Voronezh Region, Governor Alexander Gusev said on his Max channel.
- At least 18 unmanned aerial vehicles were intercepted in the Smolensk Region overnight, Governor Vasily Anokhin said on his channel on Max.

- He specified that the drones were downed over the territories of the Kuybyshevsky district, as well as the Babyninsky, Borovsky, Dzerzhinsky, Zhizdrinsky, Spas-Demensky, Sukhinichsky, Khotynetsky and Yukhnovsky municipal districts, and on the outskirts of Kaluga.
Aftermath
- A fire broke out at an oil refinery in the Yaroslavl Region due to a drone attack, Governor Mikhail Yevrayev said on his Max channel.
- The fires that broke out have now been completely extinguished.
- Due to the discovery of drone debris, traffic was restricted for safety reasons on the road out of Yaroslavl toward Moscow, starting from the intersection of Moscovsky Prospekt and the Southwestern Bypass.
- Yevrayev noted that drivers should refrain from traveling in that direction and the surrounding area or choose a route around the affected section.
- The detour is via Gagarin Street.
- In addition, falling debris shattered windows in several apartment buildings.
- Cars were also damaged.
- A transformer substation was damaged by falling debris, leaving four districts of Rostov-on-Don without power, Governor Yury Slyusar said on his channel on Max.
- He specified that power supplies were disrupted in the Voroshilovsky, Leninsky, Oktyabrsky and Kirovsky districts of the city.
- Windows, roofing and glazing at six private houses, as well as outbuildings, were damaged.
- Slyusar added that drone debris was found at various locations in Rostov-on-Don and the Myasnikovsky District, including on roads and on the grounds of private households.
- The disrupted power supply is due to be restored by the end of the day, the press service of the Rostov Region Ministry of Industry and Energy told TASS.
- Falling debris damaged the glazing of several residential buildings and caused other non-critical damage to civilian infrastructure in the Nizhny Novgorod Region, Governor Gleb Nikitin said on his channel on Max.
- The assessment of the damage is ongoing, with emergency services working at the sites of the incidents.

India vows ‘determined’ response to US sanctions pressure
India has said it remains “firmly committed” to ensuring energy security for its 1.4 billion people, in response to the threat of steep new tariffs from the Russia sanctions bill that cleared the US Congress on Wednesday. 
“The Indian side has also made clear its determination to take all necessary measures to protect its trade and economic interests,” the Indian Foreign Ministry said in a statement on Thursday. 
The new US bill mandates up to 100% additional trade tariffs on the top buyers of Russian oil. India is the second-largest buyer of Russian oil, after China. 
Russian crude accounted for 45% of Indian oil imports in August, at around 2.1 million barrels per day. New Delhi bought $40.8 billion of Russian crude in the financial year that ended in March, or about 30.3% of its total crude imports, according to the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI) think tank. 
The House of Representatives passed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 in a 262-159 vote on Wednesday, following the bill’s approval by the Senate last month. The legislation now goes to US President Donald Trump to be signed into law.
Our statement on passage of the Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act in the US Congress
🔗 https://t.co/kD0Yg9sWbUpic.twitter.com/rSc21AqwEh
The Indian Foreign Ministry said the issue had been discussed at high levels in recent months with US officials, and that New Delhi had clearly conveyed the potential implications for both bilateral relations and the international energy market.
The Indian government will work closely with trade and industry bodies to deal with the implications, the Foreign Ministry said, adding New Delhi would continue to ensure energy security through diversified sourcing and on the basis of evolving market dynamics.
The pressure on India to cut off Russian oil also comes amid the conflict in the Middle East, triggered by the US-Israeli attacks on Iran, which have disrupted energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz and stoked energy prices.
The legislation does not automatically impose additional tariffs on Russian energy buyers, although it does give Trump the authority to impose extra duties on the top five importers of Russian-origin crude oil or natural gas. India has held off on signing a trade deal with the US despite months of negotiations.
Analysts have said Trump could use the new tariff bill to pressure India to make unilateral trade concessions. The bill, named after late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, a known Russia hawk, also targets Russia’s energy and defense industries and vessels Washington claims are used to evade existing sanctions, while extending sanctions on Iran.

U.S. Congress Passes ‘Sanctions From Hell’ Bill Against Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
07:50:42 UTC
16:50:42 KST

The U.S. House of Representatives on Wednesday passed a sweeping sanctions and tariff bill intended to increase economic pressure on Russia over its invasion of Ukraine, sending the bill to U.S. President Donald Trump to sign into law more than a year after the late Senator Lindsey Graham first introduced it.
The bill, now called the "Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026" to honor the South Carolina Republican, passed the Senate last month. The House passed it by 262 to 159, as 58 Democrats broke with party leaders to join all but seven Republicans in favor.
The legislation targets Russia's energy and defense industries, as well as its "shadow fleet" of tankers that evade existing sanctions, in order to deprive Moscow of funds used to pay for its war against Ukraine.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Thursday that further U.S. sanctions against Russia would make it harder to reach a peace deal in Ukraine.
"We are, of course, monitoring the progress of this bill. It falls under the category of unfriendly actions, and of course the imposition of any additional sanctions by the U.S. would certainly complicate efforts to find a peace settlement in Ukraine," Peskov told reporters.
The legislation faced opposition from House Democrats because it also authorizes Trump to impose stiff tariffs of up to 100% on China, India and other countries to reduce their dependence on Russian oil and gas, as well as to extend sanctions on Iran. They argue that Trump already has the authority he needs to impose sanctions on Russia, but has chosen not to do so.
Democrats likewise say the bill makes it too easy for the U.S. president not to impose sanctions by declaring that doing so is not in the national interest, a much broader presidential power than in most sanctions bills.
House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said the legislation had so many loopholes that sanctions harming Russia might not be applied. "What this legislation will do is give Donald Trump, perhaps, unfettered authority to unleash tariffs on the American people," the New York lawmaker said as he announced he would vote no.
But backers said the bill, a rare piece of legislation to pass with significant support from both parties, will send an essential message to Russia — and the world — that Washington continues to support Ukraine, helping to force Moscow to negotiate.
"Today, we are now one step closer to securing Lindsey's vision of enduring peace in Ukraine and beyond," Republican Representative Michael McCaul of Texas, a lead sponsor of the legislation, told the press conference after the House vote.

Pentagon wants new mobile radar to track hypersonic weapons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
07:47:54 UTC
16:47:54 KST

The Missile Defense Agency wants industry to build a new mobile radar that can be flown into a war zone aboard a C-17, set up within hours and torn down again in minutes, according to a pre-solicitation notice posted September 16.
The program, called Forward Based Mode Radar Next, is meant to replace or supplement current forward-deployed missile-tracking radars with a system that can move fast enough to survive against an adversary trying to target it. The notice comes from the agency’s Mobile Land-Based Sensors Project Office and lays out plans to run the effort through NOBLE, the Missile Defense Agency’s existing Other Transaction Authority vehicle for prototype work.
The radar’s job is to provide early warning and tracking against ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and hypersonic weapons, then feed that data into the wider missile defense network. The agency says current forward-based radars are largely static or only semi-mobile, which makes them vulnerable to counterattack and slow to reposition as a fight evolves.
FBM Radar Next is meant to close that gap. Beyond fitting inside a C-17 and tactical ground vehicles, the notice calls for a design that can run with a minimal onsite crew, monitor its own health automatically, and reconfigure itself as either one large radar array or several smaller ones spread across a wider area. The agency also wants the system engineered to keep its physical, thermal and electromagnetic signatures low enough to avoid being easily targeted once deployed.
Cost is a central requirement rather than an afterthought. The notice specifically asks companies to show a path to high-volume, affordable production, framing the radar as something the military may need to replace quickly and repeatedly in a heavily contested environment rather than field as a small number of exquisite, expensive units.
Before any company can compete for the program, it has to clear what the agency calls an Entry Gate. That requires showing a fully documented subarray design and working hardware at the array element level, backed by real test data on things like transceiver performance and signal path continuity. Purely theoretical designs or software simulations without hardware behind them will not qualify.
Companies that clear the Entry Gate then move through four prototyping cycles, each ending in a competitive down-select. Cycle 1 covers concept development, Cycle 2 focuses on manufacturing readiness, Cycle 3 calls for a subscale prototype paired with modeling and simulation, and Cycle 4 culminates in a full-scale prototype and operational demonstration. The agency has not set specific timelines for any of the cycles, and no cost or contract value has been disclosed.
The Missile Defense Agency also flagged that only companies that complete the prototype effort will be eligible for what it describes as a likely sole-source follow-on production contract, and offerors will need to obtain a Facility Security Clearance before starting Cycle 1.
The agency stressed that the September 16 notice is not a request for proposals and does not commit it to a formal solicitation. It said it is not currently accepting questions or feedback on the notice, and a timeline for issuing an actual solicitation has not been announced.
