North Korea accused of using overseas workers finance nuclear weapons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
07:44:28 UTC
16:44:28 KST

A report has found that North Korean overseas workers raised between $US450 million ($633 million) and $US800 million last year for the authoritarian state's nuclear weapons program.
The Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team report — co-signed by a range of Western governments and US allies — details "systemic evasion of UN sanctions by the DPRK [Democratic People's Republic of Korea] and other countries through a global network of unlawful overseas labour".
It says the overseas labourers were working primarily in China and Russia and numbered anywhere between 35,000 and 101,000 workers.
A host of Western governments and US allies say North Korea's network of illegal labourers in Russia and China raised between $US450 million ($633 million) and $US800 million last year for Kim Jong Un's nuclear weapons program, helping Pyongyang evade United Nations sanctions.
Human rights groups have long decried North Korea's forced labour program, saying thousands of workers are subjected to control, abuse and coercion as they earn hard cash for the regime.
In 2024 a coalition of developed countries set up the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team (MSMT) to monitor North Korea's efforts to dodge sanctions after Russia used its Security Council veto to dismantle a UN panel of experts tracking the issue.
This morning that same coalition — which draws in Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, New Zealand, the Republic of Korea, the US and the UK — issued a report detailing the "systemic evasion of UN sanctions by the DPRK [Democratic People's Republic of Korea] and other countries through a global network of unlawful overseas labour".
The report says that North Korea maintains an army of between 35,000 and 101,000 labourers overseas.
While at least 17 countries are "suspected of continuing to host labourers" from North Korea the vast majority are working in Russia and China.
China has always denied hosting illegal workers from North Korea — and pushed out at least 10,000 workers between 2023 and 2025 — but human rights groups and investigative reporters have documented how thousands can still be found working in Chinese factories, plants and fishing fleets.
The MSMT report estimates that China still hosts between 20,000 and 70,000 North Korean labourers.
North Korea is also sending increasing numbers of labourers to Russia, which the report says has created a student visa scheme to "camouflage" North Korean labourers.
Moscow and Pyongyang have formed an increasingly tight military and strategic partnership in the last three years, with North Korea emerging as one of Russia's key backers in its invasion of Ukraine.
The MSMT report estimates there are between 15,000 and 30,000 working in Russia "as of the end of 2025", with North Korean labourers manufacturing military drones on Russian soil to bolster Vladimir Putin's war effort.
"Overseas North Korean labourers face low wages, work 12 to 18 hours per day, six or seven days per week, and are required to forfeit 80-90 per cent of their income — or more — to the DPRK government," the report says.
"Labourers are also charged an additional fee of up to 30 per cent of the funds they send as remittances to family, in addition to paying other fees, including those related to travel, food, and lodging.
"Often, this amounts up to complete wage confiscation."
Lara Strangways from the international human rights foundation Global Rights Compliance called the report "alarming" and said it validated the work done by several watchdog groups.
"North Korean workers are being channelled through Russian labour brokers into a system built on debt bondage, confiscated documents and constant surveillance, generating hard currency for Pyongyang," she said.
"This is a problem which must be urgently confronted as the scale and breadth of state-sponsored forced labour expands due to the DPRK's intensifying need for foreign currency.
"The labour brokers facilitating these arrangements, and the companies profiting from this exploitation, must be identified and sanctioned."
The governments behind the joint report have not committed to any new sanctions on Russian or Chinese companies, but said in their joint statement they were "sharing this information with the international community to highlight the significant risks associated with employing North Korean overseas labourers and the need to deter the employment of such labourers".
"We encourage all UN member states to raise awareness and hold responsible parties and facilitators accountable for UNSCR [UN Security Council Resolution] violations, including through domestic action," they said.

Cyber flaws in solar systems pose risks to Swiss power grid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
07:43:37 UTC
16:43:37 KST

Cyber flaws in solar systems pose risks to Swiss power grid
Solar power is a cornerstone of Switzerland’s energy transition, with more than 338,000 photovoltaic systems connected to the grid. But according to experts at the National Test Institute for Cybersecurity (NTC), weaknesses in critical components could be exploited to disrupt parts of the national power network.
The warning comes from an as-yet unpublished NTC study obtained by Swiss public television SRF.
The concern centres on the inverter, the device that controls the photovoltaic system and converts the direct current generated by solar panels into alternating current needed by the Swiss electricity grid. The inverter is effectively the system’s brain.
According to experts from the Swiss non-profit organisation, that’s precisely where the risk lies. Most modern inverters are permanently connected to the internet through integrated communication modules and communicate directly with servers operated by their manufacturers.
More
Swiss among top performers in renewable energy
Andreas Leisibach, a cybersecurity expert at NTC, says those connections allow inverters to be controlled remotely.
“This can be used for legitimate purposes, but also maliciously, for example to switch off or manipulate a device,” he told SRF.
The NTC has, for the first time, examined the cybersecurity of solar inverters used in Switzerland. It concludes that the vulnerability is particularly worrying because a large share of devices comes from only a handful of manufacturers, creating what experts describe as a concentration risk.
Heavy reliance on Chinese-made inverters
The Federal Office of Energy estimates that around 100,000 Swiss solar installations are equipped with inverters from the same country of origin: China. Detailed data has only recently begun to be collected, but the market share of the two Chinese manufacturers Huawei and Sungrow has risen to more than 60%.
For Raphael Reischuk, founder of the NTC, that concentration is problematic.
“Whoever controls the inverter controls the entire installation, and ultimately has influence over the electricity grid,” he said.
Reischuk says that a simultaneous shutdown of all devices from a major manufacturer while operating at full capacity could threaten the stability of Switzerland’s power grid. He stresses that manufacturers themselves may have no economic incentive to do so. But they could potentially be forced into such actions by state actors or by cybercriminals seeking to extort them.
The scenario is not purely theoretical. In a previous case, a Chinese manufacturer remotely disabled large numbers of inverters in the United States and other countries during a commercial dispute. Affected users were confronted with an error message stating: “Not allowed to use”.
More
Cyberwar brings frontline to heart of European infrastructure
Today, more than one in every two newly installed inverters in Switzerland comes from Huawei.
At the Bern vocational school, for example, solar company Clevergie is currently installing a new rooftop photovoltaic system using Huawei inverters. CEO Lukas Meister says the products are both reliable and competitively priced.
The concentration risk created by thousands of similar installations, however, is not something that individual customers or even the industry can solve on their own, he argues.
Manufacturers reject security concerns
What do Chinese manufacturers say about the safety concerns?
Sungrow did not answer questions submitted by SRF. Huawei declined an on-camera interview but stressed in writing that cybersecurity is its “highest priority”.
It wrote: “The operation of our systems in Switzerland is carried out by our customers (…). Depending on the requirements, these systems can be operated via a secure, encrypted connection to the manufacturer’s management system (…) or in offline mode.”
For cybersecurity experts, however, offline operation is often impractical.
US and EU are taking action
Other countries are already responding to the risks. In the United States, President Donald Trump declared a national emergency relating to the high-voltage electricity grid. Among other measures, new rules prohibit the installation of grid-connected inverters from countries subject to an arms embargo or sanctions, including China. Operators could even be required to remove already installed devices.
The EU is also starting to take action. Projects using Chinese inverters are no longer eligible for certain funding programmes. EU Commission spokesperson Siobhan McGarry says security risk assessments have confirmed the potential threat, including the possibility of manipulation of electricity production. In practice, this could mean a remote shutdown of the grids and thus nationwide blackouts.
More
Switzerland juggles fighting crime against threat to tech-privacy industry
Underlying these concerns is Chinese legislation, requiring companies to cooperate with state security agencies. Critics say that Beijing could force manufacturers to remotely disable solar systems in Europe in the event of a conflict.
Swiss intelligence service issues warning
In Switzerland, the Federal Intelligence Service (FIS) has also raised concerns. In a recent report, it warns that if Switzerland protects its critical infrastructure less effectively than the EU, the country could become a preferred target for cyberattacks.
Yet public authorities continue to rely on Chinese technology. The canton of Bern’s building department structured the tender for the cantonal vocational school in such a way that effectively only left Huawei as the only viable option for an inverter. The department rejects the claim that a specific manufacturer was prescribed. But it acknowledges that cybersecurity is “still not very well anchored” in procurement processes. Excluding Chinese manufacturers could amount to discrimination, since public contracts must be awarded to the “most advantageous offer”.
Reischuk stresses that the NTC study should not be interpreted as an argument against the expansion of renewable energy. But it is intended as an appeal for more caution when choosing technologies.
The Swiss Federal Office of Energy broadly agrees with the findings, acknowledging that the risk of a coordinated attack cannot be ruled out. Industry association Swissolar has also reached a similar conclusion and is calling for binding cybersecurity standards as well as a central registry tracking the share of electricity generation that can be controlled remotely.

US Fed hikes interest rates, hints more may be on the way
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
07:43:16 UTC
16:43:16 KST

Breadcrumb
US Fed hikes interest rates and hints more increases may be on the way
The US Federal Reserve hiked its main interest rate for the first time in three years and suggested more may be ahead as it tries to get the nation’s high inflation under control.
In response, the S&P 500 fell 0.4% after giving up a modest gain from earlier in the day. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 631 points, or 1.2%, and the Nasdaq composite was nearly unchanged after edging down by less than 0.1%.
Investors generally prefer lower interest rates because higher rates slow the economy’s growth and undercut prices for stocks and other investments.
The US stock market initially held onto its modest, early gains after the Fed announced its decision. The short-term pain of a slower economy may be worth it if it starves inflation of its fuel and gets further increases for the cost of living back to the Fed's 2% target.
But stock prices weakened later in the day as Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said repeatedly in a press conference that inflation remains too high and the US economy appears to be strengthening. That could imply the economy is solid enough to withstand more hikes to rates, and other officials at the Fed provided their own forecasts suggesting rates may need to go still higher.
The median Fed official expects the federal funds rate to end this year at 4.1%, according to forecasts published after the central bank’s meeting. That’s up from its current range of 3.75% to 4% following Wednesday’s increase, and it’s up from the median forecast of 3.8% that Fed officials gave three months ago.
Traders, meanwhile, suspect the Fed may go even further. They’re betting on a 38% probability the Fed could hike the federal funds rate to a range of 4.25% to 4.50% by the end of the year, according to data from CME Group.
"Our decision comes at a time when the American economy appears to be strengthening," Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said in his press conference.
He pointed to solid US hiring trends, corporate profits and investments by businesses. A report on Wednesday morning, meanwhile, showed shoppers spent much more at US retailers last month than economists expected.
"The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long," Warsh said. He later added, "Today‘s action starts to show we’re serious about this."
It's the first hike by the Fed to interest rates in three years. The central bank had been on pause for months following cuts to rates in 2024 and 2025, even though inflation has consistently remained above the Fed’s 2% target.
President Donald Trump has been lobbying for interest rates to go lower rather than higher.
On Wall Street, bank stocks fell to some of the market's sharper losses. A slower US economy could mean less demand for loans from them. Banks also get hurt when the gap narrows between short-term interest rates and longer-term ones because the industry makes profit off the difference.
Following the Fed's announcements, the two-year Treasury yield jumped to 4.74% from 4.67% late Tuesday. It tends to closely follow expectations for what the Fed will do with the federal funds rate.
The yield on the longer-term 10-year Treasury, meanwhile, takes into account expectations for economic growth and inflation years down the line. It had a more modest increase, ticking up to 5.01% from 5.00% late Tuesday.
Huntington Bancshares fell 5.6%, Citizens Financial Group sank 4.8% and JPMorgan Chase slipped 1%.
The largest loss in the S&P 500 came from J.B. Hunt Transport Services, which lost 13.3%. Its chief financial officer told a conference of analysts late Tuesday that it’s facing higher costs and expects its earnings to drop 5% to 10% from the second quarter to the third.
Stocks of oil companies also weighed on the market after the price for a barrel of Brent crude fell 2.7% to $105.83. It was the first drop of the week for Brent, which has gotten near $110 in recent days.
Helping to limit the market’s losses were gains for some influential stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry.
Nvidia rose 0.8%, and Advanced Micro Devices climbed 1.6% to recover more of their losses from earlier in the week. AI stocks slid worldwide Monday after leaders of the AI industry called for a slowdown in development to address safety issues for humanity.
All told, the S&P 500 fell 33.92 points to 7,551.81. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 631.21 to 51,461.90, and the Nasdaq composite slipped 3.15 to 25,978.42.
In stock markets abroad, indexes rose across much of Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi climbed 1.4% for one of the world’s biggest gains.
Inflation is a worldwide problem, and the European Central Bank hiked rates last week to help diminish it.

Next has thanked warmer weather for an “unexpected” boost in sales, leading the clothing retailer to raise its profit forecasts for the fourth time this year.
The FTSE 100 company, which owns the UK rights to the US brands Gap and Victoria’s Secret as well as stakes in labels including Reiss and Joules, raised its expectations for full-year profits by £12m to £1.26bn.
It is the fourth time Next has raised profit forecasts this year, with the company having last ratcheted up its expectations in early August as Europe faced a series of heatwaves.
Next, which has more than 500 stores across the UK, said in a stock market update on Thursday: “The first half was much better than we originally anticipated, both in the UK and overseas.
“It is important to acknowledge that part of this overperformance has been the result of two unusually warm summers in the UK. The rest of the overperformance is, we believe, largely the result of fulfilling the aims we outlined at the beginning of the year.”
That has included some cost-cutting efforts, particularly across Next’s warehouses.
Overall, total sales across the group were up 9% in the six months to July, helping push pre-tax profits for the half-year up by 11% to £566m.
Next said the performance over the past six months was “all the more unexpected given the strength of sales last year”. It made £1bn of annual profits for the first time in the year ending January 2025.
However, the retailer cautioned on the impact of the rising cost of living and prospects for the jobs market.
“Our primary concerns are rising inflation, higher mortgage interest costs and a weak employment market. These worries will only be compounded if they are accompanied by tax increases,” it said, in an apparent reference to John Healey’s first budget as chancellor on 28 October.
“It seems likely that it [the government] will have to increase taxes in order to fund its expenditure.”
While the group said it was deploying AI across the business, including its tech division, Next said it was ensuring fashion designs were still led by humans.
“In a world where AI is able to do more and more, our experience suggests that consumers prefer the authentic creativity of human beings,” it said. “That means we are putting more emphasis on designers using techniques that connect them directly to the artwork – painting, drawing, screen printing, etc. That is a big investment in time, and requires a higher level of creative talent than is needed to operate CAD [computer aided design] or prompt AI.”
Despite the strong results, the company lowered sales growth expectations in the UK, which accounts for three-quarters of total sales, from 2.8% to 2% for the six months to the end of January.
“We are looking at what’s ahead and it is sensible to moderate our expectations,” said the Next chief executive, Simon Wolfson. “We are not talking about [consumer spending] falling off a cliff. I think things are likely to get worse rather than better. Unlike in the past when the government has been able to help it doesn’t have any room for manoeuvre. It has a £100bn deficit. That means not only can we not expect the government to necessarily alleviate the problem, but potentially make it worse.”
He added that the escalation of hostilities in the Middle East has not triggered a further increase in further potential cost increases for Next.
“We are not expecting shipping costs to get higher, there is already a surcharge we are paying,” Wolfson said. “All those cost increases are baked in [since the start of the conflict in February], and if anything are not as bad as March.”
Aarin Chiekrie, an equity analyst at Hargreaves Lansdown, said: “Next delivered its first-half results in style, with sales growth accelerating over the period and breezing past the fashion company’s original guidance. In the UK, hotter-than-expected weather and more effective marketing saw customers logging in to refresh their summer wardrobes online, helping offset a small decline in-store.”

Ukraine's Defence Intelligence reveals foreign equipment used by Russia to produce Geran drones
Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) has released data on 20 pieces of foreign technological equipment used to produce various modifications of Geran attack drones at the Alabuga Special Economic Zone in Russia's Tatarstan, located about 1,200 km from the front line.
Details: War&Sanctions portal, an open-access online database that catalogues individuals, entities, and assets linked to Russian military aggression against Ukraine; DIU on social media
Quote: "Today's publication includes lathes, milling and drilling machines, machining centres, industrial robots, automatic component placement machines, soldering robots and other equipment from Chinese, German, Japanese, Swiss and Iranian manufacturers."
More details: DIU reported that the production facility uses a VMC 1000Q vertical machining centre from the Chinese company SMTCL (Shenyang Machine Tool Co.) and an RS-1R automatic component placement machine from Japan's JUKI.
DIU also identified a mechatronic production line from Germany's Festo, fitted with a Melfa industrial robot made by Japan's Mitsubishi.
The foreign equipment is used for machining metal and other materials, mounting SMD components onto printed circuit boards, and training personnel on specialised production lines, DIU said.
It has called on manufacturers of high-tech equipment to strengthen oversight of the end users of their products and their actual place of use, including through on-site inspections at the addresses they provide. The agency also proposed that spare parts, components, software, updates and servicing be subject to enhanced control procedures.
In addition, DIU called for regular checks of distributors, dealers, and other intermediaries to identify re-exports or changes in end users, as well as investigations into cases where manufacturers' products are found in Russia's military-industrial complex and the tracing of their supply chains.

Background:
- It was reported earlier that Russia continues to expand the industrial site at the Alabuga Special Economic Zone, where production of attack drones is concentrated. New production halls are being built and infrastructure expanded in the southern part of the economic zone.
- DIU previously released a detailed breakdown of Russia's new Geran-4 jet-powered attack drone, covering its foreign-made components and key tactical and technical specifications, alongside an interactive 3D model.

Netanyahu calls ex-AG Mandelblit as defense witness in corruption trial

2026-09-17

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s defense team has asked the court overseeing his corruption trial to summon former attorney general Avichai Mandelblit as its next witness, setting his testimony to begin just over two weeks before the Oct. 27 election.
In a request filed with the court, Netanyahu’s lawyers asked that Mandelblit be ordered to testify on Oct. 11, Oct. 12 and again from Oct. 18 through Oct. 22.
Mandelblit has not previously testified in the long-running trial, which began in 2020 and centers on three separate cases known as Cases 1000, 2000 and 4000. Netanyahu completed his own testimony in June after 98 hearings over about 18 months, and the trial has continued with additional defense witnesses.
Mandelblit is a particularly significant witness because, as attorney general, he oversaw the legal process that led to Netanyahu’s prosecution. He approved the investigations and ultimately decided in November 2019 to indict Netanyahu in all three cases after a pre-indictment hearing.
Netanyahu faces charges of fraud and breach of trust in all three cases and an additional bribery charge in Case 4000. He has denied wrongdoing and has repeatedly argued that the investigations and prosecution were politically motivated.
Mandelblit’s expected appearance could put the origins and handling of the investigations at the center of the proceedings in the final weeks of the election campaign.
The three cases
Case 1000, commonly known as the “gifts case,” concerns allegations that Netanyahu and his wife received luxury goods, including cigars and champagne, from wealthy businessmen, principally Hollywood producer Arnon Milchan and Australian billionaire James Packer. Prosecutors allege Netanyahu used his public position to assist Milchan on several matters while receiving gifts worth hundreds of thousands of shekels. Netanyahu is charged with fraud and breach of trust in the case.
Case 2000 centers on conversations between Netanyahu and Arnon “Noni” Mozes, publisher of the Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper. Prosecutors allege the two discussed a potential arrangement under which Netanyahu would receive more favorable coverage in exchange for using his political influence to weaken Yedioth’s main competitor, the free daily Israel Hayom. Netanyahu is charged with fraud and breach of trust.
Case 4000, the only case in which Netanyahu faces a bribery charge, involves allegations that he advanced regulatory decisions benefiting telecommunications giant Bezeq while serving as prime minister and communications minister. Prosecutors allege that in return, Netanyahu and his family received favorable treatment from the Walla news website, then controlled by Bezeq’s controlling shareholder, Shaul Elovitch. Netanyahu is charged with bribery, fraud and breach of trust.
Mandelblit, a former military advocate general who later served as Netanyahu’s Cabinet secretary before becoming attorney general, announced the final indictment in November 2019. The trial formally opened the following year.
His scheduled testimony on Oct. 11 would come 16 days before Israelis are due to vote on Oct. 27, putting one of the central figures behind Netanyahu’s prosecution on the witness stand during the closing stretch of the election campaign.

Israel killing Hamas officials will not lead to group's elimination, BoP source tells 'Post'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
07:38:28 UTC
16:38:28 KST

Israel’s targeted killings of Hamas operatives may be justified, but it will not cause the terrorist organization to be dismantled, according to a source close to the Board of Peace (BoP).
“The government’s policy is targeted eliminations while leaving Hamas with its army and its rule,” the source told The Jerusalem Post. “The Board of Peace wants the complete dismantling and elimination of Hamas. Israel is eliminating individual Hamas members but not Hamas itself.”
The source’s remarks come amid a dispute over how the next stage of the Gaza process should proceed, following the agreement between Hamas and the BoP on a framework for the terrorist group’s phased disarmament.
The agreement, announced by US President Donald Trump on July 30, called for Hamas and other armed factions in Gaza to surrender their weapons as part of a broader process that would eventually see IDF troops withdraw and civilian and security responsibilities transferred to new Palestinian and international structures. An implementation mechanism was to be prepared during an initial 14-day period.
Agreement reached after months of negotiations
The agreement followed months of negotiations between Hamas and the BoP, with Qatar, Egypt, and Turkey playing roles in the mediation process.
Under the framework, the disarmament process would include an inventory and storage of weapons and the dismantling of Hamas’s military capabilities and other armed factions in Gaza. An international mechanism would oversee the process and link it to the broader transfer of governance and security responsibilities.
Israel has said it does not accept the framework as currently formulated.
“Israel rejects the 15-point plan for Gaza,” Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said at a cabinet meeting in August. “The IDF will not withdraw until Hamas is genuinely disarmed.”
Against that backdrop, senior BoP officials sought to persuade Israel to observe a 14-day period of calm to allow the disarmament process to begin. The proposal included an exception for what the BoP described as “immediate threats.”
Israel initially appeared to observe that principle, although the government did not publicly endorse the arrangement.
Israel targets Hamas' terrorists, clashes with BoP officials
In recent weeks, Israel has resumed targeting Hamas operatives, including members accused of participating in the October 7 massacre, holding hostages, and serving in senior positions.
According to Israeli officials, Hamas had used the “quiet period” – in which Israel was limiting its strikes primarily to immediate terrorist threats – to rebuild and strengthen its military capabilities rather than prepare for the disarmament process envisioned by the BoP.
The source close to the BoP said the Israeli approach was “a policy similar to that of the period before October 7.”
The BoP is presenting its proposal – the complete dismantling of Hamas’s military infrastructure and an end to its rule in Gaza – as an alternative to continued Israeli military operations.
“The way to do this is 14 days of calm, apart from operations against immediate threats, and full cooperation by the government in all the preparatory and logistical steps for voluntary disarmament,” the source told the Post.
“If Hamas begins dismantling itself at a rapid pace and provides all the coordinates of the tunnels, that would be excellent,” the source said. “If it does not disarm, then the IDF receives international backing to do so by force.”
In recent weeks, the Israeli security establishment has reported a series of targeted killings and arrests of senior Hamas field commanders and members of its military and security apparatus.
Among the most prominent recent operations cited by Israeli officials was the killing of Nael Abu Obeid, identified as the commander of Hamas’s Rafah Brigade, alongside other field commanders at the battalion and Nukhba cell levels.
Israeli special forces also carried out a raid in Gaza City in which they captured Muin al-Arbid alive. He was identified as the head of Hamas’s General Security apparatus.
Such operations, even when successful against individual commanders, do not resolve the broader issue of Hamas’s continued military and political presence in Gaza, the BoP source said.
The disagreement reflects a broader question facing the Gaza framework: whether disarmament can be achieved through a negotiated and internationally supervised process, or whether Israel will continue using military force to degrade Hamas’s capabilities until it is satisfied that it can no longer threaten Israel.
For the BoP, the distinction is significant. Its framework is based on the assumption that Hamas’s military and governmental structures ultimately need to be dismantled as part of a transition to a new governing and security system in Gaza. The BoP has described its broader role as promoting stability, lawful governance, and reconstruction in Gaza.
For Israel, however, the concern is that any prolonged pause in military operations could allow Hamas to recover and reorganize.

Usama Ghanem, 22, will return to KCL this fall, nearly 18 months after university officials suspended him indefinitely and moved to withdraw his visa sponsorship over allegations concerning his involvement in student-led pro-Palestinian demonstrations.
Ghanem reportedly received an email from the university in late August stating that it continued to uphold its finding of non-academic misconduct against him, while also informing him that he had committed “no breaches” of the terms of his exclusion.
“The conditions set have been met and there is no reason for your suspension or exclusion to remain in place,” the email said. “Accordingly, you will be invited to re-enrol for the 2026/27 academic year and will be permitted access to King’s College London.”
The university also reaffirmed that it would begin the process of reinstating Ghanem’s visa sponsorship in a separate memo sent in early September.
Ghanem’s case reportedly drew public criticism from some academics, who raised concerns over a crackdown by US and UK universities that disproportionately affects Muslim students and students of color for lawful expressions of Palestinian solidarity and criticism of Israel.
Ghanem told CNN he “unequivocally” denied the misconduct allegations, saying the outcome of the review set “a huge precedent.”
He added that he would continue to advocate for “Palestinian rights, and the fight for divestment from all weapons and from all complicit actors with the genocide in Gaza.”
Meanwhile, a KCL spokesperson told CNN that a review of Ghanem’s suspension had always been scheduled to take place one year after it was imposed as part of the university’s standard procedures.
“Following that review, a panel determined that he had met the conditions agreed for suspension, and that re-enrolment was now the appropriate outcome,” the spokesperson said, and added: "We will always apply a fair approach to misconduct proceedings, and have a duty to act where behaviour breaches safeguarding and security regulations, or puts others at risk.”
The spokesperson also noted that decisions on visa sponsorship are made by UK Visas & Immigration, rather than the university, which has a legal obligation to notify the agency of changes in a student’s status.
As Ghanem prepares to return to the university, a legal case he filed against KCL remains ongoing. The case claims breaches of human rights, assault, personal injury, discrimination and harassment on the part of the university.
Despite a ceasefire agreement that has been in place since October 2025, Israel continues airstrikes, shelling, and gunfire in different parts of the Gaza Strip.
Since the ceasefire took effect, Israeli forces have killed 1,381 Palestinians in what Palestinian authorities describe as repeated violations of the truce.
Israel launched its war on Gaza on Oct. 8, 2023, killing more than 73,000 Palestinians and injuring over 174,000, according to Palestinian figures. About 90% of the enclave's infrastructure has been damaged, according to Palestinian authorities.

U.S. Navy buys first HFORCE backup radios that skip satellites
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
07:38:20 UTC
16:38:20 KST

The U.S. Navy has ordered the first production run of a new long-range radio system designed to keep ships and units communicating even when satellites are jammed or unavailable.
Naval Air Warfare Center Aircraft Division in Lakehurst, New Jersey, awarded MaXentric Technologies a $9.6 million firm-fixed-price order for 12 low-rate initial production kits of the High Frequency Over-the-Horizon Communication system, known as HFORCE. The order also covers further development work, integration with a companion amplifier system, performance testing, and ongoing maintenance and sustainment support. Work is split evenly between Fort Lee, New Jersey, and MaXentric’s home base in La Jolla, California, with an estimated completion date of March 2028.
HFORCE uses high frequency radio, the 3 to 30 megahertz band that can bounce signals off the ionosphere to reach receivers far beyond the horizon, without relying on satellites. That makes it a fallback option for military communications if satellite links go down or come under attack, a capability the Navy has been pushing to modernize as HF technology had seen little investment for decades compared with satellite and cellular systems.
The order integrates HFORCE with a High Dynamic Range Multi-Carrier Amplifier, or HDR MCA, a system the Navy first put out for development in 2018 under a Small Business Innovation Research solicitation. That original program asked companies to build an amplifier capable of handling up to 36 simultaneous radio channels across the VHF and UHF bands without the channels interfering with each other, a limitation of older shipboard radio setups that require a separate amplifier for every channel in use. MaXentric was the company selected to develop that technology, reaching a mid-range technology readiness level by 2022 as it worked toward a production-ready design.
This latest award falls under the Navy’s SBIR Phase III authority, which lets the government award follow-on production contracts to a company without competition once that company has proven a technology through the earlier SBIR phases. That is why the Navy did not compete this order.
The contract does not specify which ships or units will receive the 12 initial kits, or whether the Navy plans to order more once this low-rate production run is complete. Fiscal 2025 Defense-wide procurement funds are covering the full $9.6 million, all of which was obligated at the time of the award.

The 22-year-old returned a positive roadside reading for cocaine after he was pulled over by police on Sydney's Anzac Bridge on July 24.
He had been driving at 109 kilometres per hour in a 60km/h zone.

Volpato has maintained his innocence, insisting he never knowingly ingested the substance.

US Congress approves Russia sanctions that impact China and India
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
07:31:32 UTC
16:31:32 KST

US lawmakers have approved sweeping new sanctions targeting Russia's economy and Putin's inner circle, with Trump set to sign a bill that also threatens steep tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil, including China and India.
The US House of Representatives approved a major new package of sanctions against Russia on Wednesday, clearing the way for President Donald Trump to sign into law the most significant American legislative action against Moscow since he returned to the White House.
Lawmakers passed the measure 262 to 159, following the Senate's own overwhelming approval, 86 to 11, last month. Trump has indicated he will sign it.
The sanctions target Russia's energy and defence industries, President Vladimir Putin and senior officials around him, and the so-called "shadow fleet" of tankers Moscow uses to evade existing Western restrictions.
Crucially for global energy markets, the bill also grants Trump the power to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries that continue buying large volumes of Russian oil and gas — a measure aimed squarely at China and India, two of Moscow's biggest remaining customers.
That tariff provision proved contentious even among supporters of Ukraine in Washington. Some Democrats, while backing tougher action against Russia, objected to giving the president such broad authority over trade policy.
Gregory Meeks, the senior Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, criticised the bill's drafting, arguing it prioritised presidential tariff powers over binding sanctions commitments. He said he would have supported the legislation had the tariff measures been stripped out, but Republicans blocked attempts to amend them.
Despite these reservations, most Democrats ultimately voted for the bill, while a small number of Republicans opposed it on free-market grounds. Supporters say the added pressure is necessary as Russia's full-scale invasion enters its fifth year with no ceasefire in sight.
Kyiv welcomes the bill but India holds firm
The vote came as Russian drone strikes hit civilian transport in southern Ukraine on Wednesday, killing five people, according to officials in Kyiv — an attack that added urgency to calls from pro-Ukraine campaigners for the bill's passage.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky had lobbied Congress directly to pass the sanctions, arguing that only sustained economic pressure would push Moscow toward negotiations. Speaking in Washington in July, he said Russia was losing around 30,000 soldiers a month but showed no sign of ending the war, adding that the initiative on the battlefield had shifted out of Putin's hands.
India responded on Thursday by signalling it would not change course, saying it would continue purchasing Russian oil "through diversified sourcing and on the basis of evolving market dynamics."
Russia remains one of India's most important strategic and military partners, complicating Washington's efforts to isolate Moscow economically.
The legislation also targets companies and foreign entities supporting Russia's military effort and extends existing sanctions related to Iran. It follows more than a year of delay, reflecting Trump's general preference for retaining personal control over sanctions and tariff policy rather than ceding it to Congress.
Ukrainian advocacy groups welcomed the bill's passage while urging swift enforcement. "Once the bill is quickly signed and becomes law, we hope for strong US enforcement to finally end the cash flows to the Kremlin's war chest," said Svitlana Romanko of the energy lobby group Razom We Stand.
"Every day of delay is a day we in Ukraine must bury more people."

17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
Türkiye’s Financial Stability Committee said Thursday that there is no fundamental or structural risk to the functioning of Borsa Istanbul or the country’s capital markets, pledging swift measures to ease liquidity pressures and prevent contagion.
The committee, chaired by Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Simsek, met to discuss recent developments in the capital markets.
It concluded that the recent market volatility stemmed from credit and liquidity problems at certain funds managed by a limited number of portfolio management companies, according to an official statement.
“There is no fundamental or structural risk concerning the functioning of Borsa Istanbul and our capital markets,” the committee said.

The committee evaluated measures that could be taken to maintain the healthy functioning of markets and safeguard macrofinancial stability.
“All necessary measures within this scope will be swiftly implemented by our relevant institutions,” it said.
The measures will primarily aim to alleviate liquidity constraints and prevent the problems from spreading to other parts of the financial system.
The committee also said regulatory and supervisory authorities would continue to exercise their powers “with determination” against those found to have engaged in market-disruptive activities.
It urged the public to rely solely on statements issued by official sources during the process.
“The committee will closely monitor developments and regularly inform the public,” the statement added.

U.S. Navy, Coast Guard buys new Saab radars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
07:30:14 UTC
16:30:14 KST

The U.S. Navy has awarded Saab a $51.5 million contract modification to keep building the radar system it supplies to the Coast Guard’s newest patrol ships, with the Navy also picking up part of the bill for its own vessels.
Naval Sea Systems Command’s modification exercises a production option on an existing contract with Saab, Inc., covering more Multi-Mode Radar units, engineering support and spare parts. Work will be split between Saab’s radar facility in Gothenburg, Sweden, which handles 51 percent of the effort, and its Syracuse, New York plant, which handles the rest. The contract runs through an estimated completion date of December 2028.
Funding for the deal comes from four separate accounts. Coast Guard procurement, construction and improvement money covers just under half the total, at $24.8 million. The remainder comes from three Navy funding lines: $10 million in fiscal 2026 other procurement funds, $9.8 million in fiscal 2026 shipbuilding and conversion funds, and $6.5 million in fiscal 2025 other procurement funds. All of it was obligated at the time of the award.
The radar in question is Saab’s Sea Giraffe Multi-Mode Radar, a three-dimensional, electronically scanned phased array system the company originally developed for the Coast Guard’s Heritage-class Offshore Patrol Cutter under a contract first awarded in 2017. The radar tracks both air and surface targets simultaneously, giving a ship’s crew a single picture of threats ranging from low-flying aircraft to small boats, and Saab has marketed it as effective from open ocean down to crowded coastal waters.
Saab has since expanded the radar’s reach into the Navy fleet. A version of the same technology, designated AN/SPS-77, equips the Navy’s Independence-class littoral combat ships, and the company has delivered Sea Giraffe systems for the Expeditionary Sea Base ships operated by Military Sealift Command. That spread across multiple ship classes explains why this latest order draws on both Coast Guard and Navy funding accounts rather than one alone, though the announcement does not break down which specific Navy ships this production run will equip.
Saab has built its U.S. radar business almost entirely around this single product line, with the Syracuse facility handling final integration and testing for systems bound for American ships while the core radar technology comes from Sweden. The company has picked up incremental production orders roughly every year or two since the original 2017 award as the Coast Guard has continued taking delivery of new Offshore Patrol Cutters.
Deliveries under the contract will continue through the end of 2028.

“There are countries with which we want to deepen our relationship,” Metsola said.
"I don't doubt that it will include other countries, and others will come knocking at our door...In such times of uncertainty, having friends matters."
The EU already has trade agreements with both countries, providing a potential starting point for closer cooperation. A similar relationship has been proposed with Canada, which signed a comprehensive trade agreement with the EU in 2016.
Asked about the technicalities of what associate membership would look like, Metsola acknowledged that talks are still at an early stage, while pointing to deeper trade relations, access to critical raw materials and common regulations on issues that “like-minded” countries care deeply about, such as social media and the protection of minors.
On Wednesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed “associate membership” for Canada in her annual State of the Union address.
Canadian Prime Minister Carney is exploring closer ties with the bloc amid a trade war with the US, Canada’s biggest trading partner, with prohibitive tariffs in place. Under pressure from President Donald Trump, Ottawa is rethinking its place in the world, while Carney has been vocal in calling for an alliance of “middle powers”.
No reason for retaliation
After the announcement, Trump told reporters he would consider imposing fresh tariffs on the European Union if the bid for associate membership turns "hostile".
Washington and Brussels have a trade deal in place, under which the EU faces a 15% tariff on goods.
Metsola played down the threats, saying the EU views its relationships with the two countries separately. She said that the EU does not work against anyone but acts as an advocate for rules-based cooperation.
She also pointed to the trade deal agreed last summer and ratified this year.
Separately, a spokesperson for the European Commission said: “The proposed strengthening of our partnership is not against anyone, but for our common strength.”
Carney is due to address the European Parliament on Thursday at 11.30am.

Green by Law? Rethinking Sustainability and Architectural Responsibility Across Borders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
07:30:00 UTC
16:30:00 KST

Sustainability in architecture is often discussed as though it were a universal standard—and, in principle, it should be. Buildings are increasingly evaluated through energy performance, embodied carbon, certification systems, material efficiency, biodiversity, and whole-life impact. Yet the rules determining what must actually be done remain highly local. A project designed in London, New York, or Copenhagen may be shaped by stringent energy codes, environmental review, disclosure requirements, planning controls, and increasingly ambitious carbon targets. The same practice working elsewhere may encounter a very different regulatory landscape.
This creates a difficult question for international architecture: when sustainability is not enforced to the same degree by law, what standards should architects carry with them?

After two deaths: malaria warning in Frankfurt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
07:26:03 UTC
16:26:03 KST

Since July 2026, eight people in Germany have contracted malaria, two fatally. Frankfurt now urges residents with such symptoms to consider malaria and consult a doctor.
Frankfurt am Main's public health authority has issued a warning after the city recorded two further cases of malaria, bringing the total number of people who have fallen ill since July to six. Malaria is a tropical disease transmitted by mosquitoes. Two of the cases in Frankfurt have proved fatal.
The new cases involve people from the Schwanheim district, close to the airport, and the public health authority is investigating whether there is a link. Airport employees have been particularly affected by recent infections. It is thought that mosquitoes from malaria-affected regions occasionally travel on flight routes, survive in Frankfurt and then transmit the disease when they bite.
What is malaria?
Malaria, a tropical disease, can be treated effectively if is diagnosed early. At first, however, the symptoms resemble flu or a common cold. "It is therefore crucial to consider a possible malaria infection at an early stage when such symptoms occur," the city of Frankfurt am Main said.
Typical symptoms of malaria infection include fever, shivering, headaches, and pain in the limbs, as well as gastrointestinal complaints. "Such signs are therefore often mistaken as a flu-like infection or a stomach and intestinal infection," the Robert Koch Institute also explains.
Not all types of malaria are fatal, such as malaria tertiana, quartana or Plasmodium knowlesi malaria. The most dangerous form is malaria tropica, which can be deadly without prompt diagnosis and treatment and Germany's Federal Foreign Office describes it as a life-threatening disease.
The illness is not contagious from person to person; transmission requires the bite of an infected mosquito. When malaria is not contracted in an endemic area but instead reaches other countries via mosquitoes carried on flights, it is often referred to as airport malaria.
Recommendation: consult a doctor if you develop unexplained fever
People who work at Frankfurt Airport or in its surroundings, spend time there or live close to the airport should see a doctor if they develop unexplained fever.
During the consultation, it is important to mention their place of residence or any stay in the vicinity of the airport.
Residents of Frankfurt am Main can also obtain information via the public health authority's hotline, which can be reached by phone from 9 am to 6 pm on 069/212-30030.
Preventive measures are also possible by protecting yourself from mosquito bites, for example, through the use of insect repellents. Products containing diethyltoluamide (DEET) and icaridin have so far proved effective worldwide, according to a guide from the Federal Foreign Office. Wearing long clothing and using insect nets can also help over the longer term.
Airport malaria in Europe
According to the Robert Koch Institute, cases of airport malaria are very rare in Germany. A recent study also shows that more than 99% of malaria cases recorded in Europe were imported from endemic regions.
From 1969 to early 2024, databases recorded 145 malaria cases in which the patients were infected within Europe. More than two-thirds of these were classified as airport malaria. The countries most affected were France (52 cases), Belgium (19 cases) and Germany with nine cases, eight of them in Frankfurt and one in Munich.
Here, too, many of those affected had links to an international airport. According to the city, the two newly infected people from Frankfurt's Schwanheim district are currently being treated in hospital.

U.S. Navy orders new engine cores for its P-8A fleet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
07:23:12 UTC
16:23:12 KST

The U.S. Navy has awarded CFM International a $490 million contract to supply up to 24 replacement engine cores for its P-8A Poseidon patrol aircraft, with half reserved for the Navy’s own fleet and half for allied militaries that fly the same plane.
The Naval Air Systems Command deal covers up to 12 CFM56-7B27AE core engines for the U.S. Navy and up to 12 more for Foreign Military Sales customers, plus a single CFM56-7B24E core engine for the Navy’s C-40A transport jet. It is a firm-fixed-price, indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contract, meaning the Navy sets a ceiling now and places individual orders against it as money becomes available. No funds are obligated yet. The contract also covers engine covers, stands and cradles used to ship and store the hardware, and runs through an estimated completion date of September 2031.
A core engine is the inner section of a jet engine, the compressor, combustion chamber and turbine, without the fan and surrounding nacelle. Navy and contractor maintenance depots typically swap in a new core rather than replace an entire engine when a Poseidon’s powerplant needs a major overhaul, which cuts cost and downtime compared with buying complete replacement engines.
The P-8A is Boeing’s militarized version of the 737-800, built for the Navy to hunt submarines and surface ships and replace the older P-3C Orion. Both the Poseidon and the C-40A, the Navy’s own 737-based transport aircraft, fly on variants of the CFM56-7B, the same engine family that powers commercial 737 Next Generation jets. CFM International, a joint venture between GE Aerospace and France’s Safran Aircraft Engines, is the sole producer of that engine, which is why the Navy did not compete this contract.
The Foreign Military Sales side of the deal reflects how far the P-8 program has spread beyond the U.S. Navy. Australia, the United Kingdom, India, Norway, South Korea and New Zealand already fly the Poseidon, and Canada signed on in 2023 for up to 16 aircraft under its Canadian Multi-Mission Aircraft project, with first delivery expected this year. More than 160 P-8s have been delivered worldwide, according to Boeing, logging over 560,000 combined flight hours.
Work under the new contract will be split across three sites: 53 percent at Safran’s Villaroche plant in France, 43 percent at a GE Aerospace facility in Durham, North Carolina, and 4 percent at GE’s Peebles, Ohio, test facility. The Navy has not said how the 24 engine cores will be divided among individual Foreign Military Sales customers, or which countries’ aircraft the orders will support first. Those details, along with the pace of individual task orders, will be determined as the contract runs through 2031.

A federal immigration officer wanted on assault charges for shooting and wounding a Venezuelan man in Minneapolis was arrested there on Wednesday, eight months after a confrontation that became a flashpoint over US President Donald Trump's deportation sweeps.
US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent Christian Castro was taken into custody by agents of the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension in downtown Minneapolis and was booked into the Hennepin County jail on his outstanding arrest warrant, the agency said.
Castro had been released on bond from federal custody earlier this month, after an initial appearance in US District Court in McAllen, Texas, on charges of lying to investigators about the circumstances of the January 14 shooting.
Under an agreement with Minnesota law enforcement, Castro voluntarily drove to Minneapolis from Texas to turn himself in to state authorities at his attorney's office but ended up being arrested minutes before he was due to arrive, the lawyer, Daniel Gerdts, told Reuters.
Another lawyer representing the ICE agent, Rolando Cantu, said his client always had intended to answer the charges in Minneapolis. He disputed Hennepin County prosecutors' assertions that Castro might flee to Mexico, saying, "He wants his day in court."
Case stems from Operation Metro surge
The federal indictment charging Castro with making false statements marked the first US Justice Department prosecution of a federal law enforcement officer accused of wrongdoing arising from the massive Minneapolis ICE deployment dubbed Operation Metro Surge.
That operation, part of Trump's wider immigration crackdown, drew weeks of protests and clashes between ICE and demonstrators, leading to the fatal shootings of two US citizens by federal agents.
Castro already faced state assault charges in Minnesota stemming from the confrontation in which he shot Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis, a Venezuelan national, in the leg through the door of the man's apartment while children were present inside the home.
The state charges also include false reporting of a crime after Castro allegedly told superiors at the US Department of Homeland Security that Sosa-Celis and others attacked him with a snow shovel and broom, which was disproved by video evidence.
Initial efforts to arrest Castro were thwarted when the ICE agent returned to his home state of Texas, leading Minnesota officials to issue a warrant for his arrest.
Castro was apprehended by Texas Rangers, but Texas Governor Greg Abbott, a Republican and supporter of Trump's mass deportation sweeps, refused to sign extradition papers sent by Minnesota Governor Tim Walz, a Democrat.
Abbott questioned whether Castro could be considered a fugitive from justice, and thus subject to extradition, because DHS had reassigned him to his home state of Texas after the Minneapolis shooting.
The ICE agent ultimately spent 90 days in a Texas county jail and was released on August 27 after a federal judge in Texas denied a request from Minnesota to immediately order his extradition. Castro was re-arrested in Texas following his federal grand jury indictment in early September.
DHS has suspended Castro from ICE, and a person familiar with the case has said a civil rights investigation into the Sosa-Celis shooting had been opened.
Castro was expected to make his first state court appearance in Minneapolis on Thursday. He will then make an initial appearance in US District Court in neighboring St. Paul, the state capital, on Friday morning to face charges in the federal indictment.
"Governor Abbott’s attempt to shield Mr. Castro from accountability has failed. We look forward to commencing our prosecution," Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty, who brought the state case, said in a statement.

High prices delay Estonia's fuel replenishment, but reserves still solid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
07:20:00 UTC
16:20:00 KST

High prices delay Estonia's fuel replenishment, but reserves still solid
In March the Estonian Stockpiling Agency released about ten percent of its reserves to the market — mostly gasoline, with smaller amounts of diesel and aviation fuel. Currently there are no plans to buy back that fuel, as prices are high and such purchases could push them even higher.
The task of the Estonian Stockpiling Agency is to ensure that we have sufficient supplies of gasoline, diesel, and natural gas, as well as aviation fuel. A large share of the world's oil moves through the Persian Gulf, which is why the International Energy Agency and its member states — including Estonia — decided in spring to release some reserves.
The head of the Stockpiling Agency, Ando Leppiman, said Estonia's fuel reserves are currently in good condition and the volumes are quite large.
"We have state‑owned operational fuel reserves, and we also collect information on how much fuel companies or importers have in stock. As of the end of August, we had enough gasoline and diesel for nearly 120 days," Leppiman said.
Leppiman added that Estonia has not yet repurchased the fuel it released to the market in March. Reserves will be replenished once prices fall. It is difficult to say when that might happen, as the Middle East crisis has not yet ended.
Leppiman is currently in Croatia at the annual meeting of fuel‑reserve agencies. According to discussions at the meeting, the biggest problem has become the limited availability of diesel, which has driven diesel prices to record levels.
In addition to state reserves, Estonian fuel companies have their own commercial stocks. Alan Vaht, member of the management board of the fuel company Terminal, explained that retail fuel inventories generally cover one to seven days of consumption.
"That is the only reserve retail fuel chains have," Vaht said. "It is mistakenly assumed that the chains have huge reserves somewhere in fuel terminals. That is simply not true."
There is no fuel shortage expected at Estonian fuel stations. The reason reserves are kept small is that no one wants to store fuel at today's high prices. In the coming months, fuel prices may fall — and then the fuel would have to be sold off at the lower price.

====================================================================================================

Houthi gains at Bab el-Mandeb expose Israel's unresolved Eilat shipping crisis - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
07:19:55 UTC
16:19:55 KST

The Houthis' takeover of key points along Yemen's western coast and of Perim Island, in the heart of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, has brought renewed attention to a threat Israel knows well and has been paying a price for nearly three years, as the group's latest advances turn the Red Sea shipping threat into an increasingly urgent strategic problem for Saudi Arabia as well.
Even before the threat to Saudi oil routes prompted Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to seek US assistance, the Houthis had already registered a significant strategic achievement against Israel by almost completely disrupting regular commercial shipping to the Port of Eilat.
Nearly three years have passed since the problem emerged, and no solution remains. The IDF has repeatedly struck Houthi targets in Yemen, the state has provided assistance to the port, and an alternative import route has been established through Aqaba. None of this has brought international shipping companies back to regular, direct sailings from the East to Eilat.
Based on publicly available information, no cabinet decision has defined the restoration of commercial freedom of navigation to Eilat as a security and diplomatic objective, nor has the government presented an approved plan to bring ships back to the port.
Recent developments have changed the circumstances in which Israel is confronting the problem. The Houthi threat to Bab al-Mandab has become an urgent strategic issue for Saudi Arabia as well, and the Saudi crown prince has already requested military assistance from the US.
Israel and Saudi Arabia now have parallel diplomatic and strategic interests concerning the same maritime route. From Israel's perspective, Saudi Arabia's predicament creates an opportunity that did not previously exist to the same extent: to harness a regional effort around Bab al-Mandab to restore shipping to Eilat as well.
The Houthis captured Mocha, advanced along the coast, and took control of Perim, the island located inside the Bab al-Mandab Strait. They also seized Greater Hanish and Lesser Hanish islands, strengthening their hold around one of the world's most important maritime chokepoints.
Traffic through the strait continues, and the Houthis do not currently control the passage in a way that would allow them to halt all shipping. Their new positions do, however, improve their ability to monitor maritime traffic and selectively threaten vessels they choose to target.
Bab al-Mandab is a passage only about 18 miles wide, connecting the Gulf of Aden to the Red Sea and from there to the Suez Canal. In normal periods, oil equivalent to roughly 7% of global production passes through it.
Control of Mocha, Dhubab, Perim, and the Hanish islands improves the Houthis' ability to monitor and threaten traffic in the strait. Shipping companies and insurers price that risk into insurance premiums, and in some cases simply forgo the voyage when the destination or vessel is perceived as a potential target.
Eilat port shipping interrupted by Houthi attacks since 2023
For Israel, the problem has persisted since November 2023, when the Houthis began attacking and threatening vessels linked to Israel. Major shipping companies stopped calling at Eilat along the previously standard route. The port continued to operate on a limited basis, but the commercial activity it relied on was severely damaged.
In 2023, the Port of Eilat recorded 132 ship calls and unloaded approximately 150,000 vehicles. In 2024, the port recorded only 16 ship calls, and it unloaded no vehicles. Port revenue, which stood at approximately NIS 212 million in 2023, fell by about 80% the following year.
The figures demonstrate how effective the Houthi threat was without requiring physical control of the shipping route. The threat to ships alone was enough for shipowners, insurers, financiers, and line operators to conclude that sailing to the Israeli port was not worthwhile.
The strikes carried out by the IDF in Yemen have also failed so far to bring the shipping companies back. Ultimately, the decision on whether to return to Eilat lies with shipping companies and insurers, and depends in part on their assessment of the risk along the route.
This year, a solution was found that allowed some vehicle-import activity to return to Eilat without the large car carriers themselves returning to the port. Ships arriving from the East docked in Aqaba, Jordan, where the vehicles were unloaded and then transferred to Eilat on smaller vessels.
In March alone, 5,905 vehicles were unloaded in Eilat, followed by another 3,142 in April.
The arrangement through Aqaba restored activity to the port and eased its predicament, but the direct shipping route from the East has not resumed. International shipping lines still do not call directly at Eilat as they did before the war. The large car carriers stop in Aqaba, and the cargo continues from there to Eilat.
Since 2023, Israel has addressed the problem through several channels. The IDF has struck Houthi targets in Yemen, and the defense establishment deals with the threat from Yemen on an ongoing basis. Israeli strikes have focused on damaging Houthi capabilities and responding to attacks against Israel.
Publicly available information does not indicate the existence of an approved plan in which restoring regular commercial shipping to Eilat was defined as an objective in its own right.
MK Forer pushes for action to fully reopen shipping route to Eilat
The issue was raised unusually prominently during a Knesset Economic Affairs Committee hearing in June. MK Oded Forer argued that the shipping route to Eilat was effectively closed because of the Houthis and that the government had not made reopening it a diplomatic and security objective.
"It doesn't matter who the operator is. If ships don't enter the port, there will be no port," he said.
Eilat Mayor Eli Lankri said the port was almost completely shut down.
For more than two years, a significant share of government efforts has focused on the port's economic distress. The state allowed payment deferrals, provided a loan guarantee, and approved direct assistance.
It also formulated a plan to subsidize the arrival of car carriers, under which it approved about half a million dollars per ship, aiming the bring four ships a month for three months, at a total cost of up to NIS 21 million.
The plan was not implemented. During Knesset discussions in early 2026, the situation was described as a "dead end." According to figures presented by the port management, its debts had reached approximately NIS 30 million, while the monthly gap between expenses and revenue stood at around NIS 5 million.
Most government efforts focused on financing the port's continued operation and trying to restore cargo traffic. Publicly available information does not indicate that any specific government body was given overall responsibility for restoring the direct shipping route to Eilat.
At the same time, the port tried to promote additional solutions. Its management examined the possibility of US assistance, approached Egypt, and attempted to advance mechanisms that would make it easier for ships to arrive through a safer or more heavily subsidized route.
None of those efforts have brought international shipping lines back to regular, direct operations in Eilat so far.
Port of Eilat's future remains undecided
The port's future also remains undecided. The current operator's concession is due to expire in 2028, and the state has yet to decide what the operating model will look like afterward.
The debate over the identity of the next operator is taking place while the issue that determines whether the port can function at all - the return of ships - remains unresolved.
This also has implications for the role of the Port of Eilat in Israel's national security doctrine. Eilat cannot replace Ashdod and Haifa in every scenario. It is not a major container port, and its infrastructure is limited.
Its importance derives largely from geography: It is Israel's only commercial port facing the Red Sea. If activity at the Mediterranean ports is disrupted or restricted, an operational southern maritime gateway could provide Israel with an additional route.
For it to be usable in an emergency, Israel must also maintain infrastructure, workers, equipment, and a functioning logistics system during routine periods.
Israel has already been paying a direct price at the Port of Eilat for nearly three years because of the Houthi threat. The Houthis' latest advance now makes the threat to Red Sea shipping routes a far more urgent problem for Saudi Arabia as well.
In the background lies a fact that has almost disappeared from Israel's public agenda: An Iran-backed organization, operating from roughly 2,000 kilometers away, succeeded in prompting international shipping companies to stop calling regularly at Eilat.
Even after a long series of Israeli strikes in Yemen, the ships have not returned. Nearly three years after regular shipping to Eilat was disrupted, the government has invested money and effort to preserve the port and prevent its collapse.
It succeeded in keeping the port alive. It has still not brought the ships back.

Former MoD permanent secretary: Datasel contract followed 10 months of preparations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
07:19:00 UTC
16:19:00 KST

Former MoD permanent secretary: Datasel contract followed 10 months of preparations
Former Defense Ministry Secretary General Kusti Salm told ERR about how the contract with Datasel was signed. He stressed that the defense minister bears responsibility for decisions made in procuring ammunition for Ukraine.
Salm said providing military support to Ukraine has been important to Estonia and that the decisions related to it were made by politicians.
"These have all been decisions made by politicians and they are all decisions that the Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK), the Ministry of Defense, the foreign ministry's dedicated diplomats and the Government Office have faithfully carried out. And it has not been purely altruistic. The politicians who made these decisions have also reaped the political benefits," he said.
According to the former permanent secretary, the level of risk involved in sourcing ammunition for Ukraine was so high that procuring such items with Estonia's own money would have been out of the question.
"Now one of those risks has materialized. And we are in a situation where the very same people who did their jobs successfully in dozens or hundreds of other cases are now being lined up one by one and essentially portrayed as criminals in front of the Estonian public," Salm said.
According to Salm, there is no one in Estonia other than the defense minister — Reform's Hanno Pevkur held the post at the time — who can bear responsibility for such decisions.
"There are no other people who have a mandate from the public to spend €2.4 billion every year. The minister decides. The permanent secretary's role in this respect is to implement the minister's decisions," he said.
"As for these specific transactions, I was involved in them and I absolutely take full responsibility for the proposals I made, just as I take responsibility for the things that were done during that period and for some of the things that were left undone," Salm said.
The former permanent secretary pointed out that it took 10 months to enter into a contract with Datasel.
"People traveled to Italy, people traveled to India. The entire process took 10 months at a time when, in reality, there was a great deal of urgency," he said.
Salm explained that at the time, major ammunition manufacturers were charging several times the usual price, while producing the ammunition would have taken years. Ukraine also had many Soviet-origin weapons and Russia was also seeking ammunition compatible with them. Such ammunition was available from countries including India, Pakistan and countries in North Africa.
Asked whether the bar for following standard procedures had been deliberately lowered, Salm said: "This was not some general agreement, but a detailed instruction from the defense minister that this was exactly how these matters were to be handled because the risks were known."
"My task was to put the necessary processes in place and make sure that RKIK carried out its duties," he added.
According to Salm, the contact with Datasel came from the defense minister, Hanno Pevkur, who recently left office.
"Today, there is no question about that whatsoever. It came through the defense minister, which is completely normal," he said.
The former permanent secretary stressed that Pevkur led the process of procuring ammunition for Ukraine.
"The minister managed the process of assisting Ukraine in detail and in a very hands-on way. He had his own instructions and views on matters. People who know Hanno Pevkur know that he is a proactive person. He gets into the details, he keeps himself informed and that is exactly how he operated in this case. He was also generally very firm in his instructions," Salm said.
Background
In 2024, the Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) signed four procurement contracts with Datasel S.R.L., an Italian company acquired earlier that year by Indian-owned Neco Defence Munitions. Despite neither Datasel nor its parent firm having any prior track record of manufacturing or selling artillery shells, RKIK wired roughly €70 million in advance payments.
The contracts meant to deliver desperately needed ammunition to Ukraine using EU European Peace Facility funding suffered severe delivery delays. Ammunition that did arrive was flagged as incomplete and of substandard quality, leading RKIK to terminate the agreements and launch legal efforts to recoup the money. Datasel has denied wrongdoing, claiming it delivered tens of millions of euros' worth of goods and was left with financial losses.
The European Public Prosecutor's Office has since launched an investigation into the use of European Peace Facility funds by Estonia.
The scandal was part of Minister of Defense Hanno Pevkur's recent decision to resign, alongside wider accounting and oversight issues at the Estonian Defense Forces and other parts of the ministry's administrative area.

Trump threatens EU over Canada 'associate membership' proposal

07:18:52 UTC
16:18:52 KST

US President Donald Trump has threatened to impose heavy tariffs on the European Union or halt some trade with the bloc after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed making Canada its first associate member.
Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Trump said his response would depend on whether he viewed the proposal as a hostile act.
"I think it's laughable," he said. "If they do that, if I think it's at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe, on many things."
He added: "If it's a good intention, that's fine. If it's a bad intention, we'll put very heavy tariffs on Europe, which is a possibility."
The proposal comes as Brussels and Ottawa seek to reduce their reliance on the United States amid trade tensions under Trump's leadership.
Von der Leyen floated the idea during her annual State of the European Union address in Strasbourg, attended by Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, the first non-European head of government to join the event.
"I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU," she told Carney, drawing a standing ovation in the European Parliament.
She said Brussels and Ottawa needed to draw closer as democracies faced a "fracture in the international rules-based system".
A broader alliance
Carney is due to address the European Parliament on Thursday, with his visit intended to build momentum ahead of an EU-Canada summit in Montreal next month.
He has pursued closer ties with the bloc as Canada becomes increasingly embroiled in a trade war with the United States.
Von der Leyen called for the relationship to move beyond trade cooperation towards a broader "alliance for the future", with closer ties in technology, defence and energy.
"We will work on intelligent manufacturing. We will create a tech alliance. We will integrate defence industrial bases. We will make the Arctic a flagship joint project," she said.
She also identified critical minerals, batteries, artificial intelligence, cyber security and economic security as areas for cooperation.
"This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength," she said.
Both Canada and the EU have faced US tariffs and territorial threats, alongside competition from China.
"In a more dangerous and divided world, Canada is forging stronger relationships with trusted partners," Carney's office said in a statement.
What would associate membership mean?
EU treaties make no provision for "associate membership", leaving the scope of von der Leyen's proposal unclear.
"We don't really know yet what it means," said Tobias Cremer, a centre-left German member of the European Parliament and the main sponsor of a resolution calling for stronger EU-Canada cooperation.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz first floated the idea for Ukraine earlier this year, but it received a cool reception from Kiev, which is seeking full membership.
Under that proposal, Ukraine would have been able to attend EU summits, have a representative in the European Commission and access parts of the bloc's budget, without full voting rights.
Any partnership with a non-EU country requires approval from member states, and it remains unclear how much support von der Leyen's proposal would receive from their governments.
Brussels and Ottawa already have close ties. Their CETA free-trade agreement, which abolished almost all tariffs, has been credited with helping boost trade in goods and services by more than 80 percent since 2016.
Canada also became the first non-EU country to join the bloc's flagship defence loan programme this year.
Following von der Leyen's address, Carney travelled to Britain for his first meeting with new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham. The two attended a football match between Everton and Wolverhampton before Carney's return to Strasbourg for his speech on Thursday.
