After petitioning SC on Aug 25 raising questions about the judgement, govt has now asked CAT to modify its Aug 19 order
NEW DELHI: Centre has begun to disentangle itself from the seemingly contradictory positions it has taken before Supreme Court and Central Administrative Tribunal on the implementation of the March 11 Rohit Nathan judgement on creamy layer for OBCs from PSU family background.Rohit Nathan judgement paved way for the induction of those OBC candidates in the elite civil services who passed exams over past 10 years but were still left out. The judgement laid down that "salary" cannot be added to "income" to decide if a candidate from PSU background falls in "creamy layer" - like it is done for OBCs from non-PSU families.After petitioning SC on Aug 25 raising questions about the judgement, govt has now asked CAT to modify its Aug 19 order where Centre had committed to implement the Nathan judgement.In an affidavit filed in CAT Monday, govt said its earlier submission "that a decision has been taken to implement the judgement in Rohit Nathan requires to be suitably clarified" because a modification application is pending before SC. Govt said the judgement's implementation would depend on the outcome of pending application in SC.
Govt has told CAT that if its earlier order stays on record in its unqualified form, "it is likely to create an inconsistent position" suggesting govt has undertaken to implement the judgement that it has assailed before SC.
TOI had reported how Centre has taken a contradictory stand before SC and CAT in the wake of OBC candidate Basant Singh pushing the tribunal to enforce its order that he be inducted in civil services. Singh's case is similar to the candidates in whose favour SC delivered the Nathan judgement. Quoting the fresh affidavit, Vikram Hegde, lawyer for Singh, said, " Govt is seeking to set the clock back."As per the 1993 office memorandum, "salary" and "agricultural income" are not included in computing "income" of a family. The case pertains to how DoPT has been taking "salary" into consideration for candidates with parents in PSUs.

Sleeping too little, or too much, could speed up aging
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
02:59:38 UTC
11:59:38 KST

Researchers analysed data from about 5,00,000 UK Biobank participants and examined 23 biological aging clocks
NEW DELHI: Sleeping too little, or even too much, may be linked to faster biological aging and a higher risk of death, according to a large study of nearly 5 lakh adults aged 37 to 84 years. People sleeping less than six hours had a 50% higher hazard of death from any cause, while those sleeping more than eight hours had a 40% higher hazard, compared with six to eight hours.The study, published in Nature, did not establish that sleep extremes directly cause earlier death or faster aging.
Researchers analysed data from about 5,00,000 UK Biobank participants and examined 23 biological aging clocks based on magnetic resonance imaging, plasma proteins and metabolic markers. They found a U-shaped relationship between sleep duration and biological age gaps. The lowest gaps were generally recorded between 6.4 and 7.8 hours, depending on organ and sex. Among clocks showing a significant relationship, the lowest gaps occurred between 6.5 and 7.8 hours for women and 6.4 and 7.7 hours for men. The pattern was significant in 9 of 23 clocks, involving the brain, heart, lungs, liver, immune system, skin, endocrine system, fat tissue and pancreas.
"Sleep is not just about duration. Timing, depth and continuity also matter. There is no single ideal number of hours for everyone. Consistently sleeping too little or too much, particularly less than six or more than 9 hours, may indicate non-restorative sleep or an underlying sleep disorder, which can raise cardiovascular and metabolic risks and affect healthy aging," said Dr J C Suri, director and head, department of pulmonary, critical care and sleep medicine, Sitaram Bhartia Institute of Science and Research.
The study identified 153 significant associations between abnormal sleep duration and future disease outcomes. Short sleep had broad links with mental health, metabolic, cardiovascular, pulmonary and digestive diseases. Researchers suggested disrupted sleep and circadian rhythms may affect inflammatory, metabolic, vascular, hormonal and tissue-repair pathways. Questions remain about young people's exposure to irregular schedules, artificial night light, late-night eating, shift work and "social jet lag". Sleep duration was self-reported, and sleep quality, interruptions, timing, architecture or regularity were not measured.
Anuja Jaiswal is a Senior Assistant Editor at The Times of India, with an impressive 18-year career in narrative journalism. She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Over the years, she has worked in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh and West UP, gaining diverse on-ground experience that shapes her storytelling.

HCs backlog: 65 lakh cases, countless years of waiting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
02:56:13 UTC
11:56:13 KST

NEW DELHI: Unhappy with a Jodhpur labour court award, a health worker from Jalore district, Rajasthan, engaged on a daily wage basis and whose services were terminated in 1999 had moved Rajasthan HC in 2004.The petition is yet to be heard, 22 years later.With pendency in HCs crossing the 65 lakh mark, there is a steady stream of petitions before the Supreme Court pleading for directions to the HCs concerned, not for expeditious adjudication of their grievance but for early hearing on their petitions after prolonged wait for justice. Nearly 15 lakh such cases have remained pending in HCs for over a a decade.Most applications come from Allahabad HC and Rajasthan HC, where the pendency of cases is 12.5 lakh and 7 lakh respectively.In Allahabad HC, each judge/bench takes up an average of 150-200 cases every day for hearing, but the monstrous pendency appears to be overwhelming the judicial decision-making capacity. The erstwhile health worker from Jalore made a similar plea before a bench headed by CJI Surya Kant Wednesday.Given the constitutionally independent status of HCs and realising the daily case list before each judge in HCs, the CJI-led bench passed the standard order, "We see no ground to entertain the petition but give liberty to the petitioner to move an application seeking early hearing of the petition."
The SC is aware that it is not superior to HCs on the administrative side and the chief justices concerned of HCs, as per the SC's own ruling, are the masters of roster, prohibiting it from directing them to list certain cases for early hearing.
Moreover, if the SC requests an HC to hear one case out of turn considering the number of years for which it had remained pending, then the scale of equality would mandate early hearing of all similarly old petitions.After Allahabad and Rajasthan HCs, Bombay HC has the largest pendency of 6.4 lakh cases, followed by Madras HC with 5.6 lakh cases, Madhya Pradesh HC with 4.9 lakh, Karnataka HC with 3.3 lakh, and Andhra Pradesh HC with 2.5 lakh. Compared to Bombay and Madras HCs, the HCs of Delhi and Calcutta have relatively low pendency of cases at 1.2 lakh and 1.9 lakh cases.

US-Israeli strikes on Iran and Israeli attacks on Lebanon have killed thousands and displaced millions.

Army, CRPF, J&amp;K police launch joint operation in J&amp;K's Udhampur after input on suspicious movement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
02:50:08 UTC
11:50:08 KST

NEW DELHI: Two terrorists were neutralised during an overnight counter-terrorism operation in Jammu and Kashmir’s Udhampur district, the Army said on Thursday.The operation, code-named Operation Sohan, was launched during the intervening night of September 16 and 17 following confirmed intelligence inputs about the presence of terrorists in the general area of Brattal, the Army’s White Knight Corps said.
Despite hostile weather, difficult terrain and poor visibility, troops of the White Knight Corps, Jammu and Kashmir Police and the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) launched a targeted operation in the area, the Army said.
Official said that a joint search operation was launched in the remote Bratel Soan and Khubban areas of Majalta around 9 pm on Wednesday following information about the movement of suspected terrorists.A few rounds of firing and blasts, reportedly carried out by security forces while targeting a suspected hideout, were heard in the forest shortly after the operation began, officials said.The area remained largely quiet through the night before the lull ended on Thursday morning, when the terrorists opened heavy fire in an attempt to break the security forces’ cordon.Security forces retaliated, triggering an encounter that continued in the forested area.
The Army later said the operation resulted in the neutralisation of two terrorists. Search and surveillance operations are continuing in the area, while security forces remain deployed to track and neutralise any remaining threat, the White Knight Corps said.The operation comes amid heightened security activity in the Pir Panjal region following the recent busting of an alleged overground worker (OGW) network linked to the Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) in Rajouri.On September 15, Rajouri Police arrested three people in connection with an alleged terror module operating in the Pir Panjal region. According to police, the three were allegedly involved in providing logistical support, safe transit and other ground-level assistance to terrorists operating in the region.
Preliminary investigation found that the accused allegedly worked as guides and helped facilitate the movement of terrorist groups towards the Kashmir Valley, police said. They were also suspected of providing ground support to terrorists linked to multiple high-profile attacks, including an attack targeting civilians.Police also recovered an improvised explosive device (IED) based on information provided by one of the accused.According to officials, preliminary findings indicated that the IED had allegedly been handed over to the accused by members of a terrorist group for safe custody and possible use in a targeted attack.The recovery of the IED and the arrests have provided investigators with leads into the wider terror network operating in the region, police said.

Taiwan's Winbond looks beyond traditional memory cycle for growth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
02:50:00 UTC
11:50:00 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Winbond Electronics Corp.’s growth is becoming less dependent on the traditional memory cycle, CTEE reported Thursday.
Higher memory prices and expanded 16-nanometer DRAM production are expected to support its memory business. At the same time, new AI-related products, including advanced packaging applications, are opening additional growth sources for the company next year.
Major global DRAM suppliers continue to shift resources toward more advanced memory chips. As a result, supplies of DDR4 and other products made using mature processes are declining.
Meanwhile, data centers, networking equipment, and edge AI devices are using more memory, keeping the market for commodity memory products tight. Winbond is among the suppliers expected to benefit from these supply constraints.
Another potential growth driver is the expansion of Winbond’s 16-nm DRAM production. The company plans to raise monthly capacity at its Kaohsiung plant from 15,000 wafers to 24,000 wafers by the end of the year. As it installs new equipment, analysts expect Windbond's shipments to increase significantly in 2027.
The company is also targeting applications such as AI inference and edge servers with a memory product designed to deliver high bandwidth while consuming less power. This would allow the company to expand beyond its traditional specialty DRAM market into AI-related memory applications.
A fourth growth driver is silicon capacitors, or Si-Cap. As AI chips consume more power and advanced semiconductor packaging becomes increasingly dense, demand for high-density silicon capacitors is expected to grow. Winbond has been developing dedicated Si-Cap capacity, which can operate relatively independently of its DRAM production lines.

Taipei transport department says most Puma Shen proposals already underway
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
02:49:37 UTC
11:49:37 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taipei’s transport department said Wednesday that most transport policies proposed by DPP mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) are already being carried out by the city government.
CNA reported that Shen unveiled four proposals Wednesday covering school zones, bus safety, bicycle commuting, and the inclusion of shared electric scooters in Tpass. He said the measures would make walking, buses, bicycles, and shared electric scooters safer and more convenient for daily travel.
The department responded later that day, saying it welcomed Shen’s support for the direction of existing city policies. However, it said proposals covering measures already underway or completed should reflect the city’s current progress.
On school safety, Shen proposed setting common standards for school zones and completing them around all elementary schools within eight years. He said central government guidelines recommend creating school zones within 150 meters of schools, but the guidelines are not mandatory, per UDN.
The department said Taipei has been improving pedestrian areas around 280 schools since 2023. It added that the city began developing school zones in 2025 with measures including narrower traffic lanes, smaller intersections, speed-reduction markings, pedestrian refuge islands, and relocated crosswalks.
On bus safety, Shen proposed tying government subsidies for driver salaries to working conditions, redesigning driver seats, providing rest areas at major turnaround points, and reviewing routes by district. The department said the city has already introduced measures to improve staffing, vehicle safety, road conditions, and bus operations, per Liberty Times.
The city said bus drivers have received an NT$8,000 (US$251) monthly pay increase, while 3,384 buses have been equipped with advanced driver assistance systems. Other safety measures include active door systems, blind spot warnings, and redesigned bus stop areas that give buses more room to enter and leave stops.
Shen also proposed improving Taipei’s bicycle commuting network by closing gaps between riverside routes and city streets, strengthening maintenance, and expanding support for YouBike services. He also proposed building a bicycle bridge across the Keelung River to connect riverside routes with the Neihu Technology Park, per Economics Daily News.
The department said Taipei currently has 1,794 YouBike stations and 27,629 bicycles, with stations generally 150 to 200 meters apart in urban areas. It said the city is continuing work to connect bicycle routes and use riverside paths to improve commuting links between Taipei and New Taipei.
The city said it studied the proposed Keelung River bicycle bridge in 2024. It found that construction could require relocating water and electricity infrastructure and closing two traffic lanes for more than two years, which could affect Neihu traffic.
Shen’s fourth proposal would include shared electric scooters in Tpass to give commuters another transport option. The department said Taipei cannot make the change on its own because Tpass involves central government subsidies, the legal definition of public transport, and nationwide regulations, per CTS News.

Morocco’s 2026 election: A test of political trust and engagement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
02:47:53 UTC
11:47:53 KST

Morocco’s 2026 election: A test of political trust and engagement
Youth unemployment, living costs and public services are key issues before the September 23 vote.
Rabat, Morocco – Morocco’s parliamentary election campaign began on September 10, with 27 political parties competing for 395 seats in the House of Representatives. More than 15.8 million voters are registered for the September 23 vote, which will determine Parliament’s composition and play a central role in forming the next government.
But beyond the competition between parties, the election raises a deeper question: whether citizens believe the political system can respond to the problems shaping their daily lives.
That question is particularly important for younger Moroccans. An Afrobarometer survey published in March found that roughly a third of Moroccans aged 18 to 35 expressed trust in Parliament, the head of government and political parties. At the same time, young people were more likely than older Moroccans to post political content on social media and participate in demonstrations.
That does not necessarily mean young Moroccans are disengaged. The more important issue is whether they see electoral politics as an effective way of addressing the problems they face.
An election within a distinctive system
Morocco’s electoral politics operate within the constitutional framework established in 2011. The constitution defines Morocco as a constitutional, democratic, parliamentary and social monarchy and establishes a separation and balance of powers while preserving the monarchy’s central institutional role.
Under Article 47, the king appoints the head of government from the political party that comes first in elections to the House of Representatives. The king also presides over the Council of Ministers, while the government exercises executive power and Parliament exercises legislative and oversight functions.
Winning the largest number of seats, therefore, matters for forming the government, but the parliamentary result does not by itself determine the full distribution of political power.
A younger electorate, an older political system
The age profile of the electorate makes the question of political engagement more consequential.
Official figures show that voters aged 18 to 24 account for 4 percent of those registered, while people aged 60 and above account for 29 percent. But those figures describe the electoral roll, not turnout, but they show how heavily the registered electorate is weighted towards older citizens.
Morocco also faces a substantial youth employment problem. The IMF estimates that unemployment stood at 13 percent in 2025, while unemployment among 15-to-24-year-olds reached 37.3 percent. It estimates that 25.2 percent of young people were not in employment, education or training in the third quarter of 2025. The IMF also points to skills mismatches, limited private-sector dynamism and pronounced gender disparities in labour-market participation.
For young people struggling to enter the labour market, promises about growth, jobs and purchasing power are not abstract campaign issues. They are measures of whether the political system can deliver opportunities visible in everyday life.
When economic frustration becomes political
Those pressures have also surfaced outside formal electoral politics.
In late July, roughly 60,000 people entered the autonomous Spanish city of Ceuta from Morocco in the largest such surge in recent history, according to the news agency Reuters. The report linked the crossings to economic hardship, social unrest and misinformation circulating on social media, alongside migration aspirations and false expectations about Spanish court rulings.
While this episode may not have been a direct measure of electoral opinion or evidence of a single political cause, it illustrated how economic expectations, migration aspirations and perceptions of opportunity can intersect.
That provides a wider context for the election’s economic debate: whether Morocco’s recent growth and major development projects are producing opportunities that younger citizens can see in their own lives.
The economy has been growing strongly. The IMF estimates that real GDP grew by 4.9 percent in 2025 and projects growth of 4.4 percent in 2026. Yet high unemployment, particularly among young people, has remained a significant challenge.
Strong growth has not translated into sufficient job creation.
What the parties are promising
Employment and purchasing power feature prominently in the programmes of the three parties that have formed the governing coalition since 2021: the National Rally of Independents (RNI), the Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) and Istiqlal.
The RNI’s 2026–2031 programme promises one million jobs and a gradual increase in the minimum wage to 5,000 dirhams (about $530) per month. PAM has pledged at least one million jobs and put the cost of its five-year programme at 350 billion dirhams ($37.1bn). Istiqlal has placed purchasing power and public services at the centre of its campaign, alongside proposals on healthcare, housing, employment, water management and food security.
The programmes differ in emphasis, but their common focus is revealing: Employment, household purchasing power and public services have become central measures of political credibility.
The challenge for the next government will be turning investment and growth into more productive jobs and higher living standards.
The PJD tries to recover
The Justice and Development Party (PJD), led by former head of government Abdelilah Benkirane, enters the election seeking to rebuild support after its dramatic losses in 2021.
The party fell from 125 seats in the previous parliament to 13. In the September 2021 election, the RNI won 102 seats, followed by PAM with 87 and Istiqlal with 81. The three parties subsequently formed the governing coalition.
The PJD has presented a programme built around five axes and 467 measures covering institutional, economic, social and foreign policy. The programme emphasises concrete reforms and measures rather than extensive numerical targets, covering areas including public services, employment, purchasing power and institutional reform.
Its return adds another dimension to the contest as the governing parties defend their record since 2021 and the PJD attempts to rebuild its electoral base.
What the election will test
The election will test whether Morocco’s political system can maintain a credible connection between an ambitious development agenda and the expectations of citizens who want to see its benefits in everyday life.
For younger Moroccans, the relatively low trust in political institutions alongside very high youth unemployment points to traditional electoral politics facing competition from other forms of political expression at a time when employment and living standards are increasingly important.
At a time when employment and economic standards are central to political party platforms, economic researcher Nouh El Harmouzi argues that the challenge extends beyond what parties can promise during an election campaign.
“Morocco’s economic problems are fundamentally structural and cannot be resolved through short-term electoral promises.”

Netanyahu proposes stripping IDF critics of Israeli citizenship
Israelis should be stripped of citizenship if they are found guilty of slandering the military, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said, as the IDF faces new accusations of killing Palestinian civilians in Gaza.
In a video address on Wednesday, Netanyahu lashed out at the recently released documentary ‘NAZA’, which alleges that the Israeli military and intelligence services used AI-assisted systems to select targets and treated potential civilian deaths as acceptable collateral damage. The film by Oscar-winning Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor premiered at the Venice Film Festival on September 10 and won the Special Jury Prize.
Netanyahu vowed to introduce two bills punishing those who he said are causing “immense damage” to the IDF.
“The first, to revoke the citizenship of anyone who defames [Israeli] soldiers, and the second to hit them in their pockets and increase the statutory damages for defamation they can be sued for by 20 times,” he said, as quoted by Reuters.
“Hit them both in the pocket and through their citizenship, because they have no place among us,” Netanyahu added, according to Ynet.

Netanyahu also mentioned Yifat Tomer-Yerushalmi, who was removed as the IDF’s chief military advocate after admitting that she authorized the leaking of a video allegedly showing the abuse of a Palestinian detainee at an Israeli detention facility.
The team behind ‘NAZA’ stood by their investigation, which they said was based on interviews with Israeli service members. “It’s important as Israelis that we recognize what our government has done in Gaza,” Abraham said.
A number of countries, the UN, and human rights groups have accused Israel of indiscriminately killing civilians. Nearly 74,000 people have been killed in Gaza since the war broke out in October 2023 following a surprise attack by Hamas against Israel.
The International Criminal Court (ICC) has outstanding arrest warrants for Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity. The International Court of Justice (ICJ) is hearing a genocide case brought against Israel over its conduct in Gaza.
Israel denies the allegations, while acknowledging some civilian killings as isolated violations of IDF protocols, and accuses Hamas of using civilians as human shields. Israeli officials have also accused UN agencies of aiding Hamas and argued that the group counts fighters among civilian casualties.

Hidden “immune organ” in the skull may help fight brain cancer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
02:43:01 UTC
11:43:01 KST

Hidden “immune organ” in the skull may help fight brain cancer
Hidden immune “security stations” inside the skull may help the brain fight cancer before the rest of the immune system even gets the signal.
- Date:
- September 16, 2026
- Source:
- WashU Medicine
- Summary:
- Scientists discovered a hidden “immune organ” inside the skull that acts as a rapid first responder against brain cancer in mice. Strengthening this local immune defense improved tumor rejection and survival, raising the possibility of new treatments that target the skull directly.
- Share:
Researchers at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis have identified previously unknown lymph node-like immune structures in the skull bone marrow of mice. The findings suggest these nearby immune hubs can respond rapidly to brain cancer, becoming active before more distant lymph nodes even receive signals that something is wrong.
The team also found evidence of similar immune cells in human skull bone marrow, suggesting that this local defense system may not be limited to mice.
Scientists once believed that the brain was largely isolated from the immune system. That view has changed dramatically in recent years. The new findings suggest the brain not only communicates with immune cells, but may also have specialized immune "security stations" positioned unusually close by.
Published in Nature, the study is the first to identify immune hubs of this kind inside bone.
"This study reveals that the skull bone marrow is far more than just a structural framework -- it harbors previously unrecognized hubs for brain-specific immune responses," said senior author Jonathan Kipnis, PhD, the Alan A. and Edith L. Wolff Distinguished Professor of Pathology & Immunology and a BJC Investigator at WashU Medicine. "Uncovering this localized immune niche changes how we view neuroimmune interactions and opens exciting new avenues for treating brain tumors and other neurological diseases."
A Local Immune Defense for the Brain
Earlier work from Kipnis' laboratory helped overturn the long-standing idea that the brain was separated from the immune system. The group discovered lymphatic vessels in the dura mater, the protective outer layer of tissue surrounding the brain just beneath the skull.
More recently, the researchers found tiny physical channels bridging the skull, dura, and brain tissue. Those channels provide a direct route through which immune cells and cellular waste can travel between the brain and nearby skull bone marrow.
In the new mouse study, the scientists followed proteins as they moved out of the brain, through these channels, and into the skull bone marrow. There, they discovered organized immune structures resembling those normally found in lymph nodes.
Lymph nodes serve as important coordination centers for immune activity. Within them, T follicular helper cells support B cells, which can then produce large quantities of antibodies that help the body fight infections and disease. Finding comparable structures in healthy bone marrow was unexpected.
"We have never seen such structures in healthy bone marrow before," said Jang Hyun Park, PhD, the study's first author and a postdoctoral research fellow in the Kipnis lab who is starting his own lab at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology this fall. "It is an exciting discovery that points out that a complex brain requires its own specialized immune structures to defend it."
Skull Immune Hubs Respond to Brain Cancer
The researchers next investigated whether these newly identified immune centers actually help protect the brain from disease.
They used a mouse model of glioblastoma, an aggressive form of brain cancer, and interfered with the skull immune hubs using a drug. Tumors grew more quickly in mice whose immune hubs had been disrupted than in animals whose hubs remained intact.
The mice with impaired skull immune defenses also had shorter survival, providing evidence that these local immune structures play an active role in responding to brain cancer.
Boosting the Skull's Immune Response
The team then explored whether the immune hubs could be deliberately strengthened.
Researchers created a targeted treatment intended to increase antibody production within skull bone marrow. They combined three immune-boosting proteins in a gel and placed it directly beneath the scalp.
The treatment triggered a surge of immune activity against the tumors. Importantly, the response appeared first in the immune hubs inside the skull bone marrow and only later emerged in nearby lymph nodes outside the skull.
Mice treated with the gel rejected tumors more effectively and survived longer than control animals.
A New Route for Treating Neurological Disease
The discovery could have implications beyond brain cancer. Because these immune hubs sit directly next to the brain, researchers believe they could eventually provide a way to influence immune activity in neurological diseases without broadly affecting the rest of the body.
"The finding fundamentally changes our current understanding of neuroimmunology," said Kipnis. "Knowing that the brain relies on first responders in the surrounding skull for defense has the potential to change how we think about developing therapies for many neurological conditions, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, schizophrenia, long COVID, and many others that have an immune component to them. Such therapies could access these immune hubs directly through the skull, without major peripheral side effects."
Story Source:
Materials provided by WashU Medicine. Original written by Marta Wegorzewska. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Jang Hyun Park, Daviti Abramishvili, Gustavo Gastão Davanzo, Ruben Silva, Xingxing Gu, Siling Du, Daniel D. Lee, Bernd H. Zinselmeyer, Jackson S. Turner, Gwendalyn J. Randolph, Igor Smirnov, Jonathan Kipnis. Functional role of skull lymphoid structures in CNS immunosurveillance. Nature, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-10951-4

101 illegally kept wildlife specimens seized in Singapore, 13 found dead
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:42:05 CST
11:42:05 KST

SINGAPORE, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- Singapore has seized 101 illegally kept wildlife specimens, 13 of which were found dead and many others in poor health, and is investigating six people for suspected illegal sale and possession of wildlife, the National Parks Board (NParks) said on Wednesday.
This has been one of NParks' largest seizures of illegally kept wildlife in recent years, it said.
The animals were seized during raids on residential premises on Monday and included lizards, newts, pythons, tarantulas and turtles. All were non-native species that cannot legally be sold, offered for sale or kept as pets in Singapore. Some are also protected under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora.
Many of the surviving animals were found in poor health, NParks said. One leopard gecko was found with a ruptured and infected eye and was unable to shed its skin fully.
Such conditions were "highly indicative of a long period of time captive under poor conditions," NParks said. One leopard gecko had to be euthanised on animal welfare grounds.
The 13 specimens found dead at the premises may have died because of conditions including insufficient space, poor ventilation and inadequate access to food and water, the agency said.
The remaining wildlife have been moved to NParks' Center for Wildlife Rehabilitation, where they are being housed and cared for.
As the animals came from unknown sources and may carry infectious diseases, they will undergo a period of quarantine. NParks will then assess whether they are suitable for repatriation or donation to animal establishments such as zoos.
Euthanasia will be considered as a last resort, the agency said. ■

GENEVA, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- The International Olympic Committee (IOC) on Wednesday confirmed that ice sports competitions at the 2030 Winter Olympic Games will be staged in Lyon, with some Alpine skiing events to be held in the French resorts of Courchevel and Val d'Isere.
The IOC Coordination Commission held its second annual meeting after visiting venues in Lyon to finalize the sports venue master plan, following the IOC Executive Board's June decision to relocate the ice cluster to Lyon and allocate two Alpine skiing venues to the Savoie cluster.
Ice hockey will be held at the Decines-Charpieu Arena and Hall Tony Garnier, while curling, figure skating and short track will take place at the Eurexpo Convention Center in Lyon. A housing development project in Oullins-Pierre-Benite was also confirmed as the Olympic Village in Lyon.
Courchevel will host the downhill and super-G, while Val d'Isere will stage the giant slalom and slalom. The women's and men's team combined events will take place in Courchevel.
Pierre-Olivier Beckers-Vieujant, chair of the IOC Coordination Commission, said the site visits and discussions demonstrated "real progress" by the organizing committee and that the Games now has "a clear vision, a striking visual identity, a compelling sports program, an optimized venue plan and solid economic foundations."
"The delegation was able to assess the quality of the work carried out by the Committee in recent months and fully appreciate the potential of its five outstanding clusters: Lyon, Haute-Savoie, Savoie, the Brianconnais region and Thialf in the Netherlands, with particular attention given to the ice venues and infrastructure," said Vincent Roberti, Interim President and Chief Executive Officer of 2030 Winter Olympics.
The 2030 Olympic Winter Games will take place from Feb. 1 to 17, followed by the Paralympic Winter Games from March 1 to 10. ■

Ukraine: Russian strikes injure several in Kyiv, Odesa

"An air raid alert has been declared in Kyiv due to the threat of missile strikes. We urge residents to proceed to the nearest shelters," the Kyiv City Military Administration wrote on Telegram.

Mediated talks ahead?
The strikes continue even as Russia and Ukraine recently signalled their readiness to resume talks under US mediation. Earlier this week, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's office said officials were preparing for talks in October. Similar signals came from Moscow, which said it did not rule out such a possibility.
The last round of trilateral talks took place in January and February 2026 in Abu Dhabi and Geneva, without producing a breakthrough, as the issue of territory control in eastern Ukraine remained unresolved.

Fiji declares HIV a national crisis as diagnoses surge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Fiji declares HIV a national crisis as diagnoses surge
WELLINGTON, Sept 17 - Fiji has declared HIV a national crisis after new diagnoses climbed 27% last year, intensifying concern that an epidemic once concentrated among people who inject drugs is spreading more widely through the Pacific island nation.
The government said in a statement posted on Facebook that 2,016 people were diagnosed with HIV in 2025 and estimated that one in 60 adults was living with the disease.
Fifty-nine babies were born with HIV last year and 18 died before their first birthday, it also said.
Authorities said expanded testing had helped uncover infections, enabling earlier treatment. Fiji now plans to widen access to free, voluntary and confidential testing, prevention medicines, as well as harm-reduction services for injecting drug users and treatment.
Fiji, a country of around 900,000 people, is experiencing one of the world's sharpest rises in new infections, according to UNAIDS. It estimates that 9,100 Fijians were living with HIV last year and that only 39% knew their status and that 22% were receiving antiretroviral treatment.
"Fiji has recognized the urgency of the moment and is stepping up its response," UNAIDS Executive Director Winnie Byanyima said. "It is also a stark reminder to the world that AIDS is not over."
Among cases with a known transmission route, more than half were linked to sexual transmission and over 42% to injecting drug use, UNAIDS said. The agency welcomed government plans for a needle-and-syringe programme and expanded access to pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), medicine used to lower the risk of contracting HIV.
The government has set up a five-minister Cabinet subcommittee to remove barriers to action. It said discrimination against people living with HIV is illegal and services are available nationwide.
Fiji's estimate of one in 60 adults living with HIV remains below parts of Africa, where nearly 1 in 35 adults are living with HIV, according to the World Health Organization. REUTERS

Do whales grieve? Rare footage of humpback alongside stillborn calf suggests they might | Olaf Meynecke for the Conversation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
02:22:11 UTC
11:22:11 KST

It was a tragic sight.
One day last July, a newborn humpback whale calf lay motionless on the seafloor, just a kilometre off Australia’s Gold Coast. The encounter was captured through underwater video.
For more than an hour, the mother repeatedly returned to the same spot, gently touching the calf with her head and pectoral fin and resting beside it eye-to-eye. Our new research suggests this is the first described case of a humpback whale mother caring for her deceased newborn calf.
The encounter offers a rare window into one of the least understood aspects of whale behaviour: how these highly social animals respond to death.
And it raises the question: do whales, and other highly social animals such as elephants, grieve?
Caring creatures
Humpback whales are known for their spectacular migrations and acrobatic breaches. However, they are equally remarkable for the way they respond to other animals in distress.
Humpback whales often defend their calves from killer whales. Researchers have also observed them remaining alongside whales that are injured or entangled in nets, circling them, resting nearby and attempting to assist. Humpback whales may even intervene when killer whales attack seals, sea lions and grey whale calves.
These responses of care and attention are known as epimeletic behaviour and are common among cetaceans, a group of marine mammals including whales, dolphins and porpoises. Dolphins and killer whales often remain close to distressed companions, evidence of their strong social bonds. These animals may even risk their own lives for others. This happened in April off Scotland’s north-west coast, when multiple pilot whales became stranded after following a birthing female.
When a whale loses a calf
Killer whale mothers have repeatedly been observed carrying their dead calves for hours, days and, in exceptional cases, weeks. The most famous example is the killer whale Tahlequah, who in 2018 carried her dead calf for 17 days over more than 1,500 kilometres. Scientists have observed similar behaviour in pilot whales and dolphins.
Such prolonged responses illustrate the strength of the bond between mother and calf. Maternal instincts and hormonal changes after birth may contribute to mothers remaining with their deceased offspring. But exactly what the animals understand about death remains unknown.
Until now, scientists have almost exclusively documented these epimeletic behaviours towards deceased calves in toothed whales. The research on baleen whales, including humpback whales, is scarce. This is likely because dead newborn baleen whales often sink quickly, making it extremely difficult to observe such cases.
Humpback whale mothers give birth after almost a year of pregnancy and spend the next few months feeding their calf with nutrient-rich milk. Right after the delivery, mothers often lift their calf to the surface to help it take its first breath. During the first months of its life, a calf relies entirely on its mother for nourishment, protection and guidance during migration.
Tragically, some calves don’t survive. This may be due to disease, pollutants or a mother’s lack of fat reserves that help female whales cope better with pregnancy and better care for their calves.
A first for humpback whales
Our new study aimed to help fill this research gap.
We observed two adult whales off the Gold Coast of north-east Australia. The two whales stayed in the same area for several hours, after what appeared to have been a stillbirth. The female humpback whale released an ammoniac membrane shortly after the birth, but a placenta was not seen.
Underwater footage revealed the calf resting motionless on the seafloor while the presumed mother repeatedly approached it. She remained close to the calf, continuing to touch it with her head and pectoral fin. A second adult whale, likely an escort, also stayed nearby.
The humpback mother did not try to lift the calf to the ocean’s surface. This may indicate that she recognised the calf had died or was unable to carry it up from the seabed.
Members of the public reported two adult humpback whales remaining in the area over the next two days. However, our research team could not confirm they were the same animals.
Do whales grieve?
To our knowledge, this is the first detailed scientific study of a humpback whale mother attending her deceased newborn calf. It provides crucial insight into how baleen whales cope with death.
Many of the behaviours we observed – including remaining close to the calf and suspending normal behaviours such as travelling or socialising with other whales – resemble how other species respond to death. Elephants, great apes and some toothed whale species care for dead offspring in similar ways.
However, we can’t directly measure the emotional state of whales. The behaviours we observed could represent grief, but they could also reflect maternal attachment, confusion or instinctive caregiving. For this reason, researchers use broader terms – such as postmortem attentive behaviour – rather than concluding that whales grieve in the human sense.
Nevertheless, these behaviours reveal that humpback whales maintain strong maternal bonds even after the death of a calf. Our study suggests similar cases may have gone unnoticed because scientists rarely observe whale births at sea.
In good news, researchers are increasingly able to observe these animals as whale populations recover and scientific equipment makes at-sea studies more feasible.
So while there’s much more to learn about whales, their emotional lives may be infinitely more complex than we once imagined.
- 
  Olaf Meynecke is a research fellow in marine science and manager of the whales and climate program at Griffith University. This article was first published in the Conversation

diagonal forms and illuminated curves outline 2050 coffee shop along osaka’s midosuji axis

Diagonal geometries shift the movement of Midosuji upwards
Set along Osaka’s iconic Midosuji, 2050 Coffee’s new branchby TEKI Design introduces a new angle to the city’s historic axis. Through diagonal geometries and a vertical spatial experience, the café transforms everyday movement into discovery while reflecting 2050 Coffee’s vision for a more sustainable future.
Midosuji, the boulevard running through Shinsaibashi, began in the Edo period as a pilgrimage route connecting the Kita Mido and Minami Mido temples. During the early Showa era, it developed into Osaka’s primary north–south axis, linking Umeda and Namba and contributing to the city’s subsequent urban growth. Today, the boulevard remains a major urban artery and a defining element of Osaka. Situated alongside the shopping arcade, 2050 Coffee Shinsaibashi draws on the movement of the surrounding street and reinterprets its horizontal flow within the vertical organisation of the café. The spatial experience shifts movement upwards, creating a different relationship between the compact interior and the dense urban setting.
Curves and diagonal lines reshape movement through the café
The design does not attempt to replicate Midosuji’s strong linear character. Instead, it introduces diagonal lines, curves, and angled geometries that contrast with the boulevard’s straight north–south axis. These elements alter the direction of movement and views through the space, creating a sequence that encourages visitors to experience the café through changing perspectives. The contrast between the linear boulevard and the café’s angled geometry establishes a distinct spatial identity while maintaining a connection to its urban context. The vertical arrangement extends the movement of the surrounding city into the interior, turning circulation into part of the architectural experience.
This approach also relates to the identity of 2050 Coffee, which considers the future of coffee and the development of a more sustainable coffee culture. At Shinsaibashi, this idea is expressed through a spatial intervention that introduces a different angle to the established urban axis of Midosuji. By combining diagonal geometries, curves, and vertical movement, studio TEKI Design creates a new perspective within one of Osaka’s most established urban settings, positioning the space as both a destination and a point of connection within the city.

Western powers use ICC to keep their former colonies ‘in line’ – ex-Duterte spokesman
The Western powers have used the International Criminal Court (ICC) to keep former colonies “in line” while shielding their own nationals from its justice, Harry Roque, former spokesman for Philippines President Rodrigo Duterte, told RT on Wednesday.
His comments came after Duterte made his first public appearance since his arrest in March 2025 and transfer to The Hague on an ICC warrant alleging crimes against humanity during his war on drugs.

He argued that this had fueled perceptions in former colonies such as the Philippines that the ICC serves as a means for former colonial powers to continue influencing newly independent states.
“The powers behind the ICC want their former colonies to stand in line, but they don’t want their own nationals to be subjected to justice,” Roque said.
Roque also accused the ICC of having a “schizophrenic personality,” arguing that it seeks to dispense international justice despite several of the world’s most powerful countries remaining outside its jurisdiction.
Russia, China, India, and the US are not parties to the Rome Statute – the treaty that established the court.
According to Roque, the imbalance is unlikely to change unless nuclear-armed powers agree to submit to the ICC’s jurisdiction.

Large genetic study links GLP-1 receptor activation to improved mental well-being
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
02:00:27 UTC
11:00:27 KST

A new study provides evidence that activating the GLP-1 receptor, the biological target of popular weight-loss and diabetes medications, is associated with better mental health and a lower risk of conditions like depression and bipolar disorder. The research also suggests a potential protective effect against substance use disorders, hinting at psychiatric benefits that go beyond simple weight loss. These findings were published in Translational Psychiatry.
The glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor is a protein found on the surface of cells in various parts of the body, including the pancreas and the brain. When activated, it helps regulate blood sugar and sends fullness signals to the brain, reducing appetite. Medications that activate this receptor, known as GLP-1 receptor agonists, have become widely used for managing type 2 diabetes and obesity. Because these drugs act on the central nervous system, scientists have been investigating whether they might also influence mental health.
Early clinical research hinted at potential psychiatric benefits. For instance, an early 2016 clinical study found that the GLP-1 medication liraglutide improved cognitive problems in patients with mood disorders. Following up on that, a 2017 experimental study showed that GLP-1 treatment produced physical changes in brain areas that regulate mood in people with mood disorders. More recently, a 2023 review of clinical trials showed that GLP-1 drugs can reliably reduce symptoms of depression.
These observations prompted researchers to ask whether activating the GLP-1 receptor genuinely protects against psychiatric and substance use disorders, or if the mood improvements were simply a side effect of patients feeling better about losing weight. To answer this, a research team led by Guoyi Yang conducted a large-scale genetic study to isolate the biological effects of GLP-1 receptor activation.
“GLP-1R agonists, such as semaglutide, have transformed how we treat obesity and type 2 diabetes,” said Yang, a postdoctoral researcher at the Division of Translational Medicine and Human Genetics, Department of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania. “Concerns were raised about the risk of suicidal ideation and self-injury in people using GLP-1R agonists. In contrast, clinical trials suggested that these medications reduced depressive symptoms. To better understand the psychiatric effects of GLP-1R agonists, we used genetic variants as proxies for GLP-1R activation, the intended target of these drugs, to evaluate whether activating this receptor influences mental health outcomes,” he told PsyPost.
The researchers used a technique called Mendelian randomization. This method acts like a natural clinical trial by looking at genetic variations that people are born with. Because genes are assigned randomly at birth and are not influenced by lifestyle choices or environmental factors, they can help establish whether a specific biological mechanism directly influences an outcome. The team focused on specific genetic variants near the GLP1R gene that mimic the effects of taking a GLP-1 drug.
This approach uses genetics to predict what happens when you intervene on a specific biological target. “Our research uses genetics as a tool to predict the impact of GLP-1R activation – we aren’t saying that GLP-1R activation is only relevant to people with a certain genetic background,” Yang explained. “We hypothesize that the genetic variants that we consider in this paper affect the same mechanism that the drug affects – and so the genetic variants tell us what happens if you intervene on this target using the drug.”
Yang and colleagues identified two sets of these natural genetic proxies. The first set lowers body mass index, which is a common measure of body fat based on a person’s height and weight. The second set lowers glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c), which is a measure of average blood sugar levels over several months. They analyzed data from massive genetic databases, including the UK Biobank, which contained information from hundreds of thousands of people of European ancestry. The researchers examined how these GLP-1-activating genetic variants related to a broad spectrum of mental health outcomes.
The mental health outcomes included general well-being, comprising life satisfaction, positive affect, neuroticism, and depressive symptoms. The researchers also looked at diagnosed mental health disorders like major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Finally, they examined the risk of substance use disorders, such as alcohol dependence and cannabis use disorder. To ensure their results were robust, they compared the effects of the specific GLP-1 variants against general genetic variants from across the entire genome that simply lower body weight or blood sugar.
The findings indicate that genetically predicted GLP-1 receptor activation through the body mass index pathway is associated with widespread mental health benefits. Specifically, for every 1-kilogram per square meter decrease in body mass index driven by GLP-1 receptor activation, individuals experienced a 0.06 standard deviation improvement in overall mental well-being. This included higher life satisfaction and lower levels of neuroticism and depressive symptoms.
The researchers also found a reduced risk for severe psychiatric conditions. A 1-kilogram per square meter decrease in body mass index via the GLP-1 pathway was associated with an odds ratio of 0.82 for major depressive disorder, meaning a roughly 18% lower risk. The association with bipolar disorder was even stronger, showing an odds ratio of 0.61, or a 39% reduction in risk. There was also suggestive evidence that this specific biological pathway lowers the risk of ADHD and postpartum depression.
“We were surprised by just how broadly GLP-1R activation seems to benefit mental health, extending to depression, bipolar disorder, and potentially substance use disorders,” Yang said. “The effect on bipolar disorder was striking, showing almost a 40% lower risk (odds ratio of 0.61). These results highlight GLP-1R agonists as promising candidates for future psychiatric therapies.”
Notably, these mental health benefits were much stronger than the effects seen from general, genome-wide genetic variants that just lower body mass index. This suggests that the psychiatric advantages of GLP-1 receptor activation are not entirely explained by weight loss alone. The receptor’s direct activity in the brain, potentially regulating stress responses and neuroinflammation, likely plays an independent role in improving mood. Interestingly, genetic variants that mimicked the blood-sugar-lowering effects of GLP-1 activation did not show these same broad mental health benefits.
The study also provided suggestive evidence that GLP-1 receptor activation is associated with a lower risk of substance use disorders and fewer reported alcohol problems. These findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2025, which examined actual prescription records and hospitalizations rather than genetic proxies, and similarly found evidence linking GLP-1 pathway activity to a lower risk of substance use disorders.
The new results are also consistent with another study covered by PsyPost in 2026. That study, which also used Mendelian randomization to analyze genetic proxies for GLP-1 receptor activation, found no evidence of increased risk for major psychiatric conditions like depression and bipolar disorder, alleviating early concerns that the medications might provoke psychiatric distress.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting the results. The Mendelian randomization approach relies on the assumption that the selected genetic variants only affect the outcomes through the GLP-1 receptor. It is possible that these specific genes also influence neighboring biological pathways, which could independently affect mental health. The researchers used statistical tests to check for this, but the possibility cannot be completely ruled out.
“A key limitation of this method (Mendelian randomization) is that it relies on rigorous assumptions that cannot be verified,” Yang pointed out. “While we carefully selected genetic variants in or near GLP1R to mimic the drug target, we cannot rule out the possibility that nearby genes might also play a role. Clinical trials are needed to determine whether these psychiatric benefits directly translate to patients.”
Additionally, looking at genetic variants measures the effect of lifelong exposure to slightly altered GLP-1 receptor activity. This is quite different from an adult taking a concentrated, high-dose medication over a few months or years. While the genetic data suggests that activating this pathway is safe and potentially beneficial for mental health over a lifetime, clinical trials are needed to confirm whether GLP-1 medications produce these exact psychiatric benefits in real-world patients.
“The effect size reflects the lifelong genetic effect of GLP-1R activation in the general population,” Yang noted. “In contrast, patients in the real world usually take GLP-1R agonists for shorter periods. Therefore, our numbers should not be viewed as the exact risk reduction patients will experience when taking these medications.”
Looking ahead, the research team aims to dive deeper into how these medications work in the body. “Our immediate next step is to understand the biological mechanisms underlying these psychiatric effects of GLP-1R activation,” Yang said. “In the long term, our goal is to define the multifaceted effects of GLP-1R agonists across organs and to identify novel, genetically validated drug targets for cardiovascular, kidney, and metabolic diseases.”
You can follow Yang’s work on X (formerly Twitter) at @yanggy_hku.
The study, “Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor activation and mental health: a drug-target Mendelian randomization study,” was authored by Guoyi Yang, Stephen Burgess, and C. Mary Schooling.

Don’t get ‘locked in’ by EU rules, top nuclear adviser warns Burnham
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

LONDON — Britain should not feel “locked into” pre-Brexit EU environmental rules as it tries to rapidly boost its nuclear power capacity, a top adviser to the government has warned.
John Fingleton, author of an influential government-commissioned review into how red tape is blocking new U.K. nuclear projects, said in an interview that Whitehall should not dampen efforts to boost domestic capacity through “risk aversion.”
“I think on some of the environmental things there’s a risk that people in the system legally think we’re locked into EU regulation circa 2022 when we left [the EU],” he said.
Advertisement
“When the reality is that member states within the European Union have a lot of freedom to be flexible within the EU framework. And I don’t think the U.K. should, in its discussions with the European Union, accept less flexibility than a member state has in terms of our ability to comply with that.”
The Labour government has promised to bring forward a “golden age of nuclear,” signing off on both Sizewell C and Rolls-Royce’s small modular reactors since entering office in July 2024.
But it still faces four of the U.K.’s five existing power stations closing down by 2030. Hinkley Point C will be the first new nuclear power station in the U.K. since Sizewell B opened in 1995.
Fingleton’s 2025 review urged ministers to bring forward a “radical reset” of the U.K.’s nuclear regulations, including scrapping duplication across existing environmental laws.
The U.K. is currently negotiating a post-Brexit “reset” in relations with the European Union. As part of those talks, both parties are seeking so-called “dynamic alignment” across electricity markets. This would mean the U.K. potentially following EU rules on electricity, while making it easier to trade electricity in and out of the trading bloc.
Fingleton stressed that the U.K. should not impose more stringent interpretations of these regulations than rival nuclear markets in the EU. This follows supplier EDF paying out up to £700 million to protect marine life at Hinkley Point C — including an infamous “fish disco.”
“We don’t always have a trade-off between the environment and building things, but we often create an artificial one by making it very site-specific,” Fingleton warned.
He argued that with a reformed nuclear framework developers could have instead spent “a fraction of that on other measures to improve fish in the river,” this would “have a better environmental outcome and less delay … and lower costs for nuclear.”
Message to Burnham
Fingleton also said that ministers should not rush to implement all the recommendations of his 2025 review, saying Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s new crop of ministers have time to make future legislation as effective as possible — and should use it.
“I think it’s really important to get the legislation right rather than to rush it,” Fingleton said. “So probably, if I was asked: ‘Should you take an extra few months to get this right rather than rush it through?’ I would ease the time limit in order to get the right answer — because it’s important rather than urgent.”
Former Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s response to Fingleton’s report committed to “implementing everything [in the recommendations] by the end of 2027, subject to legislative timelines.” Governments have historically been “too cautious and too slow” on nuclear reform, Starmer wrote back in March.
“We are taking forward the recommendations of the Nuclear Regulatory Review and have published our implementation plan, with all reforms expected to be completed by the end of 2027,” a DESNZ spokesperson said.

In Germany’s east, a rare center-left star looks to stem the far right’s rise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

In Germany’s east, a rare center-left star looks to stem the far right’s rise
State premier Manuela Schwesig is close to stopping the AfD’s advance ahead of Sunday’s regional elections — but at a great cost to Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Manuela Schwesig, Premier of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and German Social Democrat stands at the harbour in Rostock on September 14, 2026. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images
ROSTOCK, Germany — Manuela Schwesig, a popular center-left politician, is within striking distance of stopping the far-right’s advance in the former East Germany.
Her success is coming, however, at a steep price for embattled Chancellor Friedrich Merz and the ailing national coalition her party helps sustain.
Ahead of an election in the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on Sunday, Schwesig, the sitting premier of the state and the lead candidate for the left-leaning Social Democratic Party (SPD), has narrowed the far-right Alternative for Germany’s lead to just a few percentage points in some polls.
Advertisement
It’s emblematic of just how far mainstream parties have fallen across large swaths of Germany that Schwesig is considered a rare and remarkable success for simply managing to keep her SPD — a sinking party that has suffered a string of historic defeats — within range of beating the far right on Sunday in what would amount to a major upset. “Manuela Schwesig could be Germany’s savior,” ran the headline of one column in Der Spiegel magazine.
Schwesig, a former tax inspector who has risen to become one of Germany’s most well-liked politicians, has thrived by casting herself as a bulwark against the far right — employing the slogan “Frau gegen Blau” — “Woman against Blue,” a reference to the AfD’s party color.
To help her cause, she has also frequently attacked the deeply unpopular Merz as out of touch with ordinary people and their financial struggles — exhibiting a populist streak that both distances her from a historically unpopular federal coalition while blunting the AfD’s ability to capitalize on the widespread anti-Merz sentiment that propelled itsregional election victory in Saxony-Anhalt earlier this month.
Schwesig’s approach has effectively turned the election in her state into a two-party race that has greatly weakened Merz’s conservatives. Her strategy was clear during a “citizen dialogue” with a few hundred supporters held in a tent on the waterside in the port city of Rostock one evening this week.
When someone from the crowd asked what she would do to halt rising gasoline prices, Schwesig, dressed in the bright red of her SPD, called it “fully unacceptable” that Merz had failed to implement a price cap to lower costs for consumers in her rural state, where people often need to drive long distances to get to work.
“I’m pretty angry at Chancellor Merz,” she said.
Advertisement
Schwesig’s success is creating an unprecedented challenge for Merz’s conservatives — and may hasten the demise of the coalition he shares with the SPD. Recent polls show Merz’s conservative Christian Democratic Union has crashed to around 7% support in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania in recent days, as the race increasingly morphs into a contest between the strongest mainstream candidate and the far right.
That level of support for the CDU would already constitute the worst result for the party in any state or federal election in Germany’s postwar history. A further decline would put the party at risk of failing to meet the 5% vote threshold required to enter the state parliament. A CDU collapse on this scale will almost certainly intensify internal debate that has been roiling since the summer over replacing Merz in a so-called Kanzlertausch.
Conservative leaders are blaming Schwesig’s “Frau gegen Blau” campaign for effectively taking them out of the running in the state as centrist voters rally around the SPD candidate to prevent an AfD victory.
A woman walks past an election campaign billboard that shows Manuela Schwesig, Premier of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and German Social Democrat, prior to state elections in Rostock September 14, 2026. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images
“Her attempt to keep the CDU in check with a personalized campaign weakens the political center and ultimately helps the AfD,” the party’s general secretary, Franziska Hoppermann, told the German Press Agency.
From Schwesig’s perspective, however, the CDU and Merz have no one to blame but themselves. A vote for her and the SPD, she said during her campaign event in Rostock, “is the only real chance to prevent the AfD from becoming the strongest party.”
‘Heart for the vulnerable’
Schwesig is by no means simply a local politician. Having served as Germany’s family minister for a three-and-a-half-year stint under former Chancellor Angela Merkel, she has a national profile and a high degree of influence within the SPD. Before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Schwesig was a strenuous advocate of importing natural gas from Russia via the Nord Stream pipelines, though she has since argued her state’s future lies with renewable energy.
Advertisement
If she’s able to defeat the AfD on Sunday, it will raise her national stature immensely — and likely lead to calls for her to run for chancellor.
But her popularity in her home state and beyond stems mainly from her ability to project herself as an empathetic, relatable politician at a time when many in Germany view their government as out of touch with the concerns of regular citizens.
“She’s close to the people,” 64-year-old Simone Kroh, a former elder caregiver, said outside of Schwesig’s campaign event in Rostock. “She’s one of us.”
Schwesig, by contrast, projects herself as a politician who understands the struggles of everyday people. Born and raised in the former East Germany, she often tells the story of how her family struggled after her father lost his job in construction around the time of the fall of the Berlin Wall — an experience many families from the region can identify with.
As premier of her state, she has pushed through measures to make pre-schools free for all families and to give young people in vocational training and seniors a €20 discount on monthly train passes — a measure she says makes a big difference in the lives of retirees who often survive on small state pensions.
Advertisement
She has also criticized Merz’s federal reform drive as punishing hard-working people, even though her own party has enabled it nationally, pushing back against one proposal in particular from the coalition to curtail early retirement for people who have worked 45 years.
“Reforms, yes, but they must be fair, and they must also be reasonable,” Schwesig told the crowd at her campaign event in Rostock. “What we currently have on the table regarding pensions, long-term care, and health care — we are not satisfied with this, and it is our duty to represent the interests of the people here.”
The message clearly resonated with many people in the crowd, particularly in a time of rising prices and slow growth. Following her talk in Rostock, supporters approached Schwesig to ask her about their financial worries. A school social worker asked whether funding for her job would be guaranteed. A university student asked whether state money to cover living costs during his studies would be cut.
For Kroh, the former elder caregiver, Schwesig’s criticisms of Merz and the government were absolutely justified.
Schwesig, she said, recognized people’s struggles.
“Merz,” she added, “just doesn’t have a heart for the vulnerable.”

Friedrich Merz’s endgame: All the scenarios, rated
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

BERLIN — German Chancellor Friedrich Merz faces the threat of being ousted as soon as this weekend, just 16 months after entering office promising an ambitious reform agenda and vowing to bring back German leadership in Europe.
Ahead of two key state elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin this Sunday, where Merz’s center-right Christian Democratic Union risks painful defeats, senior party members are privately discussing whether Germany needs a so-called Kanzlertausch — a change of chancellor — to arrest a rapidly accelerating decline in support for the government.
That same poll shows the far-right Alternative for Germany leading with 29%. The AfD also finished first in a recent state election in Saxony-Anhalt, coming close to winning an absolute majority, while Merz’s CDU lost more than half of its voter support.
European and international allies are watching with bewilderment as Germany — once a bastion of stability during the 16 years of Angela Merkel’s leadership — potentially faces its second quick-fire change of leadership (Merz’s predecessor Olaf Scholz saw his ruling coalition collapse in November 2024).
Merz canceling his trip to the U.N. General Assembly next week threw the scale of his domestic crisis into sharp focus. “His presence is required in Berlin,” said a senior German official, as the chancellor fights for his political survival.
POLITICO analyzed five scenarios for how the German leadership tumult could unfold — and rated their likelihood.
1. Merz resigns lacking party support
The chancellor has convened a high-stakes meeting of his party’s leadership on Sunday at 5 p.m., which will coincide with the state election exit polls at 6 p.m. At that meeting, Merz reportedly wants to ask his party allies whether they still back him and his reform plans. If not, he wants to urge them to put forward the name of a potential successor.
By seeking the confrontation, Merz will try to exploit a weakness of his critics: There is no clear consensus on who should take over.
Advertisement
North Rhine-Westphalia’s Minister-President Hendrik Wüst (CDU) is frequently mentioned, but he has elections in his populous home state coming up in April — so the timing isn’t great for him. An alternative would be Markus Söder of the Christian-Social Union, the CDU’s Bavarian sister party, but he isn’t short of critics. Other, less probable potential candidates are Hesse’s Minister President Boris Rhein (CDU) and Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt (CSU).
However, should the elections Sunday be a total disaster for Merz’ conservatives — the party could even miss the 5% hurdle to enter parliament in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, for the first time in any state election — frustration within the CDU/CSU could boil over and lead to broad calls for Merz to resign.
The showdown does not necessarily have to happen Sunday but could follow within the next days or weeks. Should Merz accept that fate, he could inform German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier of his intention to step down. Steinmeier would then most likely ask him to remain in office in a caretaker function until a new chancellor is elected by parliament.
However, this ain’t easy: Any successor for Merz would need the votes of the CDU/CSU’s coalition partner, the Social Democrats, who would likely ask concessions in return — triggering a time-consuming renegotiation of the coalition treaty. It also means Merz could still remain in power for months and represent Germany on the international stage, for example in EU budget talks.
Adding to the complications, the coalition’s majority in the Bundestag is thin: There’s always a risk of defectors during the secret ballot, as happened to Merz himself during the first election round last year.
Likelihood:
Advertisement
2. No-confidence vote forces Merz out
Pressure from within the party cannot actually force Merz to resign. For historical reasons, the German constitution provides elected chancellors with a very stable position.
Given that, the only possibility to forcibly oust him would be through a no-confidence vote. However, the German constitution requires that such a vote must be “constructive,” meaning an opposing candidate must at the same time receive a majority to replace Merz.
This makes such a scenario very unlikely. Apart from the negative public image that the CDU/CSU would display by openly seeking to topple their chancellor in parliament, it seems unlikely that any candidate could immediately get the required votes amid the thin majority of the coalition and the negotiations that would likely have to happen first with the SPD.
Likelihood:
3. Merz seeks a confidence vote
Merz could also call for a vote of confidence himself, seeking to show that he still has sufficient support within the coalition — or otherwise open the door to snap elections. It’s a scenario that has happened in the past, most recently with Scholz in December 2024.
Should Merz lose the vote, Steinmeier could decide to dissolve the Bundestag within 21 days — but only if Merz proposes it to him. However, given the strong position of the AfD in current polls, neither the CDU nor SPD has an interest in new elections at this stage.
Advertisement
It would also be possible to elect a new chancellor within those 21 days, if there is a quick majority for a successor.
All in all, not too likely.
Likelihood:
4. Far-right support against Merz
Theoretically, it would be possible for a Merz successor to get the necessary majority in parliament by receiving indirect backing from the AfD (minority government) or even form a coalition with the far-right party.
CDU/CSU and AfD would enjoy a comfortable majority in parliament, but it would mean breaking with Germany’s anti-far-right “firewall.”
However, it’s an idea that is unacceptable for many in the party leadership. Merz himself has also ruled out staying in power with far-right support.
Advertisement
Likelihood:
5. Merz clings to power
Contrary to the Saxony-Anhalt election aftermath, where the chancellor seemed discouraged and delivered an unconvincing speech in the Bundestag, he now appears to want to fight for his leadership.
Merz’s position was bolstered by a letter Wednesday from eight center-right state premiers — including Wüst and Rhein, but not Söder — in which they wrote that “Germany needs reliability and action” instead of “discussions about personnel.” The letter also refers to elections in France, Italy, Poland, Spain and Greece next year, noting that “a stable and strong Germany” is now needed in Europe.
The letter is far from an unwavering support for Merz; in fact, it doesn’t even mention his name and may also be an attempt to quell internal debates ahead of the important elections on Sunday. However, it may also mean that there isn’t sufficient appetite among senior party leaders to oust Merz at this point. Instead, the party may seek to close ranks and regain popularity by urging the SPD to pursue even more vigorous social reforms.
